## Commentary on the Dukanipāta
## Anguttara Nikāya
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Dukanipāta
## 1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsaka
## 1. Kammakāraṇavagga
## 1. Vajjasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Dukanipāta, "vajjāni" means faults or offenses. "Diṭṭhadhammikaṃ" refers to the result arising in this very existence, in this present life. "Samparāyikaṃ" refers to the result arising in a future existence. "Āgucāriṃ" refers to one who does evil, an offender.

"Kings, having seized (the thief), cause various punishments to be inflicted" means that although the king's men seize the thief and inflict various punishments, it is said that the kings cause them to be done. This person sees that thief being thus punished. Therefore, (the Blessed One) said: "He sees a thief, an offender, whom kings have seized and are causing to undergo various punishments."

"Addhadaṇḍakehi" means with clubs, or with short sticks obtained by cutting a four-cubit staff into two pieces to accomplish the act of beating.

"Bilaṅgathālika" (The Vinegar-Pot torture) is a punishment like a vinegar pot. Those who perform it remove the skull-cap, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and place it inside the brain; because of that, the brain boils and overflows.

"Saṅkhamuṇḍika" (The Conch-Shave torture) is a punishment that makes the head as bald and white as a conch shell. Those who perform it cut the skin from the upper lip, the two temples, and the area of the throat, tie all the hair into a single knot, wrap it around a stick, and pull it out. The skin comes off along with the hair. Then they rub and wash the skull with coarse gravel until it has the white appearance of a conch shell.

"Rāhumukha" (Rāhu's Mouth torture) is a punishment like the sun entering the mouth of Rāhu. Those who perform it pry open the mouth with a spike and light a lamp inside the mouth. Or, starting from the temples, they carve the mouth with a chisel; blood flows and fills the mouth.

"Jotimālika" (The Garland of Fire torture) is wrapping the whole body in old oil-soaked cloths and setting it on fire. "Hatthapajjotika" (The Hand-Lamp torture) ...
2: ...boils and overflows. "Saṅkhamuṇḍika" is a punishment that makes the head as bald and white as a conch shell. In that punishment, they cut the skin from the upper lip, the two temples, and the throat area, tie all the hair into a single knot, wrap it around a stick, and pull it out. The skin comes off along with the hair. Then they rub and wash the skull with coarse gravel until it is as white as a conch shell. "Rāhumukha" is a punishment like the sun entering the mouth of Rāhu. In that punishment, they open the mouth with a spike and light a lamp inside the mouth. Or, starting from the temples, they carve the mouth with a chisel so that blood flows and fills the mouth. "Jotimālika" is wrapping the whole body in old oil-soaked cloths and setting it on fire. "Hatthapajjotika" is wrapping the hands in old oil-soaked cloths and making them burn like lamps. "Eraka-vattika" (The Grass-Mat torture) is a punishment with strips of skin removed from the body like eraka grass. In that punishment, starting from below the neck, they slice the skin in a circular fashion down to the ankles. Then they bind the person with ropes and pull him; the person falls as he repeatedly steps on his own strips of skin. "Cīrakavāsika" (The Bark-Dress torture) is a punishment by making the person wear a garment of skin removed from the body. In that punishment, in the same manner, they slice the skin in a circular fashion down to the waist. Then, starting from the waist, they slice it down to the ankles. With the skin from the upper part, the lower body appears as if dressed in a bark garment. "Eṇeyyaka" (The Black-Antelope torture) is a punishment to make one like the creature called the Eṇī antelope. In that punishment, they place iron rings on both elbows and both knees and drive in iron spikes. The person remains supported on the ground by the four iron spikes. Then they surround him and set a fire. In the teaching where it says "Eṇeyyako jotipariggaho yathā," this very punishment like the Eṇī antelope is meant. Sometimes they remove the spikes and leave him supported only by the four ends of the bones. Such punishments do not exist elsewhere. "Baḷisamaṃsika" (The Fish-Hook torture) is pulling out the skin, flesh, and tendons by hooking them with double-headed fish-hooks. "Kahāpaṇika" (The Penny-Piece torture) is slicing the whole body with sharp adzes, starting from the extremities, into pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa coin. "Khārāpatacchika" (The Alkali-Wash torture) is piercing the body in various places with weapons and rubbing in alkali-salt water with brushes. The skin, flesh, and tendons melt away, leaving only a skeleton. "Palighaparivattika" (The Bolt-Pivot torture) is making the person lie on one side, driving an iron spike through the ear-hole to fix him to the ground, and then taking him by the feet and spinning him around. "Palālapīṭhaka" (The Straw-Chair torture) is...
3:
A skilled executioner, without cutting the inner or outer skin, crushes the bones with small stones, and when he lifts the person by the hair, they become just a mass of flesh. Then, they wrap that person with their own hair, making them like a bundle of straw, and wrap them again. 'Also by dogs' means they let hungry dogs, who have not been fed for several days, devour them. Those dogs make them into a mere skeleton in an instant. 'Placing on a stake' means impaling on a stake.

'Does not go about plundering the gifts of others' means even if he sees a bag of a thousand coins belonging to others, brought in their absence, or even dropped in the middle of the street, he does not go about plundering it, thinking, "I will live by this." Instead, he rolls it away with the top of his foot and moves on, thinking, "What use is this to me?"

'Pāpaka' means mean or low. 'Dukkha' means undesirable. 'What is that reason?' means what kind of reason could it be. 'Yāhaṃ' means 'because of which I'. 'Bodily misconduct' (kāyaduccarita) refers to the three types of unwholesome bodily actions such as killing living beings. 'Bodily good conduct' (kāyasucarita) refers to the three types of wholesome actions that are the opposite of that. 'Verbal misconduct' (vacīduccarita) refers to the four types of unwholesome verbal actions such as false speech. 'Verbal good conduct' (vacīsucarita) refers to the four types of wholesome actions that are the opposite of that. 'Mental misconduct' (manoduccarita) refers to the three types of unwholesome mental actions such as covetousness. 'Mental good conduct' (manosucarita) refers to the three types of wholesome actions that are the opposite of that. 'Carries a pure self'—here, purity is of two kinds: conventional (pariyāya) and absolute (nippariyāya). By taking refuge (saraṇagamana), one is said to carry a pure self conventionally. Likewise, by the five precepts, the ten precepts, the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), the first jhāna... up to... the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry... up to... the path of Arahantship, one is said to carry a pure self conventionally. However, an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who is established in the fruit of Arahantship, even while bathing, feeding, eating, sitting, or lying down with the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha) whose roots [of rebirth] are severed, should be understood as carrying or tending to a pure and stainless self in the absolute sense.

'Therefore' means because these two are indeed faults and not non-faults. 'Those who fear faults' means those who are afraid of faults. 'Those who see danger in faults' means those who have the habit of seeing faults as danger. 'This liberation is to be desired' means liberation from all these faults is to be desired; it means this will certainly happen. 'Yaṃ' is just a particle, or it is an explanatory word meaning 'the reason by which one will be liberated from all faults.' By what reason will one be liberated? One will be liberated by the fourth path and the fourth fruit. Indeed, one is being liberated by the path of Arahantship; when one reaches the fruit of Arahantship, one is liberated. If it is asked, "Does unwholesome kamma not ripen for an Arahant?" the answer is "It does ripen." However, that ripening unwholesome kamma is only the kamma performed before becoming an Arahant. Such ripening occurs only in this present existence; in the life hereafter, there is no such thing as the fruit of kamma for that Arahant.
4:
...will be liberated from all faults. By what reason will one be liberated? One will be liberated by the fourth path and the fourth fruit. Indeed, one is being liberated by the fourth path; upon reaching the fruit, one is liberated. If it is asked, "Does unwholesome kamma not ripen for an Arahant?"—it does ripen. But that ripening unwholesome kamma is the kamma performed before reaching Arahantship. Such ripening occurs only in this present existence; in the life hereafter, there is no such thing as the fruit of kamma for that Arahant. The commentary on the first sutta ends.

## 2. Padhānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'padhānāni' means efforts (vīriya). Indeed, it is called 'padhāna' because it should be exerted or because it is the cause of exertion. 'Durabhisambhavāni' means difficult to endure, difficult to fulfill, or difficult to do. 'Agāraṃ ajjhāvasataṃ' means those living in a house. It shows the meaning that effort for the purpose of offering the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines—is difficult to achieve. Indeed, even to say "Please give to others" or to take out and give a worn-out cloth of four cubits, or alms-food cooked with a mere handful of rice, or a leaf-roofed hut of four cubits, or even a small amount of medicine such as oil, ghee, or fresh butter, is very difficult; it is like entering a battlefield where two sides are arrayed. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

Giving and battle, they say, are equal;
Even few, being virtuous, conquer many.
If one gives even a little, having faith,
By that alone, he becomes happy in the hereafter.

'Agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitānaṃ' means those who have left the home and entered the homeless life, which is free from activities that bring worldly gain such as plowing and cattle-rearing. 'Sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggatthāya padhānaṃ' means the effort associated with insight (vipassanā) and the path (magga) for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions (upadhi), namely: the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), and the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi). 'Tasmā' means because these two kinds of effort are difficult to achieve. The commentary on the second sutta ends.

## 3. Tapanīyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "tapanīyā" means those things that cause burning or torment in this present life as well as in the life hereafter; thus they are called "tapanīya" (tormenting states). "Tappati" means one burns with mental distress or feels remorse. This occurs because of having committed bodily misconduct, as in the cases of Nanda the Yakkha, Nanda the youth, Nanda the butcher, Devadatta, and the two brothers.

Those two brothers killed a cow and divided the meat into two portions. Then the younger brother said to the elder, "I have many children; please give these intestines to me." The elder brother replied, "All the meat has been divided into two; why do you want more?" and he struck him, causing his death. When he turned back and saw that his younger brother was dead, the thought "I have committed a grave deed" arose, and intense remorse came upon him. Whether standing or sitting, he kept reflecting only on that evil deed and could find no peace of mind. Even the nutrients from whatever food or drink he consumed did not nourish his body, and he was left with only skin and bones.

Then a thera saw him and asked, "Lay follower, though you have plenty of food and drink, you are left with only skin and bones; is there some tormenting evil deed you have done?" He replied, "Yes, venerable sir," and related everything. Then the thera said, "Lay follower, you have committed a grave deed; you have offended against one who was innocent." That man, having passed away with that very evil kamma, was reborn in hell. Due to verbal misconduct, one suffers like King Suppabuddha the Sakyan, Kokālika, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others. The remaining words in this and the fourth sutta are clear in meaning. The explanation of the third sutta ends.

## 5. Upaññātasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "dvinnāhaṃ" means "dvinnaṃ ahaṃ" (I [have known] two things). "Upāññāsiṃ" means having approached, I knew the quality, I realized, I penetrated. Now, wishing to show those things that were known, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "yā ca asantuṭṭhitā." Indeed, the Teacher attained omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) based on these two things; therefore, wishing to show the power of those things, he spoke thus.

Among them, by the words "dissatisfaction with wholesome states," he explains this point: "I was not satisfied with mere jhāna or mere signs of light (obhāsa-nimitta), but strove to produce the Path of Arahatship. As long as that had not arisen, I was not satisfied. And being without weariness in striving, remaining without retreating, I performed the act of striving." To show this meaning, he spoke the words beginning with "yā ca appaṭivānitā." In that context, "appaṭivānitā" means not turning back, not retreating. Appaṭivānī...
6:
In the phrase "sudāhaṃ, bhikkhave, padahāmi," the word "suda" is merely a particle. "Monks, when I was a Bodhisatta, remaining in unrelenting effort and aspiring for omniscience, I strove"—this is the meaning here.

Now, to show the manner in which he performed that striving, he spoke the words beginning with "kāmaṃ taco ca." In that phrase, by "pattabbaṃ," he shows the collection of qualities to be attained. By the words "purisathāmena" and so on, the strength of a man's wisdom, energy joined with wisdom, and endeavor joined with wisdom are spoken of. "Saṇṭhānaṃ" means stopping, not proceeding, retreating, or subsiding. By this much, he spoke of the undertaking of energy endowed with four factors. Indeed, here "kāmaṃ taco ca" (let only skin remain) is one factor; "nhāru ca" (and sinews) is one factor; "aṭṭhi ca" (and bones) is one factor; "maṃsalohitaṃ" (flesh and blood [dry up]) is one factor; these are the four factors. The words "purisathāmena" and so on are synonyms for supreme energy. Thus, being endowed with the four factors mentioned earlier, the energy thus undertaken is to be known as "the undertaking of energy endowed with four factors." By this much, he spoke of his preliminary practice (āgamanīyapaṭipadā) at the Bodhi-throne.

Now, to speak of the qualities attained through that practice, he spoke the words beginning with "tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave." In that phrase, "appamādādhigata" means attained through diligence (appamāda), which is characterized by the non-absence of mindfulness. It was not attained by one who was negligent or drowsy. "Sambodhi" refers to the four Path-knowledges and Omniscience. Indeed, it is not possible for one who is negligent or drowsy to attain this. Therefore, he said, "Sambodhi is attained through diligence." "Anuttaro yogakkhemo" means not only Bodhi, but also the supreme security from the four bonds, which is the Fruit of Arahatship and Nirvāṇa, is attained only through diligence.

Now, wishing to encourage the Saṅgha of monks in the qualities he himself had attained, he spoke the words beginning with "tumhe cepi bhikkhave." In that phrase, "yassatthāya" means for the sake of which (benefit of Arahatship), wishing to dwell having attained which. "Tadanuttaraṃ" means that supreme (Arahatship). "Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ" means the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala) which is the consummation of the holy life of the Path. "Abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having known with higher knowledge and having realized with supreme wisdom. "Upasampajja viharissatha" means you shall dwell having attained and reached it. "Tasmā" means because this unrelenting striving is of great benefit and achieves the supreme goal.

## 6. Saṃyojanasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, the phrase "saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu" means in the things that are the causes of the ten fetters, which exist within the three planes of existence. "Assādānupassitā" means the state of seeing by way of gratification. "Nibbidānupassitā" means the state of seeing by way of weariness or by way of disenchantment. "Jātiyā" means due to the arising of the five aggregates. "Jarāyā" means due to the ripening of the five aggregates. "Maraṇenā" means due to the breaking up of the five aggregates. "Sokehi" means due to sorrows characterized by inner burning. "Paridevehi" means due to lamentations characterized by wailing and crying based on that sorrow. "Dukkhehi" means due to the collection of bodily sufferings that oppress the body. "Domanassehi" means due to mental displeasures, also called mental exhaustion. "Upāyāsehi" means due to despairs characterized by excessive distress. "Dukkhasmā" means from the entire suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). "Pajahatī" means one abandons by means of the Path (magga). Regarding the word "pahāya," it refers to the moment of Fruition (phala). In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. The sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Kaṇhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, the word "kaṇhā" (dark) does not mean dark because of color; rather, they are called dark because they lead to the four dark woeful states (apāya) (or because they result in dark consequences). Alternatively, by their own nature, all unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) are indeed dark. Because of the arising of those unwholesome states, the mind is not radiant. "Ahirikaṃ" means the state of being shameless. "Anottappaṃ" means the state of having no dread (of wrongdoing). The seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Sukkasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, the word "sukkā" (bright) does not mean bright because of color; rather, they are called bright because they lead to bright happy destinations (sugati) (or because they result in bright consequences). Alternatively, by their own nature, all wholesome states (kusala dhamma) are indeed bright. Because of the arising of those wholesome states, the mind is radiant and shining. In the phrase "hiri ca ottappañca," hiri is characterized by loathing evil, and ottappa is characterized by fear of evil. What should be said in detail here has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Cariyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "lokaṃ pālenti" means they well-establish, sustain, and protect the world. "Nayidha paññāyetha mātā" means that in this world, the mother who gave birth would not be recognized (known) through the power of honoring and respecting her as "This is my mother."
8:
The mother would not be recognized through the power of honoring her as "mother." The same method applies to the remaining terms (such as step-mother, etc.). "Sambheda" means confusion or the breaking of boundaries. Just as among goats, sheep, and so on, these beings do not know through the power of respect that "This is my mother" or "This is my maternal aunt." Although they arise depending on those objects (parents), they behave wrongly towards those very objects. Therefore, bringing an analogy, the Buddha taught "yathā ajeḷakā" (just as goats and sheep), and so on. The commentary on the ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Vassūpanāyikasutta-vaṇṇanā
The tenth sutta was taught because of a specific occasion that arose. What was that occasion? It was because of the criticism of the people. Indeed, for the first twenty years of the Buddha's enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi), the entering of the Rains Retreat (vassūpanāyika) had not yet been prescribed. Monks wandered as they pleased during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons without a fixed residence. Seeing those monks, people criticized them, saying: "How can the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan, wander on tour during the winter, summer, and the rains? They trample the green grass, injure one-sensed life (plants), and cause the destruction of many small creatures. Even those of other sects (titthiya) whose Dhamma is poorly taught stay in residence during the rainy season; even birds make nests in the treetops and stay in residence during the rainy season," and so on.

When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One, taking that occasion as the basis and wishing to teach this sutta, first said only this much: "Monks, I allow you to enter the Rains." Then, knowing the thought that arose in the monks, "When should we enter the Rains?", He spoke again: "Monks, I allow you to enter the Rains during the rainy season." Then, the thought arose in the monks, "How many (types of) entering the Rains are there?" They reported this matter to the Blessed One. Hearing that, and wishing to teach this entire sutta, He said, "Monks, there are these two (types of) entering the Rains," and so on.

In that teaching, "vassūpanāyikā" means the enterings of the Rains. "Purimikā" (the earlier rains) is the first three-month period to be entered from the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha until the full moon of Kattika (Thadingyut). "Pacchimikā" (the later rains) is the later three-month period to be entered from one month after the full moon of Āsāḷha (the day after the full moon of Sāvaṇa) until the full moon of the following month (Tazaungmon).

## Kammakāraṇa-vagga, the First.

## 2. Adhikaraṇavagga-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the second chapter, in what sense are they called 'powers' (balāni)? They are called powers in the sense of being unshakable. Likewise, they are called powers in the sense of being difficult to overcome and in the sense of being impossible to crush. 'The power of reflection' (paṭisaṅkhānabala) is the power consisting of investigation. 'The power of development' (bhāvanābala) is the power consisting of cultivation and growth. The phrase 'suddhaṃ attānaṃ' should be understood in the same manner as explained below. 'Tatra' means 'among those two powers'. 'Yamidaṃ' is the word-splitting of 'yaṃ idaṃ'. 'Sekhānametaṃ balaṃ' means this is the power of knowledge of the seven trainees (sekkhas). "Monks, that trainee, depending on the trainee's power" means taking as object, intending, and depending on the power of knowledge of the seven trainees. 'Pajahati' means one abandons by the Path. By the word 'pahāya', the Fruit is spoken of. 'Yaṃ pāpaṃ' means whatever evil or unwholesome state. Because one can reach the Fruit of Arahatship by developing both these powers, it should be understood that the title of 'foremost' (etadagga) is not mentioned in this sutta.

In the second sutta, in the words "cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness" and so forth, the following are the explanations of the meanings by way of terms that have not appeared below: 'Vivekanissitaṃ' means depending on seclusion. Seclusion (viveka) is the state of being secluded. That seclusion is of five kinds: seclusion by substitution (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). Among those five kinds of seclusion, in the term 'vivekanissitaṃ', the meaning should be understood as: one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on seclusion by substitution, depending on seclusion by eradication, and depending on seclusion by escape. Indeed, a practitioner (yogī) who is devoted to the development of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on seclusion by substitution by way of function at the moment of insight (vipassanā), and depending on seclusion by escape by way of inclination. At the moment of the Path, however, one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on seclusion by eradication by way of function, and depending on seclusion by escape by way of object. Some teachers say that one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on all five kinds of seclusion. These teachers do not only bring forth the enlightenment factors at the moments of powerful insight, the Path, and the Fruit, but also bring them forth in the meditations of the kasinas, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), foulness (asubha), and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), which are the bases for insight. The commentators (aṭṭhakathā-teachers) also do not prohibit such bringing forth. Therefore, according to their view, at the moment of the occurrence of those meditations, one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness depending on seclusion by suppression by way of function. Just as it was said, "depending on seclusion by escape by way of inclination at the moment of insight", so too it is proper to say, "one also cultivates it depending on seclusion by tranquillization". This same method applies to the terms 'virāganissitaṃ' (depending on dispassion) and so forth. For dispassion and the like have the same meaning as seclusion.
10:
In this context (of 'virāganissitaṃ' etc.), the word 'relinquishment' (vossagga) is of two kinds: relinquishment as abandoning (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Among these two, 'relinquishment as abandoning' is the abandoning of defilements by way of substitution at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the Path. 'Relinquishment as entering into' is the entering into Nibbāna by way of inclining towards it at the moment of insight, and by way of taking it as an object at the moment of the Path. Both of these are appropriate in this method of explanation which mixes the mundane and the supramundane. This is because this enlightenment factor of mindfulness abandons defilements in the manner already described and enters into Nibbāna. By the entire phrase "vossaggapariṇāmī" (ripening towards relinquishment), it is meant: inclining and having inclined, maturing and having matured for the sake of relinquishment. This monk, devoted to the development of the enlightenment factors, cultivates that enlightenment factor of mindfulness in such a way that it matures for the sake of relinquishment as abandoning defilements and for the sake of relinquishment as entering into Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes matured. This same method applies to the remaining enlightenment factors.

In this specific context, however, Nibbāna alone is called 'seclusion' (viveka) because it is secluded from all conditioned things; it is called 'dispassion' (virāga) because it is the state where all conditioned things are absent; and it is called 'cessation' (nirodha) because it is the state of their ceasing. Only the Path is called 'ripening towards relinquishment'. Therefore, one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness as 'depending on seclusion' because it occurs by taking seclusion (Nibbāna) as an object; likewise, it is 'depending on dispassion' and 'depending on cessation'. Because it arises at the moment of the Noble Path, that enlightenment factor of mindfulness should be understood as having matured and ripened by way of abandoning defilements through total eradication and by way of entering into Nibbāna. This same method applies to the remaining enlightenment factors. Thus, these seven enlightenment factors are taught here as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. Regarding these two powers as well, the state of being 'foremost' (etadagga) should be understood in the manner already described.

## In the third sutta,
the entire Pali meaning and the method of development of the four jhanas, beginning with "secluded from sensual pleasures" (vivicceva kāmehi), have already been explained in detail in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga. A certain monk develops these four jhanas for the sake of one-pointedness of mind; another for the sake of being a basis for insight; another for the sake of being a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā); another for the sake of being a basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); and another for the sake of a special state of existence. In this sutta, however, those jhanas which are the basis for insight are intended. For this monk, having attained these four jhanas and having emerged from the attainment, contemplates conditioned formations (saṅkhāras) and performs the discernment of the root cause and the supporting condition...
11:
Having distinguished mind and matter along with their causes, and having combined the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, one attains the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, these jhānas are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. Regarding these two powers, the state of being foremost (etadagga) should be understood in the manner already described.

In the fourth sutta, by the words "briefly and in detail," it is shown that there are only two types of Dhamma teaching: the brief Dhamma teaching and the detailed Dhamma teaching. Therein, a teaching given by referring to a matrix (mātikā) is called a brief teaching. A teaching that analyzes and explains that very matrix in detail is called a detailed teaching. Alternatively, a teaching that analyzes in detail, whether setting down a matrix or not, is called a detailed teaching. Of these two, the brief teaching is taught for the sake of a person of great wisdom, while the detailed teaching is taught for one of dull wisdom. For a person of great wisdom, a detailed teaching is like a great proliferation. For one of dull wisdom, a brief teaching is like the leaping of a hare; they can reach neither the end nor the goal. The brief teaching is taught for the sake of an ugghaṭitaññū person (one of quick understanding), while the detailed teaching is for the other three types of persons. Indeed, the entire Tipiṭaka is included within these two: the brief teaching and the detailed teaching.

In the fifth sutta, "monks, in whatever legal issue" refers to whichever of these four legal issues: legal issues arising from disputes (vivāda), from accusations (anuvāda), from offenses (āpatti), and from duties (kicca). "And a monk who has fallen into an offense" refers to a monk who has committed an offense. "In that legal issue, this matter" means in that legal issue, that legal issue of dispute. "For the sake of long duration" means for the purpose of lasting for a long time. "For the sake of harshness" means for the purpose of using harsh words such as "slave," "unvirtuous one," "outcaste," or "bamboo-weaver." "For the sake of ferocity" means for the purpose of being harsh through striking with hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so on. "Monks will not live in comfort" means that within a Saṅgha of monks engaged in mutual disputes, those who wish to learn the Pali text, those who wish to inquire about the commentaries, or those who wish to practice meditation will not live in comfort. For when the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies are suspended in the Saṅgha, those who desire to learn the Pali text and so on cannot do so; the thoughts of those practicing insight (vipassanā) are not one-pointed, and consequently, they cannot produce any special attainment. Thus, "monks will not live in comfort." In the phrases "not for the sake of long duration" and so on, the meaning should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated.
12:
"Idha" means in this Dispensation (sāsana). "Iti paṭisañcikkhati" means he reflects thus. In the phrase "akusalaṃ āpanno," "unwholesome" refers to an offense; it means he has fallen into an offense. "Kañcideva desaṃ" means not every offense, but a certain part of an offense, a certain type of offense. "Kāyena" means with the physical body (karajakāya). "Anattamano" means having a dissatisfied mind. "Anattamanavācaṃ" means dissatisfied speech. "Mam'eva" means only me. "Tattha" means in that matter. "Accayo accagamā" means a fault has overcome and overwhelmed me; I alone am the offender here. "Like a tax-payer regarding goods" means just as when goods are taken while evading a customs station, the fault overcomes the tax-payer; he alone is the offender there, not the kings or the king's men.

This is what is meant: When someone evades a customs station established by the king and carries goods, they are seized along with the cart of goods and shown to the king. In that case, there is no fault in the customs station, nor in the king, nor in the king's men; the fault lies only with the one who went evading it. In the same way, regarding the offense that the monk has committed, there is no fault in the offense itself, nor in the accuser. However, due to three reasons, the fault lies only with that monk. For he has a fault because of having committed the offense, a fault because of his dissatisfaction with the accuser, and a fault because of informing others while being dissatisfied. As for the accuser, there is no fault in his seeing that monk committing the offense. However, there is a fault in accusing with a dissatisfied mind. Without attending to that point, this monk, reflecting only on his own fault, thinks: "Thus, a fault has overcome and overwhelmed me alone, just as a fault comes upon a tax-payer regarding his goods." This is the meaning of "he reflects thus." In the second instance, there are two faults: the accuser's dissatisfaction and the fact of being accused with a dissatisfied mind; in connection with these, the phrase "accayo accagamā" should be applied. The rest is clear.

## 6. Chaṭṭha Sutta
"Aññataro" refers to a certain brahmin whose name is not well-known. In the phrase "yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī," "yena" is an instrumental case used in the sense of the locative case. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as "he approached the place where the Blessed One was." Alternatively, it should be understood as "he approached the Blessed One for the reason that he should be approached by gods and humans." For what reason should the Blessed One be approached?...
13:
For what reason should one approach the Blessed One? Just as flocks of birds approach a great tree that is always fruiting with the intention of consuming its delicious fruit, one approaches with the intention of attaining various special qualities and virtues. 'Upasaṅkami' means 'he went' or 'he approached'. The word 'Upasaṅkamitvā' indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it means that having approached in this way, the brahmin went to a very close place, known as the vicinity of the Blessed One.

'He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One' means that just as the Blessed One asked him about his health and so on, he too shared in that mutual joy with the Blessed One, becoming one like cold water mixing with hot water. He exchanged greetings with words such as: "Master Gotama, is it bearable? Is it supportable? Are Master Gotama and his disciples free from illness and affliction? Are they light, strong, and living in comfort?"

Because it gives rise to joy and delight and is suitable for rejoicing, it is called 'sammodanīya' (rejoicing). Because it is worthy of being remembered for a long time and practiced continuously due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, and because it is memorable, it is called 'sāraṇīya' (courteous/memorable). Alternatively, it is 'sammodanīya' because it is pleasant to hear, and 'sāraṇīya' because it is pleasant to remember. Likewise, it is 'sammodanīya' due to the purity of phrasing and 'sāraṇīya' due to the purity of meaning. Having thus concluded the exchange of many kinds of rejoicing and courteous talk, wishing to ask about the purpose for which he came, he sat down on one side.

'Ekamantaṃ' is an adverbial neuter usage, as in the sentence "The moon and sun revolve unevenly (visamaṃ)." Therefore, it should be understood here that he sat in such a way that his sitting was 'on one side'. Alternatively, this word 'ekamantaṃ' uses the accusative case (upayogavacana) in the sense of the locative (bhummatthe). 'Nisīdi' means he sat down nearby. For wise men, having approached a person worthy of respect, sit on one side due to their skill in sitting. This brahmin was one of those wise men; therefore, he sat on one side.

How does one sit so as to be sitting 'on one side'? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. They are: too far, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, and directly behind. If one sits too far and wishes to speak, one must speak with a loud voice. If one sits too near, physical contact...
14:
...occurs. If one sits upwind, one troubles the other with body odor. If one sits on high ground, it shows a lack of respect. If one sits directly in front and very close, and wishes to look, one must look eye-to-eye. If one sits directly behind and very close, and wishes to look, one must stretch one's neck to look. Therefore, this brahmin also sat down avoiding these six faults of sitting. With reference to such sitting, it is said, "He sat down on one side."

Regarding "He said this," there are two types of questions: the layperson's question and the monastic's question. Among them, the layperson's question comes in the manner of: "Venerable Sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?" The monastic's question comes in the manner of: "Venerable Sir, are these the five aggregates of clinging?" But this brahmin, wishing to ask a layperson's question suitable for himself, said these words: "Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the condition?"

In that context, both 'hetu' (cause) and 'paccayo' (condition) are synonyms for 'reason'. 'Adhammacariyā-visamacariyā-hetu' means because of uneven conduct known as unrighteous conduct; for that reason, due to that condition. The meaning of the words is: Adhammacariyā is the practice of what is not Dhamma; it means the cause of unrighteousness. Visamacariyā is uneven practice, or the practice of uneven actions. That which is unrighteous conduct is also uneven conduct. In this way, the meaning should also be understood for the wholesome side. In essence, here 'adhammacariyā-visamacariyā' refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action, and 'dhammacariyā-samacariyā' refers to the ten wholesome courses of action.

In the phrase "Excellent, Master Gotama!", the word 'abhikkanta' is seen in the senses of exhaustion, excellence, beauty, and great delight. It is seen in the sense of exhaustion in such phrases as: "Venerable Sir, the night is exhausted (ended), the first watch has passed, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time." It is seen in the sense of excellence in such phrases as: "Among these four types of persons, this one is more excellent and more sublime."

"Who is this that worships my feet, shining with psychic power and glory, illuminating all directions with a most beautiful (abhikkantena) complexion?"

In phrases such as "Excellent, Master Gotama!", it is seen in the sense of great delight. Therefore, it should be understood to mean "Master Gotama, it is very good."
15:
The word 'Abhikkanta' is used in the sense of 'excellence' in such passages as 'ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro ca' (this one is more excellent and more refined than these four persons). In passages such as 'abhikkantena vaṇṇena', it is used in the sense of 'surpassing beauty'. In passages such as 'Abhikkantaṃ, bhante', it is used in the sense of 'great appreciation' (rejoicing). Here too, it is used only in the sense of great appreciation. Because it is used in the sense of great appreciation, it should be understood to mean, 'Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent!'.

According to the rule: 'A wise man should repeat a word twice in times of fear, anger, praise, haste, wonder, joy, sorrow, and devotion,' it should be understood that the word 'Abhikkanta' is spoken twice here due to the power of devotion and praise. Alternatively, 'Abhikkanta' means that which is greatly desired, greatly heart-pleasing, and exceedingly good.

Of those two utterances of 'Abhikkanta', one praises the teaching (desanā) and the other praises one's own devotion. The intention here is: 'Master Gotama, this Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama is excellent; my devotion that has arisen depending on the Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama is also exceedingly delightful.' Or, it praises the words of the Blessed One himself by intending two meanings for each: the words of Master Gotama are excellent because they destroy faults, because they lead to the attainment of virtues, and likewise because they generate faith, because they generate wisdom, because they are endowed with meaning, because they are endowed with phrasing, because they have clear words, because they have deep meaning, because they are pleasant to the ear, because they go to the heart, because they are free from self-exaltation, because they are free from disparaging others, because they are cool with compassion, because they are pure with wisdom, because they are delightful upon encounter, because they withstand investigation, because they are pleasant to hear, and because they bring welfare when reflected upon. Thus, it should be understood by connecting with such terms.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching itself with four metaphors. Among those metaphors, 'nikkujjita' means placed face down or turned downwards. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to make it face upwards. 'Paṭicchanna' means covered with grass, leaves, etc. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover or open. 'Mūḷha' refers to one who is confused about the directions. 'Showing the way' means taking one by the hand and saying, 'This is the path.' 'Darkness' refers to the fourfold gloom caused by the midnight of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a dense forest, and a thick layer of clouds. This is first the literal meaning of the words.

The application of the meaning is as follows: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, even so, by raising me up from the false Dhamma, I who had turned my back on the true Dhamma and fallen into the false Dhamma; just as one might reveal what was hidden, even so, by revealing the Dispensation (Sāsana) which had been covered by the forest of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; just as to one who is lost...
16:
...by revealing the Dispensation (Sāsana) which was covered by the forest of wrong views; just as one might point out the way to one who is lost, even so, by making manifest the path to heaven and liberation to me who had entered upon the wrong path and the path of falsehood; just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, even so, by lighting the lamp of the teaching which destroys the darkness of delusion that covered those jewels, for me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and could not see the nature of the jewels such as the Buddha—Master Gotama has made the Dhamma manifest in many ways through these methods.

Having thus praised the teaching, and having a heart devoted to the Triple Gem because of this teaching, he speaks the words beginning with 'Esāhaṃ' while performing an act of devotion. In that passage, 'Esāhaṃ' means 'I, such as I am'. 'I go to Master Gotama as a refuge' means that Master Gotama is my refuge, my resort, the remover of my suffering, and the provider of my welfare; with this intention, 'I go to, I resort to, I serve, and I attend upon Master Gotama.' Or, it means 'I know thus, I understand thus.' This is because roots having the meaning of 'going' also have the meaning of 'knowing'. Therefore, this meaning of 'I know, I understand' is stated for the word 'gacchāmi'.

In the phrase 'and to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha (I go for refuge)', 'Dhamma' is so called because it upholds (dhāreti) beings who practice according to the instruction—having attained the Path and realized Cessation—so that they do not fall into the four woeful states. That Dhamma, in terms of essence, is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. For it has been said: 'Monks, as far as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost of them,' and so on in detail. 

Not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of scriptural learning (pariyatti) together with the Noble Fruits is called 'Dhamma'. In the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna, it is said:
'Go for refuge to this Dhamma which is the fading of lust, free from craving, sorrowless, unconditioned, free from disturbance, sweet, well-practiced, and well-analyzed.'

In this verse, the word 'rāgavirāga' (fading of lust) refers to the Path. The words 'aneja' (free from craving) and 'asoka' (sorrowless) refer to the Fruit. The word 'dhamma-masaṅkhata' (unconditioned Dhamma) refers to Nibbāna. The words 'appaṭikūla' (free from disturbance), 'madhura' (sweet), 'paguṇa' (well-practiced), and 'suvibhatta' (well-analyzed) refer to all the aggregates of Dhamma as analyzed in the Three Piṭakas. The 'Saṅgha' is so called because it is joined together by the unity of views and virtue. That Saṅgha, in terms of essence, is the group of the eight noble individuals. In that very Vimāna, it is said:
'Wherein what is given is said to have great fruit, among the four pairs of pure men; these eight individuals see the Dhamma of the Noble Ones; go for refuge to this Saṅgha.'
17:
The assembly of monks is called the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. With this much speech, the Brahmin made known his arrival at the three refuges.

Now, for the sake of proficiency in those goings for refuge, this procedure should be understood: the refuge (saraṇa), the going for refuge (saraṇagamana), the person who goes for refuge, the classification of the going for refuge, the fruit of the going for refuge, the defilement, and the breach.

What is this procedure? Firstly, in terms of the meaning of the word, it is called 'refuge' (saraṇa) because it destroys [suffering]. For those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, it kills and destroys fear, trembling, suffering, and the misery of the woeful planes; this is the meaning. This is a designation for the Triple Gem itself. Alternatively, the Buddha is so called because he destroys the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and preventing what is not to their benefit. The Dhamma is so called because it rescues the world from the wilderness of existence and provides relief. The Saṅgha is so called because it causes even small meritorious deeds to yield abundant fruit. Therefore, for these reasons also, the Triple Gem is the refuge (saraṇa). The arising of consciousness, which has defilements dispelled through faith and reverence for those three gems and which occurs in the mode of having them as the mainstay, is 'going for refuge' (saraṇagamana). The being endowed with that consciousness is the one who goes for refuge. By means of the aforementioned arising of consciousness, one approaches thus: "These three gems are my refuge, these are my mainstay"; this is the meaning. Thus, firstly, these three—the refuge, the going for refuge, and the person who goes for refuge—should be understood.

Regarding the classification of the going for refuge, there are two kinds: the supramundane (lokuttara) and the mundane (lokiya). Of these two, the supramundane going for refuge, for the Noble Ones who have seen the Truth, is accomplished at the moment of the Path by the absolute cutting off of the defilements of the going for refuge; in terms of object, it takes Nibbāna as its object, and in terms of function, it is accomplished regarding the entire Triple Gem. The mundane going for refuge is accomplished for worldlings (puthujjanas) by the suppression of the defilements of the going for refuge, taking the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object. In essence, it is the acquisition of faith in the objects such as the Buddha, and it is called 'straightening of view' (diṭṭhijukamma) among the ten bases of meritorious action, being right view rooted in faith.

That mundane going for refuge occurs in four modes: by self-dedication (attasanniyyātana), by having them as the mainstay (tapparāyaṇatā), by acceptance of discipleship (sissabhāvūpagamana), and by prostration (paṇipāta). Among these, self-dedication means the renouncing of oneself to the Buddha and so forth, thus: "From this day forth, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha." Being the mainstay means the state of having them as one's resort, thus: "From this day forth, please remember me as one who has the Buddha as my mainstay, the Dhamma as my mainstay, and the Saṅgha as my mainstay." Acceptance of discipleship means: "From this day forth, I..."
18:
“...please remember me as a disciple of the Buddha, a disciple of the Dhamma, and a disciple of the Saṅgha”; this is the acceptance of discipleship (sissabhāvūpagamana). Prostration (paṇipāta) means the supreme humility shown toward the Buddha and so forth, thus: “From this day forth, please remember me as one who performs acts of salutation, rising up, salutation with joined palms, and proper homage only toward these three objects, the Buddha and so forth.” Indeed, for one who performs even one of these four modes, the going for refuge is truly acquired.

Furthermore, self-dedication (attasanniyyātana) should also be understood thus: “I renounce myself to the Blessed One, I renounce myself to the Dhamma, I renounce myself to the Saṅgha; I renounce my life. My self is indeed renounced, my life is indeed renounced. I go to the Buddha for refuge until the end of my life; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, and my protection.” Acceptance of discipleship should be understood as in the case of the going for refuge of the Venerable Mahākassapa: “Indeed, I would see the Teacher, I would see only the Blessed One; indeed, I would see the Sugata, I would see only the Blessed One; indeed, I would see the Sammāsambuddha, I would see only the Blessed One.”

“As such, I shall wander from village to village, from city to city,
paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and to the excellence of the Dhamma.”
In this way, being the mainstay (tapparāyaṇatā) should be understood as in the case of the going for refuge of Āḷavaka and others. Prostration (paṇipāta) should also be understood thus: “Then the Brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, massaged them with his hands, and announced his name: ‘I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, O Master Gotama; I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, O Master Gotama.’”

That prostration is of four kinds: due to kinship, fear, a teacher, or one worthy of offerings. Among these four, the going for refuge occurs only through prostration to one worthy of offerings, not through the others. For one takes refuge only by virtue of [the object's] excellence, and the refuge is breached only by virtue of [the object's] excellence. Therefore, whether it be a Sakyan or a Koliyan who pays homage thinking, “The Buddha is our kinsman,” the refuge is not truly acquired. Or if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and is of great power; if I do not pay homage, he might do me harm,” the refuge is not truly acquired. Or if one remembers having learned some art in the presence of the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta, or even during his time as the Buddha...
19:
“One portion should be enjoyed; two portions should be applied to one’s occupation (such as farming or trade); and the fourth portion should be stored and buried for use when dangers arise.” If one learns such worldly advice and pays homage thinking, “This person is my teacher,” the taking of refuge (saraṇagamana) is not established. Only when one pays homage thinking, “This person is the supreme field of merit in the world,” is the refuge truly taken.

For a male or female lay follower who has thus established the refuge, the refuge is not broken even if they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth in a non-Buddhist sect, thinking, “This person is my relative.” This is even more so in the case of a relative who has not gone forth. Likewise, the refuge is not broken for one who pays homage to a king out of fear. This is because the king is one honored by the nation, and if not paid homage, he might cause harm. Similarly, the refuge is not broken even if one pays homage to a non-Buddhist teacher who teaches some secular art or science, thinking, “This person is my teacher.” In this way, the distinctions in the taking of refuge should be understood.

Among these, for the supramundane (lokuttara) taking of refuge, the primary results (vipāka-phala) are the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), and the beneficial result (āniśaṃsa-phala) is the destruction of all suffering. Thus it has been said:

“He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcending of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This indeed is the safe refuge; this is the supreme refuge. Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.”

Furthermore, the beneficial result of that refuge should also be understood by way of the impossibility of viewing things as permanent, and so forth. Thus it has been said:

“It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view (diṭṭhisampanna) should look upon any formation (saṅkhāra) as permanent; should look upon any formation as pleasurable; should look upon any phenomenon (dhamma) as self; should deprive his mother of life; should deprive his father of life; should deprive an Arahant of life; should, with a corrupted mind, shed the blood of a Tathāgata; should cause a schism in the Saṅgha; or should point to another as his teacher. This is not possible.”
20:
The result of the mundane (lokiya) taking of refuge is the perfection of future lives and the perfection of wealth. Thus it has been said:

“Whoever have gone to the Buddha for refuge,
They shall not go to a state of woe.
Having discarded the human body,
They shall fill the hosts of devas.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.37)

It is also stated elsewhere: “Then Sakka, the lord of devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... To Sakka, the lord of devas, who was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: ‘It is good, O lord of devas, to go to the Buddha for refuge. Because of going to the Buddha for refuge, O lord of devas, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world. They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine life-span, beauty, happiness, fame, and power; and in divine sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches.’” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.341)

The same principle should be understood for the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Furthermore, the special excellence of the result of taking refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. In this way, the result of taking refuge should be understood.

Between those two types of refuge, the mundane refuge becomes defiled by ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the three objects (the Triple Gem). Therefore, it is not of great luster or of great influence. The supramundane refuge, however, has no defilement.

The breach of the mundane refuge is of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. Among them, the blameworthy breach occurs through such acts as dedicating oneself to another teacher (non-Buddhist), and so forth. That breach yields undesirable results. The blameless breach occurs through death. Since it has no further result to give, it is said to be without result. In the supramundane refuge, however, there is no breach at all. This is because even in a future life, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not point to another as his teacher. In this way, the defilement and the breach of the taking of refuge should be understood.
21:
The meaning is: "May the Venerable Gotama remember me as 'this person is a lay follower'; may he know me as such." Furthermore, in this context, to be skilled in the procedures regarding a lay follower, one should know these miscellaneous points: "Who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure (vipatti)? What is his accomplishment (sampatti)?"

Regarding those miscellaneous points, to the question "Who is a lay follower?": Any householder who has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem is called a lay follower. Thus it has been said: "Mahānāma, when a lay follower has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, and has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge, to that extent, Mahānāma, he is a lay follower" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033).

"Why is he called a lay follower?": Because he attends upon (upāsana) the Triple Gem. Indeed, he is called a lay follower because he attends upon the Buddha. He is called a lay follower because he attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

"What is his virtue?": It is the five abstinences (veramaṇī). As the Buddha said: "Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from the use of wines, liquors, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033).

"What is his livelihood?": It is living righteously and equitably, having abandoned the five types of wrong trade (micchā-vaṇijjā). Thus it has been said: "Monks, these five types of trade should not be undertaken by a lay follower. Which five? Trade in weapons, trade in beings (humans), trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poison. Monks, these five types of trade should not be undertaken by a lay follower" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177).

"What is his failure (vipatti)?": The failure of that very virtue and livelihood is the failure of this lay follower. Furthermore, the failure by which he becomes an outcaste lay follower (upāsaka-caṇḍāla), a stain of a lay follower (upāsaka-mala), and a social pariah of a lay follower (upāsaka-patikuṭṭha) should also be known as his failure. In essence, those are the five qualities beginning with lack of faith (assaddhiya). As the Buddha said...
22:
"Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is an outcaste lay follower, a stain of a lay follower, and a social pariah of a lay follower. Which five? He lacks faith; he is immoral; he is superstitious regarding omens; he relies on omens and not on kamma; and he seeks for those worthy of offerings outside of this dispensation and performs his primary service there" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175).

What is accomplishment (sampatti)? His accomplishment in virtue and accomplishment in livelihood is called accomplishment. Also, the five qualities beginning with faith, which make one a 'gem' and so forth, are called accomplishment. With reference to this meaning, the Buddha said: "Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a gem of a lay follower, a red lotus of a lay follower, and a white lotus of a lay follower. Which five? He has faith; he is virtuous; he is not superstitious regarding omens; he relies on kamma and not on omens; he does not seek for those worthy of offerings outside of this dispensation; and he performs his primary service here (within the dispensation)" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175).

In the term 'ajjatagge', this word 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning (ādi), tip (koṭi), portion (koṭṭhāsa), and best (seṭṭha). In passages such as "Friend gatekeeper, from today (ajjatagge) onwards, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.70), it is seen in the sense of 'beginning'. In passages such as "One should touch that fingertip (aṅgulagga) with that same fingertip; the tip of sugarcane, the tip of bamboo" (Kathāvatthu 441), it is seen in the sense of 'tip'. In passages such as "A portion of sour taste, a portion of sweet taste, or a portion of bitter taste" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.374), and "Monks, I allow you to divide by portion of dwellings or portion of precincts" (Cūḷavagga 318), it is seen in the sense of 'portion'. In passages such as "Monks, among beings without feet... the Tathāgata is declared the best (agga) of them" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34), it is seen in the sense of 'best'.

In this context, however, this word 'agga' should be understood in the sense of 'beginning'. Therefore, 'ajjatagge' should be understood as 'starting from today'. 'Ajjataṃ' means the state of today. There is also a reading 'ajjadagge', where the letter 'da' acts as a euphonic conjunction (sandhi); it carries the meaning 'starting from today'.

'Pāṇupetaṃ' means attending (the Triple Gem) with one's life. May the Venerable Gotama remember me and know me as a lay follower who attends as long as my life lasts, who has no other teacher, who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, and who performs what is allowable (kappiya-kāraka). Even if my head were cut off with a sharp sword, I would never say the Buddha is 'not the Buddha', or that the Dhamma...
23:
"I shall not say 'It is not the Dhamma' regarding the Dhamma, nor 'It is not the Saṅgha' regarding the Saṅgha." Having thus taken refuge by surrendering himself, inviting [the Buddha] with the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

In the seventh sutta, "Jāṇussoṇi" is a certain official title. Whichever clan obtains that title is called the Jāṇussoṇi clan. This brahmin is called "Jāṇussoṇi" because he was born into that clan and because he received the honor and title of Jāṇussoṇi from the king. Having heard that "the ascetic Gotama is wise, clever, and very learned," he thought, "If he knows the distinctions of gender (liṅga), case endings (vibhatti), and syntax (kāraka), etc., he will only know what we already know; what could he know that is unknown to us? He will only speak of what is known; what could he speak of that is unknown?" Thus, raising the banner of pride and lifting the horn of pride, surrounded by a large retinue, he approached the Blessed One.

"Brahmin, because of what is done and because of what is not done..." Hearing the brahmin's words, the Teacher thought, "This brahmin has not come here seeking the goal with a desire to know; he has come raising the banner of pride and lifting the horn of pride. If I explain the meaning of the question so that he understands, will it be for his benefit? Or if I explain it so that he does not understand, will it be for his benefit?" Knowing that "it will be for his benefit only if I explain it so that he does not understand," he said, "Brahmin, because of what is done and because of what is not done."

Hearing those words, the brahmin thought, "The ascetic Gotama says that one is reborn in hell because of both what is done and what is not done. Since this is taught as rebirth in one place due to both reasons, it is like a great darkness that is hard to understand; I have no footing in this matter. If I remain silent with only this much, when speaking among brahmins, they might say to me, 'You went to the ascetic Gotama raising the banner of pride and lifting the horn of pride, yet you remained silent after just one word and could not say anything; why do you speak here?' Therefore, though defeated, I will act as if undefeated and ask again the question about going to heaven." Thinking thus, he began the second question: "Venerable Gotama, who then..."
24:
It also occurred to that brahmin: "Through the upper question, I shall know the lower question; through the lower question, I shall know the upper question." For that reason, he asked this question again. The Teacher, thinking in the same way as before, spoke in a manner that he could not understand, saying once more: "Brahmin, it is because of what is done and because of what is not done." Being unable to find a footing in that either, the brahmin decided: "Friends, it is not right to come to such a man and leave without understanding. I shall abandon my own view, follow the ascetic Gotama, seek my own benefit, and clear the path to the next world." Having made this resolution, wishing to entreat the Teacher, he spoke the words beginning with "Na kho ahaṃ." Then, knowing that his pride was humbled, the Teacher, wishing to expand the teaching further, spoke the words beginning with "Tena hi, brāhmaṇa." Therein, "Tena hi" (Therefore) is an indication of the reason. It means "Because you do not understand the meaning of what was spoken in brief and entreat for a detailed teaching, therefore..." The rest of the words in this sutta have clear meanings.

In the eighth sutta, "Āyasmā" (Venerable) is a term of endearment. "Ānanda" is the name of that Elder. "Ekamsena" means certainly. "Anuvicca" means having entered into (investigated). "Viññū" means the wise. "Garahanti" means they blame or speak of dispraise. All the remaining words in this eighth and ninth suttas have clear meanings.

In the tenth sutta, "dunnikkhittañca padabyañjanaṃ" refers to Pali words taken out of order. Because the word itself expresses the meaning, it is called "byañjana" (phrasing). Both "pada" and "byañjana" are names for the Pali text. "Attho ca dunnīto" refers to the Commentary (Atthakathā) taken out of order and reversed. "Monks, the meaning of wrongly placed Pali words is also difficult to grasp" means that the Commentary of the Pali that is taken out of order and reversed is difficult to understand, difficult to follow, and difficult to explain. In the eleventh sutta, the meaning should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated.

## The Second Chapter: Adhikaraṇavagga.

## 3. Commentary on the Bālavagga

In the first sutta of the third chapter, "accayaṃ accayato na passati" means not seeing one's own fault, thinking "I have failed and committed an offense." It refers to not asking for forgiveness (not making amends) by performing the penalty after saying "I have committed an offense." "Accayaṃ desentassa" refers to one who asks for forgiveness (one who apologizes) by performing the penalty after saying thus...
25:
The meaning is not forgiving after having brought about a penalty. "Accayaṃ desentassa" means for one who, having spoken thus and brought about the penalty, asks for forgiveness. "Yathādhammaṃ nappaṭiggaṇhāti" means that even when it is said, "I will not do this again, please forgive me," he does not accept this fault in accordance with the Dhamma or in accordance with the nature of things. It means not saying, "From now on, do not do such a thing again; I forgive your fault." The wholesome side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite method of what has been stated.

In the second discourse, "abbhācikkhanti" means they speak by overpowering [the truth] or speak with what is untrue. "Dosantaro" means one who has anger fallen within the mind. Indeed, such a person, like Sunakkhatta, misrepresents the Blessed One by saying, "The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states (jhāna, path, or fruit)," and so on. Or "saddho vā duggahitena" means one who is excessively faithful with faith devoid of wisdom, or one who is blindly devoted, also misrepresents the Blessed One by taking up a wrong view in such a way as: "The Buddha is entirely supramundane; even the thirty-two parts of the body of that Blessed One, such as the hair, are purely supramundane." The third discourse has a clear meaning.

In the fourth discourse, "neyyatthaṃ suttantaṃ" refers to a discourse whose meaning is to be inferred. To declare it as "nītattho suttanto" means saying, "This discourse is one with a direct meaning." Among those discourses, such discourses as "Monks, one person...", "Monks, two persons...", "Monks, three persons...", "Monks, four persons..." are called neyyattha (discourses whose meaning is to be inferred). In these discourses, although the Blessed One spoke saying "Monks, one person," and so on, the meaning must be inferred that in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no such thing as a "person." However, this person, due to his own foolishness, declares, "This discourse is nītattha (one with a direct meaning)." Indeed, [he thinks] if there were no person in the ultimate sense, the Blessed One would not have spoken words such as "Monks, one person," and so on. Because the Blessed One spoke thus, he assumes that a person exists in the ultimate sense and declares that neyyattha discourse to be a nītattha discourse. "Nītatthaṃ" refers to a discourse with a direct meaning such as "impermanence, suffering, and non-self." Indeed, in such a discourse, the meaning is just impermanence, just suffering, and just non-self. However, this person, due to his own foolishness, says, "This discourse is neyyattha; I will infer its meaning," and assuming that "there is permanence (nicca), there is happiness (sukha), there is a self (atta)," he declares a nītattha discourse to be a neyyattha discourse. The fifth discourse has a clear meaning.
26:
In the sixth discourse, "paṭicchannakammantassa" means of one who performs evil deeds. They perform evil deeds by concealing them. Even if they do not perform them by concealing, an evil deed is still said to be concealed. "Nirayo" (Hell) refers to the aggregates (khandhas) together with their location. In the animal realm, only the aggregates are obtained. The seventh and eighth discourses have clear meanings.

In the ninth discourse, "paṭiggāhā" means those who receive; the meaning is that two places receive an immoral person.

In the tenth discourse, "atthavase" means causes. "Araññavanapatthāni" means forests and large jungle thickets far from people. In that text, although it is stated in the Abhidhamma in a direct sense that "everything situated outside the threshold is called a forest," it should be understood that here it refers only to a dwelling that fulfills the forest-dweller's practice (āraññakanga), which is said to be "at least five hundred bow-lengths away." "Vanapattha" (jungle lodging) is a place beyond the vicinity of a village, not frequented by people, and where there is no plowing or sowing. "Pantāni" means remote places that are very far away. "Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra" means dwelling happily in both mundane and supramundane states. "Out of compassion for the later generations" means having compassion and care for my future disciples.

In the eleventh discourse, "vijjābhāgiyā" means states that belong to the category of true knowledge. "Samatha" (serenity) is the one-pointedness of mind. "Vipassanā" (insight) is the wisdom that comprehends conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras). "What benefit does it experience?" means what purpose does it achieve, accomplish, or fulfill? "The mind is developed" means the path-mind (maggacitta) is developed and increased. "Whatever lust there is, it is abandoned" means lust that occurs through the power of attachment is abandoned. Indeed, lust is the opposite of the path-mind, and the path-mind is the opposite of lust. When lust occurs, the path-mind is not present; when the path-mind occurs, lust is not present. When lust arises, it prevents the arising of the path-mind and cuts off its basis. When the path-mind arises, it arises only by uprooting lust along with its root and completely destroying it. Therefore, it is said, "lust is abandoned."

"Monks, insight is developed" means insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) is developed and increased. "Wisdom is developed" means path-wisdom (maggapaññā) is developed and increased. "Whatever ignorance there is, it is abandoned" means the great ignorance that is the root of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) regarding the eight bases is abandoned. Indeed, ignorance is the opposite of path-wisdom, and path-wisdom is the opposite of ignorance. When ignorance occurs, path-wisdom
28:
...placing the father (on the shoulder), a son with a lifespan of a hundred years might carry them while living for the entire hundred years. That son would serve those parents, while they are still on his shoulders, by anointing them with perfumes to remove bad odors, by massaging them with hands to relieve fatigue, by bathing them with hot and cold water during cold and hot seasons, and by rubbing their hands and feet, which is called "kneading." Those parents, while sitting right there on his shoulders, would void their excrement and urine. Monks, even by doing this, it is not considered that enough has been done for the parents or that the debt has been repaid.

"In kingship with supreme authority" is said with reference to the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). "Āpādaka" means those who make one grow, the protectors. Indeed, children are made to grow and are protected by their parents. "Posaka" means those who nourish, making the limbs grow and feeding them with the milk that is their heart's blood. Indeed, children are nourished, supported, and looked after with food and drink by their parents. "Showers of this world" means that if parents, on the very day of birth, were to take the child by the feet and throw them into the forest, a river, or a precipice, the child would not see pleasant or unpleasant objects in this world. Because they did not do so, but instead nurtured and nourished them, the child sees pleasant and unpleasant objects in this world depending on the parents. Therefore, parents are called the "showers of this world" for that child. "Samādapeti" means to make them undertake (to make them take up). In this sutta, faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom, which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are discussed. A monk who is like the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, should be understood as one who establishes parents in those qualities.

In the third sutta, "tenupasaṅkami" means that Brahmin thought, "It is said that the ascetic Gotama answers whatever is asked; there is no such thing as him failing a question. I will devise a question that will make him fail." After eating excellent food, he closed the door of his chamber and sat down to think. Then it occurred to him, "In this place, there is much noise and great sound; the mind cannot be one-pointed. I will have an underground house built." Having built the underground house and entered there, he took one (thought) and then another, thinking, "If asked this, he will answer that; if asked that, he will answer this..."
29:
That Brahmin, though he strove to solve the problem, could not see any solution for the whole day. In this manner, four months passed for him. Only after those four months had elapsed did he see a two-pronged (inescapable) problem. Then, he thought: "I shall approach the ascetic Gotama and ask, 'What is your doctrine?' If he says, 'I am a kiriyavādī (one who holds the doctrine of action),' I will rebuke him by saying, 'Do you say that all unwholesome deeds should be done?' If he says, 'I am an akiriyavādī (one who holds the doctrine of non-action),' I will rebuke him by saying, 'Do you say that wholesome deeds should not be done?' When asked such a two-pronged question, he will be able neither to spit it out nor to swallow it. Thus, victory will be mine, and the ascetic Gotama will be defeated." Having thought this, he rose from his seat, clapped his hands, and emerged from his underground chamber. Thinking, "One who is to ask such a question should not go alone," he had a proclamation made throughout the city and, surrounded by the townspeople, approached the Blessed One.

"Kiṃvādī" means what view does he hold. "Kimakkhāyī" is asking what kind of practice he teaches to his disciples. Then, the Blessed One, knowing that the Brahmin had prepared the question for four months and had come with pride, thinking, "I have seen the problem that will defeat the ascetic Gotama," shattered that question with a single statement, saying, "Brahmin, I am a kiriyavādī," and so on. Then the Brahmin, discarding his pride, entreated the Blessed One and asked, "How then...?" and so forth. The remaining meanings in this sutta are clear.

## The Fourth Sutta
In the fourth sutta, "dakkhiṇeyya" means that an offering is called "dakkhiṇā," and it asks how many persons are worthy of receiving that offering. By the word "sekho," the seven types of noble learners (sekha) are shown. Here, even a virtuous worldling is included within the Stream-enterer. "Āhuneyyā yajamānānaṃ honti" means they are recipients worthy of offerings brought from afar by those giving gifts. "Khettaṃ" means a foundation or place, signifying the place where merit grows.

## The Fifth Sutta
In the fifth sutta, "Pubbārāme" refers to the monastery located on the eastern side of Sāvatthī. "Migāramātupāsāde" refers to the palace of the female lay devotee Visākhā. She is called "Migāramātā" (Migāra's Mother) because the banker Migāra placed her in the position of a mother, and also because the name of her eldest son was the same as his grandfather, the banker Migāra. The palace with a thousand rooms built and donated by her is called "Migāramātupāsāda."
30:
The Elder Sāriputta was residing in that (Migāramātupāsāda) palace. "Tatra kho āyasmā Sāriputto" refers to the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, who was residing in that palace.

"Bhikkhū āmantesi"—at what time did he address them? To elaborate, some suttas were spoken in the morning, some in the afternoon, some in the first watch, some in the middle watch, and some in the last watch. This Samacittappaṭipadā Sutta, however, was spoken in the afternoon (pacchābhatta). Therefore, he addressed them in the evening.

This sutta was not spoken by the Elder Sāriputta alone; it was also spoken by the Blessed One. Where was he sitting when he spoke it? He spoke it while sitting in Visākhā's Jewel Palace (Ratanapāsāda). For twenty years after his enlightenment, the Blessed One had no fixed residence (anibaddhavāsa); he went and stayed wherever it was comfortable.

During the first rains retreat (vassa), he turned the Wheel of Dhamma in the Isipatana Deer Park, and after letting eighteen crores of Mahābrahmās drink the nectar of the Dhamma, he stayed in Isipatana, depending on Benares. During the second rains retreat, he stayed at the Veḷuvana monastery, depending on Rājagaha; he stayed in that same Rājagaha for the third and fourth retreats as well. During the fifth rains retreat, he stayed in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Wood (Mahāvana), depending on Vesālī. During the sixth rains retreat, he stayed on Makula Mountain; during the seventh, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; during the eighth, in the Bhesakaḷā forest, depending on Susumāragira in the Bhagga country; during the ninth, in Kosambī; and during the tenth, in the Pālileyyaka forest thicket.

During the eleventh rains retreat, he stayed in the Brahmin village of Nālā; during the twelfth, in Verañjā; during the thirteenth, on Cāliya Mountain; during the fourteenth, in the Jetavana monastery; and during the fifteenth, in Kapilavatthu. During the sixteenth rains retreat, after taming the ogre Āḷavaka and letting eighty-four thousand beings drink the nectar of the Dhamma, he stayed in the city of Āḷavī. During the seventeenth, he stayed in Rājagaha itself; during the eighteenth, on Cāliya Mountain itself; likewise for the nineteenth.
