For the twentieth rains retreat, however, he stayed depending on Rājagaha itself. Thus, for twenty years, he stayed wherever it was comfortable without a fixed residence.

From then on, he made two dwellings his permanent residences. Which two? Jetavana and Pubbārāma. Why? Because of the great virtues of the two families. Considering the virtues of Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, and because of those virtues, the Teacher used those dwellings as permanent residences. Even though he would wander on a walking tour during the cold and hot seasons, he would stay only in those two dwellings during the rains retreat. Thus...
31:
The Blessed One, while residing [there], would stay at the Jetavana monastery at night, and on the following day, surrounded by the community of monks, he would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the South Gate, exit through the East Gate, and spend the day at the Pubbārāma monastery. Having stayed at the Pubbārāma monastery at night, on the following day, he would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the East Gate, exit through the South Gate, and spend the day at the Jetavana monastery. However, on that particular day, the Blessed One stayed only at the Jetavana monastery. For the Blessed One, wherever he resides, he never neglects the fivefold duties (the five Buddha-kicca). These duties have been explained in detail below. Among those five duties, during the time of performing the duties of the last watch (pacchima-yāma), the Blessed One, while surveying the world, saw the potential for the realization of the Four Noble Truths in countless beings living in Sāvatthī and in places within a distance of one gāvuta, half a yojana, and one yojana around Sāvatthī.

Thereafter, while considering, 'At what time will the realization of the Four Noble Truths occur?' he saw that it would be 'in the evening.' Then, considering, 'Will the realization occur while I am preaching, or while a disciple is preaching?' he saw that it would occur 'while the Elder Sāriputta is preaching.' Then, considering, 'At what place will it occur while [he] is sitting and preaching?' he saw that it would occur 'while [he] is sitting in Visākhā’s Palace of Gems (Ratana-pāsāda).' Furthermore, he saw: 'For Buddhas, there are three types of gatherings of disciples; for the Chief Disciples, there is one. Among those gatherings, today will be the gathering of disciples for the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta.' Having seen this, early in the morning, after attending to his physical needs, he adjusted his lower robe, put on the robe of the Sugata, took his stone bowl, and surrounded by the community of monks, entered the city through the South Gate. While wandering for alms, he ensured that the community of monks easily obtained alms-food, and then, like a boat driven by the wind, he turned back, exited through the South Gate, and stood outside the gate. Then, the four assemblies—the eighty great disciples, the community of bhikkhunīs, the community of laymen (upāsakas), and the community of laywomen (upāsikās)—surrounded the Teacher.

The Teacher addressed the Elder Sāriputta: 'Sāriputta, it is proper for you to go to the Pubbārāma monastery; take your assembly and go.' The Elder replied, 'Very well, Bhante,' and together with his retinue of five hundred monks, he went to the Pubbārāma. In this manner, [the Buddha] sent the eighty great disciples to the Pubbārāma monastery, while he himself went to the Jetavana monastery accompanied only by the Elder Ānanda. The Elder Ānanda, having performed his duties for the Teacher at the monastery and paid homage, said, 'Bhante, I shall go to the Pubbārāma.'
32:
'Do so, Ānanda,' [the Teacher] said. Having paid homage to the Teacher, [Ānanda] went to that very place (the Pubbārāma). The Teacher remained alone at the Jetavana monastery.

Indeed, on that day, the four assemblies desired to hear only the Dhamma talk of the Elder [Sāriputta]. King Kosala also went to the Pubbārāma, surrounded by his army. Similarly, Anāthapiṇḍika, with a retinue of five hundred lay followers, [went there]. The great laywoman Visākhā went surrounded by two thousand attendants. In the city of Sāvatthī, where five million seven hundred thousand families resided, only the house-guards were left behind, while the rest of the people took scented powders, flowers, and so on, and went to the Pubbārāma. All the people living in the villages at the four gates, within a distance of one gāvuta, half a yojana, and one yojana, also went to the Pubbārāma, carrying scented powders, flowers, and so on in their hands. The entire monastery appeared as if covered with a mixture of various flowers.

The General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, also went to the monastery and stood in the open space of the monastery courtyard. The monks prepared a seat for the Elder. The Elder sat there, and after his attendant monk had performed the major and minor duties, he gave an exhortation to the community of monks, entered the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), and remained there absorbed in meditative attainment (samāpatti). When the predetermined time had passed, the Elder Sāriputta emerged from the attainment, went to the Aciravatī River, washed away the dust and dirt from his body, and being free from distress, ascended from the same landing place where he had gone down. He then changed his lower robe, put on his double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭī), and stood there. The community of monks also went down from the places directly in front of them, washed away the dust and dirt from their bodies, came back up, and surrounded the Elder. Inside the monastery, they prepared a Dhamma-seat for the Elder. The four assemblies, knowing their respective places, sat down, leaving a path clear.

The Elder Sāriputta, together with his retinue of five hundred monks, proceeded to the Dhamma Hall and sat down facing the East on a jeweled throne carved with lion heads, over which a white parasol was raised, holding an ornate fan. Having sat down, he surveyed the assembly and thought: 'This assembly is indeed very large; a brief Dhamma teaching of little measure is not suitable for this assembly. What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable?' While reflecting on the Three Pitakas, he saw this Saṃyojana-pariyāya Dhamma teaching.
33:
Having reflected on the teaching in this way and desiring to preach it, he addressed the monks, saying, "Friends, monks." Indeed, addressing as "Bhikkhave" (Monks) without saying "Āvuso" (Friends) is the manner of the Buddhas' speech. However, this Venerable [Sāriputta], thinking, "I will not use an address equal to that of the Ten-Powered One," out of respect for the Teacher, used the address of disciples and said, "Friends, monks." "He said this" means he spoke this phrase of Dhamma teaching: "Friends, I shall preach about the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters."

In that gem palace, there was a certain Sotāpanna deity residing there. That deity, as soon as the Buddhas or disciples began a teaching, would know: "This teaching will be clear; this teaching will be profound. This teaching will be based on jhāna; this teaching will be based on insight (vipassanā). This teaching will be based on the Path (magga); this teaching will be based on the Fruition (phala); this teaching will be based on Nibbāna." On that day too, as soon as the Elder began the teaching, he knew: "By whatever method my lord, the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta, has begun the teaching, this teaching will delve into insight; he will preach insight through six aspects. At the conclusion of the teaching, a hundred thousand crores of deities will attain Arahantship, while the number of deities and humans who become Sotāpannas and so forth will be beyond measure. I shall give a cry of approval to my lord in a manner suitable to the teaching." Thinking thus, he made a great sound through his divine power and said, "Sādhu, sādhu, Bhante!"

When the king of deities gave the cry of approval, all the deities residing in the thousand surrounding palaces also gave their approval. Because of their sound of approval, all the deities residing in the Pubbārāma monastery, and because of their sound, the deities within a league (gāvuta), and then by the same method, at half a yojana, one yojana, and so on, the deities in one world system, two world systems, three world systems, up to ten thousand world systems gave their approval. Because of their sound of approval, the nāgas dwelling on earth and the deities dwelling in the sky, and then the cloud-deities (abbhavalāhaka), the heat-deities (uṇhavalāhaka), the cold-deities (sītavalāhaka), the rain-deities (vassavalāhaka), the four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika realm, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, Sakka the king of deities, the Yāma deities, and Suyama the king of deities...
34:
...the king of deities, the Tusitā deities, Santusita the king of deities, the Nimmānaratī deities, Sunimmita the king of deities, the Vasavatti deities, Vasavatti the king of deities, the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas, the Brahmapurohita Brahmas, the Mahābrahmas, the Parittābhā Brahmas, the Appamāṇābhā Brahmas, the Ābhassara Brahmas, the Parittasubhā Brahmas, the Appamāṇasubhā Brahmas, the Subhakiṇhā Brahmas, the Vehapphala Brahmas, the Avihā Brahmas, the Atappa Brahmas, the Sudassā Brahmas, the Sudassī Brahmas, and the Akaniṭṭha deities—excluding the non-percipient beings and the beings of the formless realm, all the deities and Brahmas in the places where the ear-base functions gave their approval.

Thereafter, the Arahant Great Brahmas, reflecting, "This sound of approval is indeed great; it has reached from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. For what reason has this sound arisen?" realized, "The General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta, is seated in Visākhā's gem palace in the Pubbārāma monastery and has begun preaching the Saṃyojana-pariyāya Dhamma teaching. It is fitting that we too should be present there as witnesses." Thinking thus, they went there. The Pubbārāma was crowded with deities. In the surroundings of the Pubbārāma, for a league, half a yojana, and a yojana, up to the edge of the world system, the area was filled without any gap by deities who had gathered from ten thousand world systems, from the earth below to the horizontal limits of the world systems. Even in a space the size of a needlepoint, sixty deities, having created subtle forms, stood at the upper limit.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, reflecting, "This tumult is indeed great; what could it be?" saw that the deities from ten thousand world systems had gathered in a single world system. At that time, while the Buddhas have no need for a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and can see and make their voices heard according to the extent of the assembly, for the disciples, a determination is necessary. Therefore, the Elder entered into a meditative attainment, and having emerged from it, he determined with a lofty mind (mahaggata-citta): "May the entire assembly up to the edge of the world system see me, and may they hear the sound of me preaching the Dhamma." From the moment he made the determination, whether one was sitting by his right knee or at the circular edge of the world system, there was no reason to ask, "What is the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāriputta, like? Is he tall or short? Is he dark-complexioned or fair?" He appeared clearly right in front of all the deities and Brahmas in all directions, like the moon stationed in the middle of the sky. The Dhamma...
35:
While he was preaching, all the devas and brahmās sitting at the side of the Venerable Sāriputta’s right knee and at the edge of the world-boundary heard his voice clearly.

Having made this determination, the Venerable Sāriputta began this Dhamma teaching: "Friends, the internal fetter..." (Āvuso ajjhattasaṃyojanañca). In that teaching, "internal" (ajjhatta) refers to the sensuous realm (kāmabhava). "External" (bahiddhā) refers to the fine-material realm (rūpabhava) and the immaterial realm (arūpabhava). Indeed, beings reside in the sensuous realm for only a short time (only for the duration of the incalculable aeon of staying evolved, which is one-fourth of a great aeon). For the remaining three parts, the sensuous realm is empty and void. They reside in the fine-material realm for a long time. Nevertheless, for those beings, deaths and rebirths are frequent in the sensuous realm, but few in the fine-material and immaterial realms. Where deaths and rebirths are frequent, there is also much clinging (ālaya), longing (patthanā), and desire (abhilāsa). Where they are few, these are few. Therefore, the sensuous realm is called "internal," and the fine-material and immaterial realms are called "external."

Thus, the desire and lust (chandarāga) occurring in the sensuous realm, called "internal," is the "internal fetter" (ajjhattasaṃyojana). The desire and lust occurring in the fine-material and immaterial realms, called "external," is the "external fetter" (bahiddhāsaṃyojana). Alternatively, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya) are called the "internal fetter." The five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya) that produce rebirth in the fine-material and immaterial realms are called the "external fetter." In this context, the etymological meaning is: the sensuous element (kāmadhātu) is called "lower" (ora); because they produce rebirth in that low sensuous element, they are called "lower-part-fettering" (orambhāgiya) as they cling to that lower realm. The fine-material and immaterial elements are called "higher" (uddha); because they produce rebirth in those higher realms, they are called "higher-part-fettering" (uddhambhāgiya) as they cling to that higher realm.

A person associated with the internal fetter as described is called an "internally fettered person" (ajjhattasaṃyojanapuggala). A person associated with the external fetter is called an "externally fettered person" (bahiddhāsaṃyojanapuggala). Both these names do not apply to the general worldly people who are dependent on the round of suffering. They are names only for the Noble Disciples—Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners—who have delimited their existence into two types.

For example, in a great forest, trees like catechu (khadira) or sal (sāla) cannot be called "pillars," "beams," or "rafters"; they are only called "catechu forest" or "sal forest." But when the trees from that forest are cut with a sharp axe and fashioned into the shapes of pillars and so on, only then do they receive the names "pillar," "beam," or "rafter." In the same way, a worldling (puthujjana) with thick defilements who has not yet delimited existence cannot receive these names. Only those like Stream-enterers, who have delimited existence and thinned their defilements, receive these names.

To clarify this meaning, the simile of the calf pen (vacchakasāla) should be understood. Having made a calf pen, stakes are driven inside, and calves are tied to those stakes with ropes. When there are not enough ropes, they catch them by the ears and lead them into the pen. When there is not enough space inside the pen, they drive stakes outside as well and do the same. In that simile, some calves, though tied inside, lie down outside. Some, though tied outside, lie down inside.
36:
They bind the calves with ropes and tether them to those stakes. When there are not enough ropes, they catch them by the ears and lead them into the pen. When there is not enough space inside the pen, they drive stakes outside as well and do the same. In doing so, some calves, though tied inside, lie down outside. Some, though tied outside, lie down inside. Some are tied inside and lie down inside. Some are tied outside and lie down outside. Some wander about without being tied either inside or outside. Among those calves, the rope of the calf tied inside but lying outside is long. This is because that calf, oppressed by heat and so on, goes out and lies down in the midst of other calves. The same applies to the calf tied outside but lying inside. If a calf is tied inside and lies down inside, its rope is short. The same applies to the calf tied outside and lying outside. Both these types of calves spend the whole day circling the stake and sleep right there. The calf that is not tied inside wanders in the midst of the calves within that pen. This well-behaved calf, even if released among the calves by being held by the ear, does not go elsewhere all day but wanders right there. The same applies to the calf that is not tied outside and wanders right there.

In this simile, the three realms of existence (bhava) should be understood as the calf pen. The stake of ignorance (avijjā) is like the stake in the pen. The ten fetters (saṃyojana) are like the ropes for tying the calves. Beings born in the three realms are like the calves. Stream-enterers and Once-returners in the fine-material and immaterial realms are like the calf tied inside but lying outside. For although they reside in those realms, their fetters are bound only to the sensuous realm. In what sense? In the sense of not yet being abandoned by the Path. Worldlings in the fine-material and immaterial realms are also included among these. For although they reside there, their fetters are bound only to the sensuous realm. A Non-returner (anāgāmi) in the sensuous realm is like the calf tied outside but lying inside. For although he resides in the sensuous realm, his fetters are bound only to the fine-material and immaterial realms. Stream-enterers and Once-returners in the sensuous realm are like the calf tied inside and lying inside. For they themselves reside in the sensuous realm, and their fetters are also bound only to the sensuous realm. A Non-returner in the fine-material and immaterial realms is like the calf tied outside and lying outside. For he himself resides in those realms, and his fetters are also bound only to those realms. An Arahant (khīṇāsava) in the sensuous realm is like the calf that is not tied inside and wanders inside. [Like the calf] not tied outside...
37:
An Arahant in the fine-material and immaterial realms should be understood like a young calf wandering outside. Among the fetters, these three—personality belief, doubt, and clinging to rites and rituals—obstruct the being who is going and bring back the being who has gone. However, these two fetters—sensual desire and ill will—cannot cause rebirth in the fine-material and immaterial realms without being suppressed by meditative attainment or completely eradicated by the Path.

Regarding the words "Friends, how is it?", the Elder Sāriputta, like a man who places two jewel boxes by his side and, filling both hands, distributes the seven kinds of jewels to the assembled crowd, first giving from the first jewel box and then likewise from the second, even so, having established these two terms, "Friends, I shall teach the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters," as the table of contents (mātikā), he now begins the detailed explanation to demonstrate it to the eightfold assembly.

In that detailed explanation, "in this" means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). "Is virtuous" means one is endowed with virtue through the fourfold purification virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). Thus, the Elder Summa, a resident of Dīpavihāra, said that the Elder Sāriputta, having briefly indicated the fourfold purification virtue with this sequence of words, then explained the foremost virtue among those four with the passage "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint."

However, his pupil, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: "In both the brief and detailed accounts, only the Pātimokkha restraint is spoken of. Indeed, only the Pātimokkha restraint is called virtue; there is no place where the other three are called virtue." Being unwilling to concede, he further said: "What is called restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors; purity of livelihood is merely the arising of the four requisites in accordance with the Dhamma; and that which is dependent on requisites is merely the reflecting on the purpose of the acquired requisites before using them. In the primary sense, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. If that Pātimokkha restraint is broken, it cannot be said that such a person will protect the remaining virtues like restraint of the faculties, just as a man whose head is cut off cannot protect his hands, feet, and the rest. But if that Pātimokkha restraint is healthy, such a person can protect the remaining virtues like restraint of the faculties by restoring them to their original state, just as a man whose head is not cut off can protect his life. Therefore, having briefly indicated the Pātimokkha restraint with the word 'virtuous,' he spoke the words 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint' and so forth, wishing to explain it in detail."
38:
In the passage beginning with "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint," "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint" means endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint. "Perfect in conduct and resort" means endowed with both conduct and resort. "In the slightest" means in small matters. "Faults" means unwholesome states. "Seeing danger" means one who habitually sees danger. "Having undertaken" means having properly taken up. "Trains in the training rules" means having undertaken those specific training rules, one trains.

Alternatively, "having undertaken, trains in the training rules" means having properly taken up and training in all training rules that should be practiced by way of body or speech, whether in the training rules or in the categories of training. This is the summary here. In detail, however, all these terms such as Pātimokkha restraint have been explained in the Visuddhimagga, and the fourfold purification virtue has been shown by analyzing it in every aspect.

"A certain group of devas" refers to one of the six classes of sense-sphere devas. "One who returns" means one who returns to the lower sense realm. "Coming to this state" means one who returns only to this state of the five human aggregates. It shows that there is no rebirth in one's own current realm nor rebirth in higher realms, but one only returns again to the lower sense realm. By this factor, the two lower Paths and the two lower Fruits are spoken of for a monk who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and whose meditation subject is the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhāna).

"A certain peaceful liberation of mind" refers to one of the eight attainments, specifically the fourth jhāna attainment. Indeed, that fourth jhāna attainment is called "peaceful" (santā) because of the calming of opposing defilements, and it is called "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) because the mind is liberated from those same defilements. "A certain group of devas" refers to one of the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). "Not coming to this state" means not coming again to this state of the five aggregates; it shows that there is no rebirth in the lower sense realm, but there is rebirth in the higher Pure Abodes, or one attains Parinibbāna in that very place of rebirth. By this factor, the three Paths and the three Fruits are spoken of for a monk who is devoted to concentration (samādhi).

"For the sake of revulsion towards sense desires" means for the sake of being weary of or disgusted with both types of sense desires (objective and subjective). "For the sake of fading away" means for the sake of the fading of passion. "For the sake of cessation" means for the sake of making them non-existent. "Is one who has practiced" means one has undertaken the practice. By this sequence of words, the insight for the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga-vipassanā) is spoken of for the sake of the destruction of the fivefold sensual lust of the Stream-enterer and the Once-returner. "Towards existences" means towards the three types of existence. By this term, the insight for the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-vipassanā) is spoken of for the sake of the destruction of the Non-returner's lust for existence. By the term "is one who has practiced for the destruction of craving," the insight for the Path of Non-returning is also spoken of for the sake of the destruction of the craving for the fivefold sensual pleasure of the Stream-enterer and the Once-returner.
39:
By the phrase "taṇhākkhayāya paṭipanno hoti" (he is practicing for the destruction of craving), the insight for the path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga) is taught for the purpose of ending craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure specifically for Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī). By the phrase "so lobhakkhayāya" (he [practices] for the destruction of greed), the insight for the path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga) is taught for the purpose of ending greed for existence for Non-returners (Anāgāmī). "Aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ" (a certain group of deities) refers to one of the Brahma realms among the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). "Anāgantā itthattaṃ" (not returning to this state) means not returning to the state of these five aggregates, no longer being reborn in the lower sensual realms, but being reborn in the higher Pure Abodes or attaining Parinibbāna right there.

Thus, by the first factor, the lower two paths and fruits are taught for the monk who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) meditating on the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhāna). By the second factor, the three paths and fruits are taught for the monk engaged in the practice of concentration (samādhi). By the phrase "so kāmānaṃ," the insight for the higher path of Non-returning is taught for Stream-enterers and Once-returners to end lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. By the phrase "so bhavānaṃyeva," the insight for the higher path of Arahantship is taught for Non-returners. By the phrase "so taṇhākkhayāya," the insight for the higher path of Non-returning is taught for Stream-enterers and Once-returners to end craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure. By the phrase "so lobhakkhayāya," the insight for the higher path of Arahantship is taught for Non-returners to end greed for existence. In this way, having taught insight through these six methods (mukha), the Buddha concluded the teaching in accordance with the sequence (anusandhi). At the conclusion of the teaching, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship. The number of those who became Stream-enterers and so forth was beyond limit. Just as in this assembly one hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship and the number of deities and humans who became Stream-enterers and so forth was limitless, so too in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, and the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained Arahantship, and the number of deities and humans who became Stream-enterers and so forth was limitless.

"Samacittā devatā" (even-minded deities) means they are called even-minded because they are equal in the subtle nature of their minds. To elaborate, all those deities created their own forms (attabhāva) to be as subtle as their minds. Therefore, they are known as "Samacittā." They are also called "Samacittā" for another reason: "The Elder Sāriputta has only taught the meditative attainments (samāpatti), but he has not yet taught the power (thāma) of those attainments. We shall invite the Buddha and have him teach the power of the attainments." Thus, all of them were of one mind. Another reason is that they looked to see who had arrived and who had not yet arrived at this assembly, and seeing that the Tathāgata had not yet arrived, they thought, "We [shall invite] the Tathāgata..."
40:
"Let us invite the Buddha and make the assembly complete"—thus all the deities were of one mind; therefore, they are called "Samacittā" (those of even mind). Another reason: in the future, some monk, nun, deity, or human might show disrespect, thinking, "This teaching was spoken by a disciple (sāvaka)." Therefore, let us invite the Buddha and make this teaching one spoken by the Omniscient One (Sabbaññu). By doing so, this teaching will be held in high esteem in the future—thus all the deities were of one mind; therefore, they are called "Samacittā." Another reason: all those deities were attainers of the same meditative attainment (samāpatti) or attainers of the same object; thus, they were of even mind.

"Haṭṭha" means being delighted, joyful, and exceedingly glad. The word "Sādhu" is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of requesting. "Anukampaṃ upādāya" (out of compassion) does not mean it was based on compassion or pity for the Elder Sāriputta, for there was no need to show compassion to the Elder in this situation. The reason is that on the day the Elder Sāriputta was fanning the Buddha while standing at the entrance of the Sūkarakhata cave, as the Buddha was teaching the meditation on feelings (vedanākammaṭṭhāna) to the Elder's nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, the Elder reached the very peak of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), like one who satisfies hunger by eating food prepared for another, or like one who places an ornament prepared for another on his own head. On that very day, he had already been the recipient of the Buddha's compassion. However, out of compassion for the other deities and humans who had arrived at that place, they requested the Buddha, saying, "May the Blessed One please come."

In the phrase "balavā puriso" (a strong man), a weak person cannot quickly bend or extend his limbs, but only a strong man can. Therefore, it is said, "a strong man." "Sammukhe pāturahosi" means he appeared clearly right in front of them. "Bhagavā etadavoca" means the Buddha stated the reason for his arrival by the method beginning with, "Here, Sāriputta, in this Dispensation." It is said that the Buddha had this thought: "If some foolish or ignorant monk, nun, male lay follower, or female lay follower should think, 'The Elder Sāriputta has gained a large following; the Buddha, unable to tolerate such a large following, has come out of envy (usūyā) to disperse the assembly,' such a person would be reborn in the states of misery (apāya) because of having a corrupted mind toward me." Therefore, wishing to explain the reason for his arrival, he spoke the words beginning with, "Here, Sāriputta, in this Dispensation."
41:
Having thus stated the reason for his coming, he now said, "Sāriputta, those deities, being in groups of ten," and so forth, to explain the power of meditative attainment (samāpatti). In that statement, the meaning should be taken either by the power of retinue or by the power of meditative attainment. Firstly, by the power of retinue, deities of great power stood in groups of ten in a single place; deities of lesser power than them stood in groups of twenty in a single place; deities even less powerful than them... stood in groups of sixty in a single place. However, by the power of meditative attainment, those deities who had developed noble attainments stood in groups of sixty in a single place. Deities who developed attainments inferior to them stood in groups of fifty... those who developed even more inferior attainments... stood in groups of ten in a single place. Or, those who developed inferior attainments stood in groups of ten in a single place. Those who developed more noble attainments than them stood in groups of twenty; those more noble than them... stood in groups of sixty in a single place.

"The size of a point made by the tip of an awl" means in a space as small as where the tip of an awl falls. "They do not obstruct one another" means that even though they stand in such a crowded place, they do not obstruct or collide with one another, remaining without pressure or congestion. There was no reason to say, "Your hand is hurting me, your foot is hurting me, you are standing on me." "Indeed in that existence" means indeed in that Brahma realm. "Thus the mind was developed" means the mind was developed in that manner. "Those deities" means that with the mind thus developed, those deities, being in groups of ten... stand and do not obstruct one another. "Only in this Dispensation" is a locative case meaning either in the Dispensation or in the human world; the meaning is "only in this very Dispensation, only in this very human world." For those deities developed that mind in this very human world and in this very Dispensation, because of which they were reborn in the peaceful realm of form (rūpabhava), and having come from there, they stand having created such subtle bodies. In this regard, although there are deities reborn in the Brahma realm after attaining the three paths and fruits during the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, because the instruction of all Buddhas is one and the Dispensation is one, he said, "Sāriputta, only in this Dispensation," treating the Dispensation of other Buddhas as this very Dispensation. By this much, the Tathāgata has explained the power of meditative attainment.
42:
Now, wishing to give an instruction by way of the sequence of the text concerning the Elder Sāriputta, he said, "Therefore, Sāriputta." In that phrase "Therefore, Sāriputta," etc., "therefore" means because those deities, having produced peaceful meditative attainments only here in this human world and in our Buddha's Dispensation, were reborn in the peaceful realm of form; therefore (is the meaning). "Calm faculties" (santindriyā) means they have calm faculties because the five faculties, such as faith, are peaceful, quenched, and noble. "Calm minds" (santamanasā) means they have calm minds because the mind is peaceful, quenched, and noble. "We shall offer only a calm offering" means we shall offer an offering of body and mind that is only peaceful, quenched, and noble. "Among fellow Dhamma-farers" (sabrahmacārīsu) means among those who lead the holy life together, such as having the same recitation of the Pātimokkha. With this much of the section, "Thus, Sāriputta, you should train," the Blessed One made the discourse one spoken by the Omniscient One. "Perished" (anassu) means ruined or destroyed. "Those who did not hear this Dhamma discourse" means those wanderers of other sects who, relying on their own evil, empty, and useless wrong views, did not get to hear such a Dhamma teaching as this. Thus, he concluded the discourse in accordance with the sequence of connections.

In the sixth sutta, "dwelling at Varaṇā" means there is a city named Varaṇā; he dwells depending on that city. "Due to the cause of adherence to sensual lust, bondage to sensual lust, entanglement in sensual lust, obsession with sensual lust, and total absorption in sensual lust" means due to the cause of adherence to sensual lust, due to the cause of bondage to sensual lust, due to the cause of entanglement in sensual lust, due to the cause of obsession with sensual lust, and due to the cause of total absorption in sensual lust. This is what is meant: the sensual lust that arises depending on the five cords of sensual pleasure, due to the cause of adherence to it, etc. Because of being adhered to by sensual lust, being bound by it, being entangled in it like in a great bog, being entered into it, being obsessed and seized by that very sensual lust, and being totally absorbed by sensual lust, having swallowed and completely seized it—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the terms "lust for views" (diṭṭhirāga), etc. Furthermore, in the term "lust for views," the lust that arises depending on the sixty-two wrong views should be understood. "In the eastern districts" means from the place where the Elder resided, the district of Sāvatthī is in the eastern direction, and even when the Elder sat, he sat facing that direction; therefore, he said thus. "Uttered an inspired utterance" means he spoke an inspired speech. To clarify that speech: just as oil that a measuring vessel cannot contain flows out and is called "overflow" (avasesaka), and just as water that a tank cannot contain overflows...
43:
Just as water flows over and is called 'ogha' (a flood), so too, words born of joy that arise when the heart cannot contain it, becoming excessive and unable to stay within, break out externally. Such words are called 'udāna' (inspired utterances). It means he uttered such words born of joy.

## In the Seventh Sutta, in the forest named Gundāvana.

'Upasaṅkami' means: "It is heard that the Elder Mahākaccāna, even upon seeing those as old as his father or grandfather, does not pay homage, does not rise to greet them, and does not invite them to a seat. One cannot reach a conclusion with just this much; I will approach and investigate that elder." Thinking thus, after eating his morning meal, he approached where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was. 'Jiṇṇa' is being worn out by old age. 'Vuddha' is being aged in years. 'Mahallaka' is being senior by birth. 'Addhagata' is having passed through a long stretch of time. 'Vayoanuppatta' is having reached the final stage of life.

"O Kaccāna, that behavior which we had only heard of is now consistent with what is seen. Therefore, it is just as heard, not otherwise." This refers to himself. "Even seeing us who are so aged, there is not even a mere salutation, nor a rising to greet, nor an invitation to a seat from the Venerable Kaccāna." This was the Brahmin's intention. 'Na sampannameva' means it is certainly not proper, it is certainly not suitable.

The Thera, hearing the Brahmin's words, thought, "This Brahmin knows neither the elder nor the young; I will explain to him about the elder and the young." Expanding the teaching, he said, "Brahmin, there are..." and so on. In that context, 'jānatā' means by knowing all that should be known. 'Passatā' means by seeing that very Dhamma like an āmalaka (emblic myrobalan) placed on the palm of the hand. 'Vuddhabhūmi' is the reason why one is called an elder. 'Daharabhūmi' is the reason why one is called young.

'Āsītika' is one who is eighty years old. 'Nāvutika' is one who is ninety years old. 'Kāme paribhuñjati' means enjoying both types of sensual pleasures—objective (vatthukāma) and subjective (kilesakāma)—with desire. 'Kāmamajjhāvasati' means living as a master of the house amidst both types of sensual pleasures. 'Kāmapariyesanāya ussuko' means being devoted to the search for both types of sensual pleasures. 'Bālo na therotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati' means such a person is reckoned only as a fool, an ignorant one, and does not reach the reckoning of an 'elder'. Indeed, the Blessed One said this:
44:
The Blessed One, who knows all that should be known and who sees all those things like an āmalaka on the palm of his hand, knows the ground of elderhood (vuddhabhūmi) and the ground of youth (daharabhūmi). Even if one is eighty or ninety years old, if one still enjoys the two types of sensual pleasures—objective and subjective—with desire, lives as a master of the house amidst sensual pleasures, and is devoted to seeking sensual pleasures, such a person is reckoned only as a fool, an ignorant one, and does not reach the reckoning of an elder. Indeed, the Blessed One said this:

“He is not an elder just because his head is grey;
His age is ripe, but he is called 'one grown old in vain'.”

'Dahara' means young. 'Yuvā' means one endowed with youth. 'Susu kāḷakeso' means one with very black hair. By the phrase "endowed with auspicious youth," it shows that the youth by which one is a young man is auspicious and beautiful. In the context of "in the first stage of life," the first stage of life is thirty-three years; it means being endowed with that age. Only such a person reaches the reckoning of a "wise one" and an "elder." The Blessed One also said this:

“In whom there is truth, Dhamma, non-violence, restraint, and self-control,
That wise one who has washed away impurities is indeed called an 'elder'.”

In the Eighth Sutta, "thieves are powerful" means they are well-equipped with factions, followers, wealth, hideouts, and vehicles. "At that time, kings are weak" means when those thieves are powerful, kings are weak due to the lack of such resources. It is not easy to enter the city at any desired moment after wandering on tour in the countryside outside. Thinking, "Thieves are plundering and crushing the countryside, we will stop them," it is not convenient to set out in the first watch, middle watch, or last watch. From then on, thieves beat and rob people and go away. It is also not pleasant to travel in the border districts to establish villages, build bridges, dig ponds, or build rest-houses, etc. It is not easy for the Brahmins and householders living inside the city to carry out their work in orchards and fields outside the village. "Evil monks are powerful" means they have factions, fame, merit, and are endowed with many male and female attendants, and they rely on kings and great ministers. "At that time, virtuous monks are weak" means when those evil monks are powerful, the virtuous monks are weak due to the lack of such resources. Those monks remain silent in the midst of the Saṅgha.
45:
"Saṅkasāyantī" means sitting silently in the midst of the Saṅgha, unable to open one's mouth to speak even a single word, sitting as if brooding. "Tayidaṃ" refers to that very cause. The wholesome side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meaning.

In the ninth sutta, "micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu" means due to the cause of practicing wrongly. "Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ" refers to the Path (magga) together with insight (vipassanā). A person of such nature is unable to attain, fulfill, or complete the Path together with insight. The wholesome side should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meaning. In this sutta, the Path together with insight is taught.

In the tenth sutta, "duggahitehi" means because of (suttas) that are wrongly grasped out of order. "Byañjanappatirūpakehi" means because of (syllables) that are counterfeit in terms of sound, obtained through the ornateness of letters. "Atthañca dhammañca paṭibāhanti" means they obstruct the meaning and the Pali text of well-grasped suttas. They present only the meaning and the Pali text of the suttas they have wrongly grasped as being superior. The wholesome side should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meaning. In this sutta, the growth and decline of the Dispensation (Sāsana) are taught.

## Samacitta Vagga, the Fourth.

## 5. Commentary on the Parisa Vagga

In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, "uttānā" refers to an assembly that is open and not concealed. "Gambhīrā" refers to an assembly that is deep and concealed. "Uddhatā" refers to those endowed with a restless mind. "Unnaḷā" means those who are uplifted by empty pride, like raising a banner of conceit. "Capalā" refers to those endowed with frivolity, such as decorating bowls and robes. "Mukharā" refers to those who are harsh-mouthed and have rough speech. "Vikiṇṇavācā" refers to those with unrestrained speech, who talk nonsense all day long. "Muṭṭhassatī" refers to those who are unmindful. "Asampajānā" refers to those lacking wisdom. "Asamāhitā" refers to those who do not obtain even a mere moment of one-pointedness of mind. "Pākatindriyā" refers to those endowed with faculties that are left open as usual and are unguarded. The wholesome side should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meaning.
46:
In the second sutta, "bhaṇḍanajātā": the behavior prior to a quarrel (such as muttering) is called "bhaṇḍana"; because that behavior has arisen in them, they are called "bhaṇḍanajātā." Furthermore, they are those in whom a quarrel has arisen due to speaking words such as "We will have you punished, we will have you bound," etc. This is the way regarding laypeople. For monks, however, those who cause a quarrel by speaking words of committing an offense (āpatti) are called "kalahajātā." "Vivādāpannā" means having fallen into conflicting views. "Mukhasattīhi vitudantā": words spoken badly because they cut away virtues are called "mouth-spears" (mukhasatti); piercing and striking with those mouth-spears. "Samaggā" means being endowed with harmony through performing the same ecclesiastical act (kamma), the same recitation (uddesa), and having the same training (sikkhā). "Piyacakkhūhi" means looking with eyes associated with loving-kindness (mettā).

In the third sutta, "aggavatī" means an assembly that has noble persons, or an assembly endowed with the highest or noble practice. An assembly opposite to that is called "anaggavatī." "Bāhulikā" refers to those who practice primarily for the abundance of robes and so forth. Those who take up the Dispensation laxly are called "sāthalikā." In the phrase "okkamane pubbaṅgamā," the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are called "okkamana" because they lead down to the sensual realm; thus it means those who take the lead in fulfilling those five hindrances. "Paviveke" refers to Nibbāna, which is the seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviviveka). "Nikkhittadhurā" refers to those who have laid down the burden (lacking effort) in all three types of seclusion. "Na vīriyaṃ ārabhanti" means they do not exert effort in both body and mind. "Appattassa pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining the special qualities of jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala) that have not been reached before. The remaining two terms are just synonyms for that same meaning. "Pacchimā janatā" refers to co-residents and pupils. "Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī" means following the practice of the teachers and preceptors that one has seen, by imitating the actions performed by them. The remaining points should be understood by the way of the opposite of what has been stated.

In the fourth sutta, "ariyā" refers to the assembly of noble disciples. "Anariyā" refers to the assembly of worldlings (puthujjana). "They do not know as it really is: 'This is suffering'" means that, excluding craving (taṇhā), the five aggregates of the three planes are called the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); it means not knowing according to nature that "this much is suffering, there is no suffering beyond this." This method is the same in all places. In the remaining terms, the previous craving that gives rise to that suffering is called "Origin" (samudaya). The absolute destruction and non-arising of that craving, or of both those truths, is called the "Cessation of Suffering" (dukkha-nirodha). The Noble Eightfold Path is the "Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering" (dukkha-nirodhagāminī paṭipadā).
47:
In this way, in this sutta, the four paths and the four fruits are taught by means of the four truths.

## Pañcama Sutta

'Parisākasaṭa' means an assembly like dregs, an assembly like rubbish, or an assembly like chaff. 'Parisāmaṇḍa' means a clear assembly or an assembly like the essence. 'They go to a wrong course through favoritism (chanda)' means they go to an improper path out of affection; it means they do what should not be done. In the remaining terms, the same method should be noted. These four ways of going astray (agati) are found in the distribution of goods and in the place of legal decision.

Between those two, in the distribution of goods, first, when an undesirable item arrives for monks who are one's own burden (dependents), one who exchanges that item and gives a desirable one is said to go to a wrong course through favoritism. When a desirable item arrives for monks who are not one's own burden, one who exchanges that item and gives an undesirable one is said to go to a wrong course through hatred. One who does not know the items to be distributed or the established rules is said to go to a wrong course through delusion. One who gives a desirable item by exchanging it out of fear, thinking, "If I give an undesirable item to these harsh-spoken people or those who rely on kings and so on, they might even do me harm," is said to go to a wrong course through fear. But one who does not go thus, being like a scale or a measure and remaining neutral towards all, giving to each person exactly what is due to them, is said not to go to the four wrong courses.

In the place of legal decision, one who speaks of a grave offense (garukāpatti) as a light offense (lahukāpatti) for someone who is one's own burden is said to go to a wrong course through favoritism. One who speaks of a light offense as a grave offense for another is said to go to a wrong course through hatred. One who does not know the rehabilitation from an offense or the collection of offenses is said to go to a wrong course through delusion. One who speaks of a grave offense as light out of fear of a harsh-spoken person or one honored by the king, thinking, "If I speak of this person's offense as grave, he might even do me harm," is said to go to a wrong course through fear. But one who speaks only according to the truth to everyone is said not to go to the four wrong courses.

## Chaṭṭha Sutta

'Okkācitavinītā' means those who are difficult to discipline. 'No paṭipucchāvinītā' means those who are not disciplined through questioning. 'Gambhīrā' means teachings that are deep in terms of the Pali text, like the Salla Sutta. 'Gambhīratthā' means teachings that are deep in terms of meaning, like the Mahāvedalla Sutta. 'Lokuttarā' means...
48:
...they explain the meaning known as supramundane. "Suññatapaṭisaṃyuttā" means teachings like the Asaṅkhata Saṃyutta, which clarify only the ultimate reality (paramattha) devoid of a being. "Na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti" means they do not apply their minds for the sake of understanding; or they sleep, or they are occupied with other objects. "Uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ" refers to what should be learned and what should be mastered. "Kavitā" means teachings composed by poets. The other term (kāveyya) is just a synonym for that "kavitā". "Cittakkharā" means teachings with ornate syllables. The other term (cittabyañjanā) is just a synonym for that "cittakkharā". "Bāhirakā" means teachings outside the Dispensation (Sāsana). "Sāvakabhāsitā" means teachings spoken by the disciples of those outsiders. "Suṃssūsanti" means they listen with delight because of the ornateness of the syllables and the excellence of the sound.

"Na ceva aññamaññaṃ paṭipucchanti" means they do not question each other about the meaning, the connection (anusandhi), or the sequence. "Na ca paṭivicaranti" means they do not wander about for the sake of inquiry. "How is this?" means asking "How should this phrasing (byañjana) be established? In what way should it be established?" "What is the meaning of this?" means asking "What is the meaning of this spoken Pali? What is the connection? What is the sequence?" "Aviwaṭaṃ" means a matter that is concealed. "Na vivaranti" means they do not open it up. "Anuttānīkataṃ" means a matter that is not made plain. "Na uttāniṃ karonti" means they do not make it plain. "Kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu" means in matters that are the cause of doubt. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the reverse of the dark side already mentioned.

In the seventh sutta, "Āmisagaru" refers to an assembly that stands by taking the supramundane Dhamma as inferior while giving weight to the four requisites. "Saddhammagaru" refers to an assembly that stands by taking the four requisites as inferior while giving weight to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. "Ubhatobhāgavimutto" is one liberated by both parts (the physical body and the mental body). "Paññāvimutto" is a dry-insight Arahant liberated by wisdom. "Kāyasakkhī" is one who stays having touched the touch of jhāna with the mental body and later having realized Nibbāna, the cessation of defilements. "Diṭṭhippatto" is one who has reached the end of the path of stream-entry, seeing Nibbāna. Both of these are found in six instances. "Saddhāvimutto" is one liberated through faith. This person is also found in six instances. One is called "Dhammānusārī" because of following the Dhamma of the path of Arahantship. One is called "Saddhānusārī" because of following faith. Both of these are persons endowed with the path of stream-entry. "Kalyāṇadhammo" is one of good character. "Dussīlo pāpadhammo" is an immoral person of evil character. Why is this immoral person accepted? The reason is that if all virtuous people were to exist simultaneously and equally...
49:
If all virtuous ones appear at the same time, strong respect does not arise; only when some non-virtuous ones are present does strong respect for the virtuous ones arise—thinking thus, they take [that position]. Those monks obtain gains by doing so. Those monks obtain the four requisites by speaking of the virtues of some and the faults of others. 'Gathitā' means bound by craving (infatuated). 'Mucchitā' means dazed or infatuated by the power of craving alone. 'Ajjhopannā' means remaining swallowed and finished by craving. 'Anādīnavadassāvino' refers to those who do not see the danger in consumption without reflection. 'Anissaraṇapaññā' refers to those lacking the wisdom of escape, which removes intense lust (rāga) for the four requisites, and who do not know, 'This is the purpose, this is the requisite.' 'Paribhuñjantī' means they consume while having intense lust.

In the 'bright side' (sukkapakkha), the brief explanation of these seven types of Noble Persons (ariya-puggala) is given through terms such as 'ubhatobhāgavimutta'. A monk, having striven with wisdom as the lead, attains the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) and reaches the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). At that moment, he is called a 'dhammānusārī' (dhamma-follower). In the six stages starting from the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), he is called a 'kāyasakkhī' (body-witness). At the moment of the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala), he is called an 'ubhatobhāgavimutta' (liberated in both ways). This means he is liberated from two parts (the form-body and the name-body), or liberated twice: by the liberation of suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) through meditative attainments and by the liberation of eradication (samuccheda-vimutti) through the path.

Another person, though striving with wisdom as the lead, is unable to attain the meditative attainments and reaches the path of stream-entry as a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka). At that moment, he is called a 'dhammānusārī'. In the six stages starting from the fruit of stream-entry, he is called a 'diṭṭhippatta' (one attained to vision). At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, he is called a 'paññāvimutta' (liberated by wisdom).

Another person, having striven with faith (saddhā) as the lead, attains the eight meditative attainments and reaches the path of stream-entry. At that moment, he is called a 'saddhānusārī' (faith-follower). In the six stages starting from the fruit of stream-entry, he is called a 'kāyasakkhī'. At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, he is called an 'ubhatobhāgavimutta'.

Another person, though striving with faith as the lead, is unable to attain the meditative attainments and reaches the path of stream-entry as a dry-insight practitioner. At that moment, he is called a 'saddhānusārī'. In the six stages starting from the fruit of stream-entry, he is called a 'saddhāvimutta' (liberated by faith). At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, he is called a 'paññāvimutta'.

## 8. In the eighth sutta, 'visamā' (uneven/unjust) is so called because of the sense of slipping or stumbling. 'Samā' (even/just) is so called because of the sense of not slipping. 'Adhammakammāni' are actions not in accordance with the Dhamma. 'Avinayakammāni' are actions not in accordance with the Vinaya.
50:
In the ninth sutta, 'adhammikā' refers to those who are devoid of Dhamma (not associated with Dhamma). 'Dhammikā' refers to those who are associated with Dhamma.

In the tenth sutta, 'adhikaraṇa' refers to the four types of legal issues, such as disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa). 'Ādiyanti' means they take up (the legal issue). 'Saññāpenti' means they make others know. 'Na ca saññattiṃ upagacchanti' means they do not assemble for the purpose of making others know (or satisfying others). 'Na ca nijjhāpenti' means they do not make others look (or reflect). 'Na ca nijjhattiṃ upagacchanti' means they do not assemble for the purpose of making each other look (or agree). 'Asaññattibalā' means they are called so because their strength lies in not being convinced (or not being satisfied).

'Appaṭinissaggamantino' refers to those who, if they had the thought, "If the legal issue we have taken up is in accordance with Dhamma, we will keep it; if it is not in accordance with Dhamma, we will relinquish it," would be called 'paṭinissaggamantino' (those who consult to relinquish). These people, however, do not consult (or intend) in that way, and thus are called 'appaṭinissaggamantino'. 'Thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissā' means firmly taking to heart through the strength of a view and through misapprehending a view. "Only this is true" means "Only this word of ours is true." "Other [words] are vain" means "The words of others are vain and empty." The bright side (sukkapakkha) is quite clear in its meaning.

## 2. The Second Fifty (Dutiya-paṇṇāsaka)
## (6) 1. Commentary on the Puggalavagga
In the first sutta of the Second Fifty, because [the Buddha] is taken together with the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), it was not preached as "for the compassion of the world" (lokānukampāya). Between these two—the Wheel-turning Monarch and the Buddha—due to the appearance of a Wheel-turning Monarch, people obtain two types of bliss: celestial bliss and human bliss. Due to the appearance of the Buddhas, they obtain all three types of bliss (celestial, human, and Nibbāna).

In the second sutta, 'acchariya-manussā' refers to humans never before encountered in the world, wonderful humans who appear without having existed before.

In the third sutta, 'bahuno janassa anutappā hoti' means it causes remorse (or sorrow) for many people. Between those two, the passing of a Wheel-turning Monarch causes remorse for the deities and humans within one world-system. The parinibbāna of the Tathāgata, however, causes remorse in ten thousand world-systems.

In the fourth sutta, 'thūpārahā' refers to those who are worthy and suitable for a stupa to be built for them. By attending to and honoring the stupa of a Wheel-turning Monarch, people obtain two types of bliss. By attending to and honoring the stupa of the Buddhas, they obtain all three types of bliss.

In the fifth sutta, 'buddhā' refers to those who have realized the Four Noble Truths by their own extraordinary power.

In the sixth sutta, 'phalantiyā' means when making a sound (roaring). 'Na santasantī' means they are not afraid. Between the Arahant and the noble elephant, the Arahant is not afraid because he has eradicated self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi). The noble elephant, however, is not afraid because of the strength of his self-identity view. The same method applies to the seventh and eighth suttas.

In the ninth sutta, 'kiṃpurisā' refers to Kinnaras. 'Mānusiṃ vācaṃ na bhāsantī' means they do not speak the language of humans. To elaborate, it is said that people brought a Kinnara and showed him to King Dhammāsoka. The King said, "Make that Kinnara speak." However, the Kinnara did not wish to speak. A man said, "I will make this Kinnara speak," and went down from the palace, struck two stakes into the ground, and placed a rice pot on them. The pot tilted and fell to both sides. Seeing that, the Kinnara said, "[Why not] another stake..."
52:
"It is not proper to strike," he said only this much. Later, at another time, two Kinnaras were brought and shown. The King said, "Make them speak." Those Kinnaras did not wish to speak. A man said, "I will make them speak," and taking those Kinnaras, he went to the market. In that market, one Kinnara saw ripe mangoes and fish; the other saw wood-apples and tamarind. Between the two, the first Kinnara said, "Humans eat great poison, yet why do they not get skin diseases such as pway, nyin, or tin-teik?" The other said, "These humans consume these wood-apples and tamarind, yet why do they not get leprosy?" Thus, although they were able to speak the language of humans, they did not speak because they saw two benefits.
In the tenth sutta, "appaṭivāno" means not being weary, not drawing back.
In the eleventh sutta, "asantasaṃnivāsaṃ" means living together with the wicked, not the virtuous. "Na vadeyya" means one should not speak by way of admonishing or instructing; the meaning is "let him not speak." "Therampāhaṃ na vadeyyaṃ" means "I too would not speak to an elder monk by way of admonishing or instructing." "Ahitānukampī" means one who desires harm. "No hitānukampī" means one who does not desire welfare. "No'ti naṃ vadeyyaṃ" means saying to that elder, "I will not follow your words." "Viheṭheyyaṃ" means harassing by not following the words. "Passampissa nappaṭikareyyaṃ" means "even if I see or know, I will not follow that elder's words." In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sentences. In the bright side (sukkapakkha), "sādhūti naṃ vadeyyaṃ" means saying to that elder, "You have spoken well, it is very good," while greatly rejoicing in his words.
In the twelfth sutta, "ubhato vacīsaṃsāro" means speech that occurs repeatedly by way of mutual abuse and counter-abuse on both sides. "Diṭṭhipaḷāso" is the conceit (paḷāsa) characterized by grasping at pairs, which arises depending on wrong view. "Cetaso āghāto" means anger. That anger arises while harassing and oppressing the mind. "Appaccayo" is the state of being displeased, meaning dejection (domanassa). "Anabhiraddhi" is anger itself. That anger is called "anabhiraddhi" because it does not accomplish the welfare of oneself or others. "Ajjhattaṃ avūpasantaṃ hotīti sabbampetaṃ" means all these, such as the cycle of speech (vacīsaṃsāra), are not calmed within one's own mind or in the minds of one's followers.
53:
It is not calmed within one's own internal continuity, called one's own mind, nor within one's own followers, called co-residents and pupils. The term "tasmētaṃ" should be analyzed as "tasmiṃ etaṃ." The remaining meaning should be understood in the manner already stated.
## The first, the Puggalavagga, is finished.
## (7) 2. Commentary on the Sukhavagga.
In the first sutta of the second vagga, "gihisukhaṃ" refers to the happiness of laypeople, which has the fulfillment of all sensual pleasures as its root. "Pabbajitasukhaṃ" refers to the happiness of monastics, which has the state of renunciation as its root.
In the second sutta, "kāmasukhaṃ" is the happiness that arises depending on sensual pleasures. In the term "nekkhammasukhaṃ," renunciation is called "nekkhamma"; it refers to the happiness that arises depending on that renunciation.
In the third sutta, "upadhisukhaṃ" is the happiness included within the three realms. "Nirupadhisukhaṃ" is the happiness included within the supramundane states.
In the fourth sutta, "sāsavasukhaṃ" is the happiness included in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), which is a condition for the four taints (āsavas). "Anāsavasukhaṃ" is the happiness that has Nibbāna, the cessation of the round, as its object, which is not a condition for those four taints.
In the fifth sutta, "sāmisaṃ" is the happiness that leads to the round of rebirth, oppressed by defilements. "Nirāmisaṃ" is the happiness that leads to Nibbāna, free from defilements.
In the sixth sutta, "aryasukhaṃ" is the happiness of noble persons (ariyas) who are not worldlings. "Anariyasukhaṃ" is the happiness of worldlings (puthujjanas).
In the seventh sutta, "kāyikaṃ" is the happiness associated with body-consciousness. "Cetasikaṃ" is the happiness occurring at the mind-door. That happiness occurring at the mind-door is taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
In the eighth sutta, "sappītikaṃ" is the happiness associated with the first and second jhānas. "Nippītikaṃ" is the happiness associated with the third and fourth jhānas. Between these two, mundane happiness without rapture (nippītika) is superior to mundane happiness with rapture (sappītika). Likewise, supramundane happiness without rapture is superior to supramundane happiness with rapture. In this way, the state of superiority should be understood without mixing the levels of the realms.
54:
In the ninth sutta, "sātasukha" is the happiness occurring in the three jhānas. "Upekkhāsukha" is the happiness occurring in the fourth jhāna.
In the tenth sutta, "samādhisukha" is the happiness attained in either absorption (appanā) or access (upacāra) concentration. "Asamādhisukha" is the happiness that does not reach either of those two (access or absorption).
In the eleventh sutta, "sappītikārammaṇa" is the happiness that arises for one who reviews the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. In "nippītikārammaṇa," the method is the same. In the twelfth sutta also, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
In the thirteenth sutta, "rūpārammaṇa" is the happiness having the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as its object, or the happiness arising by taking any material form as an object. "Arūpārammaṇa" is the happiness having the immaterial sphere jhānas as its object, or the happiness arising by taking any mental state as an object.
## The second, the Sukhavagga, is finished.
## (8) 3. Commentary on the Sanimittavagga.
78-79. In the first sutta of the third vagga, "sanimittā" means those occurring with a cause. In the second sutta and so on, the method is the same. Indeed, all these terms—nidāna, hetu, saṅkhāra, paccaya, and rūpa—are synonyms meaning "cause" (kāraṇa).
In the seventh sutta, "savedanā" means they arise only when there is associated feeling (vedanā) as a condition, and not when it is absent. In the eighth and ninth suttas also, the method is the same.
In the tenth sutta, "saṅkhatārammaṇā" means they arise only by taking conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma), which are produced by causes, as an object. "No asaṅkhatārammaṇā" means they do not arise by taking Nibbāna, which is unconditioned, as an object. "Na honti" means they are said not to occur at the moment of the Path (magga); they did not occur when the Fruit (phala) was reached. Thus, in these ten instances, the teaching is given up to the attainment of Arahantship.
## The third, the Sanimittavagga, is finished.
55:
## (9) 4. Dhamma-vagga-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, cetovimutti (liberation of mind) refers to the concentration (samādhi) occurring in fruition (phala). Paññāvimutti (liberation by wisdom) refers to the wisdom (paññā) occurring in fruition.

In the second sutta, paggāha (exertion) refers to energy (vīriya). Avikkhepa (non-distraction) refers to one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).

In the third sutta, nāma (name) refers to the four immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandhā). Rūpa (form) refers to the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha). Thus, in this sutta, the insight knowledge that distinguishes the groups of phenomena (dhammakoṭṭhāsaparicchedañāṇa) is taught.

In the fourth sutta, vijjā (knowledge) refers to the knowledge occurring in fruition. Vimutti (liberation) refers to the remaining states associated with that fruition-knowledge.

In the fifth sutta, bhavadiṭṭhi (view of existence) refers to eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). Vibhavadiṭṭhi (view of non-existence) refers to annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The sixth and seventh suttas have clear meanings.

In the eighth sutta, dovacassatā (difficult to admonish) refers to the state of being difficult to speak to. Pāpamittatā (bad friendship) refers to the state of associating with evil friends. The ninth sutta should be understood by the opposite of the aforementioned meaning.

In the tenth sutta, dhātukusalatā (skill in elements) refers to knowing the eighteen elements as elements. Manasikārakusalatā (skill in attention) refers to knowing those same elements by applying the three characteristics such as impermanence (anicca).

In the eleventh sutta, āpattikusalatā (skill in offenses) refers to knowing the five and seven groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha). Āpattivutthānakusalatā (skill in rehabilitation from offenses) refers to knowing the emergence from offenses either through confession (desanā) or through formal act (kammavācā).

## (10) 5. Bāla-vagga-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, "anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahati" (he carries a burden that has not yet arrived) means—the ten duties of an elder (therabhāra), namely: "Sweeping, lighting lamps, providing drinking and washing water and arranging seats, conveying consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi), announcing the season, counting the monks, announcing the exhortation to the nuns, and reciting the Pātimokkha." A junior monk who performs these ten duties of an elder...
56:
...being a junior monk and performing them without being urged by an elder, is said to be carrying a burden that has not yet arrived. "Not carrying a burden that has arrived" means that an elder who does not perform those ten duties himself nor encourages others to do so is said to not carry the burden that has arrived at him. In the second sutta, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

In the third sutta, "perceiving the unallowable as allowable" (akappiye kappiyasaññī) means perceiving unallowable meat such as lion meat as "this meat is allowable." "Perceiving the allowable as unallowable" (kappiye akappiyasaññī) means perceiving allowable meat such as crocodile meat or cat meat as "this meat is unallowable." The fourth sutta should be understood by the same method already mentioned.

In the fifth sutta, "perceiving an offense where there is no offense" (anāpattiyā āpattisaññī) means perceiving actions that do not constitute an offense—such as washing requisites after asking permission, baking a bowl, cutting hair, or entering a village—as "this is an offense." "Perceiving no offense where there is an offense" (āpattiyā anāpattisaññī) means perceiving actions that do constitute an offense because they were done without asking permission as "this is not an offense." In the sixth sutta, the meaning should be understood by the same method already mentioned. The seventh and subsequent suttas have clear meanings.

In the eleventh sutta, "āsava" (taints) refers to defilements (kilesa). "Na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ" (should not be worried about) means that although not managing or not investigating the use of Sangha property is something one should not be worried about, one becomes worried about it. "Kukkuccāyitabbaṃ" (should be worried about) means that although managing or investigating that same Sangha property is something one should be worried about, one does not become worried about it. The twelfth and subsequent suttas should be understood by the same method already mentioned below.

## 3. Tatiya-paṇṇāsaka
In the first sutta of the Third Fifty (Tatiya-paṇṇāsaka), "āsā" refers to craving (taṇhā). "Duppajahā" refers to that which is hard to abandon or hard to remove. Because craving for gain (lābhāsā) is hard to abandon, beings serve kings for ten, twenty, or sixty years, thinking, "We shall receive today, we shall receive tomorrow." They engage in farming and so on, rush into battlefields where two armies are arrayed, enter goat-paths and spike-paths (ajapatha, saṅkupatha), and enter the great ocean by boat. Because craving for life (jīvitāsā) is hard to abandon, even when the time of death arrives, they think of themselves as living for a hundred years. Even when that dying person sees kamma and the signs of kamma (kamma-nimitta), and is told by compassionate relatives, "Give alms, perform worship," he does not listen to anyone's words due to the craving that "I shall not die, I shall live."

In the second sutta, "pubbakārī" refers to one who does a favor first. "Kataññūkatavedī" refers to one who knows the favor done by that person and later reciprocates. Among those two, the pubbakārī thinks, "I shall give a loan," while the one who reciprocates later thinks, "I shall settle the debt."

In the third sutta, "titto ca tappetā ca" (satisfied and satisfying) means that a Paccekabuddha and an Arahant disciple of the Buddha are called "titta" (satisfied). The Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, is called both "titta" (satisfied) and "tappetā" (satisfying others).

In the fourth sutta, "duttappayā" means they are hard to satisfy by a donor; it is not easy to satisfy them. "Nikkhipati" means storing away and not consuming. "Vissajjeti" means giving to others.

In the fifth sutta, "na vissajjeti" means not giving all of one's wealth to others, but taking only enough for one's own subsistence and giving the remainder.

In the sixth sutta, "subhanimitta" refers to a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa).
58:
In the seventh sutta, paṭighanimitta (the sign of repulsion) means an undesirable object (aniṭṭhanimitta).

In the eighth sutta, parato ca ghoso (a voice from another) means hearing the false Dhamma (assaddhammasavana) from another.

In the ninth sutta, parato ca ghoso (a voice from another) means hearing the true Dhamma (saddhammasavana) from another. The meaning of the remaining words in all these suttas is clear.

## (12) 2. Commentary on the Āyācana-vagga

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "one who aspires well should aspire thus" means a faithful monk should stand up and aspire: "Just as the Elder Sāriputta is in wisdom, may I also be like him. Just as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is in psychic power, may I also be like him." Aspiring, admiring, and wishing in this way is called right aspiration (sammā-patthanā) because it is an aspiration for existing qualities. If one aspires to qualities beyond this, it would be wrong aspiration (micchā-patthanā). This is because it is an aspiration for qualities that do not exist.

For what reason? Monks, these qualities of Sāriputta and Moggallāna are like a scale; they are like a measure. Just as a scale is needed for one weighing gold or silver, and a measure (bushel) is needed for one measuring grain—where the scale is the standard for weighing and the measure is the standard for measuring—likewise, among my disciple monks, Sāriputta and Moggallāna are like a scale and a measure. Based on these elders, one can weigh or measure oneself, thinking, "May I be of such measure in terms of knowledge or psychic power." It cannot be otherwise.

The same method applies to the second sutta and those following. However, there is this distinction: among the bhikkhunīs, Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Khemā is foremost in wisdom and Uppalavaṇṇā is foremost in psychic power. Therefore, "In wisdom...
59:
...or in psychic power, may I be like her," a faithful laywoman should aspire. Similarly, Citta the householder is foremost in wisdom, and Prince Hatthaka is foremost in having great psychic power. Therefore, "In wisdom or in psychic power, may I be like these (Citta and Hatthaka)," a faithful layman should aspire. Khujjuttarā is foremost in having great wisdom, and Nandamātā is foremost in having great psychic power. Therefore, "In wisdom or in psychic power, may I be like these (Khujjuttarā and Nandamātā)," a faithful laywoman should aspire.

In the fifth sutta, "khataṃ" (uprooted) means a person who is uprooted because their virtues are uprooted. "Upahataṃ" (ruined) means a person who is ruined because their virtues are ruined; it means one whose virtues are cut off or whose virtues have vanished. "Attānaṃ pariharati" (carries oneself) means one looks after or guards one's virtue-less self. "Sāvajjo" means blameworthy. "Sānuvajjo" means with reproach. "Pasavati" means obtains. "Ananuvicca" means without knowing, without judging. "Apariyogāhetvā" means without penetrating with wisdom. "Avaṇṇārahassa" (of one deserving dispraise) refers to a heretic or a disciple of a heretic who practices wrongly and is worthy of dispraise. "Vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati" (speaks praise) means speaking of virtues, saying, "This person practices well, practices rightly." "Vaṇṇārahassa" (of one deserving praise) refers to one of the persons such as the Buddha who practices rightly. "Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati" (speaks dispraise) means speaking of lack of virtue, saying, "This person practices badly, practices wrongly." "Speaks dispraise of one deserving dispraise" means a certain person in this world speaks of the lack of virtue of heretics or their disciples who practice badly or wrongly, saying, "They practice badly for such reasons; they practice wrongly for such reasons." "Speaks praise of one deserving praise" means speaking of the virtues of the Buddhas or their disciples who practice well and rightly, saying, "They practice well for such reasons; they practice rightly for such reasons."

In the sixth sutta, "appasādanīye ṭhāne" means in a matter that does not inspire faith. "Pasādaṃ upadaṃseti" (shows faith) means causing faith to arise in a bad or wrong practice, saying, "This practice is a good practice, a right practice." "Pasādanīye ṭhāne appasādaṃ" means causing a lack of faith to arise in a good or right practice, saying, "This practice is a bad practice, a wrong practice." The rest of the words in this sutta are clear.

In the seventh sutta, "dvīsu" means in two places or for two reasons. "Micchāpaṭipajjamāno" means one who practices wrongly. "Mātari ca pitari ca" means towards the mother, like Mittavindaka, and towards the father, like King Ajātasattu (practicing wrongly). The "white side" (virtuous side) should be understood by the same method already mentioned.

In the eighth sutta, "tathāgate ca tathāgata-sāvake ca" means towards the Tathāgata, like Devadatta, and towards the Tathāgata's disciple, like Kokālika (practicing wrongly).
60:
In the wholesome side (sukkapakkha), it should be understood that the Elder Ānanda has devotion in the Blessed One, and the merchant's son Nanda Gopālaka has devotion in the disciples of the Blessed One.

In the ninth sutta, 'sacittavodāna' means the purification of one's own mind, and it is a name for the eight attainments. 'Does not cling to anything in the world' means not grasping or misinterpreting even a single phenomenon among the phenomena such as form (rūpa) in the world. Thus, in this sutta, the second quality called non-clinging (anupādāna) arises. The tenth and eleventh suttas have meanings that are already clear.
