## (13) 3. Dānavaggavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Chapter on Giving)

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'dānāni' means gifts by way of giving; it is a name for the objects to be given (deyyadhamma). Alternatively, volition (cetanā) together with the object is called giving (dāna); it is a name for the relinquishing of one's possessions (sampattiparicccāga). 'Āmisadāna' (material gift) refers to the four requisites by way of giving. 'Dhammadāna' (gift of Dhamma) means, in this Dispensation, some person teaches and gives the practice leading to the Deathless Nibbāna; this is called the gift of Dhamma.

In the second sutta, just as the four requisites are called 'yāga' (sacrifice/offering) by way of offering, the Dhamma should also be known as 'yāga' by way of offering.

In the third sutta, the relinquishing of material things is called 'āmisacāga'; the relinquishing (teaching) of Dhamma is called 'dhammacāga'. In the fourth sutta, there is a distinction only in the prefix (upasagga) (i.e., pari-).

In the fifth sutta, the enjoyment of the four requisites is called 'āmisabhoga'; the enjoyment of Dhamma is called 'dhammabhoga'. In the sixth sutta, there is a distinction only in the prefix (i.e., saṃ-).

In the seventh sutta, the distribution of the four requisites is called 'āmisasaṃvibhāga'; the distribution of Dhamma is called 'dhammasaṃvibhāga'.

In the eighth sutta, favoring with the four requisites is called 'āmisasaṅgaha'; favoring with Dhamma is called 'dhammasaṅgaha'.
61:
In the ninth sutta, supporting with the four requisites is called āmisānuggaha; supporting with Dhamma is called dhammānuggaha.

In the tenth sutta, compassion with the four requisites is called āmisānukampā; compassion with Dhamma is called dhammānukampā.

## The Chapter on Giving is the third chapter.

## (14) 4. Santhāravaggavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Chapter on Greeting)

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, greeting by way of covering the gap between oneself and others with the four requisites is called āmisasanthāra; greeting with Dhamma is called dhammasanthāra. In the second sutta, only the prefix (upasagga) paṭi- is distinct.

In the third sutta, seeking the aforementioned various material things is called āmisesanā; seeking Dhamma is called dhammesanā. In the fourth sutta, only the prefix pari- is distinct.

In the fifth sutta, because it reaches the summit, searching for material things is called āmisapariyeṭṭhi; because it reaches the summit, searching for Dhamma is called dhammapariyeṭṭhi.

In the sixth sutta, honoring with material things is called āmisapūjā; honoring with Dhamma is called dhammapūjā.

In the seventh sutta, "ātitheyyāni" refers to gifts given to guests. There is also a reading "atitheyyāni".

In the eighth sutta, material things are called āmisiddhi by way of fulfillment and complete fulfillment; Dhamma is also called dhammiddhi by way of fulfillment and complete fulfillment.

In the ninth sutta, growth through material things is called āmisavuḍḍhi; growth through Dhamma is called dhammavuḍḍhi.

In the tenth sutta, because of the sense of producing delight, material things are called āmisaratana; Dhamma is called dhammaratana.
62:
In the eleventh sutta, accumulating and increasing material things such as alms-food and robes is called āmisasannicaya. Accumulating and increasing Dhamma is called dhammasannicaya.

In the twelfth sutta, the state of abundance of material things is called āmisavepulla. The state of abundance of Dhamma is called dhammavepulla.

## The Chapter on Greeting, the fourth, is finished.

## (15) 5. Samāpattivaggavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Chapter on Attainments)

In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, samāpattikusalatā (skill in attainments) is the state of being skilled in entering attainments after investigating the suitability of food (āhārasappāya) and the suitability of climate (utusappāya). Samāpattivutthānakusalatā (skill in emerging from attainments) is the state of being skilled in emerging, being one who is capable of emerging when the time is up as determined.

In the second sutta, ajjava is the state of being upright. Maddava is the state of being gentle.

In the third sutta, khanti is patience (adhivāsanakhanti). Soracca is the state of being a person who delights in beautiful conduct of body and speech by way of having good virtue.

In the fourth sutta, sākhalyam is the state of being joyful by way of gentle speech. Paṭisanthāra is greeting (hospitality) either with material things or with Dhamma.

In the fifth sutta, avihiṃsā is the quality that occurs in the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā). Soceyya is the state of being pure by way of virtue (sīla). The sixth and seventh suttas have meanings that are already clear.

In the eighth sutta, paṭisaṅkhānabala is the power of reflection.

In the ninth sutta, mindfulness itself is called satibala (power of mindfulness) due to non-shaking caused by forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca). Concentration itself is called samādhibala (power of concentration) due to non-shaking caused by restlessness (uddhacca).

In the tenth sutta, samatha is one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). Vipassanā is the knowledge that comprehends conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
63:
In the eleventh sutta, 'failure in virtue' (sīlavipatti) means immorality (dussīlya). 'Failure in view' (diṭṭhivipatti) means wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

In the twelfth sutta, 'attainment in virtue' (sīlasampadā) means the state of having perfected virtue. 'Attainment in view' (diṭṭhisampadā) means the state of having right view. By the term 'attainment in view', all five types of right view are included: right view of ownership of action (kammassakata-sammādiṭṭhi), right view of meditative absorption (jhāna-sammādiṭṭhi), right view of insight (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi), right view of the path (magga-sammādiṭṭhi), and right view of the fruition (phala-sammādiṭṭhi).

In the thirteenth sutta, 'purification of virtue' (sīlavisuddhi) means virtue that leads to purification. 'Purification of view' (diṭṭhivisuddhi) means the right view associated with the four paths that leads to purification, or otherwise, the five types of right view.

In the fourteenth sutta, 'purification of view' (diṭṭhivisuddhi) means only the right view that leads to purification. 'Striving in accordance with the view' (yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ) means the effort associated with the lower paths. Because that effort is in accordance with that view, it is called 'striving in accordance with the view'.

In the fifteenth sutta, 'lack of contentment with wholesome states' means the state of not being content with wholesome states other than the path of Arahantship.

In the sixteenth sutta, 'forgetfulness' (muṭṭhassacca) means the state of lost mindfulness. 'Lack of clear comprehension' (asampajañña) means the state of not knowing (ignorance).

In the seventeenth sutta, the state characterized by not wobbling (non-forgetfulness) is mindfulness (sati). The state characterized by clear understanding is clear comprehension (sampajañña).

## 1. Kodhapeyyālaṃ
In the chapters following this Third Fifty, such as the Chapter on Anger (Kodhavagga), the characteristic of being furious is anger (kodha). The characteristic of binding enmity is hostility (upanāha). The characteristic of obliterating the recognition of past favors is denigration (makkha). The characteristic of rivalry (assuming equality) is domineering (palāsa). The characteristic of envying the prosperity of others is envy (issā). The state of the five types of stinginess, such as stinginess regarding dwellings, is stinginess (macchariya). All such stinginess has the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity. The characteristic of hiding the faults one has committed is deceit (māyā). The characteristic of being crooked and treacherous is fraud (sāṭheyya). The manner of not being ashamed of misconduct is shamelessness (ahirika). The manner of not fearing the blame of others is fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). Non-anger (akkodha) and so forth should be understood by way of being the opposites of anger and so forth.

'For a monk in higher training' (sekkhassa bhikkhuno) means that for the seven types of persons in higher training (sekha), these states lead to the decline from higher and higher qualities; however, for a worldling (puthujjana), it should be understood that they lead to decline from the very beginning. 'For non-decline' (aparihānāya) means for the purpose of not declining from higher and higher qualities.

'As if carried and dropped' (yathābhataṃ nikkhibto) means it should be understood as being established in hell just as if one were carried and dropped there.

'A certain person' (ekacco) means that a person who possesses these states such as anger is called 'a certain person'.

## The Repetitive Series on Anger (Kodhapeyyālaṃ) is finished.

## 3. Vinayapeyyālaṃ

Monks, 'dependent on two reasons' (dveme bhikkhuve atthavase paṭicca) means, monks, relying on two benefits and intending two causes. 'The training rule was laid down' (sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ) means the body of training was established. 'For the excellence of the Saṅgha' (saṅghasuṭṭhutāya) means for the good state of the Saṅgha, with the meaning of accepting and acknowledging by saying, 'It is well, Bhante'. 'For the comfort of the Saṅgha' (saṅghaphāsutāya) means for the purpose of the Saṅgha living in comfort. 'For the ill-behaved' (dummaṅkūnaṃ) refers to those who are immoral. 'For the well-behaved' (pesalānaṃ) refers to those who have dear virtue.

'For the taints in the present life' (diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ) refers to the dangers known as the suffering of execution, imprisonment, etc., which are to be received in this very existence due to transgressions. 'For the restraint' (saṃvarāya) means for the purpose of closing off those dangers. 'For the future life' (samparāyikānaṃ) refers to the taints that will arise in the future life known as the suffering of the lower realms of such nature. 'For the warding off' (paṭighātāya) means for the purpose of prohibiting those dangers. 'For enmities' (verānaṃ) refers to both unwholesome enmities and personal enmities. 'For faults' (vajjānaṃ) means for defects. Alternatively, those very states of suffering are intended here as 'faults' (vajja) because they should be avoided. 'For fears' (bhayānaṃ) refers to both the fears of mental terror and those very states of suffering which are the causes of fear. 'For unwholesome states' (akusalānaṃ) refers to the states of suffering called unwholesome because they are difficult to endure.

'Out of compassion for the laity' (gihīnaṃ anukampāya) means that a training rule laid down when laypeople criticize is said to be laid down out of compassion for the laity. 'For the breaking up of the factions of those with evil desires' (pāpicchānaṃ pakkhupacchedāya) means that monks with evil desires might split the Saṅgha by relying on a faction; it is for the purpose of cutting off their faction so that this does not happen. 'For the inspiring of those not yet inspired' (appasannānaṃ pasādāya) means for the purpose of generating inspiration in wise people who were not previously inspired, upon seeing the perfection of the laying down of training rules. 'For the increase of those already inspired' (pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya) means for the state of increasing inspiration in those who are already inspired. 'For the endurance of the True Dhamma' (saddhammaṭṭhitiyā) means for the purpose of the long endurance of the True Dhamma. 'For the support of the Vinaya' (vinayānuggahāya) means for the purpose of supporting the fivefold Vinaya.

202-230. 'The Pātimokkha was laid down' (pātimokkhaṃ paññattaṃ) means the two kinds of Pātimokkha—the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha—were laid down. 'The recitation of the Pātimokkha' (pātimokkhuddeso) means the nine recitations of the Pātimokkha—five for monks and four for nuns—were laid down. 'The suspension of the Pātimokkha' (pātimokkhaṭṭhapanaṃ) means the suspension of the Uposatha. 'The invitation was laid down' (pavāraṇā paññatta) means the two kinds of invitation—that of the fourteenth and that of the fifteenth—were laid down. 'The suspension of the invitation was laid down' (pavāraṇāṭṭhapanaṃ paññattaṃ) means the laying down of the suspension of the invitation when the invitation motion is being made for a monk who has an offense.

The Act of Censure (tajjaniya-kamma) was prescribed for the monks named Paṇḍukalohitaka, who were in the habit of stabbing and attacking other monks with the weapons of their tongues. The Act of Subordination (nissaya-kamma) was prescribed for the monk named Seyyasaka, who was foolish and incompetent. The Act of Banishment (pabbājaniya-kamma) was prescribed on account of the monks named Assaji and Punabbasukā, who were corrupters of families. The Act of Reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya-kamma) was prescribed for the Elder Sudhamma, who used to abuse laypeople. The Act of Suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) was prescribed for such cases as the refusal to see an offense. The granting of probation (parivāsa) was prescribed for a monk who has committed a grave offense (garuka-āpatti) and concealed it. Sending back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana) was prescribed for a monk who commits an intervening offense while undergoing probation. The granting of penance (mānatta) was prescribed for that offense, whether it was concealed or not. Rehabilitation (abbhāna) was prescribed for a monk who has completed his penance. Reinstatement (osāraṇီya) was prescribed for a monk who conducts himself properly. The Act of Removal (nissāraṇīya-kamma) was prescribed for such cases as improper conduct.

Eight types of ordination (upasampadā) were prescribed: ordination by the 'Come, monk' formula (ehibhikkhu-upasampadā), ordination by going for the three refuges (saraṇagamana-upasampadā), ordination by accepting exhortation (ovāda-upasampadā), ordination by answering questions (pañhābyākaraṇa-upasampadā), ordination by a motion and three resolutions (ñatticatuttha-kamma-upasampadā), ordination by accepting the heavy rules (garudhamma-upasampadā), ordination by both Saṅghas (ubhatosaṅghe-upasampadā), and ordination by a messenger (dūtena-upasampadā). The motion (ñatti-kamma) was prescribed in such a way that it goes to nine instances. The motion and one resolution (ñattidutiya-kamma) was prescribed in such a way that it goes to seven instances. The motion and three resolutions (ñatticatuttha-kamma) was prescribed in such a way that it goes to seven instances. The primary rule (paṭhamapaññatti) of the first Pārājika and others was prescribed before the training rule had been laid down. The supplementary rule (anupaññatti) of those same first Pārājika and others was prescribed following the primary rule after it had been laid down. The verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) was prescribed by virtue of the fourfold presence: the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, the presence of the Saṅgha, and the presence of the individuals. The verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) was prescribed for an Arahant who has attained abundance of mindfulness, so that he may not be accused. The verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya) was prescribed for a monk who is insane. The verdict based on admission (paṭiññātakaraṇa) was prescribed so that a monk who is accused without admitting it may not be dealt with by the offense. The verdict by majority (yebhuyyasikā) was prescribed for the purpose of settling a legal issue by taking the view of the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma. The verdict of further misconduct (tassapāpiyasikā) was prescribed for the purpose of punishing a person of many evil qualities. The verdict of covering over as with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-kamma) was prescribed for the purpose of settling the remaining offenses—excluding gross offenses (thullavajja) and those connected with laypeople—of monks who, on account of quarreling and so forth, have committed many unseemly acts and fallen into offenses.

## 4. Rāgapeyyāla

'Monks, for the direct knowledge of lust' means for the purpose of knowing with direct knowledge and for the purpose of realizing the lust that arises in the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'For the full understanding' means for the purpose of fully understanding. 'For the complete destruction' means for the purpose of reaching complete destruction. 'For the abandoning' means for the purpose of abandoning. 'For the ending and vanishing' means for the purpose of reaching ending and vanishing. 'For dispassion' means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate. 'For cessation' means for the purpose of cessation. 'For relinquishment' means for the purpose of relinquishing. 'For giving up' means for the purpose of giving up once more.

232-246. 'Obstinacy' (thambha) refers to the state of being stubborn by the power of anger and conceit. 'Impetuosity' (sārabha) refers to impetuosity characterized by excessive action. 'Conceit' (māna) refers to the ninefold conceit. 'Arrogance' (atimāna) refers to the conceit of thinking highly of oneself by overestimating. 'Pride' (mada) refers to pride in the form of intoxication. 'Negligence' (pamāda) refers to the loss of mindfulness and the letting loose of the mind in the five cords of sensual pleasure. In all the remaining discourses, the meaning is clear.

## 1. Bālavagga
## 1. Explanation of the Bhaya Sutta

In the first sutta of the Tikanipāta, among the words beginning with 'bhayāni', 'bhaya' (fear) refers to mental terror. 'Upaddava' (calamity) refers to the state of lacking one-pointedness (distraction). 'Upasagga' (adversity) refers to the state of being afflicted, the state of clinging to various objects.

The distinction between these—fear, calamity, and adversity—should be understood as follows: Robbers dwelling in uneven places such as mountains send a message to the inhabitants of a district, saying, "We will attack and loot your village on such-and-such a day." From the moment they hear this news, the inhabitants of that district fall into fear and terror. This is called mental terror (bhaya).

Thinking, "Those robbers might get angry and cause us harm," they take their jewelry and wealth, and together with people and livestock, enter the forest and sleep on the ground in various places. They suffer from the bites of gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, and when entering thickets, they tread on stumps and thorns. The distracted state of those people as they wander about in this manner is called the state of lacking one-pointedness (upaddava).

Then, when the robbers do not arrive on the appointed day, they say, "It must have been a false report; let us return to the village," and they re-enter the village with their belongings. Thereupon, the robbers, knowing that they have returned, surround the village, set fire to the gates, kill the people, loot all their wealth, and depart. Among them, those who remain unkilled extinguish the fire and sit in various places such as the shadows of granaries or walls, grieving over their lost wealth. This is called the state of being afflicted or clinging (upasagga).

'Naḷāgārā' refers to houses thatched and covered with reeds. In these houses, the remaining structural components apart from the roof are made of wood. The same method applies to grass-thatched houses (tiṇāgāra). 'Kūṭāgārāni' refers to houses with peaked roofs (pinnacled houses). 'Ullittāvalittāni' refers to houses plastered both inside and out. 'Nivātāni' refers to houses where the entry of wind is prevented. 'Phusitaggaḷāni' refers to those where skilled carpenters...
70:
...because they are well-made, there are door-leaves that are well-fitted to the door-frame. 'Pihitavātapānāni' means being equipped with windows. By these two words, it does not mean that the door-leaves and windows are always kept closed, but rather it speaks of their excellence. Whenever desired, those doors can be closed and opened.

'Bālato uppajjanti' means that dangers arise only because of the fool. Indeed, a foolish person, lacking wisdom, desiring kingship, the status of viceroy, or some other great position, gathers a few rogues (sons of widows) like himself, makes them carry heavy weapons, and says, "Come, I will make you rulers." Basing himself in mountains and forests, he attacks remote villages to make his status as a rebel known, and gradually attacks towns and districts. People abandon their homes and flee, seeking a safe place. Monks and nuns who live depending on those people also abandon their respective dwellings and depart. Wherever they go, alms-food and lodgings are difficult to obtain. In this way, fear comes to the four assemblies. Among the monastics as well, two foolish monks start a dispute with each other and begin making accusations. Thus, a great quarrel arises, like that of the residents of Kosambī. Fear indeed comes to the four assemblies. In this way, whatever fears arise, they all arise because of the fool; thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching according to the sequence of the discourse.

## 2. Explanation of the Lakkhaṇa Sutta

In the second sutta, the action (kamma) occurring in the body-door and so on is called 'kammalakkhaṇa' because it is the cause for recognition (characteristic). 'Apadānasobhanī paññā' means that wisdom is beautified by the conduct (effort) that knows faults. The meaning is that fools and wise persons become manifest only through their own behavior and conduct.

Indeed, the path taken by a fool is like the path of a fire that goes along burning trees, bushes, villages, and towns; only the burnt place, full of charcoal and ash, is evident. The path taken by a wise person is like the path of a great rain cloud raining over the four islands, filling the hollows and pools and bringing about the abundance of various crops. Just as in the path of that rain, full reservoirs of water and various fruits and crops are evident in those various places, so too, in the path taken by a wise person, only successes (sampatti) are evident, not failures (vipatti). The remaining words have clear meanings.
71:
## 3. Cintīsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "bālalakkhaṇāni" means the signs of a fool, as they are recognized or known by these (such as thinking bad thoughts). These very things are called "bālanimittāni" because they are the causes for recognizing that fool. "Bālāpadānāni" refers to the behaviors (conduct) of a fool. "Duccintitacintī" means one who, when thinking, thinks only ill-thought thoughts by way of covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view. "Dubbhāsitabhāsī" means one who, when speaking, speaks only ill-spoken words such as falsehood and so on. "Dukkaṭakammakārī" means one who, when acting, performs only ill-done deeds by way of killing and so on. The words "paṇḍitalakkhaṇāni" and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In this context (of the signs of a wise person), terms such as "sucintitacintī" should be applied by way of mental good conduct and so on.

## 4. Accayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "accayaṃ accayato na passati" means not seeing one's own fault as a fault. "Accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ nappaṭikaroti" means that even though one knows "I have transgressed," one does not act according to the Dhamma to remedy that fault, does not perform the required penalty, does not confess the fault, and does not ask for forgiveness. "Accayaṃ desentassa yathādhammaṃ nappaṭiggaṇhāti" means not forgiving another who, knowing "I have transgressed," performs the required penalty and asks for forgiveness. The bright side (the wise person's side) should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

## 5. Ayonisosutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "ayoniso pañhaṃ kattā hoti" means one who asks a question unwisely. For instance, when asked, "Udāyī, how many bases of mindfulness (anussatiṭṭhāna) are there?", one thinks, "Past lives (pubbenivāsa) must be a base of mindfulness," and like the Elder Lāḷudāyī, by thinking inappropriately, makes a non-question into a question. "Ayoniso pañhaṃ vissajjetā hoti" means that when answering such a thought-out question, one answers unwisely like that same Elder, saying, "Here, venerable sir, a monk recollects many kinds of past lives, that is, one birth..." and so on, speaking of a non-question as a question. In the phrase "parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi," the word (pada) itself is called "padabyañjana" because it clarifies the meaning (byañjana). When it is spoken by completing the syllables and without diminishing the ten types of articulation (byañjanabuddhi)...
72:
...it is called "parimaṇḍala" (well-rounded/complete). The meaning is "with such words and syllables." "Siliṭṭhehi" means smooth/polished due to the smoothness of the words. "Upagatehi" means words that have approached both the meaning and the cause. "Nābbhanumoditā" means not rejoicing or delighting in another's question that has been answered by fulfilling all reasons in a proper manner, just as the Elder Lāḷudāyī did regarding the question of the Elder Sāriputta.

As it was said: "Friend Sāriputta, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person who has surpassed the company of devas who subsist on solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) and has been reborn in a certain mind-made body (the formless realm) could enter into or emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha); there is no such possibility."

In the words "yoniso pañhaṃ kattā" and so forth, it refers to one who thinks about a question wisely and answers wisely, like the Elder Ānanda. Indeed, when the Elder was asked, "Ānanda, how many bases of mindfulness are there?", he thought wisely, "This will be the question," and wishing to answer wisely, he said: "Here, venerable sir, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Venerable sir, this base of mindfulness, when thus developed and thus cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life." "Abbhanumoditā hoti" means one who rejoices wisely like the Tathāgata. Indeed, when the question was answered by the Elder Ānanda, the Tathāgata said: "Good, good, Ānanda! In that case, Ānanda, you should also remember this sixth base of mindfulness. Here, Ānanda, a monk goes forward mindfully and returns mindfully," and so on. The suttas starting from the sixth have clear meanings.

## 9. Khatasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, the bright side (sukkapakkha) is defined in the preceding part by the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha), and in the latter part, it is obtained up to the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). In the phrase "bahuñca puññaṃ pasavati" (generates much merit), merit that is a mixture of mundane and supramundane is spoken of.

## 10. Malasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the state of being immoral is "dussīlya" (immorality). Immorality itself is a stain, thus "dussīlyamala" (the stain of immorality). In what sense is it a stain? It is a stain in the sense of burning (anudahana), in the sense of having a foul odor (duggandha), and in the sense of causing defilement (kiliṭṭhakaraṇa). That state of immorality is a stain also in the sense of burning because it burns one in woeful states such as hell. (A person endowed with that stain of immorality is loathsome to parents, in the midst of the Saṅgha, and in places where the Bodhi tree and pagodas stand. That person...)
73:
A person endowed with the impurity consisting of the state of being immoral is loathsome in the presence of parents, in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and in the precincts of Bodhi trees and stupas. In all directions, the scent of dispraise—the report that 'such a person has committed such an evil deed'—spreads. Thus, it is called a stain (mala) in the sense of having a foul odor. A person endowed with that stain experiences only distress wherever they go. Their bodily actions and so forth are impure and lack radiance. Thus, it is called a stain in the sense of causing defilement. Furthermore, that stain causes the prosperity of devas and humans, as well as the attainment of Nibbāna, to wither. Thus, it should be understood as a stain in the sense of causing withering. The same method applies to the stain of envy (issā-mala) and the stain of stinginess (macchera-mala).

## 2. The Chapter of the Wheelwright (Rathakāravagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Ñāta Sutta

In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'ñāta' means known or famous. 'Ananulomika' means unsuitable because it does not conform to the Teaching; it refers to that which is not in conformity. 'Kāyakamma' (bodily action) refers to bodily misconduct such as killing living beings. Alternatively, such bodily misconduct is gross; one is unable to establish others in such bodily actions. He establishes or makes them take up such bodily actions as, 'It is proper to worship the directions' or 'It is proper to make offerings to spirits (bhūtabali).' Regarding verbal actions (vacīkamma), lying and so forth are gross. He establishes others in such verbal actions as saying, 'It is proper to speak such a deceptive lie as "I do not have it" when one does not wish to give one's own property to another.' Regarding mental actions (manokamma), covetousness and so forth are gross. However, one who speaks by distorting the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is said to establish others in dhammas that are not in conformity, like the Elder who resided at Dakkhiṇavihāra.

To elaborate, a minister's son who was a supporter approached that Elder and asked, 'When one wishes to develop loving-kindness, on what kind of person should one first develop it?' The Elder, without explaining the suitable (sabhāga) and unsuitable (visabhāga) objects, said, 'One should develop it towards a beloved person.' That man's wife was beloved and pleasing to his heart. While he was developing loving-kindness by taking his wife as the object, he fell into madness. How then does such a person who establishes others in what is not in conformity with the Teaching practice for the harm of many? To explain, the co-residents, pupils, and supporters of such a person, starting from the guardian deities and including the deities who are friends of those deities, up to...
74:
...the Brahma-world, and the remaining deities, thinking, 'This bhikkhu would not act without knowing,' follow and perform exactly what that bhikkhu does. In this way, he practices for the harm of many.

On the bright side (sukkapakkha), bodily and verbal actions should be understood by way of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth. One who teaches the meditation subject without distortion is said to establish others in dhammas that are in conformity with the Teaching, like the Elder Tissa, a knower of the four Nikāyas, who resided at Koḷitavihāra. It is said that his elder brother, Nandābhaya Thera, while residing at Potaliyavihāra, fell ill and sent for his younger brother, saying, 'Friend, please teach me a meditation subject that will make me feel at ease.' The younger brother asked, 'Venerable sir, what is the use of other meditation subjects? It is proper to contemplate material food (kabaḷīkārāhāra).' When asked, 'Friend, what is the benefit of this material food?', he replied, 'Venerable sir, material food is derived matter (upādārūpa). When one derived matter is seen, the other twenty-three types of derived matter become evident.' The Elder said, 'Friend, this much is enough,' and after sending his younger brother back, he contemplated material food, noted the derived matter, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Then, before the younger brother Tissa Thera had even left the monastery grounds, he called him back and informed him of the special attainment he had reached, saying, 'Friend, you have become a great refuge for me.' Regarding 'bahujanahitāya' (for the welfare of many), the co-residents and others of such a person, thinking, 'This bhikkhu would not act without knowing,' follow and perform exactly what that bhikkhu does. Therefore, he is said to practice for the welfare and benefit of many.

## 2. Commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta

In the second sutta, 'khattiyassa' refers to one who is a king by birth. 'Muddhāvasitta' refers to one who has been consecrated on the head through the royal anointing ceremony. 'Sāraṇīyāni bhavanti' means they are things to be remembered and not to be forgotten. 'Jāta' means born or arisen. Regarding 'yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ' (to be remembered as long as life lasts), although one cannot know it by oneself during childhood, later on, when told by parents, relatives, or servants, 'You were born in such a district, in such a city, on such a day, under such a constellation,' one remembers it from that time onwards as long as life lasts and does not forget it. Therefore, it is said, 'It is to be remembered as long as life lasts.'
75:
Monks, this second place of consecration causes great joy to the king; therefore, he should remember it as long as he lives. The same applies to the place of victory in battle. Here, *saṅgāma* means war. *Abhivijitvā* means having conquered and crushed the enemy. *Tam-eva saṅgāmasīsaṃ* refers to that very battlefield. *Ajjhāvasati* means dwelling while having overcome.

Now, although there is no duty for the King, the Fully Enlightened One, regarding his birthplace and so on, this matter is brought forward to show three types of persons in this Dispensation who are similar to that king. Therefore, wishing to show those persons, he said, "In the same way, monks," and so forth. In that text, "he has gone forth into homelessness" (*anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti*), it should be understood that the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is also dependent on the going forth. "It is memorable" (*sāraṇīyaṃ hoti*) means: "I went forth in such a country, in such a district, in such a monastery, in such a pavilion, in such a day-quarters, in such a cloister, at the foot of such a tree." Thus, it should be remembered as long as one lives; it should not be forgotten.

"This is suffering" means this much is the truth of suffering; there is no truth of suffering beyond these phenomena of the three planes. "This is the origin of suffering" means this much is the origin of suffering, which is the truth of the origin; there is no truth of the origin beyond this craving. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. Thus, in this sutta, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) is taught through the Four Truths. The preliminary work of *kasiṇa* and insight knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) are dependent on the path. "It is memorable" (*sāraṇīyaṃ hoti*) means: "I became a stream-enterer in such a country... at the foot of such a tree." It is memorable as long as one lives and should not be forgotten.

"Through the destruction of the taints" means by the ending of the taints. "Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) means the concentration of the fruit (*phalasamādhi*). "Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) means the wisdom of the fruit (*phalapaññā*). "Having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge" means having personally witnessed it with distinguished wisdom. "Entering upon it, he dwells" means having attained it, he dwells. "Memorable" means: "I attained arahantship in such a country... at the foot of such a tree." The place of one's attainment of arahantship is memorable as long as one lives and should not be forgotten. Thus, he concluded the teaching according to the sequence.

## 3. Commentary on the Āsaṃsasutta

In the third sutta, *santo* means they exist, they are found. *Saṃvijjamānā* is a synonym for that same word. *Lokasmiṃ* means in the world of beings. *Nirāso* means one without desire, one without longing.
76:
'Āsaṃso' means one who longs or one who desires. 'Vigatāso' means one whose longing has departed. 'Caṇḍālakule' means in a family of outcasts (caṇḍālas). 'Venakule' means in a family of bamboo-weavers. 'Nesādakule' means in a family of hunters who kill animals. 'Rathakārakule' means in a family of leather-workers. 'Pukkusakule' means in a family of flower-scavengers.

Having shown the lowliness of the family with these words, now, although some people are born into a low family, they may be wealthy and have much property. However, to show that this person is not such a wealthy person, He said 'dalidde' and so forth to show the deficiency of wealth. In those words, 'dalidde' means one who is endowed with poverty. 'Appannapānabhojane' means one who has little rice, drink, and food. 'Kasiravuttike' means one who lives with difficulty; it means being in a family where one must achieve a livelihood only through great effort and exertion. 'Yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhati' means being in a family where one can only obtain food such as gruel and rice, and clothing just enough to cover one's shame, with great hardship.

Now, although some people are born into a low family, they may be endowed with physical excellence and possess a perfect body. However, to show that this person is not such a perfect person, He said 'so ca hoti dubbaṇṇo' and so forth to show the deformity of the body. In those words, 'dubbaṇṇo' means one who has a complexion like a burnt stump, like a dust-goblin (paṃsupisācaka). 'Duddasiko' means one who has an unsightly appearance that is unpleasant even to his own mother. 'Okoṭimako' means one who is dwarfish. 'Kāṇo' means one who is blind in one or both eyes. 'Kuṇī' means one who has one or both hands crooked. 'Khañjo' means one who has one or both feet lame. 'Pakkahato' means one who is paralyzed or one who moves with the aid of a stool (pīṭhasappī). 'Padīpeyyassa' refers to the accessories for a lamp, such as the wick, oil, and lamp-bowl. In the phrase 'tassa na evaṃ hoti', why does such a desire not arise? It is because he was born into a low family.

'Jeṭṭho' (the eldest) is mentioned because if there is another elder, the younger one does not have the expectation to receive consecration. 'Ābhiseko' (worthy of consecration) is mentioned because even if he is the eldest, if he is not worthy of consecration, he does not have the expectation. 'Anabhisitto' (not yet consecrated) is mentioned because even if a prince is worthy of consecration and free from defects such as blindness or crookedness, if he has already been consecrated once, he does not have the expectation to be consecrated again.
77:
The commentator states "acalappatto" (one who has attained stability). Even the eldest prince, if he has not yet been consecrated and is still a tender infant lying on his back, has no desire for consecration. However, a prince who is about sixteen years of age and whose beard has begun to appear is called "acalappatta" (one who has reached stability). Such a prince is capable of administering a great kingdom. Therefore, it is said, "acalappatto." Why does such a prince think, "It would be good if I were consecrated"? It is because of his noble birth.

"Dussīlo" means being without virtue. "Pāpadhammo" means having an evil nature. "Asuci" means being endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth. "Saṅkassarasmācāro" means conduct that is suspicious or doubtful. It refers to conduct that causes others to suspect, upon seeing some unseemly behavior, "This was likely done by him," or conduct that one himself reflects upon with suspicion; the meaning is conduct accompanied by doubt. To explain, when a monk of such evil conduct sees other monks gathered in a place of daytime rest or elsewhere, discussing something, he thinks, "These monks are consulting together; could they be discussing the evil deed I have committed?" Thus, he is one of suspicious conduct. "Paṭicchannakammanto" means being endowed with evil deeds that ought to be concealed. "Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño" means that although he is not a true monk, because he has the appearance of a monk, he claims, "I am a monk." "Abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño" means that upon seeing other celibate practitioners who are well-dressed, well-robed, carrying their alms-bowls, and wandering for alms in villages, market towns, and royal capitals to make a living, he behaves in the same manner and thus acts as if he is making the claim, "I am a celibate practitioner." One who says, "I am a monk," and enters the Uposatha hall or similar places, or accepts gifts intended for the Saṅgha, is also considered to be claiming to be a celibate practitioner. "Antopūti" means that rotten deeds have entered within him. "Avassuto" means being wet with lust and so forth. "Kasambujāto" means having the rubbish of arisen lust and so forth. Why does such a person not have the thought, "I am a monk"? Because he lacks the strong support (upanissaya) for the nine supramundane states. Why does a virtuous person have such a thought? Because he is one who fulfills the great virtue.

## 4. Cakkavattisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, he is called "Rājā" (king) because he pleases the people with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called "Cakkavatti" because he turns the Wheel-treasure, or because the Wheel-treasure is turned by him. Dhammo...
78:
Because he possesses the Dhamma, he is called 'dhammika' (righteous). Because he has become king solely in accordance with the ten duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch, he is called 'dhammarājā' (righteous king). Even that Wheel-turning Monarch cannot turn the Wheel without a king (without a ruler); the meaning is that he cannot turn the Wheel without depending on another 'King of Dhamma' as his support. Thus, the Teacher, having initiated the discourse, remained silent without reaching the conclusion (anusandhi). Why? He thought, 'Monks who are skilled in the sequence of the discourse will rise and ask about the connection; there are many such monks in this place. When I am asked by them, I shall expand the teaching.' Then, a monk skilled in the sequence of the discourse asked the Blessed One, 'But who, Bhante, (is the king of the Wheel-turning Monarch?)' and so forth. The Blessed One, wishing to answer him, said, 'Monks, the Dhamma (is the king of the Wheel-turning Monarch)' and so forth.

In that passage, 'Dhamma' refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha). 'The Dhamma' (dhammaṃ) refers to that very Dhamma of the kind mentioned. 'Depending on' (nissāya) means making that very Dhamma his support with a mind established in it. 'Honoring the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ sakkaronto) means practicing that Dhamma well so that it is properly performed. 'Respecting the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ garuṃ karonto) means making it an object of esteem by generating reverence for it. 'Revering the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ apacāyamāno) means showing humility toward that very Dhamma through gestures such as salutation with joined palms. 'One for whom the Dhamma is the banner, for whom the Dhamma is the standard' (dhammadhajo dhammaketu) means that because he practices by placing the Dhamma at the forefront like a banner and raising it high like a standard, he is one who has the Dhamma as his banner and standard. 'One who holds the Dhamma as sovereign' (dhammādhipateyyo) means being one who holds the Dhamma as sovereign by the understanding that the Dhamma alone is supreme, and by performing all actions solely through the power of the Dhamma.

In the phrase 'provides righteous protection, shelter, and guard' (dhammikaṃ rakkha-āvaraṇa-guttiṃ saṃvidahati): because that king possesses the Dhamma, he is called 'dhammika'. Protection, shelter, and guard are collectively called 'rakkha-āvaraṇa-gutti'. Among these three, according to the teaching, 'One who protects others protects himself,' qualities such as patience (khanti) are called 'protection' (rakkhā). For it has been said: 'And how, monks, does one who protects others protect himself? By patience, by non-violence, by a mind of loving-kindness, and by compassion.' Clothing, housing, and so forth are called 'shelter' (āvaraṇa). Guarding to prevent dangers such as thieves is called 'guard' (gutti). To 'provide' (saṃvidahati) means to properly arrange, carry out, and establish all of these.

Now, showing to whom those protections should be provided, he said 'for the inner circle' (antojanasmiṃ) and so forth. The summary of the meaning is: establishing the wife and children, known as the inner circle, in the restraint of virtue, providing them with clothes, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and preventing all dangers for them, is what is meant by providing righteous protection, shelter, and guard. The same method applies to the nobles (khattiya) and others. However, this is the distinction: consecrated kings, noble steeds...
79:
Consecrated kings should be supported by the gift of treasures such as thoroughbred horses. Kings who are followers (not yet consecrated) should be pleased by the gift of appropriate vehicles such as chariots, elephants, and horses. The military forces should be supported by the timely provision of food and wages. Brahmins should be supported with gifts such as food, drink, and clothing; householders should be supported with the provision of food, seeds, plows, and oxen. Similarly, the town-dwellers (negama) and the country-dwellers (jānapada) [should be supported in the same way]. Ascetics and Brahmins who have calmed and warded off evil should be honored with the gift of monastic requisites. Beasts and birds should be comforted by the granting of safety.

'He rolls the wheel only by means of the Dhamma' means he rolls the wheel of treasure only by means of the ten courses of wholesome action (dasa-kusalakamma-patha). 'That wheel is one that cannot be turned back' means the wheel of authority thus set in motion by that king cannot be turned back by anyone. In the phrase 'by any human being,' since deities act only according to their own desires, they are excluded, and thus 'human being' is mentioned. 'Enemy' (paccatthika) means an opponent or adversary. 'Righteous' (dhammika) means the Wheel-turning Monarch is righteous by virtue of the ten courses of wholesome action, whereas the Tathāgata is righteous by virtue of the nine supramundane states (nava-lokuttara-dhamma). 'King of Dhamma' (dhammarājā) means he is so called because he pleases the great multitude with the nine supramundane states. 'Only the Dhamma' means relying only on the nine supramundane states, honoring them, respecting them, and venerating them. That very Dhamma is his banner (dhammadhaja) in the sense of being eminent. That very Dhamma is his standard (dhammaketu). He is called 'one who makes Dhamma the sovereign' (dhammādhipateyya) because he dwells making that very Dhamma his chief and superior. 'Righteous protection, shelter, and guard' refers to the protection, shelter, and guard that bestows both mundane and supramundane Dhamma. 'Arranges' (saṃvidahati) means he establishes and prescribes: 'Such three types of bodily misconduct should not be practiced; good conduct should be practiced.' The meaning should be understood thus in all places. 'Having arranged' (saṃvidahitvā) means having established and taught. 'He rolls the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma only by means of the Dhamma' means he rolls the incomparable Wheel of Dhamma only by means of the nine supramundane states. 'That wheel is one that cannot be turned back' means that the Wheel of Dhamma thus set in motion cannot be turned back or obstructed by even a single person among those ascetics and others. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all places.

## 5. Sacetana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'Isipatana' is so called because it is the place where the sages (isī), namely the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, alight (patana) or assemble, having come there for the purpose of setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma and for performing the Uposatha. There is also a reading 'Padana,' which has the same meaning.
80:
'Migadāya' (Deer Park) is a place donated for the purpose of providing safety to the deer. 'In a period of six months less six nights'—it is said that on the very day the king gave the order, that wheelwright prepared all the equipment and entered the forest with his apprentices. Avoiding trees standing at village gates, in the middle of villages, at shrines, or in cemeteries, as well as burnt wood or naturally fallen dry wood, he took wood from a good location that was free from all defects and suitable for the hub, spokes, and rim, and made that wheel. This much time passed in selecting and taking the wood and in the making. Therefore, it is said, 'in six months less six nights.' 'Nānākaraṇaṃ' means a distinction or difference. 'Nesaṃ' means 'na esaṃ' (not in these [wheels]). 'Atthesaṃ' means 'atthi esaṃ' (there is in these [wheels]). 'Abhisaṅkhārassa gati' means the occurrence of the preparation (effort). 'Ciṅgulāyitvā' means having revolved. 'Akkhāhataṃ maññe' means as if it were fixed onto the axle.

'Sadosā' (faulty) means [wheels] that have knots or uneven (high and low) spots. 'Sakasāvā' (with dregs) means [wheels] that have rotten heartwood or sapwood. 'Kāyavaṅka' (bodily crookedness) and so on are names for bodily misconduct and the like. 'Fall down in this way' means falling through the decline of virtues. 'Stand firm in this way' means standing firm through virtues. Among them, the mundane multitude are called 'those who have fallen,' while those such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) are called 'those who stand firm.' Among those such as Stream-enterers, the first three types [of noble disciples] are called 'those who have fallen' at the moment when defilements arise. However, Arahants are called 'those who stand firm' in an absolute sense. 'Therefore' (tasmā) is said because those who have not abandoned bodily crookedness and so on fall, while those who have abandoned bodily crookedness and so on stand firm. The abandonment of bodily crookedness and so on should be understood thus: First, these six—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, and wrong view—are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Harsh speech and ill will are abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). Covetousness and idle chatter are abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga).

## 6. Apaṇṇaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'Apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā' means a practice that is unerring, a practice that is certain, a practice leading out [of saṃsāra], a practice consistent with reason, an essential practice, a pure practice, an unopposed practice, a practice in accordance [with the truth], and a practice in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. One practices not by speculative grasping (takkaggāha) nor by inference-based grasping (nayaggāha). Indeed, a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman who practices by grasping in this way (through takkaggāha or nayaggāha) declines and perishes from the attainments of human prosperity, celestial prosperity, and the prosperity of Nibbāna.
81:
One who practices the unmistakable way (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā) does not fall away from these attainments (human, celestial, or Nibbāna). In the past, among two caravan leaders traveling through a wilderness, the foolish caravan leader believed the words of a yakkha and met with ruin along with his followers. The wise caravan leader (the Bodhisatta), however, did not believe the yakkha's words, and by convincing his followers, "Let us not discard our existing water in a place where water is merely seen," he continued the journey and reached safety. Referring to this, it was said: "Some take the sure way; the speculators speak of a second (false) way. Knowing this (the benefit and harm of these two ways), the wise person should take that which is sure." (Jātaka 1.1.1).

In the phrase "For him, the origin (yoni) is undertaken," the word 'yoni' is a name for a collection of aggregates (khandha-koṭṭhāsa), for a cause (kāraṇa), and for the birth-canal (passāva-magga). In passages such as "Sāriputta, there are these four origins (yoni)," the collection of aggregates is called yoni. In passages such as "Bhūmija, this is the cause (yoni) for the attainment of the fruit," it means cause. In the passage "I do not call one a brahmin because of his origin (yoni-ja), born from a mother's womb," and in passages such as "The karma-born winds turn that fetus upside down and deliver it to the mother's birth-canal (yoni-mukha)," it refers to the birth-canal. Here, however, 'cause' is intended. 'Āraddhā' means undertaken or fulfilled.

In the phrase "for the destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayāya)," they are called 'āsava' because they flow out (āsavanti). It means they flow or proceed from the eye... etc... and from the mind. Alternatively, they are called āsava because they flow, in terms of phenomena, up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and in terms of location, up to the peak of existence (bhavagga). It means they proceed by including these phenomena and these locations within them. For this prefix 'ā' carries the sense of 'including within'. Just as liquors (madirā) etc. are called āsava because they have been fermented for a long time, these are called āsava because they are like those liquors. In the world, liquors etc. that have been kept for a long time are called āsava. If āsava is defined by the sense of long-term fermentation, then only these (greed, wrong view, delusion) should be considered. For it was said: "Bhikkhus, the preceding point of ignorance is not known; one cannot say that before this, ignorance did not exist." Or, they are called āsava because they produce the long suffering of saṃsāra. The former definitions apply where defilements (kilesa) are called āsava; the last definition applies to karma as well. Not only are karma and defilements called āsava, but various kinds of dangers (upaddava) are also called āsava. In the Suttas, in the passage "Cunda, for the restraint of taints (āsava) belonging to the present life...", āsava refers to the defilements that are the basis of disputes.
82:
In this passage from the Dīgha Nikāya, "I teach the Dhamma," the defilements such as anger (kodha) and resentment (upanāha), which are the roots of disputes, are intended by the term "taints" (āsava).

"Those taints by which I might have been reborn as a deva, or as a gandhabba wandering the sky, or by which I might have attained the state of a yakkha, or entered into the human state—those taints are destroyed in me, demolished, and completely eliminated." (Anguttara Nikāya). In this verse, karma pertaining to the three realms and the remaining unwholesome states are meant by āsava. In the Vinaya Pārājika passage, "For the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life," āsava refers to various dangers such as the reproach of others, remorse, killing, and imprisonment, as well as the various afflictions that constitute the suffering of the woeful states.

These taints should be understood according to how they appear in various scriptures. In the Vinaya teaching, they appear in two ways: "For the restraint of taints belonging to the present life, for the warding off of taints belonging to the future life." In the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, they appear in three ways: "Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)." In other Suttas and in the Abhidhamma, they appear in four ways by including the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) along with those three. In the Nibbedhika-pariyāya Sutta, they appear in five ways: "Bhikkhus, there are taints leading to hell, taints leading to the animal realm, taints leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, taints leading to the human world, and taints leading to the deva world." In this Sutta, karma alone is called āsava. In the Chakka Nipāta, they appear in six ways, such as "Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint." In the Sabbāsava Sutta, they appear in seven ways by adding those to be abandoned by seeing (dassana—the Path of Stream-entry) along with those six. In this context (of the Abhidhamma), however, the four taints according to the Abhidhamma method should be understood as intended.

In the word "khayāya (for the destruction)," the term "destruction of taints" (āsavakkhaya) refers to the natural dissolution of the taints, the state of being destroyed, and also to the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. In the passage, "That which is the destruction, vanishing, breaking up, disintegration, impermanence, and disappearance of the taints," the natural dissolution of the taints is called "destruction of taints." In the passage, "Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees," in this passage...
83:
"I say the destruction of the taints for one who sees." In this passage, the abandoning of taints, the absolute destruction of taints, non-arising, the mode of destruction, and non-existence are called "destruction of the taints" (āsavakkhaya).

"For a trainee in training, following the straight path, first knowledge arises in the destruction [the path], and then immediate gnosis [the fruit]." In this verse, the Path (magga) is called "destruction of the taints." "By the destruction of the taints, one is a recluse." In this passage, the Fruit (phala) is meant.

"For one who constantly looks for others' faults and is always intent on complaining, their taints grow; they are far from the destruction of the taints [Nibbāna]." In this verse, Nibbāna is meant. In this sutta, however, referring to the Fruit, it is said "for the destruction of the taints," meaning for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship.

"One with guarded doors in the faculties" means having closed doors in the faculties, with the mind as the sixth. "Moderate in eating" means knowing the measure in food; it means one knows or understands the measure in receiving, consuming, and reflecting. "Devoted to wakefulness" means dividing the day and night into six parts and being devoted to the state of wakefulness in five parts; it means being intensely and continuously engaged in wakefulness.

Having established the outline (mātika) in this way, now, wishing to analyze it according to the established order, [the Buddha] said, "And how, monks, is a monk..." and so forth. Therein, the meaning of the words "seeing a form with the eye" and so forth has been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga. Likewise, the meaning of the words "reflecting wisely, he consumes food, not for play..." and so forth [has also been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga]. "From hindering states" means from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Indeed, the hindrances remain blocking the mind; therefore, they are called hindering states (āvaraṇīyā dhammā). "He takes up the lion's posture" means he sleeps like a lion. "Placing foot on foot" means placing the left foot over the right foot. For if the feet are placed evenly, knee against knee and ankle against ankle, they strike each other, and from that, painful feelings arise. Therefore, to avoid that fault, he places the foot slightly overlapping. Thus it is said, "placing foot on foot."
84:
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" (sato sampajāno) means being endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension. But how can one who is sleeping be called mindful and clearly comprehending? It is by the power of the meditation practiced prior [to sleep]. For this practitioner, while walking in meditation, recognizes the onset of sleepiness, sets aside the meditation that was in progress, lies down on a couch or a bench, and upon falling asleep and then waking up again, wakes up while picking up the meditation exactly where it was stopped. Therefore, even while sleeping, he is called mindful and clearly comprehending. This is the method according to the primary meditation (mūlakammaṭṭhāna).

Furthermore, by the power of the meditation grasped at the moment of sleeping, he is also called mindful and clearly comprehending. How? This meditating monk, recognizing the onset of sleepiness while walking in meditation, lies down on his right side on a stone slab, a bench, or a couch, and reflects thus: "This insentient body is situated on an insentient couch; the insentient couch is on the insentient earth; the insentient earth is on the insentient water; the insentient water is on the insentient wind; the insentient wind is situated in the insentient space. In that situation, the space also does not know, 'I am standing while supporting the wind'; the wind also does not know, 'I am situated in the space.' Likewise, the wind does not know, 'I am standing while supporting the water' ... (and so forth) ... the couch does not know, 'I am standing while supporting the body'; the body also does not know, 'I am situated on the couch.' Indeed, among them, there is no mutual attention, application, reflection, volition, or desire." For him who reflects in this way, that reflecting mind descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). In this way, even while sleeping, he is known as mindful and clearly comprehending.

"Reflecting on the thought of rising" means having established in the mind the perception that defines the time of rising, such as "I shall rise when the moon or the stars reach such a position." For one who sleeps after doing this will wake and rise exactly at the defined time.

## 7. Attabyābādha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, the Attabyābādha Sutta, "attabyābādhāya" means for one's own suffering. "Parabyābādhāya" means for the suffering of others. The terms "good bodily conduct" and so forth appear in the preceding stage by way of the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha), but in the higher stage, they appear without restriction up to the Fruit of Arahantship.
85:
## 8. Devalokasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, the word "aṭṭīyeyyātha" means you should be oppressed (or you should be weary). "Harāyeyyātha" means you should be ashamed. "Jigucchayyātha" means you should be repulsed, as if experiencing the repulsion felt towards excrement in regard to those words. In the phrase "iti kira," the word "iti" is used for the smooth connection of words (padasandhi), and the word "kira" is a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of hearsay or report. The connection should be understood as: "It is said (kira) that you should be weary of divine life." "Pageva kho pana" means even earlier (or how much more so).

## 9. Paṭhamapāpaṇikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "pāpaṇiko" refers to a shopkeeper. This is a designation for a merchant who opens a shop and sells various goods. "Abhabbo" means being one who is not a suitable vessel (incapable). "Na sakkaccaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhāti" means he does not attend to his business in such a way that it is well-managed; it means he does not personally supervise it with direct observation.

In this context, a shopkeeper who does not get up at dawn at the sound of footsteps, light the lamp, set out his goods, and sit [in his shop] is said to not carefully attend to his business in the morning. The reason is that thieves who have stolen goods at night go to the market to dispose of them from their hands and sell them at a low price. Also, people with many enemies who stay in the city at night go to the market very early to take goods. Furthermore, people wishing to travel to the countryside go to the market early to buy goods. Because of these reasons, that shopkeeper becomes one who is unable to obtain the potential profit.

Furthermore, one who comes to eat at the time others eat, packs up his goods early, goes home to eat and sleep, and only returns to the shop in the evening is said to not carefully attend to his business at midday. The reason is that he becomes unable to obtain the profit from goods that thieves could not dispose of early in the morning but sell at a low price during the day when others are not moving about, as well as goods that powerful and wealthy people send for at lunchtime, saying, "It is proper to get such and such from the market."

Moreover, one who does not sit in the shop with a lamp lit until the beating of the [evening] drum is said to not carefully attend to his business in the evening. This is because he...
86:
...becomes one who is not the master of the profit arising from goods that thieves were unable to dispose of (sell) in the morning or during the day, but which they bring to the market in the evening and sell at a low price.

"Does not carefully attend to the sign of concentration" (na sakkaccaṃ samādhinimittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti) means he does not enter into concentration with thoroughness and respect. In this regard, one who performs his duties at the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard early in the morning, then enters his dwelling and stays there without attaining meditative absorption (samāpatti) until the time for alms-round, is said to not carefully attend to the sign of concentration in the morning. One who, after the meal, departs from the place of eating, enters his night-quarters or day-quarters, and stays there without attaining absorption until the evening, is said to not carefully attend to the sign of concentration at midday. One who, in the evening, pays homage to the stupa, performs services for the elders, enters his dwelling, and stays there without entering into absorption throughout the first watch, is said to not carefully attend to the sign of concentration in the evening. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the opposite of the method already stated. Furthermore, in this context, where it is said "attaining absorption," even insight (vipassanā) is appropriate if absorption is absent. Regarding "the sign of concentration" (samādhinimitta), the object of concentration is also appropriate. Indeed, it has been said: "Concentration itself is the sign of concentration, and the object of concentration is also the sign of concentration."

## 10. Commentary on the Second Pāpaṇika Sutta
In the tenth sutta, "cakkhumā" (having eyes) means having eyes by way of the eye of wisdom. "Vidhuro" (capable) means one who is endowed with energy associated with knowledge, having excellent and foremost effort as his lead. "Nissayasampanno" means one endowed with support or endowed with a foundation. "Paṇiyaṃ" refers to merchandise for sale. "This much will be the capital, this much will be the profit" means that in regard to the stated merchandise, [he knows] "it was bought in this way, it is sold in this way"; the capital, known as the purchase price for which the goods were bought, will be this much. And whatever sale there is when it is sold, in that sale, there will be this much increase, this much profit—this is the meaning.

"He is skilled in buying and selling goods" means that one who goes to a place where goods are easy to find to buy them, and goes to a place where they are rare to sell them, is called skilled in this trade; he obtains a tenfold or even twentyfold profit.
87:
"Aḍḍhā" refers to rulers who are endowed with much wealth buried in the ground. "Mahaddhanā" refers to those who have much wealth in terms of daily usable items. "Mahābhogā" refers to those who have great possessions in terms of consumable and enjoyable goods. "Paṭibalo" refers to one who is capable because they are endowed with physical and intellectual strength. "Amhākañca kālena kālaṃ anuppadātuṃ" means to regularly pay us the interest on the borrowed principal. "Nipatantī" means they invite. There is also the reading "nipātentī," which has the same meaning.

"Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya" means for the fulfillment and attainment of wholesome states. "Thāmavā" means one endowed with the power of wisdom. "Daḷhaparakkamo" means one endowed with firm effort associated with wisdom. "Anikkhittadhuro" means one who has not laid down the burden, thinking, "I will not lay down this burden of energy until I reach the path of Arahantship."

"Bahussutā" refers to those who have heard much of the Buddha's word through the Nikāyas and so forth. "Āgatāgamā" refers to those who have studied, mastered, and memorized at least one of the Nikāyas (which are called Āgamas, such as one Nikāya being one Āgama, two Nikāyas being two Āgamas, and five Nikāyas being five Āgamas). "Dhammadharā" refers to those who bear the Suttanta Piṭaka. "Vinayadharā" refers to those who bear the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Mātikādharā" refers to those who bear the two Mātikās. "Paripucchati" means asking about what is beneficial or not, and what is a cause or not. "Paripañhati" means investigating and weighing, knowing "I will ask such and such a question." The meaning of the remaining words here is clear.

In this sutta, wisdom (paññā) comes first, followed by energy (vīriya) and association with good friends (kalyāṇamittasevanā). In this regard, the meaning should not be understood as reaching the fruit of Arahantship first and only then putting in effort and associating with good friends. A teaching is usually defined by either the lower stage, the higher stage, or both. Here, it should be understood that it is defined by the higher stage (the fruit of Arahantship). Therefore, in the exposition, the support of good friends (kalyāṇamitta-upanissaya) is shown first, energy is shown in the middle, and finally, the fruit of Arahantship is taught.

## The Second Chapter: Rathakāra.
88:
## 3. Puggalavagga

## 1. Commentary on the Samiddhasutta

In the first sutta of the third vagga, because one first touches the contact of jhāna and later realizes Nibbāna, the cessation of the rounds, one is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhi*). Because one has reached the end of the path of stream-entry that sees Nibbāna, one is called "one attained to vision" (*diṭṭhippatta*). Because one is liberated from defilements through faith, one is called "one liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*). *Khamati* means it pleases. *Abhikkantataro* means especially good. *Paṇītataro* means especially noble. 

"The faculty of faith is predominant" (*saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti*) means that for the Elder Samiddha, at the moment of the path of arahantship, the faculty of faith was the leader, and the remaining four conascent faculties, such as energy, were its attendants. Thus, the Elder, wishing to speak of the path he had personally penetrated, said this. For the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, however, at the moment of the path of arahantship, the faculty of concentration was the leader, and the remaining four faculties, such as faith, were its attendants. Therefore, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika also, when saying "the faculty of concentration is predominant," was speaking only of the path he had personally penetrated. For the Venerable Sāriputta, at the moment of the path of arahantship, the faculty of wisdom was the leader, and the remaining four faculties, such as faith, were its attendants. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta also, when saying "the faculty of wisdom is predominant," was speaking only of the path he had personally penetrated.

*Na khv-ettha* should be broken down as *na kho ettha*. *Ekaṃsena byākātuṃ* means to answer definitively. By the term "one practicing for arahantship" (*arahattāya paṭipanno*), he shows the person endowed with the path of arahantship. Thus, in this sutta, although the three Elders spoke only of the path they had personally penetrated, the Blessed One spoke only by way of the difference in planes.

## 2. Commentary on the Gilānasutta

In the second sutta, *sappāyāni* means things that bring benefit and cause growth. *Patirūpaṃ* means an appropriate thing. By the phrase "he does not recover from that illness" (*neva vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhā*), it refers to a sick monk who has reached the end, being afflicted with an incurable disease such as wind-ailment or epilepsy. By the phrase "he recovers from that illness" (*vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhā*), it refers to minor ailments such as sneezing, scabies, ringworm, freckles, or grass-flower-like sores. By the text "obtaining suitable food, not failing to obtain it" (*labhanto sappāyāni bhojanāni no alabhanto*), it refers to all illnesses that can be relieved by medical care. 

Here, "an appropriate attendant" (*patirūpo upaṭṭhāko*) should be understood as one who is endowed with the qualities of a sick-attendant, who is wise, skillful, and not lazy. "A sick-attendant is authorized" (*gilānupaṭṭhāko anuññāto*) means it is authorized that he should be provided by the Saṅgha of monks. When that sick monk is unable to sustain himself by his own nature...
89:
The Saṅgha of monks should request and assign one monk and one novice, saying, "Take care of this sick monk." For as long as those caregivers are looking after that sick monk, whatever material things are needed for both the sick monk and the two caregivers, all such material things are the responsibility of the Saṅgha of monks alone. "Other sick ones should also be cared for" means that the other two types of sick monks should also be made to be cared for. For what reason? If a terminally ill monk is not cared for, he might develop a mind of ill-will, thinking, "If they were to care for me, I would have comfort; but now they do not care for me," and thus be reborn in a state of misery (apāya). However, for that sick monk who is cared for, the thought occurs: "The Saṅgha of monks has done what should be done; this kind of illness is merely the result of my own kamma." That sick monk, having established loving-kindness (mettā) toward the Saṅgha of monks, will be reborn in heaven. As for a monk who is afflicted with a minor illness, whether he receives suitable requisites or not, he is able to recover; yet, for such a monk, an illness that could subside even without medicine will subside more quickly if medical treatment is provided. Because of that recovery, he will be able to learn the Buddha's word (Buddhavacana) or strive in the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). For this reason, it is said, "Other sick ones should also be cared for."

"Neva okkamati" means he does not enter. "Niyāmaṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ" refers to the state of rightness known as the certainty of the path (magga-niyāma) among wholesome states (which he does not reach). By these words, the padaparama person (one for whom the word is the most) is described. By the second turn, the ugghaṭitaññū person (one of quick intuition) is taken; this includes a person like the Elder Nālaka in the Dispensation, or one who, having received an instruction once from Paccekabuddhas during the interval between two Buddhas, penetrates the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. By the third turn, the vipañcitaññū person (one who understands through elaboration) is described; the neyya person (one who requires guidance) is indeed dependent on that vipañcitaññū person.

"Dhamma-desanā anuññātā" means that permission is granted to preach the Dhamma eight times a month. "The Dhamma should be preached to others as well" means the Dhamma should be spoken to other persons besides these. For what reason? Because even if a padaparama person is unable to penetrate the Dhamma in this existence, it will become a supporting condition (paccaya) in the future. A person who penetrates the Dhamma whether he gets to see the physical body (rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata or not, and whether he gets to hear the Dhamma-Vinaya or not—such a person penetrates it even without obtaining them. If he does obtain them, however, he will penetrate it even more quickly. For this reason...
90:
...for that reason, the Dhamma should be preached to them. To the third type of person, however, it should be preached again and again.

## 3. Saṅkhārasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'sabyābajjhaṃ' means with suffering. 'Kāyasaṅkhāraṃ' refers to the mass of volition (cetanā) occurring in the body-door. 'Abhisaṅkharoti' means he strives, he forms a mass, he forms a heap. The same method applies to the doors of speech and mind. 'Sabyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ' refers to the world of kamma that is accompanied by suffering. 'Sabyābajjhā phassā phusanti' means that resultant contacts (vipāka-phassa) accompanied by suffering touch him. 'Sabyābajjhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyati' means he experiences resultant feeling accompanied by suffering; it means that which is oppressive and without enjoyment.

'Seyyathāpi sattā nerayikā' means he experiences feeling just as beings born in hell experience purely painful feeling. If it is asked, "Is there no neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) there?", the answer is: there is. However, because the painful feeling is so powerful, that neutral feeling remains in a state that is not worth mentioning (unreckonable). Thus, hell itself is brought in as a simile for hell. This is indeed called a counterpart simile (paṭibhāga-upamā).

In the words 'seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā', the deva world (Brahma world) itself is brought in as a simile for the deva world. Since in the lower Brahma worlds the resultant of jhāna accompanied by rapture (pīti) occurs, whereas in the Subhakiṇhā worlds there is no rapture and only purely pleasant resultant, the lower Brahma worlds are not taken and only the Subhakiṇhā world is mentioned. This simile should also be understood as a counterpart simile.

'Vokiṇṇasukhadukkhaṃ' means mixed pleasure and pain. 'Seyyathāpi manussā' means that for humans, there is pleasure at times and pain at times. 'Ekacce ca devā' refers to the devas of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). For those devas too, there is pleasure at times and pain at times. This is because when those of lesser power see devas of greater power, they must rise from their seats, move out of the way, remove their shoulder-cloaks, and perform a salutation with joined palms; all such actions are indeed called suffering. 'Ekacce ca vinipātikā' refers to the mansion-dwelling ghosts (vemānika-petas). They experience divine prosperity at times and karmic retribution (suffering) at times; thus, they are those with mixed pleasure and pain. Thus, it should be understood that in this sutta, the three types of good conduct (sucarita), which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are preached.
91:
## 4. Bahukāra Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, the phrase "Monks, these three persons" refers to three types of teachers. "Are of great help to a person" means they are of great benefit to the resident pupil (antevāsika). "The Buddha" refers to the Omniscient Buddha. "Has gone for refuge" means he has gone for reliance [to escape from the suffering of saṃsāra]. "The Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma along with the scriptural tradition (pariyatti). "The Saṅgha" refers to the group of eight noble persons (ariya-puggala). Furthermore, this taking of refuge is spoken with reference to a person who has not previously taken the refuges and has not yet established a firm resolve in them.

Thus, in this sutta, three types of teachers are mentioned as being of great help: the teacher who gives the refuges, the teacher who leads one to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), and the teacher who leads one to the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Do other teachers—such as the one who gives ordination (pabbajjā), the one who teaches the Buddha's word, the Kammavācā teacher, the one who leads to the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga), and the one who leads to the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga)—not appear here because they are not of great help? No, it is not that they are not of great help. However, this teaching is classified into two categories. Therefore, all those teachers, starting from the one who gives ordination, are indeed of great help. Among them, the lack of previous resolve is applicable only to the taking of refuge. It should be understood that the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), the preliminary work on kasiṇa, and insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) are dependent on the first path (sotāpattimagga).
