The two higher paths and fruits are dependent on the Path of Arahantship.

"By this person" refers to this resident pupil. "I say it is not easy to repay" means I declare that it is not easy to perform a reciprocal service. Indeed, even if a person were to prostrate and worship with the five-point prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita) not just hundreds or thousands of times in acts of salutation and so on; or if he stands up from his seat to welcome the teacher; or if he raises his hands in homage (añjali) every single time he sees him; or if he performs appropriate acts of respect; or if he offers a hundred or a thousand robes and a hundred or a thousand alms-bowls of food every day; or if he builds a monastery made of all kinds of jewels extending to the edge of the universe; or if he provides various medicines such as ghee and fresh butter—he would still not be able to truly repay the service rendered by the teacher. Thus the meaning should be understood.

## 5. Vajirūpama Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "one with a mind like an old sore" means a person whose mind is like a chronic wound. "One with a mind like lightning" means a person whose mind is like lightning due to its momentary illumination. "One with a mind like a diamond (vajira)" means a person whose mind is like the vajira weapon because of its ability to cut through the root of the defilements.
92:
Because of the ability to destroy the very root of the defilements, he is one with a mind like a diamond (vajira). 'Abhisajjati' means to cling [with anger]. 'Kuppati' means to be agitated by the power of anger. 'Byāpajjati' means to abandon the natural state and become putrid. 'Patitthīyati' means to reach a state of rigidity or stubbornness. 'Kopa' refers to weak anger. 'Dosa' refers to a stronger anger than kopa, characterized by the intent to corrupt. 'Appaccaya' refers to displeasure or unhappiness (domanassa) characterized by dissatisfaction. 'Duṭṭhāruka' is an old sore. 'Kaṭṭhena' means with the end of a stick. 'Kaṭhalena' means with a potsherd. 'Āsavaṃ deti' means it oozes repeatedly. An old sore, by its own nature, oozes these three: pus, blood, and serum; however, when struck by a stick or similar object, it oozes those impurities even more.

In the phrase 'evameva kho', the correlation between the simile and the thing compared is as follows: An angry person should be understood as being like the old sore. The natural arising of harshness in an angry person should be understood as being like the natural oozing of the old sore. A slight word [of provocation] should be understood as being like the striking with a stick or a potsherd. The state of becoming excessively enraged, thinking, "How can this person speak thus to someone like me?", should be understood as being like the excessive oozing from the sore.

'Rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ' means in the thick mass of darkness that creates blindness by obstructing the arising of eye-consciousness at night. 'Vijjantarikāya' means in the moment of a lightning flash. Here too, the correlation of the simile is as follows: The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the man with sight. The defilements to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry should be understood as the darkness. The time of the arising of the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry is like the flash of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry should be understood as being like the man with sight seeing the surrounding forms during the flash of lightning. Again, the defilements to be abandoned by the Path of Once-returning are like the covering of darkness. The arising of the knowledge of the Path of Once-returning is like the flash of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the Path of Once-returning should be understood as being like the man with sight seeing the surrounding forms during the flash of lightning. Again, the defilements to be abandoned by the Path of Non-returning are like the covering of darkness. The arising of the knowledge of the Path of Non-returning should be understood as being like the flash of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the Path of Non-returning should be understood as being like the man with sight seeing the surrounding forms during the flash of lightning.
93:
In the case of a person with a diamond-like mind (vajirūpamacitta), the following is a comparison and illustration. In detail, the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa) should be understood as being like a diamond weapon (vajira). The defilements (kilesas) that are to be destroyed by the Path of Arahantship should be understood as being like blocks of gems or blocks of stone. Just as there is nothing that a diamond weapon cannot penetrate, whether it be a block of gems or a block of stone, it should be understood that there are no defilements that cannot be pierced by the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. Just as a hole pierced by a diamond weapon does not fill up again, it should be understood that the defilements cut off by the Path of Arahantship do not arise again.

## 6. Sevitabbasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "sevitabba" means should be associated with. "Bhajitabba" means should be resorted to. "Payirupāsitabba" means should be attended upon repeatedly by sitting nearby. "Sakkattvā garuṃ katvā" means having shown respect and having shown esteem. In the phrases such as "inferior in virtue," the state of being inferior should be understood by comparing one with another. In such a comparison, one who observes the ten precepts should not associate with one who observes the five precepts. One who observes the fourfold purifying virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) should not associate with one who observes the ten precepts. "Except out of pity, except out of compassion" means excluding pity and compassion. Indeed, for one's own benefit, such a person should not be associated with; however, it is proper to approach them out of pity and compassion.

"Sīlasāmaññagatānaṃ sataṃ" means of the virtuous who have reached the state of equality in virtue. "There will be talk on virtue for us" means that for us who are equal in virtue, there will be conversation based only on virtue. "That talk will occur for us" means that even if we speak all day, that talk will continue to occur without being interrupted or hindered. "That talk will be a comfort for us" means that the talk on virtue occurring all day will be a comfortable dwelling, a happy dwelling for us. The same method applies to talk on concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā).

"Sīlakkhandha" means the aggregate of virtue. In the phrase "I will support with wisdom in various instances," one who avoids things that are unsuitable and unhelpful for virtue and resorts to things that are suitable and helpful is said to support the aggregate of virtue with wisdom in those various instances. The same method applies to the aggregates of concentration and wisdom. "Declines" means that one who associates with a person inferior to oneself constantly and continuously declines and perishes, like water poured into a filter for alkaline water. "Tulyasevī" means one who associates with an equal. Those who bow down to a superior...
94:
One who bows down to a superior person progresses and increases quickly. "Udeti khippaṃ" means increases quickly. Therefore, "one should resort to one's superior" means that because one who bows down to a superior person progresses quickly, one should associate with a person who is particularly superior and more distinguished than oneself.

## 7. Jigucchitabbasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "jigucchitabba" means one who should be loathed like excrement. "Atha kho naṃ" means "then of him." "Kittisadda" means the sound of talk (reputation). In this context, "evam-eva kho," immorality (dussīlya) should be understood as being like a cesspool.

An immoral person should be understood as being like a rat snake (dhammani) that has fallen into a cesspool. Just as that snake, when pulled out of the cesspool, does not bite even when it climbs onto a man's body, it should be understood that even if one associates with an immoral person, one does not adopt their behavior. Just as when one catches a snake with one's body smeared with excrement, it should be understood as the time when a bad reputation spreads for the one who associates with an immoral person.

"Tindukālātaṃ" means a tinduka-wood firebrand. "Bhiyyosomattāya cicciṭāyati" means that when that tinduka-wood firebrand is burning, it naturally emits sparks and makes the sound "ciṭiciṭā," but if it is struck or bumped, it makes an even louder sound. In the same way, an angry person naturally wanders about in an agitated and fierce manner, but when hearing even a small word, they become even more agitated and fierce, thinking, "How dare they speak like this to someone like me?"

"Gūthakūpa" means a pit full of excrement or simply a heap of excrement. The comparison and illustration in this sutta should be understood in the same way as the previous method. Therefore, the statement that such a person should be ignored and not associated with is because an angry person gets angry even when closely associated with and attended upon, and also gets angry when one withdraws, thinking, "What is the use of this person?" Therefore, like a straw fire (palālaggi), they should be ignored, not associated with, and not resorted to. What is meant? One who approaches a straw fire too closely to get warm will have their body burned. For one who stays too far away to get warm, the cold will not be dispelled. Only for one who gets warm from a middle position, neither too close nor too far, will the cold be dispelled. Therefore, like a straw fire, an angry person should be ignored from a middle position, not associated with, not resorted to, and not served. "Kalyāṇamitta" means a virtuous friend. "Kalyāṇasahāyo" means...
95:
One should ignore [such a person] with an attitude of equanimity; one should not associate with, frequent, or attend to them.

'Kalyāṇamitta' means a pure friend. 'Kalyāṇasahāya' means a pure companion. 'Sahāya' refers to those who travel or live together. 'Kalyāṇasampavaṅka' means one who leans towards noble and pure persons; it means one whose mind is inclined, sloped, and directed towards them.

## 8. Gūthabhāṇīsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Gūthabhāṇī Sutta: 'Gūthabhāṇī' is one who speaks words that have a foul smell like dung. 'Pupphabhāṇī' is one who speaks words that have a pleasant fragrance like flowers. 'Madhubhāṇī' is one who speaks words as sweet as honey. 'Sabhaggato' means being present in an assembly. 'Parisaggato' means being present in a village assembly. 'Ñātimajjhagato' means being in the midst of relatives. 'Pūgamajjhagato' means being in the midst of a guild (seṇī). 'Rājakulamajjhagato' means being in the midst of the royal court, the great place of judgment. 'Abhinīto' means being brought for the purpose of questioning. 'Sakkhipuṭṭho' means being questioned as a witness. The phrase "Come, O man" is merely a form of address. 'For one's own sake or for another's sake' means for the sake of one's own or another's limbs and so on, or for the sake of wealth. In the phrase 'āmisakiñcikkhahetu', 'āmisa' refers to a bribe. 'Kiñcikkha' means any small thing; it means for the sake of a bribe as small as a partridge, a quail, a lump of ghee, or a lump of butter. 'Sampajānamosā' (deliberately lying) means one who tells a lie while knowing it to be so.

'Nelā': 'ela' is said to be a fault; that which has no 'ela' is 'nelā', meaning faultless speech. It is like the virtue mentioned in the passage "Nelango setapacchādo". 'Kaṇṇasukhā' means pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of the syllables; it does not cause pain in the ear like the piercing of a needle. 'Pemanīyā' (endearing) means it does not cause anger in the whole body but generates love due to the sweetness of its meaning. 'Hadayangamā' (heart-reaching) means it reaches the heart without obstruction and enters the mind easily. 'Porī' (polite/urbane) means speech of the city (pura) because it is full of virtues. It is also called 'porī' because it is as delicate as a woman raised in a city. It is also called 'porī' because it is the speech of city-dwellers. 'Speech of city-dwellers' refers to the proper manner of speaking used by those living in the city. City-dwellers possess proper speech.
96:
(City-dwellers) are such. They address one who is like a father as "Father", one like a mother as "Mother", and one like a brother as "Brother". Such speech is called 'bahujanakantā' because it is beloved by many people. Because it is beloved, it is called 'bahujanamanāpā' because it pleases the hearts of many people and causes the growth of the mind.

## 9. Andhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, the Andha Sutta: "Cakkhu na hoti" means the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) is absent. "Phātiṃ kareyya" means one should make it flourish or increase. "Sāvajjānavajja" refers to faulty and faultless states. "Hīnappaṇīta" refers to low and high (inferior and superior) states. "Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāga": dark unwholesome states and bright wholesome states are called counterparts (sappaṭibhāga) in the sense of being opposites, because they mutually exclude each other. The summary here is: one should know wholesome states as "wholesome states" and unwholesome states as "unwholesome states". The same method applies to faulty states and so on. Specifically, regarding the counterparts of dark and bright states, one should know dark states as "counterparts to bright states" and bright states as "counterparts to dark states" by whichever eye of wisdom; that person does not possess such an eye. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining sections as well.

"Na ceva bhogā tathārūpā" means such wealth also does not exist for that person. "Na ca puññāni kubbati" means they do not perform meritorious deeds. By this sequence of words, the absence of the eye for producing wealth and the eye for performing merit is stated. "Ubhayattha kaliggāho" means taking a loss or failure in both this world and the next. Alternatively, "ubhayattha kaliggāho" means taking a loss in both types of benefits, those belonging to the present life and those belonging to the future life. "Dhammādhammena" means by the 'dhamma' of the ten wholesome courses of action and by the 'adhamma' of the ten unwholesome courses of action. "Saṭho" means a deceitful person. "Bhogāni pariyesati" means they seek wealth. "Theyyena kūṭakammena, musāvādena cubhayaṃ" means seeking by both means among theft, fraud, and lying. How? Seeking by theft and fraud, or by theft and lying, or by fraud and lying. "Saṅghātuṃ" means to accumulate. "Dhammaladdhehi" means with wealth obtained without violating the ten wholesome courses of action. "Uṭṭhānādhigataṃ" means obtained through effort...
97:
It is attained through effort. *Avyagghamānaso* means one who has a mind free from doubt. *Bhaddakaṃ ṭhānaṃ* means the noble place of the celestial realm. *Na socati* means a place where one does not grieve with internal sorrow.

## 10. Avakujjasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the tenth sutta, the Avakujja Sutta, *avakujjapañño* means one who has wisdom like a face turned downwards. *Ucchaṅgapañño* means one who has wisdom like a lap. *Puthupañño* means one who has extensive wisdom. In the words beginning with *ādikalyāṇaṃ*, *ādi* means the initial establishment. *Majjhaṃ* means the middle of the discourse. *Pariyosānaṃ* means the conclusion of the discourse. Thus, those who preach the Dhamma to such a person do so by making it good and faultless in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end. In this context, there are the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (*desanā*), and there are also the beginning, middle, and end of the dispensation (*sāsana*). Among these two, in the teaching, the first line of a four-line verse is the beginning, two lines are the middle, and the final line is the end. For a sutta with a single connection, the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, the connection (*anusandhi*) is the middle, and the conclusion "*idamavoca*" is the end. For a sutta with many connections, the first connection is the beginning, the one or many connections after that are the middle, and the last connection is the end. This is the method regarding the teaching.

In the dispensation, however, virtue (*sīla*) is the beginning, concentration (*samādhi*) is the middle, and insight (*vipassanā*) is the end. Or, concentration is the beginning, insight is the middle, and the path (*magga*) is the end. Or, insight is the beginning, the path is the middle, and the fruition (*phala*) is the end. Or, the path is the beginning, the fruition is the middle, and Nibbāna is the end. Or, if taken in pairs, virtue and concentration are the beginning, insight and the path are the middle, and fruition and Nibbāna are the end.

*Sātthaṃ* means they preach making it endowed with meaning. *Sabyañjanaṃ* means they preach making the phrasing complete. *Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ* means they preach making it entirely complete and without deficiency. *Parisuddhaṃ* means they preach making it pure, unentangled, and without knots. *Brahmacariyaṃ pakāsenti* means that in preaching thus, they reveal the Noble Eightfold Path, which is the noble practice included in the Three Trainings (*sikkhattaya*). *Neva ādiṃ manasi karoti* means one does not attend to the initial establishment of the Dhamma teaching.

*Kumbho* means a pot. *Nikujjo* means placed face down. In the phrase *evameva kho*, the person with *avakujja* wisdom should be seen like a pot placed face down...
98:
The time of pouring water is like the time of receiving the Dhamma teaching. The time when the water is poured out is like the time of being unable to learn while sitting in that seat. The time when the water does not remain is to be understood as the time of not remembering after rising from that seat.

*Ākiṇṇāni* means the delicacies that have been put in. *Satisammosāya pakireyya* means one would scatter them due to loss of mindfulness. In this analogy, the person who is like a lap should be understood as the person with lap-wisdom (*ucchaṅgapañño*). The various delicacies should be understood as the various words of the Buddha. The time of sitting and eating various delicacies in the lap is like the time of sitting and learning in that seat. The time of scattering them due to loss of mindfulness when rising is to be understood as the time of not remembering when going away after rising from that seat.

*Ukkujjo* means a pot placed face up. *Saṇṭhāti* means it remains. In this analogy, the person who is like a pot placed face up should be understood as the person with broad wisdom (*puthupañño*). The time of pouring water is like the time of receiving the teaching. The time when the water remains is like the time of learning while sitting there. The time when the water does not pour out is to be understood as the time of remembering when going away after rising.

*Dummedho* means a person without wisdom. *Avicakkhaṇo* means one who is devoid of discerning wisdom. *Gantā* means one who has the habit of going. *Seyyo etena vuccati* means it is said that one is superior to this person. *Dhammānudhammapappaṭipanno* means one who practices the preliminary path along with virtue, which is in accordance with the nine supramundane states. *Dukkhassa* means of the suffering of the round of rebirths (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*). *Antakaro siyā* means one should be an end-maker, a definer, or one who concludes.

## The Third Chapter: On Persons (Puggala-vagga) is finished.

## 4. Devadūta-vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Sabrahmaka Sutta

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, *ajjhāgāre* means in one's own home. *Pūjitā honti* means they are served and protected with whatever things are available in the home. Thus, having shown that families who honor their parents are like those with the Great Brahmā, now...
99:
To show that they are the first teachers and so forth of those families, he said "sapubbācariyaka" and so on. In that context, the sentences such as "Brahma" are spoken to establish the status of parents as Brahma and so forth. "Bahukārā" means being of great help to children. "Āpādakā" means those who bring life into being. Indeed, the life of children is brought into being, protected, sustained, and kept going continuously by parents. "Posakā" means those who nourish, making the limbs grow and feeding them with their heart's blood (milk). In the phrase "showers of this world," I shall explain further. The seeing of pleasant and unpleasant objects in this world by children occurs depending on parents. Therefore, they are called "showers of this world."

"Brahma is a term for parents" is a designation based on excellence. Just as the four meditations—loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā)—are never abandoned by Brahma, so too these four meditations are never abandoned by parents toward their children. These should be known at various times. To elaborate, while the child is in the mother's womb, a mind associated with loving-kindness arises in the parents: "When shall we see our little son healthy and complete in all limbs?" When that child is young and lies on his back, and cries or screams because of being bitten by insects such as lice or bedbugs, or because of being oppressed by uncomfortable sleep, compassion arises in the parents upon hearing his voice. When the child runs and plays, or when he is at an attractive age, the parents' hearts, upon looking at the child, become soft like a hundred-times-beaten cotton ball dipped in clarified butter, and they are greatly delighted; at that time, muditā is found in them. When the son takes a wife and lives in a separate house, equanimity arises in the parents: "Now our little son is able to live according to his own nature." At that time, upekkhā is found. For this reason, it is said, "Brahma is a term for parents."

In the phrase "They are called first teachers (pubbācariya)," I shall explain further. From the time of birth, parents make them learn and train them, saying: "Sit like this, stand like this, go like this, sleep like this, eat like this, consume like this. This person should be called 'Father', this is 'Brother', this is 'Sister'. This should be done, this should not. This person should be approached, this one should not." Later, other teachers teach them arts such as elephant-lore, horse-lore, chariot-lore, archery, weaponry, and calculation.
100:
Another teacher gives the refuges; another teacher establishes one in the precepts; another teacher grants novice ordination; another teacher teaches the word of the Buddha; another teacher grants higher ordination; another teacher leads one to the path of stream-entry and so forth. In this way, all those teachers (who teach skills such as elephant training, horse training, etc.) are called later teachers (pacchācariya). However, parents are the very first of all teachers. Therefore, it was said: "They are called the first teachers (pubbācariya)." In that text, "vuccare" means they are called, they are spoken of. "Worthy of offerings from their children" (āhuneyyā ca puttānaṃ) means they are worthy of receiving and suitable to receive things such as rice and drinks that children have brought from afar and specially prepared to offer. Therefore, it is said, "worthy of offerings from their children." "Compassionate toward their offspring" (pajāya anukampakā) means that they provide for and protect their own children, even if it means taking the lives of others. Therefore, it is said, "compassionate toward their offspring."

"Should revere" (namasseyya) means one should perform an act of homage. "Should honor" (sakkareyya) means one should cherish them with respect. Now, wishing to show the manner of that respect, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "annena." In that passage, "with food" (annena) refers to gruel, boiled rice, and hard food. "With drink" (pānena) refers to the eight kinds of allowable drinks. "With clothing" (vatthena) refers to garments for wearing and covering. "With bedding" (sayanena) refers to providing couches and benches. "With anointing" (ucchādanena) refers to anointing to remove unpleasant odors and create a pleasant scent. "With bathing" (nhāpanena) refers to bathing the body by pouring warm water when it is cold and cold water when it is hot. "With washing of the feet" (pādānaṃ dhovanena) refers to washing the feet with warm or cold water and rubbing them with oil. "After passing away" (pecca) means having reached the next world. "Rejoices in heaven" (sagge pamodati) means that, first of all, in this world, wise people praise that person even in the present life upon seeing their service to their parents. Furthermore, after passing away and being established in the heavenly realm, that attendant of parents greatly rejoices and delights in divine splendors.

## 2. Ānandasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "of such a kind" (tathārūpo) means of that nature. "Attainment of concentration" (samādhipaṭilābho) means the attainment of one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā). In the phrase "in this body with consciousness" (imasmiñca saviññāṇake), both one's own body and the bodies of others are taken together in the sense of being possessed of consciousness and are referred to as "this body." "I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency of conceit" (ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā) refers to the wrong view (diṭṭhi) characterized by "I," the craving (taṇhā) characterized by "mine," and the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya). Regarding one's own...
101:
The defilements of others should also not arise. "And externally in all signs" (bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu) means in all such external signs as the sign of form, the sign of sound, the sign of smell, the sign of taste, the sign of touch, signs such as eternalism and so forth, the sign of a person, and the sign of phenomena (defilements should not arise). "Deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom" (cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ) refers to the concentration of fruition and the knowledge of fruition. "Siyā" means "would be" or "might be."

"Here, Ānanda, for a monk" (idhānanda bhikkhuno) means, Ānanda, for a monk in this Dispensation. With the words "This is peaceful, this is sublime" (etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ), the Buddha speaks referring to Nibbāna. Indeed, Nibbāna is called "peaceful" (santa) because defilements are stilled. Because the thought-process of one who dwells in attainment all day long, contemplating Nibbāna as peaceful, proceeds only in a peaceful manner, it is also called "peaceful." "Sublime" (paṇīta) means that because the thought-process of one who dwells in attainment proceeds only in a sublime manner, Nibbāna is called "sublime." Terms such as "the stilling of all formations" (sabbasankhārasamatha) are also merely synonyms for that Nibbāna. "The stilling of all formations" means that the thought-process of one who dwells in attainment throughout the day proceeds only as the stilling of all formations. ... Likewise, because of the absence of craving called "vāna" in the three realms of existence, it is named Nibbāna; because the thought-process of one who dwells in attainment in that Nibbāna proceeds only as Nibbāna, it receives names such as "the stilling of all formations." In these eight types of adverting and bringing to mind (ābhoga-samannāhāra), one type, two types, or all types can be obtained in this context.

"Having reflected" (sankhāya) means having known with wisdom. "Higher and lower" (paroparāni) refers to the internal bases of others and one's own internal bases. The individual existence of others and one's own individual existence are called "parāni ca oparāni ca." "For whom" (yassa) means for that Arahant. "Agitation" (iñjitaṃ) refers to these seven types of agitation, vibration, and trembling: agitation due to lust, and agitation due to hatred, delusion, pride, views, defilements, and misconduct. "Nowhere" (natthi kuhiñci) means not present in any single object. "Peaceful" (santo) means one who is stilled because opposing defilements are stilled. "Smokeless" (vidhūmo) means one who is free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and so forth. "Trouble-free" (anīgho) means one who is free from the trouble of lust and so forth. "Desireless" (nirāso) means one who is without craving. "Crossed over" (atārī) means one who has crossed, transcended, and gone beyond. "He" (so) refers to that Arahant, the khīṇāsava (one whose taints are exhausted). In this context, by taking "birth and old age" (jātijaraṃ), it should be understood that sickness and death are also included. Thus, in both the Sutta and the verse (gāthā), only the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) is taught.
102:
## 3. Sāriputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "in brief" (saṅkhittena) means by setting out the mātikā (table of contents). "In detail" (vitthārena) means by analyzing the set mātikā. "In brief and in detail" (saṅkhittavitthārena) means sometimes in brief and sometimes in detail. "Those who understand are rare" (aññātāro ca dullabhā) means that persons who can penetrate the Four Noble Truths are rare. The Blessed One spoke this with the intention, "I will touch (test) the knowledge of the Elder Sāriputta." Upon hearing those words, although the Elder did not directly say, "Venerable Sir, I will understand," he encouraged the Blessed One to teach by saying, "This is the time, Blessed One" (etassa bhagavā kālo), implying: "Venerable Sir, please teach with confidence; I shall penetrate the Dhamma taught by you through hundreds and thousands of methods; let this task be my responsibility."

Then the Blessed One began the teaching for Venerable Sāriputta with the words "Therefore" (tasmātiha). In that teaching, the phrase "In this conscious [body]" (imassiñca saviññāṇake) and so forth is just as explained previously. "He cut off craving" (acchecchi taṇhaṃ) means he cut off craving with the weapon of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. "He overturned the fetters" (vivaṭṭayi saṃyojanaṃ) means he uprooted and discarded the ten fetters along with their roots. "Through the right breakthrough of conceit, he made an end of suffering" (sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassa) means he made an end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) through the breakthrough of abandoning the nine types of conceit by the appropriate means and right practice. "And this was said by me, Sāriputta, in reference to this" (idañca pana metaṃ sāriputta sandhāya bhāsitaṃ) means, "Sāriputta, I spoke this in the Udaya-pucchā of the Pārāyana Vagga referring specifically to this attainment of fruition."

Now, wishing to show those words spoken by the Blessed One, he began with "The abandoning of perceptions of sensual pleasure" (pahānaṃ kāmasaññānaṃ). Although this term appears as "pahānaṃ kāmacchandānaṃ" (abandoning of sensual desires) in the Udaya-pucchā, here in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Aṅguttara-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Aṅguttara) have presented it as "kāmasaññānaṃ." In that regard, only the syllables (phrasing) differ, but the meaning is the same. "Perceptions of sensual pleasure" (kāmasaññānaṃ) means perceptions arisen in reference to sensual pleasures, or perceptions associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. "Both... and of distress" (domanassāna cubhayaṃ) means the abandoning of both these perceptions of sensual pleasure and of mental distress. "I declare the abandoning... liberation through final knowledge" (pahānaṃ... aññāvimokkhaṃ pabrūmi) means he taught the liberation through final knowledge, which is the fruition of Arahantship, characterized by abandoning through stilling. In the Niddesa, however, it is stated as: "The abandoning, stilling, relinquishing, and calming of both sensual desire and distress; the deathless Nibbāna." That statement is made by way of extracting the meaning. This is because "abandoning" (pahāna) refers to stilling (vūpasama) characterized by the state of exhaustion, as well as the Path that relinquishes defilements, and the calming of defilements...
103:
The fruit (phala) through which defilements are abandoned, and that deathless Nibbāna, are called pacification (vūpasama). Therefore, those terms (such as abandonment and pacification) appear in that Mahāniddesa. According to the statement 'I declare the liberation through final knowledge' (aññāvimokkhaṃ pabrūmi), only the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is intended. By the phrase 'the dispelling of sloth' (thinassa ca panūdanaṃ), only the fruit of Arahantship is intended because it occurs at the end of the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) which dispels sloth and torpor (thina-middha). 'The prevention of remorse' (kukkuccānaṃ nivāraṇaṃ) means that only the fruit is intended because it occurs immediately after the path that prevents remorse.

'Purified by equanimity and mindfulness' (upekkhā-sati-saṃsuddhaṃ) refers to the purity through equanimity and mindfulness occurring in the fruit associated with the fourth jhāna. In 'preceded by thought on the Dhamma' (dhammatakka-purejavaṃ), 'thought on the Dhamma' refers to right intention (sammā-saṅkappa). Because that right intention occurs at the beginning, in front, and as a precursor to the liberation through final knowledge, it is called 'preceded by thought on the Dhamma.' It refers to that which has thought on the Dhamma as its precursor (meaning liberation through final knowledge). 'Liberation through final knowledge' (aññāvimokkhaṃ) means the liberation that occurs at the conclusion of the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya); or it means liberation from defilements through knowing without overstepping the limit already seen by the path of stream-entry; it has the meaning of 'liberation through wisdom' (paññāvimutta). 'The breaking of ignorance' (avijjāya pabhedanaṃ) is so named because it occurs at the end of the path of Arahantship which destroys ignorance, or because it occurs by taking Nibbāna, known as the destruction of ignorance, as its object; thus it is only the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, it should be understood that by all these terms such as abandonment (pahāna), only the fruit of Arahantship is illustrated.

## 4. Nidānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'causes' (nidānāni) means origins. 'Of kammas' (kammānaṃ) means of kammas that lead to the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). 'Greed is a cause for the arising of kammas' (lobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāya) means that greed, which has the nature of attachment and intense longing, is the root cause and support for the arising and accumulation of kammas that lead to the round of suffering. 'Hatred' (doso) is hatred which has the nature of malice and intense ill-will. 'Delusion' (moho) is delusion which has the nature of confusion and intense bewilderment.

'Done through greed' (lobhapakataṃ) means kamma performed through greed, or kamma performed by one who is overwhelmed by greed and has become greedy. Because it is born of greed, it is called 'born of greed' (lobhaja). Because greed is the root cause of that kamma, it is called 'rooted in greed' (lobhanidāna). Because greed is the origin of that kamma, it is called 'originated from greed' (lobhasamudaya). 'Origin' (samudaya) means support (paccaya); it means having greed as its support. In whatever place the individual possessing that kamma born of greed has a rebirth (attabhāva), the aggregates (khandhas) manifest. In those aggregates, that kamma ripens. 'Either in the present life' (diṭṭhe vā dhamme) and so on is said to show the classification of that kamma, as it may be kamma to be experienced in the present life, kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya), or kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya). The same method applies to the remaining two (hatred and delusion).
104:
'Unbroken' (akhaṇḍāni) refers to seeds that are not split or damaged. 'Not rotten' (apūtīni) refers to seeds that have not reached the state of being non-seeds due to rotting. 'Not destroyed by wind or heat' (avātātapahatāni) refers to seeds not damaged by the wind or the heat of the sun. 'Substantial' (sārādāni) refers to seeds that have essence, are full of essence, and are not without essence. 'Well-stored' (sukhasayitāni) refers to seeds that remain in good condition because they have been properly stored and accumulated. 'In a good field' (sukhette) means in a clear and fertile field. 'In a well-prepared soil' (suparikammakatāya bhūmiyā) means in field soil that has been well-prepared by plowing with a plow and an eight-toothed harrow. 'Deposited' (nikkhittāni) refers to seeds that are placed or sown. 'Should provide' (anuppaveccheyyā) means should cause to enter. Among the terms beginning with 'growth' (vuddhi): growth by ascending upwards is called 'vuddhi'; flourishing and spreading by establishing roots below is called 'virūḷhi'; and abundance by spreading all around is called 'vepulla.'

Regarding the statement 'either in the present life' (diṭṭhe vā dhamme) and so on taught in this sutta, the classification of kamma (kamma-vibhatti) should be explained here to avoid confusion. According to the Suttanta method, eleven types of kamma are classified. They are: kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya), kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya), kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya), weighty kamma (garuka), habitual kamma (bahula), death-proximate kamma (āsanna), stored-up kamma (kaṭattā), productive kamma (janaka), stabilizing kamma (upatthambhaka), frustrating kamma (upapīḷaka), and destructive kamma (upaghātaka). Among these, in a single process of impulsion (javana-vīthi) consisting of seven consciousnesses, the first impulsion-volition (javana-cetanā), whether wholesome or unwholesome, is called kamma to be experienced in the present life. That kamma gives its result in this very life, like the wholesome kamma of the householder Kākavaḷiya and the merchant Puṇṇa; or like the unwholesome kamma of the yakkha Nanda, the youth Nanda, the cattle-butcher Nanda, Kokāliya, Suppabuddha, Devadatta, and Ciñcamāṇavikā. If it cannot give its result, it becomes 'lapsed kamma' (ahosi-kamma) and is concluded without yielding a result. This should be understood through the simile of the hunter. When a hunter sees a deer, draws his bow, and shoots an arrow, if the arrow does not miss, it brings the deer down right there. Then the hunter skins it, cuts it into pieces, takes the meat, feeds his wife and children, and goes away rejoicing. If the arrow misses, the deer runs away and does not look back at that place. This should be understood in the same way. The arrow hitting the deer without missing is like the diṭṭhadhammavedanīya kamma obtaining its turn to ripen; the arrow missing is like the kamma becoming ahosi-kamma without giving a result.

The seventh impulsion-volition, which completes the functional purpose, is called kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya). That kamma gives its result in the immediately following life. This should be understood on the wholesome side by way of the eight attainments (samāpatti), and on the unwholesome side by way of the five kammas with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma). Among these, one who attains the eight attainments is reborn in the Brahma world through one of those attainments. One who commits all five ānantariya kammas is reborn in hell through one of those kammas.
105:
The remaining attainments and the ānantariya kammas merely become ahosikamma (lapsed kamma); they do not produce results. This meaning should also be understood by the previously mentioned simile. The five javana-cetanās (volitions of the impulsion process) occurring between the first javana and the seventh javana are called aparāpariyavedanīya-kamma. This kamma produces its result whenever it finds an opportunity in the future. As long as the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) continues, it never becomes ahosikamma. All of this should be explained with the simile of the dog hunter. Just as a dog released by a hunter upon seeing a prey follows it and bites it wherever it catches up, similarly, this kamma produces its result wherever it finds an opportunity. There is no being who is liberated from this kamma.

Among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, that which is heavy among heavy and light kammas is called garuka-kamma. This garuka-kamma should be understood as mahaggata-kamma on the wholesome side and as the five ānantariya-kammas on the unwholesome side. When such garuka-kamma exists, the remaining wholesome or unwholesome kammas are unable to produce results. Only that garuka-kamma gives the result of rebirth (paṭisandhi). Just as a pebble or an iron ball the size of a mustard seed, when thrown into a pond, cannot float on the water but only sinks to the bottom, similarly, whichever kamma is heavy, whether wholesome or unwholesome, it alone takes hold of the being and proceeds.

Among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, that which is frequent is called bahula-kamma. It should be understood by the power of repeated practice over a long period. Alternatively, among powerful wholesome kammas, that which causes joy, and among unwholesome kammas, that which causes remorse, is called bahula-kamma. This bahula-kamma is like when two wrestlers enter the battlefield; the stronger one knocks down the other and proceeds. Similarly, overcoming other weak kammas, the kamma that is frequent due to repetition (bahula-kamma) or the kamma that is powerful at the time of death (āsanna-kamma) gives its result. It is like the kamma of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya.

It is said that after being defeated in the Cūḷaṅgaṇiya battle, the King fled riding a mare. His young attendant, the minister named Tissa, followed alone behind him. While sitting in a forest, being oppressed by hunger, the King said, "Brother Tissa, hunger is oppressing us greatly; what shall we do?"
106:
The minister replied, "Great King, I have a portion of rice in a small golden bowl that I brought hidden in my garment." "If so, bring it," the King commanded. The minister took it out and placed it before the King. Seeing it, the King said, "Minister, make four portions." "Great King, there are only three of us; why do you have me make four portions?" (he asked). "Brother Tissa, from the time I have been self-aware, I have never consumed food without first offering it to the Noble Ones. Even today, I will not consume it without offering it." The minister made four portions. The King said, "Announce the time (for the meal)." "Great King, in this forest abandoned by people, where shall we find Noble Ones?" (he asked). "This is not your burden. If I have faith, we shall find Noble Ones. Announce the time with confidence," the King said. The minister announced three times, "It is time, Bhante! It is time, Bhante!"

Then, the Elder Bodhimātumahātissa, hearing that sound with his divine ear, reflected, "Where is this sound coming from?" and knew, "Now King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, having been defeated in battle, is sitting in the forest and, having had a portion of rice divided into four, has had the time announced, thinking, 'I will not consume it alone.'" Thinking, "Today I should favor the King," he arrived by the power of his mind and stood before the King. Seeing him, the King was filled with faith and said, "Look, Brother Tissa!" and after paying homage to the Elder, said, "Bhante, please give me your bowl." The Elder took out his bowl. The King placed his own portion along with the portion for the Elder into the bowl and, paying homage, stood there saying, "Bhante, may there never be any hardship due to food." Minister Tissa also thought, "I cannot eat while my lord is looking on," and poured his own portion into the Elder's bowl as well. The mare also thought, "It is proper for me to give my portion to the Elder too." The King, looking at the mare, realized, "This mare also desires to put her portion into the Elder's bowl," and after putting that portion into the bowl as well, he paid homage to the Elder and saw him off. The Elder took that food and, starting from the beginning, offered it to the Sangha of monks in the form of morsels of food. The King also thought, "We are very hungry; it would be very good if he would send back the leftover grains of rice." The Elder, knowing the King's mind...
107:
The Elder, knowing the King's mind, made the remaining rice sufficient for those three people and threw the bowl into the sky. The bowl came and settled in the King's hand. The rice was as much as the three people desired. Then the King washed the bowl, and thinking, "I will not send back an empty bowl," he removed his upper robe, made it into a water-wiping cloth, placed it in the bowl, and made a resolution: "May the bowl go and settle in my master's hand," then threw it into the sky. The bowl went and settled in the Elder's hand.

Later, the King enshrined an eighth part of the Buddha's bodily relics and was building the Mahācetiya, one hundred and twenty cubits high. While the stupa was not yet completed, the time of his passing arrived. Then, as the King lay on the right side of the Mahācetiya, and the Saṅgha of monks was performing recitations according to the five Nikāyas, six chariots from the six deva worlds arrived and stood in the sky before him. The King said, "Bring the ledger of merits," and had the record of his merits read from the beginning. At that time, no merit could please the King. He said, "Read further." The reader said, "Great King, while you were defeated in the Cūḷaṅgaṇiya battle and were staying in the forest, you divided one bowl of rice into four portions and offered alms-food to the Elder Bodhimātumahātissa." The King said, "Stop," and asked the Saṅgha of monks, "Venerable sirs, which deva world is delightful?" "Great King, the Tusita heaven, the dwelling place of all Bodhisattas, is delightful." The King passed away and, standing in the very chariot that came from the Tusita heaven, went to the Tusita heaven. This is the story of the fruition of Strong Kamma (Balava-kamma).

Among wholesome and unwholesome actions, the kamma that one can remember at the time of death is called Death-proximate Kamma (Āsanna-kamma). This death-proximate kamma gives its result. For example, when the gate of a cattle pen full of cows is opened, even if there are strong young bulls in the back, the cow that is closest to the gate, even if it is a weak old cow, comes out first. In the same way, even if there are other wholesome and unwholesome kammas, because it is close to the time of death, the death-proximate kamma gives its result.

In this regard, there are these stories. In the village of Madhuaṅgaṇa, it is said that a Tamil gatekeeper went early in the morning taking a fishhook, killed fish, and made three portions. With one portion, he bought rice; with one portion, he bought curd; and one portion he cooked. In this manner, he committed the act of killing for fifty years. Later, becoming old and infirm, he reached a state of being unable to rise from his bed. At that moment, [the Elder] who used to reside at the Giri monastery...
108:
...making [the fish into three portions], with one portion he bought rice, with one portion he bought curd, and one portion he cooked and ate. Having committed the act of killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) for fifty years in this manner, he later became old and infirm, reaching a state where he lay in bed unable to rise. At that moment, Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa, who resided at the Giri monastery, thought, "May this being not perish while I am watching," and went to stand at the door of that man's house. Then his wife informed him, "Master, the Elder has arrived." [The man] said, "I have never gone to the Elder's presence for fifty years; what virtue do I have that the Elder should come? Go and tell him [to leave]." She said, "Venerable sir, please proceed (I pay my respects)." The Elder asked, "What is the condition of the lay devotee's body?" "Venerable sir, he is weak," she replied. The Elder entered the house, established mindfulness in him, and asked, "Will you take the precepts?" "Yes, venerable sir, please give them to me," he replied. The Elder gave the Three Refuges and began to give the Five Precepts. At the very moment of saying "Pañca sīlāni" (the Five Precepts), the man's tongue fell out. The Elder, reflecting, "This much [the Refuges] will suffice," departed. That man also passed away and was reborn in the Cātumahārājika heaven. At the very moment of rebirth, reflecting, "What kamma did I do to obtain this [celestial splendor]?" he realized he obtained it depending on the Elder. He came from the deva world, paid homage to the Elder, and stood at one side. When asked, "Who is this?" he replied, "Venerable sir, I am the Tamil gatekeeper." When asked, "Where were you reborn?" he said, "Venerable sir, in the Cātumahārājika heaven. If you, my master, had given me the Five Precepts, I would have been reborn in a higher deva world." The Elder said, "Dear son, what could I do? You were unable to take them." He paid homage to the Elder and returned to the deva world. This is a story regarding wholesome kamma.

In Antaragaṅgā, however, there was a lay devotee named Mahāvācakāla. For thirty years, for the sake of attaining the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), he recited the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). However, he fell into the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vippallāsa), thinking, "Even though I recite the thirty-two parts of the body like this, I have not been able to produce even a sign of light; the Buddha's dispensation must not be emancipating (aniyyānika)." When he passed away, he was reborn as a crocodile-peta, nine usabhas in length, in the Mahāgaṅgā river. On one occasion, sixty carts carrying stone pillars went by the Kacchaka ferry. That crocodile-peta ate all those oxen and the stone pillars. This is a story regarding unwholesome kamma.
109:
Kamma that is free from the three types such as weighty kamma (garuka-kamma), etc., and is done without full awareness is called kaṭattā-kamma (kamma performed through being done). For example, just as a stick thrown by a madman goes wherever it may fall, so too this kamma gives results in any existence when other major kammas are absent.

What is called janaka-kamma (productive kamma) produces a single rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) but does not produce results during the course of existence (pavatti); during the course of existence, another kamma produces the results. Just as a mother only gives birth to a child while a nurse takes care of it, so too the kamma that produces rebirth-linking is like a mother and is called janaka-kamma, while the kamma that gives results during the course of existence is like a nurse and is called upatthambhaka-kamma (supportive kamma). Supportive kamma can be found in both wholesome and unwholesome states. Some person, having performed a wholesome deed, is reborn in a happy destination (sugati). Remaining there, they repeatedly perform wholesome deeds, supporting that kamma, and thus wander in happy destinations for many hundreds of thousands of years. Some person, having performed an unwholesome deed, is reborn in a miserable destination (duggati). Remaining there, they repeatedly perform unwholesome deeds, supporting that kamma, and thus wander in miserable destinations for many hundreds of thousands of years.

Another method: Janaka-kamma can be either wholesome or unwholesome. It produces the material and immaterial resultant aggregates (vipāka-khandha) both at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Upatthambhaka-kamma, however, cannot produce resultants itself, but it supports the pleasure or pain that arises in the rebirth-linking provided by another kamma, making it last for a long time. What is called upapīḷaka-kamma (obstructive kamma) oppresses the pleasure or pain that arises in the rebirth-linking provided by another kamma and does not allow it to last long. In this regard, there is this method: while wholesome kamma is yielding its result, unwholesome kamma becomes upapīḷaka-kamma and does not allow it to yield its result. While unwholesome kamma is yielding its result, wholesome kamma becomes upapīḷaka-kamma and does not allow it to yield its result. Just as if someone were to damage or cut a growing tree, bush, or creeper with a stick or a weapon, that tree, bush, or creeper would not be able to grow further; in the same way, when wholesome kamma is yielding its result and is oppressed by unwholesome kamma, or when unwholesome kamma is yielding its result and is oppressed by wholesome kamma, it cannot yield its result. In that context, Sunakkhatta’s unwholesome kamma oppressed his wholesome kamma, and the executioner’s wholesome kamma oppressed his unwholesome kamma.

In Rājagaha, it is said that a man named Vātakāḷaka performed the duty of an executioner for fifty years. Then, people informed the King, 'Your Majesty, Vātakāḷaka is old and can no longer execute thieves.' The King said, 'Remove him from that position.'
110:
The King commanded, 'Remove him from that position of executioner.' The ministers removed him and appointed another person to that position. As long as Vātakāḷaka performed that work of an executioner, he did not have the opportunity to wear new clothes, wear fragrant flowers, eat milk rice, or enjoy anointing and bathing.

Thinking, 'I have lived in a soiled state for a long time,' he ordered his wife, 'Cook milk rice for me.' He had the bathing requisites brought, went to the bathing place, washed his head and bathed, put on new clothes, anointed himself with perfumes, wore flowers, and while returning home, he saw the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. With a joyful heart, thinking, 'I have been freed from my soiled work, and I have also seen the Noble One,' he invited the Thera to his house and served him with milk rice prepared with fresh ghee and sugar powder. The Thera gave him a talk of appreciation (anumodanā). Having heard the appreciation, he attained the knowledge of conformable patience (anulomika-khanti). While escorting the Thera and returning, he was gored by a cow with a young calf on the way, met his end, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

The monks asked the Blessed One, 'Venerable Sir, the executioner was freed from his soiled work only today and passed away today. Where has he been reborn?' 'Monks, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,' He replied. 'Venerable Sir, that executioner killed people for a long time, yet You say this. Is there no fruit of evil kamma?' they asked again. 'Monks, do not say so. Having obtained the support of a powerful good friend, having offered alms-food to the General of the Dhamma, and having heard the talk of appreciation, he attained the knowledge of conformable patience and was thus reborn in that heaven,' He said.

Having heard the well-spoken Dhamma,
The executioner of the city (of Rājagaha),
Having attained conformable patience,
Reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and rejoices.

Upaghātaka-kamma (destructive kamma), whether wholesome or unwholesome itself, kills another weak kamma, prevents its result, and makes an opportunity for its own result. When an opportunity is thus made by kamma, that resultant is said to be 'arisen' (uppanna). Upacchedaka is also a name for this same kamma. In this regard, there is this method: when a wholesome kamma is about to yield its result, an unwholesome kamma arises, cuts off that kamma, and strikes it down. Also, when an unwholesome kamma is about to yield its result, a wholesome kamma arises, cuts off that kamma, and strikes it down. This is called upacchedaka-kamma. Among such destructive kammas, the kamma of King Ajātasattu...
111:
King Ajātasattu's unwholesome kamma was kusalacchedaka-kamma, which cuts off wholesome kamma, and the Elder Angulimāla's wholesome kamma was akusalacchedaka-kamma, which cuts off unwholesome kamma. Thus, according to the Suttanta method, kamma is classified into eleven types. According to the Abhidhamma method, however, kamma is classified into sixteen types, namely: Some evil, unwholesome kammas are hindered by the perfection of destination (gati-sampatti) and do not ripen. Some evil, unwholesome kammas are hindered by the perfection of physical form (upadhi-sampatti) and do not ripen. Some evil, unwholesome kammas are hindered by the perfection of time (kāla-sampatti) and do not ripen. Some evil, unwholesome kammas are hindered by the perfection of effort (payoga-sampatti) and do not ripen. Some evil, unwholesome kammas ripen due to the failure of destination (gati-vipatti). They ripen due to the failure of physical form, the failure of time, and the failure of effort. Some good, wholesome kammas are hindered by the failure of destination and do not ripen. They do not ripen due to the failure of physical form, the failure of time, and the failure of effort. Some good, wholesome kammas ripen due to the perfection of destination. They ripen due to the perfection of physical form, the perfection of time, and the perfection of effort.

In that text, 'pāpakāni' means evil kammas. 'Kamma-samādānāni' means the undertaking of kamma. It is a name for kammas that have been undertaken. In the phrases such as 'gati-sampatti-paṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti', it means that even though there exists unwholesome kamma deserving of experiencing unpleasant objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), for one born in a happy destination, that unwholesome kamma does not ripen because it is hindered by the perfection of destination. It does not ripen because it is obstructed by gati-sampatti. Suppose a person, due to unwholesome kamma, is born in the womb of a slave woman or a female laborer, yet is endowed with physical beauty and possesses a perfect body. Then, the masters, seeing the perfection of that person's form, think, 'This person is not suitable for dirty work,' and having developed such a thought, they treat them like their own son, place them in positions such as treasurer and provide them with prosperity. The unwholesome kamma of such a person is said not to ripen because it is hindered by upadhi-sampatti. Suppose a person is born in a time of abundance (subhikkha-kāla) with easily available and delicious food, similar to the time of the first aeon; the unwholesome kamma existing in that person is said not to ripen because it is hindered by kāla-sampatti. Suppose a person lives by relying on right effort (sammā-payoga); they approach when it is time to approach, they withdraw when it is time to withdraw, they flee when it is time to flee. They give a bribe when it is time to give a bribe, and when it is time for theft...
112:
...even if they commit theft, the unwholesome kamma of such a person is said to be unable to ripen because it is hindered by the perfection of effort (payoga-sampatti). However, the unwholesome kamma of one born in a miserable destination is said to ripen due to the failure of destination (gati-vipatti). One born in the womb of a slave woman or a female laborer may be ugly and of poor physique, causing others to doubt, "Is this a yakkha or a human?" If that person is a man, they are considered unsuitable for other work and are made to look after elephants, horses, or oxen, or to carry grass and wood, or to hold a spittoon. If it is a woman, she is made to cook rice and beans for the elephants and horses, etc., or to throw away rubbish, or is made to do other disgusting work. The unwholesome kamma of such a person is said to ripen due to the failure of physical form (upadhi-vipatti). The unwholesome kamma of one born during a time of famine, a time of declining prosperity, or during an intermediate aeon (antara-kappa) is said to ripen due to the failure of time (kāla-vipatti). The unwholesome kamma of one who does not know how to accomplish effort, who does not know how to approach when it is time to approach... who does not know how to steal when it is time to steal, is said to ripen due to the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti).

Even if there is wholesome kamma deserving of experiencing desirable objects, for one who has gone to a miserable destination, that wholesome kamma is said to be unable to ripen because it is hindered by the failure of destination (gati-vipatti). Even if one is born in the house of a king or a great minister due to the power of merit, if they are blind, deformed in hands or feet, lame, or paralyzed, they are not given positions such as crown prince, general, or treasurer, being told it is unsuitable for them. Thus, the merit of that person is said to be unable to ripen because it is hindered by the failure of physical form (upadhi-vipatti). The wholesome kamma of one born among humans during a time of famine, a time of declining prosperity, or during an intermediate aeon is said to be unable to ripen because it is hindered by the failure of time (kāla-vipatti). As mentioned above, the wholesome kamma of one who does not know how to accomplish effort is said to be unable to ripen because it is hindered by the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti). However, for one born in a happy destination due to wholesome kamma, that kamma is said to ripen due to the perfection of destination (gati-sampatti). Being born in the family of a king or a great minister and with the perfection of physical form (upadhi-sampatti)...
113:
When one attains physical perfection and is established in the fulfillment of the physical body, seeing a physical body like a jeweled archway well-erected in a celestial city, people think, "The positions of sub-king, general, treasurer, and so forth are suitable for this person," and even while he is young, they grant him those positions such as sub-king, general, and treasurer. The meritorious kamma of such a person is said to ripen by depending on physical perfection (upadhi-sampatti). For one who is born in the beginning of an aeon or in a time when food and drink are easily obtainable, his meritorious kamma is said to ripen by depending on the perfection of time (kāla-sampatti). For one who knows how to fulfill effort (payoga) in the manner already described, his wholesome kamma is said to ripen by depending on the perfection of effort (payoga-sampatti). In this way, sixteen types of kamma are analyzed according to the Abhidhamma method.

Furthermore, twelve types of kamma are analyzed according to the Paṭisambhidāmagga method. What are these twelve? They are: "There was kamma, there was kamma-result. There was kamma, there was no kamma-result. There was kamma, there is kamma-result. There was kamma, there is no kamma-result. There was kamma, there will be kamma-result. There was kamma, there will be no kamma-result. There is kamma, there is kamma-result. There is kamma, there is no kamma-result. There is kamma, there will be kamma-result. There is kamma, there will be no kamma-result. There will be kamma, there will be kamma-result. There will be kamma, there will be no kamma-result."

Among those twelve types of kamma, the kamma that was performed in a past life and obtained its turn for fruition in that very past life—where the kamma producing rebirth-linking produced rebirth-linking, and the kamma producing matter produced matter—is called "There was kamma, there was kamma-result." The kamma that did not obtain its turn for fruition, where the kamma producing rebirth-linking or the kamma producing matter was unable to produce rebirth-linking or matter, is called "There was kamma, there was no kamma-result." The kamma that was performed in a past life and, having obtained its turn for fruition in the present life, exists having produced rebirth-linking and matter, is called "There was kamma, there is kamma-result." The kamma that did not obtain its turn for fruition and was unable to produce rebirth-linking or matter is called "There was kamma, there is no kamma-result." The kamma that was performed in a past life and will obtain its turn for fruition in a future life, being able to produce rebirth-linking and matter, is called "There was kamma, there will be kamma-result." The kamma that will not obtain its turn for fruition in a future life and will be unable to produce rebirth-linking or matter is called "There was kamma, there will be no kamma-result."
114:
The kamma performed in this present life that obtains its turn for fruition in this very present life is called "There is kamma, there is kamma-result." The kamma that does not obtain its turn for fruition in this present life is called "There is kamma, there is no kamma-result." The kamma performed in this present life that will obtain its turn for fruition in a future life, being able to produce rebirth-linking and matter, is called "There is kamma, there will be kamma-result." The kamma that will not obtain its turn for fruition and will be unable to produce rebirth-linking or matter is called "There is kamma, there will be no kamma-result."

The kamma that will be performed in a future life and will obtain its turn for fruition in that very future life, producing rebirth-linking and matter, is called "There will be kamma, there will be kamma-result." The kamma that will not obtain its turn for fruition and will be unable to produce rebirth-linking or matter is called "There will be kamma, there will be no kamma-result." In this way, twelve types of kamma are analyzed according to the Paṭisambhidāmagga method.

Thus, these twelve types and the sixteen types analyzed according to the Abhidhamma method, when moved from their respective positions, become only the eleven types of kamma taught according to the Suttanta method. Those eleven types, when further reduced, become only three types of kamma: kamma to be experienced in this life (diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya), kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajja-vedanīya), and kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariya-vedanīya). There is no shifting among these; they remain fixed in their respective places. For if diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya kamma could become upapajja-vedanīya or aparāpariya-vedanīya, the Teacher would not have said "diṭṭhe vā dhamme" (in this very life). If upapajja-vedanīya could become diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya or aparāpariya-vedanīya, the Teacher would not have said "upapajja vā" (in the next birth). And if aparāpariya-vedanīya could become diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya or upapajja-vedanīya, the Teacher would not have said "apare vā pariyāye" (in a subsequent sequence).

In the case of the bright side (sukkapakkha), the meaning should be understood in this same way. Here, "lobhe vigate" means when greed is gone or has ceased. "Tālavatthukataṃ" means made like a palmyra stump; the meaning is made to have the nature of not being able to grow again, like a palmyra tree with its top cut off. "Anabhāvaṃ kataṃ" means made non-existent; the meaning is made so that it does not arise again. "Evassu" means they should be thus. In the phrase "evameva kho," just like seeds...
115:
Wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be regarded as seeds. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be regarded as the man who burns those seeds with fire, and Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) should be regarded as the fire. The time of killing (burning) the defilements (kilesas) with Path Knowledge should be understood as the time of burning the seeds by applying fire. The time when the five aggregates are kept with their roots severed should be understood as the time when they are turned into ink (ashes). Just as seeds are winnowed in a great wind or carried away by a river so that they do not arise again, the five aggregates, whose roots are severed by the cessation of the continuity of the grasped (upādinnaka-santāna), cease to exist without rebirth-linking and should be known as the time when they do not take rebirth in a new existence again.

"Mohajañcāpavidassu" means one who does not know the kamma born of delusion. The meaning is: that ignorant fool performs kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion. In doing so, whether the kamma he has performed is little or much, that fool experiences that kamma in this very life (attabhāva). It means it ripens for him in this very existence. There is no other basis (vatthu) for the ripening of that kamma. This is because kamma performed by one person cannot ripen in the existence of another. Therefore, in the phrase "Tasmā lobhañca dosañca, mohajañcāpi vidassu," the wise person who knows cause and effect does not perform such kamma born of greed and so on. That monk, producing knowledge (vijjā, i.e., the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship), abandons all woeful states (duggati). By producing the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, he abandons all woeful states. This is stated as the climax of the teaching. In reality, that Arahant (khīṇāsava) also abandons happy states (sugati). Regarding the phrase "Tasmā lobhañca dosañca," it should be understood that it refers specifically to kamma born of greed and kamma born of hatred, with greed and hatred as the primary factors. Thus, in the Suttas and in the verses, only the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 5. Hatthakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Āḷaviyaṃ" means in the kingdom of Āḷavī. "Gomagge" means on a path traveled by cattle. "Paṇṇasanthare" means on a spread of leaves that have fallen naturally. "Atha" means while the Tathāgata was sitting in the cross-legged posture, having spread out His noble robe on a bed made by gathering leaves that had fallen naturally in a Siṃsapā forest near the main cattle path. "Hatthako Āḷavako" is the prince of Āḷavī who received this name because he was passed from hand to hand. "Etadavoca" means he addressed [the Buddha] saying, "Venerable Sir, is the Blessed One..." and so on.
116:
He addressed [the Buddha] with the words, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One," and so on. But why did the Fully Enlightened One go to that place and sit there, and why did the prince go there? First, the Fully Enlightened One sat there having seen the occasion for the arising of a Dhamma teaching. The prince, having risen early in the morning and being surrounded by five hundred lay followers (upāsakas), was going to attend upon the Buddha. Leaving the main road and taking the cattle path, he thought, "I will pick various flowers to worship the Buddha." While going, he saw the Teacher, approached Him, paid homage, and sat at one side. This is how he arrived at that place. "Sukhamasayitthā" means "Did you sleep happily?"

"Antaraṭṭhaka" refers to the period of eight days between the months of Māgha and Phagguṇa. The last four days of Māgha and the first four days of Phagguṇa are called "Antaraṭṭhaka." "Himapātasamaya" is the time of snowfall. "Kharā" means rough or harsh. "Gokaṇṭakahatā" refers to how, when it has recently rained, mud rises between the hooves where cattle tread. When that mud dries due to wind and sun, it becomes like saw teeth and is painful to the touch. Referring to this, He said, "Gokaṇṭakahatā bhūmi" (ground damaged by cattle hooves). It also means ground cut by the gaps between cattle hooves. "Verambho vāto vāyati" means the wind blows from all four directions. A wind blowing from one, two, or three directions is not called a Verambha wind.

Regarding the words "Tena hi rājakumāra," the Teacher said this intending, "This prince does not yet know who lives happily and who lives miserably in the world; I will make him know," and thus continued the teaching. Therein, "Yathā te khameyya" means as it would please you. "Idhassa" means it would be for him in this world. "Gonakatthatā" means spread with a black wool rug with hair longer than four inches. "Paṭikatthatā" means spread with a white wool coverlet. "Paṭalikatthatā" means spread with a wool coverlet embroidered with thick flowers. "Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo" means spread with an excellent rug made of Kadali-deer skin. It is said that such rugs are made by placing Kadali-deer skin over white cloth and sewing them together. "Sauttaracchado" means together with a red canopy fastened above. "Ubhatolohitakūpadhāno" means having red pillows placed at both ends of the couch, at the head and at the feet. "Pajāpatiyo" means wives.
117:
"Mānāpena paccupaṭṭhitā assu" means they should be present with a pleasing arrangement of service.

"Kāyikā" means agitating the collection of consciousness occurring in the five doors; "cetasikā" means agitating the mind-door. "The Tathāgata has abandoned that lust" means the Tathāgata has abandoned lust of such a nature. It does not mean that the lust present in that householder's son was abandoned by the Tathāgata. The same method should be understood regarding hatred and delusion.

"Brāhmaṇo" refers to the Arahant Brahmin who has put away evil and whose taints (āsavas) are exhausted. "Parinibbuto" means one who is extinguished through the Nibbāna of defilements. "Does not cling to sensual pleasures" means not clinging by way of the smears of craving and views to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). "Sītibhūto" means one who has become cool due to the absence of the defilements that cause burning within. "Nirūpadhi" means one who is without acquisitions due to the absence of the acquisitions of defilements.

In the phrase "having cut off all attachments," cravings are called attachments (āsatti). It means having cut off all those cravings that are variously attached to objects such as forms, etc. "Having dispelled the distress in the heart" means having dispelled and calmed the distress (daratha) based in the heart. "Having reached the peace of the mind" means having reached the Nibbāna of the mind's defilements. Alternatively, as in the Pali passages such as "sabbacetaso samannāharitvā," the word "cetasa" is taken as the instrumental case, meaning having reached Nibbāna with the mind.

## 6. Devadūtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "devadūtāni" refers to the divine messengers (devadūta). Here is the word-definition: "Deva" means Death (Maccu); the messengers of that Death are "devadūta." Indeed, because they produce spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the old, the sick, and the dead are called divine messengers because they seem to urge one, saying, "Now you must go near to Death."

They are also called divine messengers because they are messengers like gods. For example, just as the word of an adorned deity standing in the sky saying, "You will die on such and such a day," should be believed, so too, when seeing the old, the sick, and the dead, it is as if they are urging, "You too are of such a nature." Because their word is unfailing, it is like the prophecy of a deity; thus they are called divine messengers. 

They are also called divine messengers because they are messengers of the Gods of Purity (Visuddhi-deva). All Bodhisattas, only after seeing the old, the sick, the dead, and the monk, were struck with spiritual urgency, went forth, and became monks. In this way, they are also called divine messengers because they are messengers of the Gods of Purity. In this sutta, however, "devadūtāni" is used with a change of gender.
118:
Why did the Blessed One begin the discourse with "conducted himself badly in body," and so on? It was for the purpose of showing the kamma that is the cause for the interrogation regarding the divine messengers. Indeed, because of this kamma, this being is reborn in hell; then King Yama interrogates him regarding the divine messengers. In that passage, "conducted himself badly in body" means practicing the threefold misconduct through the body-door. "In speech" means practicing the fourfold misconduct through the speech-door. "In mind" means practicing the threefold misconduct through the mind-door.

Monks, in this phrase "the wardens of hell (nirayapālā) [take] him," some elders say, "There are no such things as wardens of hell; kamma itself, like a machine, inflicts the punishment." That view has already been refuted in the Abhidhamma (Kathāvatthu) by the method starting with: "Are there wardens of hell in hell? Yes. And are there punishers? Yes." Just as there are executioners and such who inflict punishment in the human world, so too there are wardens of hell in hell. In the phrase "of King Yama (yamassa rañño)," King Yama is a king of the mansion-dwelling ghosts (vimānika-peta). At one time he enjoys all prosperity such as celestial mansions, celestial wish-fulfilling trees, celestial gardens, and celestial dancers; at another time he experiences the result of unwholesome kamma. He is a righteous king. And he is not just one; there are four individuals at the four gates. "Amatteyya" means one who benefits the mother is called "matteyya," meaning one who treats the mother rightly. One who does not treat the mother rightly is "amatteyya," meaning one who treats the mother wrongly. This same method applies to the remaining terms. In the word "abrahmañña," Arahants are called "brāhmaṇa," and one who treats those Arahants wrongly is called "abrahmañña."

"Samanuyuñjati" means asking while performing the duty of interrogation. Asking to establish a view is called "samanuggāhati," and asking for the reason is called "samanubhāsati." The phrase "I did not see" is said with reference to the absence of any divine messenger sent to him personally.

Then King Yama, knowing "This person does not perceive the meaning of what is spoken," and wishing him to perceive the meaning, said "Ambho" and so on. In those words, "jiṇṇa" means worn out by old age. "Gopānasivaṅka" means crooked like a roof-rafter. "Bhōgga" means broken. By this word "bhōgga," the crookedness of his body is also indicated. "Daṇḍaparāyaṇa" means having a staff as a support, having a staff as a second. "Pavedhamāna" means trembling. "Ātura" means afflicted by old age. "Khaṇḍadanta" means having broken teeth due to the power of old age. "Palitakesa" means having grey hair. "Vilūna" means being as if the hair has been plucked out.
119: It is like a bald person. Khalitasiiraṃ means having a very bald head. Valitaṃ means wrinkled skin. Tilakāhatagattaṃ means having a body mottled with white and black spots. Jarādhamma means being subject to aging, not being free from aging. It means that aging occurs within oneself. The same logic applies to the subsequent terms byādhidhamma (subject to sickness) and maraṇadhamma (subject to death). In the context of 'having questioned the first divine messenger' (paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvā), an aged being essentially says this: 'Friends, look at me; I too was once young like you, possessed of strength in my thighs and arms, and full of speed. Those strengths and speeds of mine have vanished. Although I have hands and feet, they can no longer perform their functions. I have become like this because I am not free from aging. Not only I, but you too are not free from aging. Just as aging has come to me, so it will come to you. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds even before that aging arrives.' For this reason, this aging is called a divine messenger (devadūta). Ābādhika means afflicted with illness; dukkhita means fallen into suffering; bāḷhagilāna means severely ill. In the context of 'the second divine messenger' (dutiyaṃ devadūtaṃ), a sick being essentially says this: 'Friends, look at me; I too was once free from disease like you.
