Now, however, I am oppressed by disease, wallowing in my own excrement and urine, unable even to stand up. Although I have hands and feet, they can no longer perform their functions. I have become like this because I am not free from disease. Not only I, but you too are not free from disease. Just as disease has come to me, so it will come to you. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds even before that disease arrives.' For this reason, this sickness is called a divine messenger (devadūta). Regarding terms like ekāhamataṃ, one who has been dead for one day is called ekāhamata. The same logic applies to the next two terms. It is called uddhumātaka (bloated) because, like a leather bag filled with air, it becomes progressively swollen after life has ended. A corpse that is discolored and has a dark-blue hue due to the mixing of various colors is called vinīla; that vinīla itself is called vinīlaka. Alternatively, because it is loathsome, having a loathsome dark-blue color is called vinīlaka. Vipubbaka means festering with pus; it refers to a corpse smeared with pus oozing from ruptured places.
120: In this passage, 'the third divine messenger' (tatiyaṃ devadūtaṃ), a deceased being essentially says this: 'Friends, look at me, cast away in a charnel ground, having reached the state of being bloated and so forth after death. I have come to such a state because I am not free from death. Indeed, not only I, but you too are not free from death. Just as death has come to me, so death will come to you. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds in the time before that death arrives.' For this reason, that nature of death is called the messenger of Death. Regarding these divine messengers, who receives questioning and who does not? He who has first committed much evil goes directly to hell. But he who has committed only a little evil receives questioning (regarding the divine messengers). For example, just as when a thief is caught with stolen goods, no judgment is made and the king's punishment is simply carried out; but a person caught after investigation is taken to the place of judgment and receives a trial—this example should be understood as applicable here. Those with a small amount of evil karma can remember [their good deeds] by their own nature, or they can remember when prompted by others. Among them, a Damila man named Dīghajayanta was able to remember by his own nature. That Damila man had offered a red cloth to the Akāsacetiya at the Sumanagiri Monastery. Later, when he was reborn in the vicinity of the Ussada hell and heard the sound of the hell-flames, he remembered the cloth he had offered and went to be reborn in heaven. Another person, when donating a hemmed cloth to his young monk son, placed it at his feet. At the time of death, he took as an object the 'paṭa-paṭa' sound of the cloth. While being reborn near the Ussada hell, he remembered that cloth because of the sound of the flames and was reborn in heaven. In this way, by remembering wholesome karma by one's own nature, one is reborn in heaven. As for those who cannot remember by their own nature, they are questioned about the three divine messengers. Among them, some can remember through the first divine messenger, some through the second or third, and some cannot remember even through all three. Seeing such a person who cannot remember, King Yama himself prompts them to remember. It is said that an official, having offered a jar of jasmine flowers to the Mahācetiya, shared the merit with King Yama. Due to unwholesome karma, when that official was reborn in hell, they brought him before King Yama. When that official could not remember his merit even when questioned about the three divine messengers, King Yama himself looked and saw it, saying, 'Did you not offer a jar of jasmine flowers to the Mahācetiya and share the merit with me?' Thus he prompted him to remember. At that time, the official remembered and [went] to the celestial realm...
121:
(That minister) has gone (to the celestial realm). King Yama, even looking himself, did not see (any merit) and remained silent, thinking, "This being will indeed experience great suffering."

"Tattaṃ ayokhilaṃ" means they make the being lie on their back on a burning iron ground that is three gāvutas in size, and drive an iron stake the size of a palm tree into the right hand; likewise into the left hand and so on. Just as they make the being lie on their back and drive stakes, they also do so while making them lie on their chest, on their left side, and on their right side, performing that torture.

"Saṃvesetvā" means making the three-gāvuta body lie on the burning iron ground.

"Kuṭhārīhi" means they chop with axes as large as one side of a house roof; blood flows like a river, and flames rising from the iron ground burn the chopped places, causing great suffering. When chopping, they mark with a string as if marking wood and chop them into eight-sided or six-sided shapes.

"Vāsīhi" means (chopping) with adzes the size of a large winnowing basket.

"Rathe yojetvā" means yoking them to a chariot that is burning from all directions, along with the yoke, ropes, wheels, axle, and goad (and making them pull it).

"Mahantaṃ" means (a mountain of fire) the size of a large pinnacled house.

"Āropenti" means they make them climb while beating them with burning iron clubs.

"Sakimpi uddhaṃ" means having to go up, down, and across like rice grains placed in a well-boiling pot.

"Mahāniraye" means it occurs in the Avīci Great Hell.

"Bhāgaso mito" means divided and arranged into sections.

"Pariyanto" means surrounded on all sides.

"Ayasā" means covered from above with iron plates. That hell exists spreading for a hundred yojanas all around; it exists spreading so much that the eyes of a person standing a hundred yojanas away and looking at it would bulge out like gamboge seeds.

"Hīnakāyūpagā" means having reached a low group (or) body.

"Upādāne" means in the clinging through craving and views.

"Jātimaraṇasambhave" means (in the clingings) which are the cause of rebirth and death.

"Anupādā" means without clinging through the four types of clinging.

"Jātimaraṇasaṅkhaye" means they are liberated in Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and death.

"Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā" means they are cooled by the extinguishing of all defilements in this very life.

"Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccaguṃ" means they have transcended the entire suffering of the round of rebirth.
122:
## 7. Commentary on the Catumahārāja Sutta

In the seventh sutta, 'amaccā pārisajjā' refers to the attendant deities. 'They wander through this world' means that on the eighth day, Sakka, the King of Devas, commands the Four Great Kings: "Dear friends, today on the eighth day, wander through the human world and return after recording the names and clans of those who perform meritorious deeds." Those Great Kings go and send their own attendants: "Go, dear friends, wander through the human world and return after writing the names and clans of the merit-makers on golden plates." They do accordingly. Therefore, it is said, "They wander through this world." The words beginning with 'kacci bahū' are said to show the manner of their investigation. Thus investigating, they wander.

In that context, 'uposathaṃ upavasanti' means they undertake the factors of the Uposatha eight times a month. 'Paṭijāgaronti' means they perform the act of the Patijāgara (preparatory) Uposatha. In doing so, they perform it by way of welcoming and seeing off the four Uposatha days in one fortnight. Welcoming the fifth-day Uposatha, they observe Uposatha on the fourth day; seeing it off, they observe it on the sixth day. Welcoming the eighth-day Uposatha, they observe it on the seventh day; seeing it off, they observe it on the ninth day. Welcoming the fourteenth-day Uposatha, they observe it on the thirteenth day; seeing off the fifteenth-day Uposatha, they observe Uposatha on the first day of the next fortnight.

'Puṇyāni karonti' means they perform various meritorious deeds such as taking refuge, observing the permanent precepts (nicca-sīla), offering flowers, listening to the Dhamma, lighting a thousand lamps, and building monasteries. Having wandered thus, those deities write the names and clans of the merit-makers on golden plates and, having brought them, give them to the Four Great Kings. 'Puttā imaṃ lokaṃ anuvicaranti' means that the sons (of the Four Great Kings) wander because they are sent by the Four Great Kings in the same manner as before. 'Tadahu' means on that day. 'Uposathe' means on the Uposatha day.

"Monks, if (merit-makers) are few" means the ministers and attendants of the Four Great Kings approach various villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Then, the deities residing in those places, thinking "The ministers of the Great Kings have arrived," take gifts and go to them. Those [ministers] take the gifts and ask about the meritorious practice of humans in the manner stated: "Friends, are many humans respectful and supportive of their parents?" and so on. When it is said, "Yes, friends, in this village, such and such persons perform meritorious deeds," they record their names and clans...
123:
They go (to the presence of those Great Kings). Then, on the fourteenth day, the sons of the Four Great Kings also take that same gold plate and, wandering in the same manner, record the names and clans. On that fifteenth day, the Uposatha day, the Four Great Kings themselves also record the names and clans on that same gold plate in the same manner. By the extent of the records on that gold plate, those Great Kings know: "At this time, humans (who perform merit) are few; at this time, they are many." With reference to this knowledge, the Blessed One said: "Monks, if humans are few..." and so forth.

"Devānaṃ Tāvatiṃsānaṃ" (of the Tāvatiṃsa devas) refers to those who obtained this name based on the thirty-three young devas who first arose there. The story of their origin has been explained in detail in the Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya. "Tena" (by that) means either because of hearing such news or because of the scarcity of those performing merit. "Friends, the celestial hosts will decline" means that because new young devas are no longer appearing, the celestial hosts will diminish, and the delightful celestial city, ten thousand yojanas in extent, will become empty. "The hosts of Asuras will be filled" means that the four lower realms will be filled. Because the celestial city would be empty and the lower realms filled, they become displeased, thinking, "We shall not get the opportunity to celebrate the festival in the midst of the celestial assembly in a full celestial city." In the same manner, the meaning should be understood regarding the Sukkapakkha (the bright fortnight) when those performing merit are many.

"Monks, in the past, Sakka, the lord of devas..."—this was spoken by the Buddha with reference to the time when he himself was Sakka, the king of devas. Or, it is said that he spoke by taking the inclination of a certain Sakka. "Anunayamāno" means making them understand properly. "Tāyaṃ velāyaṃ" means at the time of making them so understand.

In the phrase "pāṭihāriyapakkhañca," what is called Pāṭihāriyapakkha is the Uposatha observed continuously for the three months of the rains retreat (vassa). For one who is unable to observe it for three months, it is the Uposatha observed continuously for one month between the two Pavāraṇā ceremonies (the full moon of Assayuja and Kattika). For one who cannot observe it even for that month, the period of one and a half months starting from the first Pavāraṇā is also called Pāṭihāriyapakkha. "Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ" means being endowed with the eight factors of virtue. "Yopissa mādiso naro" means if any being were of a nature like mine. It is said that Sakka, knowing the merit of the aforementioned Uposatha practice, would renounce the two types of celestial splendor and observe the Uposatha eight times a month. Therefore, he spoke thus. Another way: "Yopissa mādiso naro" means if any being were of such a nature, desiring to attain the prosperity I have attained...
124:
...meaning he desires to reach the prosperity already attained by me. The intention here is that by performing such Uposatha deeds, one can attain the prosperity of Sakka.

"Vusitavā" means one who has lived the holy life. "Katakaraṇīyo" means one who has completed what was to be done through the four paths (magga). "Ohitabhāro" means one who has laid down the burden—the burden of the aggregates (khandha), the burden of defilements (kilesa), and the burden of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). "Anuppattasadattho" means one who has successively attained his own goal, which is the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). "Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano" means one whose fetters of existence are destroyed, because the fetters that bind and pull one toward existences have been exhausted. "Sammadññā vimutto" means one who is liberated through knowing by way of cause and reason. "Kallaṃ vacanāya" means it is proper to say.

"A man such as I" means if there were an Arahant like me, he too would observe such an Uposatha; thus he would speak, knowing the virtue of the Uposatha practice. Alternatively, "a man such as I" means if any being were like me, he would desire to attain the prosperity I have attained. The intention here is that through such Uposatha practice, one can attain the prosperity of the Arahants. The eighth sutta is clear in its meaning.

## 9. Sukhumālasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "sukhumālo" means one free from suffering. "Paramasukhumālo" means one who is exceedingly free from suffering. "Accantasukhumālo" means one who is perpetually free from suffering. The Blessed One spoke this by taking the state of being free from suffering from the time of his birth in the city of Kapilavatthu; however, during the time he was fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), there was no end to the suffering experienced by the Bodhisatta. "Ekatthā" means in one pond. "Uppalaṃ vappati" means he plants lotuses. That pond is covered with a grove of blue lotuses (nīluppala). "Padumaṃ" refers to the white lotus (paṇḍarapaduma). "Puṇḍarīkaṃ" refers to the red lotus (rattapaduma). In this manner, the other two ponds are also covered with groves of paduma and puṇḍarīka lotuses.

It is said that when the Bodhisatta was seven or eight years old, the King asked his ministers: "What kind of play do young boys enjoy?" They replied, "Your Majesty, they enjoy playing in the water." Then the King assembled the spade-workers and had them clear sites for ponds. At that time, Sakka, the king of devas, reflecting on the matter and knowing the situation, thought: "Human use is not suitable for the Great Being (Mahāsatta); only celestial use is suitable." He then called the celestial architect Vissakamma and said: "Go, dear friend, and create ponds in the Great Being's playground." As for what kind...
125:
“O King of Devas, what should be the nature of the ponds?” (asked the celestial son Vissakamma). (Sakka replied,) “Let there be ponds free from mud and mire, with scattered gems, pearls, and corals, surrounded by walls made of the seven precious gems, and endowed with stairways having coral banisters, gem-encrusted railings, and steps made of gold, silver, and gems. Let there also be boats made of gold, silver, gems, and corals in these ponds. In a golden boat, let there be a silver couch; in a silver boat, a golden couch; in a gem boat, a coral couch; and in a coral boat, a gem couch. Let there be water-pouring vessels made of gold, silver, gems, and corals. Let them also be covered with five-colored lotuses.” Vissakamma, the celestial son, replied, “Very well, O King,” and acknowledging Sakka’s command, he descended during the night and created the ponds in that very manner at the sites designated by the King.

How did the lotuses bloom in these ponds since they were free from mud and mire? It is said that Vissakamma created small boats made of gold, silver, gems, and corals in various places within those ponds and made a resolution: “Let these small boats be filled with mud and mire, and let five-colored lotuses bloom here.” Thus, the five-colored lotuses bloomed. Clusters of pollen rose up and spread over the surface of the water. Swarms of five kinds of bees flew about humming. Having thus created the ponds, Vissakamma returned to the celestial realm. When the night had passed and dawn broke, the people saw them and thought, “These must have been created for the Great Being,” and they informed the King. The King, surrounded by a great crowd, went to see the ponds and was delighted, thinking, “These must have been created by the deities due to the power of my son’s merit.” From then on, the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) went there for water sports.

In the phrase “Yāvadeva mamatthāya,” “yāvadeva” is a term defining the limit of purpose. It means “only for my benefit; there is no other reason here.” The phrase “Na kho panassāhaṃ” should be broken down as “Na kho pana assa ahaṃ.” “Akāsikaṃ candanaṃ” refers to coarse sandalwood (not from the Kāsī region). “Kāsikaṃ, bhikkhave, su me taṃ veṭhanaṃ” means “Monks, that turban of mine was also well-made in the Kāsī region.” Here, “su” and “taṃ” are merely particles, and “me” is the genitive case showing possession. It shows that his turban was indeed fine and delicate. “Kāsikā kañcukā” means the upper garment worn was also a fine garment. “Setacchattaṃ dhārīyati” means that a white umbrella, whether human or divine, was held over him. “Mā naṃ phusi sītaṃ” means “Let not cold touch (or afflict) this Bodhisatta.” Regarding heat and so forth...
126:
...it means “Let not cold, or any other thing such as heat, afflict this Bodhisatta.”

“There were three palaces” means that when the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen, King Suddhodana thought, “I shall have palaces built as residences for my son.” He gathered craftsmen and, at an auspicious astrological moment, had the new site prepared and three palaces constructed. It is in reference to these palaces that this was said. In the terms such as “Hemantika,” the palace in which it is pleasant to live during the winter is called “Hemantika” (the winter palace). The same principle applies to the other palaces. The etymological meaning here is: “Hemante vāso hemantaṃ” (dwelling in winter is ‘hemanta’); because it is suitable for dwelling in winter, it is called “Hemantika.” The same applies to the other terms.

Among them, the Hemantika palace had nine stories. Its floors were low to capture and retain heat. The main doors and windows had well-fitted shutters with no gaps. Those performing the artwork painted images of blazing masses of fire in various places. The floor coverings here were made of wool; likewise, the curtains, canopies, clothing, wraps, and turbans were made of wool. The windows were kept open during the day to let in heat and closed at night.

The Gimhika (summer) palace had five stories. To capture coolness, the floors were high and spacious. The main doors and windows were not tightly fitted, having gaps and nets. In the artwork, only red, white, and blue lotuses were painted. The floor coverings here were made of fine cloth (dukūla); likewise, the curtains, canopies, clothing, wraps, and turbans were made of fine cloth. Near the windows of this palace, new pots were placed, filled with water, and covered with blue lotuses and the like. Water machines were installed in various places, from which streams of water flowed out as if it were raining. Inside the palace, troughs filled with mud were placed in various spots, and five-colored lotuses were planted in them. On top of the palace, dried buffalo hides were fastened, and a mechanism was turned to carry stones up to the roof and release them onto the hides. The sound of the stones rolling on the hides was like the rumbling of thunder. In this palace, the main doors and windows were kept closed during the day and open at night.
127:
The palace suitable for residing during the rainy season had seven stories. In that palace, the floors were constructed neither too high nor too low so as to maintain a balanced temperature between the two seasons of cold and heat. Some doors and windows were well-fitted and closed (to keep out the wind), while others had openings for ventilation. In certain parts of that palace, exquisite paintings were made in the form of blazing masses of fire, and in other parts, in the form of the five kinds of lotuses found in a lake. In that palace, floor coverings and such were spread with a mixture of woolen blankets and fine white silk cloth. Some doors and windows were opened at night and closed during the day, while others were opened during the day and closed at night. All three palaces were equal in height. However, there were differences in the tiered stories.

When the palaces were thus completed, King Suddhodana thought: "My son has reached maturity; I shall crown him with the white umbrella and behold his royal glory." The King sent messages to the Sakyans: "My son has reached maturity; I shall establish him in the kingship. Let all Sakyans send their daughters who have reached maturity in their respective homes to this son's house." Upon hearing the news, those Sakyans said: "The prince is merely handsome and pleasant to look at, but he knows no art or craft. He will not be able to support a wife. We will not give our daughters." The King, hearing this, went to his son and informed him. The Bodhisatta asked: "Father, what craft should I demonstrate?" The King said: "Dear son, it is fitting to string the bow that has the strength of a thousand men." The Bodhisatta said: "Then let them bring it." The King had it brought and given to him. That bow required a thousand men to string and a thousand men to unstring. The Great Being had the bow brought, and while sitting on his throne, he wound the bowstring around his big toe, pulled it, and strung the bow using only his big toe. Then, holding the bow-staff with his left hand and pulling with his right, he plucked the string. The sound was such that the whole city seemed as if it would fly up. When people asked, "What is this sound?", some said, "It is thunder." Then others said, "You do not know; it is not thunder. It is the sound of the bowstring being plucked by Prince Aṅgīrasa after stringing the bow that has the strength of a thousand men." The Sakyans were satisfied with just that much.

The Great Being asked, "What else should be done?" They said, "It is fitting to pierce an iron plate about eight finger-breadths thick with an arrow." After piercing that iron plate, he asked again, "What else should be done?" They said, "It is fitting to pierce an Asana wood plank four finger-breadths thick." After piercing that Asana wood plank, he asked again, "What else should be done?" A Udumbara wood plank one span thick...
128:
...is fitting to be pierced. After piercing that (Udumbara plank), he asked, "What else should be done?" They said, "It is fitting to pierce a hundred planks bound on a machine." After piercing those hundred planks, he asked, "What else should be done?" They said, "It is fitting to pierce dried buffalo hide sixty layers thick." After piercing that buffalo hide as well, he asked, "What else should be done?" Then they mentioned sand-carts, straw-carts, and so on. The Bodhisatta pierced both the sand-cart and the straw-cart, and shot an arrow to a distance of one usabha in water and eight usabhas on land. Then they said to him, "Now it is fitting to shoot a horsehair using a labu fruit as a mark." He said, "Then let it be tied." He said, "Friends, let it be tied at the distance of a call." Then, "Go further; let it be tied at a distance of one gāvuta." Then, "Go further; let it be tied at a distance of half a yojana." Then, "Go further; let it be tied at a distance of one yojana." He said, "Friends, let it be tied," and after having the horsehair tied with a labu fruit as a mark at a distance of one yojana, he shot an arrow during the night, which was dark and covered with clouds. That arrow went, split the horsehair at the distance of one yojana, and entered the earth. He did not demonstrate only this much craft; on that day, the Bodhisatta showed all the arts and crafts existing in the world. The Sakyan kings adorned their young daughters and sent them; there were forty thousand dancing women. The Great Being, enjoying himself like a king of gods in the three palaces, experienced great prosperity.

"Nippurisehi" means (with musical instruments) devoid of men. Here, it is not only the musical instruments that were devoid of men; all places were devoid of men. Even the door-keepers were only women; those who performed services such as bathing were also only women. The King thought, "If my son, who is enjoying such sovereignty, happiness, and prosperity, sees a man, suspicion might arise; let such suspicion not occur to my son." Thus, he placed only women in all matters of service. "Paricārayamāno" means being delighted. "Na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohāmi" means "I do not descend from the palace." Thus, for four months, no other man with a topknot could see me. "Yathā" means in such a manner. "Dāsakammakara-porisassa" means for the slaves, for the laborers who live on daily rations of food, and for the men who earn a living. "Kaṇājakaṃ" means broken rice. "Bilaṅgadutiyaṃ" means sour gruel as the second (dish).

"Evarūpāya iddhiyā" means (to the Bodhisatta) who is endowed with such power of merit. "Evarūပေန စ သုခုမာလေန" means by such a state of being free from suffering (delicacy).
129:
"Sukhumālena" is also a reading. In this way, the Blessed One spoke of the fulfillment of his own glory and prosperity to this extent. In speaking thus, he did not speak for the purpose of boasting, but for the purpose of illustrating the characteristic of heedfulness (appamāda), saying, "Even while established in such prosperity, I did not become negligent but remained heedful."

Because he wished to show the characteristic of heedfulness, he spoke the words beginning with "Assutavā kho puthujjano" (The uninstructed worldling). In those words, "paraṃ" means another person. "Jiṇṇaṃ" means an aged person. "Aṭṭīyati" means being oppressed (or weary). "Harāyati" means being ashamed or feeling bashful. "Jigucchati" means feeling disgust, seeing it like excrement. "Attānaṃyeva atisitvā" means that although one is oneself subject to aging, one overlooks one's own nature and feels oppressed or ashamed (at another's aging). "Jarādhammo" means having the nature of aging. "Jaraṃ anatīto" means not having transcended the nature of aging, remaining within the sphere of aging. "Iti paṭisañcikkhato" means for one who reflects in this way.

"Yobbanamado" is the intoxication of pride that arises depending on youth. "Sabbaso pahīyi" means it is abandoned in every way. It is shown as if it were abandoned by the Path. However, it should be understood that this intoxication of youth is spoken of as being abandoned through reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna), not by the Path. In truth, the deities showed the aged person to the Bodhisatta. From that time until reaching the Fruit of Arahantship, what is called intoxication with youth (yobbanamado) did not arise in the Great Being during the interval. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (ārogayamado and jīvitamado). Here, "ārogayamado" is the intoxication of pride that arises depending on health, thinking, "I am free from disease." "Jīvitamado" is the intoxication of pride that arises depending on life, thinking, "I shall live long." "Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya" means having renounced the training. "Hīnāyāvattati" means returning to the low state of a householder.

"Yathādhammā" means having such a nature as disease and so forth. "Tathāsantā" means being just as that nature is, having the unerring nature of disease and so forth. "Jigucchanti" means they loathe another person. "Mama evaṃ vihārino" means for me who dwells with such a habit of loathing, such loathing would not be proper or suitable. "Sohaṃ evaṃ viharanto" means that I, while dwelling thus loathing another, or I, while dwelling with such reflective wisdom. "Ñatvā dhammaṃ nirūpadhiṃ" means having known the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is free from all acquisitions (upadhi). "Sabbe made abhibhosmi" means I have conquered and transcended all three types of intoxication. "Nekkhamme daṭṭhu khemataṃ" means seeing the state of safety in Nibbāna. There is also a reading "Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato," meaning seeing Nibbāna as a safe Dhamma.
130:
"Tassa me ahu ussāho" means for me, who was looking towards that Nibbāna called renunciation from the round of suffering, there was exertion (ussāha); it means there was the effort of energy. "Nāhaṃ bhabbo etarahi kāmāni paṭisevituṃ" means I am no longer fit to indulge in the two kinds of sensual pleasures. "Anivatti bhavissāmi" means I shall not turn back from monkhood or from Omniscience; I shall be one who does not turn back. "Brahmacariyaparāyaṇo" means having the Noble Practice of the Path as one's final resort (refuge). Thus, with these verses, he spoke of his energy that leads to the attainment (of the Path-knowledge) at the seat of the Great Enlightenment.

## ၁၀။ အာဓိပတေယျသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the tenth sutta, "ādhipateyyāni" refers to things that arise from a predominant cause. Among the terms such as "attādhipateyya," the collection of virtues that arises by making oneself predominant is called self-sovereignty (attādhipateyya). The collection of virtues that arises by making the world predominant is called world-sovereignty (lokādhipateyya). The collection of virtues that arises by making the ninefold supramundane Dhamma predominant is called Dhamma-sovereignty (dhammādhipateyya). "Na iti bhavābhavahetu" means it is not for the sake of future existence or prosperity, nor for the cause of various types of success in existence (that one becomes a monk). "Otiṇṇo" means entered into or beset. One into whose interior birth (jāti) has entered is called one beset by birth. The same method applies to aging (jarā) and so forth. "Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa" means of the entire mass of suffering in the round of existence. "Antakiriyā paññāyetha" means the making of an end of suffering, the making of a limit or termination, might be known. "Ohāya" means having abandoned. "Pāpiṭṭhatare" means more vile (states). "Āraddhaṃ" means upheld or fulfilled (energy). Because of being aroused, there is no shrinking. "Upaṭṭhitā" means (mindfulness) that stands close to the object by the power of the four foundations of mindfulness. Because of being established, there is no forgetfulness. "Passaddho kāyo" means the calming and allaying of distress in both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (karajakāya). Because of being calmed, there is no agitation. "Samāhitaṃ cittaṃ" means the mind being well-placed on the object. Because of being well-placed, it is one-pointed (ekaggatā). "Adhipatiṃ karitvā" means having made predominant. "Suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharati" means one protects, tends, and guards oneself by making oneself pure and stainless. A monk practicing thus is said to protect himself purely in a figurative sense (pariyāyena) until reaching the Path of Arahantship. However, only one who has reached the Fruit is said to protect himself purely in the literal sense (nippariyāyena). The meanings of terms like "svākkhāto" have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "Jānaṃ passaṃ viharanti" means they dwell knowing and seeing that Dhamma. Monks, these three...
131:
With this term "ādhipateyyāni," the three types of supremacy (adhipati), which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are taught.

"Pakubbato" means of one who acts. "O man, your own self knows whether what you do is true or false" means that whether the nature of your action is true or not true, you yourself know it. For this reason, it should be understood that "for one who commits an evil deed, there is no such thing as a hidden place in the world." "Kalyāṇa" means beautiful (sundara). "Atimanyasi" means thinking excessively. "Attānaṃ parigūhasi" means striving with the thought, "I will hide this evil so that even I myself do not know it."

"Attādhipateyyako" means making oneself supreme. "Lokādhipo" means making the world supreme. "Nipako" means one who is wise. "Jhāyī" means one who burns away defilements (one who enters meditative absorption). "Dhammādhipo" means making the Dhamma supreme. "Saccaparakkamo" means having firm effort, true effort. "Pasayha māraṃ" means having subdued Mara. "Abhibhuyya antakaṃ" is a synonym for that same term. "Yo ca phusī jātikkhayaṃ padhānavā" means that the person with effort who burns away defilements, having subdued and conquered Mara, attains the fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of rebirth. "So tādiso" refers to that person of such a nature, established in such a manner. "Lokavidū" means one who stands having clearly known the three worlds. "Sumedho" means having good wisdom. "The sage (muni) who is unattached to craving in all things" means that because of the absence of being fashioned by that craving—known as "tammayatā"—in all things belonging to the three planes, the Arahant sage called "atammaya" (unaffected) never declines or diminishes in any way or at any place.

## Devadūta Vagga, the Fourth.
## 5. Cūḷa Vagga
## 1. Sammukhībhāva Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, "sammukhībhāvā" means by being present, by being manifest. "Pasavatī" means obtains. In the phrase "saddhāya sammukhībhāvā," if there were no faith, no gift (deyyadhamma), and no recipients known as the worthy ones (dakkhiṇeyya), how could a meritorious deed be performed? It is only because of the presence of those [faith, gift, and recipient] that it can be done. Therefore, it is said, "saddhāya sammukhībhāvā," and so on. Here also...
132:
These two things—the gift and the worthy recipient—are easy to find; however, faith (saddhā) is difficult to find. Indeed, the faith of a worldling (puthujjana) is not stable and changes in various ways with every step. For this reason, even a Great Disciple like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, being unable to provide a guarantee, said: "Friend, I can be a guarantor for you in two things: your wealth and your life; but as for faith, you yourself must be the guarantor."

## 2. Tiṭṭhānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "with the stain of stinginess removed" (vigatamalamacchereṇa) means by being free from the stain of avarice. "Generous" (muttacāgo) means one who has a liberated habit of giving. "Clean-handed" (payatapāṇī) means one whose hands are washed. For a person without faith, even if they wash their hands a hundred times, they still have "dirty hands." However, for a person with faith, because they delight in giving, even if their hands are physically soiled, they are considered to have "washed hands." "Delighting in relinquishment" (vossaggarato) means delighting in giving, which is characterized by relinquishment. "Accessible to requests" (yācayogo) means suitable to be asked, or it means one who is associated with those who ask. "Delighting in giving and sharing" (dānasamvibhāgarato) refers to one who delights in both the act of giving and the act of distributing.

"Desiring to see those possessed of virtue" (dassanakāmo sīlavataṃ) means one who would travel ten leagues, twenty leagues, thirty leagues, or even a hundred leagues to see those perfected in virtue. This is like the brahmin from Pāṭaliputta and King Saddhātissa. It is said that two brahmins staying at a rest house by the city gate of Pāṭaliputta heard of the virtues of the Elder Mahānāga who lived at Kaḷavallimaṇḍapa and discussed, "We ought to see that monk," and both set out. One died along the way. The other reached the seashore, boarded a ship, disembarked at the port of Mahātittha, arrived at Anurādhapura, and asked, "Where is Kaḷavallimaṇḍapa?" He was told, "It is in the Rohaṇa region." Traveling by stages, he reached the Elder's residence, stayed at the main house in the village of Cūḷanagara, prepared food for the Elder, and rising early, asked for the Elder's location and went there. Standing at the edge of the village, he saw the Elder approaching from afar; he bowed once right where he stood, then approached closer, and while bowing firmly grasping the Elder's ankles, he said, "Venerable sir, you are very tall." The Elder was neither too tall nor too short but of moderate proportions. Therefore, the brahmin spoke again, "Venerable sir, though you are not too tall in stature, your virtues are..."
133:
“Your honors' virtues have traveled across the surface of the dark-blue ocean and overspread the entire land of Jambudīpa. I too, while sitting at the gate of the city of Pāṭaliputta, heard the talk of your virtues,” he said. That Brahmin, having offered alms-food to the Elder and prepared three robes for himself, went forth in the presence of the Elder. Established in the Elder's advice, he attained Arahantship within just a few days.

King Saddhātissa also asked, “Venerable Sir, please tell me of an Elder who is worthy of my worship.” The monks replied, “It is Kuṭṭatissa Thera, who resides in Mangala.” The King set out on a journey of five yojanas with a large retinue. The Elder asked the community of monks, “Friends, what is this sound?” “Venerable Sir, the King is coming to see you,” they replied. The Elder thought, “What use is there for me, in my old age, with matters concerning the royal house?” and lay down on a couch in his day-quarters, scratching lines on the ground. The King asked, “Where is the Elder?” and hearing he was in the day-quarters, went there. Seeing the Elder scratching lines on the ground, he thought, “One who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) does not have fidgety hands (hatthakukkucca); this man is no khīṇāsava,” and turned back without paying respects.

The community of monks asked the Elder, “Venerable Sir, why did you cause such dissatisfaction to a King who is so faithful and devoted?” He replied, “Friends, to protect the King's devotion is not your burden; it is the burden of an old Elder like me.” Later, when he was about to attain Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), he told the community of monks, “Prepare another couch for me inside my pinnacled pavilion (kūṭāgāra).” When the couch was prepared, the Elder made a determination: “May this pinnacled pavilion not stop along the way, but descend to the ground only when the King sees it,” and then he passed away.

The pinnacled pavilion traveled through the air for a distance of five yojanas. Within that five-yojana journey, trees capable of bearing banners appeared as if they were holding banners aloft. Even the small trees and bushes stood facing toward the pinnacled pavilion. A message was sent to the King: “The Elder has passed away; the pinnacled pavilion is coming through the air.” The King did not believe it. The pinnacled pavilion, traveling through the sky, circumambulated the Thūpārāma Cetiya and reached the site of the Silācetiya. The Silācetiya, together with its base, rose up and stood atop the pinnacled pavilion. Thousands of cries of ‘Sādhu!’ rang out. At that moment, Mahāvyaggha Thera, who was sitting in the seventh-story pinnacled chamber of the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace) performing Vinaya duties for the monks, heard that sound and asked, “What is this sound?”
134:
“What is this sound?” he asked. “Venerable Sir, Kuṭṭatissa Thera of Mangala has passed away. The pinnacled pavilion has come five yojanas through the air; that is the sound of ‘Sādhu’ being shouted there,” they replied. “Friends, by relying on those with great merit, we shall receive honor and offerings,” he said. After asking his disciples for forgiveness, he traveled through the air, entered the pinnacled pavilion, sat on the second couch, and attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder. King Saddhātissa took scented powder and flowers, and seeing the pinnacled pavilion suspended in the air, he made offerings to it. At that moment, the pinnacled pavilion descended and rested on the ground. The King performed the funeral rites with great honor, took the relics, and built a cetiya. Such people are said to be “desirous of seeing the virtuous.”

“Saddhammaṃ sotumicchati” means having the desire to listen to the True Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata, like Piṇḍapātika Thera and others. It is said that thirty monks spent the rains retreat at the Gangāvanavāli courtyard. Every fortnight on the Uposatha day, they would preach the noble Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, which consists of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. One Piṇḍapātika Thera arrived later and sat in a secluded, hidden spot. Then, a viper bit the calf of his leg as if gripping it with pincers. Looking down, the Elder saw the viper and thought, “I will not create an obstacle to hearing the Dhamma today.” He caught the viper, put it in a bag, tied the mouth of the bag, placed it nearby, and continued to sit and listen to the Dhamma. The rising of the dawn, the neutralizing of the poison, the Elder's attainment of the three fruits, the poison descending from the bite and entering the earth, and the conclusion of the Dhamma talk by the preaching monk—all these occurred at the same moment. Then the Elder said, “Friends, I have caught a thief,” and untying the bag, he released the viper. Seeing this, the monks asked, “Venerable Sir, at what time were you bitten?” “Friends, it was yesterday evening,” he replied. “Venerable Sir, why did you perform such a difficult and painful task?” they asked. “Friends, if I had said I was bitten by a long-bodied creature (snake), I would not have obtained such great benefits,” he said. This is the story of Piṇḍapātika Thera.

In the region of Dīghavāpi, also, [it was said] “Mahājātakabhāṇaka Thera will preach the Mahāvessantara Jātaka, which has a thousand verses.” A resident of Tissamahāvihāra in the great village of Tissa...
135:
A young monk, having heard that the Mahāvessantara Jātaka would be preached, set out from that place and arrived after a journey of nine yojanas in a single day. At that very moment, the Elder began the Dhamma talk. Because of the physical exhaustion from traveling the long distance, the young monk was only able to grasp the concluding verse along with the opening verse. Then, when the Elder said, "Idamavoca" (This he said) and rose to leave the assembly, the monk stood weeping, saying, "My coming here has been in vain." A man, hearing those words, went and informed the Elder, "Venerable Sir, a young monk has come from Tissa-mahāvihāra to listen to your Dhamma talk. He is standing there weeping, saying that his coming has been in vain because of his physical exhaustion." The Elder said, "Go and inform him: 'We shall preach it again tomorrow.'" On the following day, having heard the Elder's Dhamma talk, that young monk attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Another woman, a resident of Ullakolikaṇṇi, while nursing her young son, heard that "The Elder Mahā Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, is preaching the practice of the Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage)," and traveled a distance of five yojanas. She entered the monastery while the daytime preacher was still seated, laid her son on the ground, and listened to the Dhamma while standing. When the reciter of the Pali rose, the Elder Mahā Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, began the Great Ariyavaṃsa concerning contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. She listened attentively while standing. The Elder preached about only three requisites and made a sign to rise. That laywoman said, "Venerable Sir, having said 'I will preach the Ariyavaṃsa,' you have partaken of fine food, drunk sweet drinks, and received medical treatment with liquorice oil and so forth; yet you rise just when it is the proper time to preach." The Elder said, "Very well, sister," and continued to preach the latter part on delight in meditation. At the moment of dawn, the Elder's concluding words "Idamavoca" and the laywoman's attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry occurred simultaneously.

Another woman, a resident of Kaḷampara, taking her young son in her arms with the thought "I will listen to the Dhamma," went to Cittala-pabbata. Leaning against a tree, she laid her son down and listened to the Dhamma while standing. At the end of the first watch of the night, a snake...
136:
While she was watching, a snake bit the child sleeping nearby with its four fangs and went away. She thought, "If I say 'My son has been bitten by a snake,' it will be an obstacle to the Dhamma. Indeed, in this wandering through the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), this child has been my son many times; I shall only practice the Dhamma well." Throughout the three watches of the night, she listened to and meditated on the Dhamma while standing, and having become established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, she performed an Act of Truth (Saccakiriya) at dawn, neutralizing the son's venom, and went away taking her son. Such persons are truly those who desire to hear the Dhamma.

## 3. Atthavasa-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, "tayo bhikkhave atthavase sampassamānena" means a person seeing three reasons. "Alameva" means it is truly appropriate. "Yo dhammaṃ deseti" means that person reveals the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Atthappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who repeatedly experiences the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) through wisdom. "Dhammappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who repeatedly experiences the Dhamma of the Pali text.

## 4. Kathāpavattī-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "ṭhānehi" means by reasons. "Pavattinī" means [the occurrence of speech] that is unobstructed and leads to liberation from the suffering of the round of rebirths.

## 5. Paṇ膽ita-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "paṇḍitapaññattāni" refers to things prescribed, taught, and praised by the wise. "Sappurisapaññattāni" refers to things prescribed, taught, and praised by virtuous persons or Great Beings (Mahāpurisa). "Ahiṃsā" refers to compassion (karuṇā) and the states preceding compassion. "Saṃyamo" refers to the restraint of virtue (sīla). "Damo" refers to the restraint of the senses, or self-taming through the observance of the Uposatha. The patience (khanti) taught by the word "dama" in the Puṇṇovāda Sutta, as well as the wisdom taught in the Āḷavaka Sutta, are also appropriate in this sutta. "Mātāpitu upaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to protecting, securing, and caring for one's parents. In this word "santānaṃ", although in other places the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (Ariya-sāvaka) are called "santa" (the peaceful), in this sutta, those who serve their parents are intended. Therefore, by the highest sense...
137:
"Santānaṃ" is the meaning of the virtuous who are called "brahmacārī" because of their noble conduct. In this context, the meaning should be understood as: "The virtuous have prescribed this service to parents." "Sataṃ etāni ṭhānāni" refers to these grounds of the superior men who have calmed their defilements. "Ariyo dassanasampanno" means that in this Sutta, one is to be known as an "Ariya" and "one endowed with vision" solely because of performing these three grounds; it does not refer to the Buddhas and others, nor to Stream-enterers. Alternatively, "Sataṃ etāni ṭhānāni" means these grounds—serving the mother and serving the father—are the causes of superior men who have calmed their defilements; thus, the meaning of this verse should be understood through the power of one who serves their parents. This is because, in this Sutta, only the one who serves their parents is called "Ariya" and "one endowed with vision." "Sa lokaṃ bhajate sivaṃ" means that person goes to the safe celestial world.

## ၆။ သီလဝန္တသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the sixth Sutta, "tīhi ṭhānehi" means by three grounds. In the words beginning with "kāyena," those who, seeing monks arriving, go out to welcome them; who follow them when they leave; who perform sweeping and plastering with cow dung in the refectory; who prepare seats; and who set out drinking water, are said to increase merit through the body. Those who, seeing the Saṅgha of monks walking for alms, say, "Give gruel, give food, give ghee, butter, and so on; honor them with scents and flowers; observe the Uposatha; listen to the Dhamma; pay homage to the stupa," are said to increase merit through speech. Those who, seeing monks walking for alms, think, "May they receive alms," are said to increase merit through the mind. "Pasavanti" means they obtain. Merit here is spoken of as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

## ၇။ သင်္ခတလက္ခဏသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the seventh Sutta, "saṅkhatassa" means of that which is conditioned, having been brought together by causes. "Saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni" means the signs or causes for recognizing that "this is a conditioned thing." "Uppādo" is arising (jāti). "Vayo" is passing away (bheda). "Ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ" is the alteration of what is present, called aging (jarā). Therein, "saṅkhata" refers to the phenomena of the three planes. Path and Fruit (magga-phala), however, are not mentioned here as conditioned because they do not come under the scrutiny of the three marks. Arising and so on are called the marks of the conditioned. Among them, at the moment of arising, it is "arising"; at the moment of presence, it is "aging"; at the moment of dissolution, it is "passing away." The mark is not the conditioned; the conditioned is not the mark.
138:
Among those moments of arising and so on, arising at the moment of arising, maturing at the moment of presence, and passing away at the moment of dissolution are called the marks of recognition. The mark is not the conditioned thing, and the conditioned thing is not the mark. Rather, the conditioned thing is delimited by the mark of recognition. For example, in elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, and so on, the brands such as spears or stakes are the signs for recognition. Those signs are not the elephants, horses, etc., nor are the elephants, horses, etc., merely the signs. Rather, by those signs, one knows, "This is so-and-so's elephant, this is so-and-so's horse, this elephant is named such-and-such, this horse is named such-and-such." The completeness of this analogy should be understood in this way.

## ၈။ အသင်္ခတလက္ခဏသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the eighth Sutta, the Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇa Sutta, "asaṅkhatassa" means of that which is not made by the coming together of causes. "Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇāni" refers to the signs for recognizing that "this is an unconditioned thing." By the words "arising is not discerned" and so on, the absence of arising, aging, and dissolution is stated. Indeed, it is by the absence of arising and so on that the unconditioned is known.

## ၉။ ပဗ္ဗတရာဇသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the ninth Sutta, the Pabbatarāja Sutta, "mahāsālā" refers to great trees. "Kulapatiṃ" refers to the head of a family. "သေလော" (Selo) refers to a mountain made of rock. "Araññasmiṃ" means in a place where there is no village. "Brahmā" means great. "Vane" means in the forest. "Vanappatī" refers to the trees that are the lords of the forest. "Having practiced the conduct called the path that leads to a good destination in this Dispensation" is the meaning.

## ၁၀။ အာတပ္ပကရဏီယသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the commentary on the tenth Sutta, the Ātappakaraṇīya Sutta, "ātappaṃ karaṇīyaṃ" means effort should be made. "Anuppādāya" means for the sake of non-arising; it means it should be done for this reason: "I will ensure the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states." In the subsequent terms, the method is the same. "Sārīrikānaṃ" means arising in the body. "Dukkhānaṃ" means those feelings that are hard to bear. "Tibbānaṃ" means thick, or harsh by way of burning pain. "Kharānaṃ" means rough. "Kaṭukānaṃ" means acute. "Asātānaṃ" means not sweet. "Amanāpānaṃ" means unable to please the mind. "Pāṇaharānaṃ" means life-taking. These refer to feelings (vedanā). "Adhivāsanāya" means for the sake of enduring, for the sake of bearing, for the sake of experiencing.
139:
In this extent, the Teacher, having given the command and set it in motion, now wishing to exhort, spoke the words beginning with "Yato kho bhikkhave." In that passage, "Yato" means "at which time." "Ātāpī" means one who possesses energy. "Nipako" means one who possesses wisdom. "Sato" means one who is endowed with mindfulness. "Dukkhassa antakiriyāya" means for the purpose of making an end to the round of suffering, which is the limit of the suffering of the round of rebirth. These three qualities, beginning with ardency (ātāpa), are spoken of as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane.

## 11. Mahācorasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the eleventh discourse, the Mahācorasutta, "Mahācoro" means a great and powerful thief. "Sandhiṃ" means (breaking through) the joints of a house. "Nillopaṃ" means a great plundering. "Ekāgārikaṃ" means plundering by surrounding only a single house. "Paripanthepi tiṭṭhati" means he commits the act of waylaying on the road. "Nadīviduggaṃ" means a river-fastness, referring to the middle of a river island where it is possible to hide along with two or three thousand infantry. "Pabbatavisamaṃ" means a mountain-fastness, referring to a mountain gorge where it is possible to hide along with seven or eight thousand infantry. "Tiṇagahanaṃ" means a place two or three leagues in extent that is overgrown and covered with grass. "Rodhaṃ" means a large, dense forest thicket where the branches are intertwined and continuous. "Pariyodhāya atthaṃ bhaṇissanti" means they will speak for his benefit by including his virtues and presenting various appropriate reasons. "Tyāssa" should be resolved into "te assa." "Pariyodhāya atthaṃ bhaṇanti" means that when someone begins to speak of some fault, they speak for his benefit, removing even a great fault by including various reasons such as, "Do not say such a thing; we have known this person for generations; he would not do such a thing." Alternatively, "pariyodhāya" also has the meaning of "covering up." Indeed, the king's ministers speak for the benefit of that great thief by covering up his faults. "Khataṃ upahataṃ" means one who is uprooted and destroyed because his virtues have been uprooted and destroyed. "Visamena kāyakammena" means by an unrighteous bodily action occurring at the bodily door, in the sense of stumbling. The same method applies to verbal and mental actions. "Antaggāhikāya" means by a wrong view that stands holding to an extreme, such as the ten types of eternalism, etc. The remaining words in all places have clear meanings.

## Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ Niṭṭhitaṃ.
140:
## 2. Dutiya-paṇṇāsaka
## (6) 1. Brāhmaṇavagga
## 1. Paṭhama-dvebrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Brāhmaṇavagga, "Jiṇṇā" means those who are decayed by old age. "Vuddhā" means those who are advanced in years. "Mahallakā" means those who are senior by birth. "Addhagatā" means those who have passed through the three stages of life (the first, middle, and last). "Vayoanuppattā" means those who have reached the final stage of life.

"They approached where the Blessed One was" means that seeing their children and wives not following their words, they thought, "We will go to the ascetic Gotama and seek the path of escape from the round of suffering," and thus they approached. In saying, "Venerable Gotama, we are Brahmins," they first made it known that they were of the Brahmin caste—not of the warrior caste, the ministerial class, or the householder class—and then spoke the words beginning with "We are old."

"Akatabhīruttāṇā" means those who have not yet performed the meritorious deeds that can prevent the fear of the lower realms. It shows that they have not yet performed the meritorious kamma which is a support and a foundation that leads to a happy destination. "Taggha" is an indeclinable used either in the sense of "certainly" or in the sense of "acceptance." It shows: "You are certainly of such a nature, and I also accept that statement." "Upanīyati" means it is brought near. Indeed, in this world of beings, birth leads to old age, old age leads to sickness, sickness leads to death, and death leads again to birth. Therefore, it is said, "Upanīyati."

Now, because those Brahmins were so old that they would not be able to fulfill the monastic duties even if they ordained, the Blessed One, wishing to establish them in the Five Precepts, spoke the words beginning with "Here, restraint by body..." In that passage, "restraint by body" means restraint through the bodily door. The same method applies to the remaining terms for restraint. "That merit is for that person who has gone to the beyond..." means that for the person who has reached the next life, that merit is a "protection" (tāṇa) because of its nature of guarding, a "shelter" (leṇa) because of its nature of providing a hiding place, an "island" (dīpa) because of its nature of being a foundation, a "refuge" (saraṇa) because of its nature of being a reliance, and a "resort" (parāyaṇa) by way of being the excellent destination. The verses have clear meanings. Thus, those Brahmins, having been established in the Five Precepts by the Tathāgata, guarded the Five Precepts for the rest of their lives and were reborn in the heavenly realm.
141:
## 2. Dutiyadevebrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'bhājanaṃ' refers to any unspecified property or goods. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first sutta.

## 3. Aññatarabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'sammodanīyaṃ' refers to speech that generates joy. 'Sāraṇīyaṃ' refers to speech associated with being worthy of remembrance. 'Vītisāretvā' means having concluded (the conversation). 'Kittāvatā' means to what extent. 'Sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti' means it is to be seen by oneself. 'Akāliko' means it does not give fruit at a time other than its own occurrence (it gives fruit immediately). 'Ehipassiko' means it is worthy of saying 'Come and see'; thus, it is an inquiry into the practice that leads to arrival. 'Opaneyyiko' means it should be brought into one's own mind. 'Paccattaṃ veditabbo' means it should be known only by oneself. 'Viññūhi' means by the wise noble persons. 'Pariyādinnacitto' means having a mind that is obsessed or seized. 'Ceteti' means thinks. The rest in this sutta has an obvious meaning. In fact, in this sutta, the Brahmin asked about the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga), and the Blessed One also explained that very supramundane path. Indeed, because that supramundane path is to be seen by oneself, it is called 'sandiṭṭhika'.

## 4. Paribbājakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'brāhmaṇaparibbājako' means a wanderer of the Brahmin caste, not a wanderer of the Khattiya caste or others. 'Attatthampi' means one's own benefit, which includes mundane and supramundane benefits, pertaining to both the present life and the future.

## 5. Nibbutasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'akālikaṃ' means it is not to be reached at a time other than its own occurrence (it is to be reached immediately). 'Opaneyyikaṃ' means it should be reached through practice.

## 6. Palokasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, 'ācariyapācariyānaṃ' refers to the benefit of the teachers and the teachers of the teachers. 'Avīci maññe phuṭo ahosī' means just as the great Avīci hell is crowded without gaps by hell-beings, similarly, it is crowded with humans. 'Kukkuṭasampātikā' means flying up from the roof of one village...
142:
...and falling onto the roof of another village; such a flight of cocks exists in those villages, market towns, or capitals, hence they are called 'kukkuṭasampātikā'. There is also a variant reading 'kukkuṭasampādikā', which means the walking of cocks from one village to another on foot exists in those places. Both of these terms indicate a very dense population. 'Adhammarāgarattā' means although lust (rāga) is strictly unrighteous (adhamma), here it does not mean lust arising for one's own requisites, but specifically lust arising for the requisites of others. 'Visamalobhābhibhūtā' means there is no such thing as 'even greed' (samalobha); greed is strictly 'uneven' (visama). However, greed arising for objects one has already acquired is called 'samalobha', while greed arising for objects acquired by others is intended as 'visamalobha'. 'Micchādhammaparetā' means being endowed with a perverted nature, which is the indulgence in what should not be indulged. 'Devo na sammā dhāraṃ anuppaveccatī' means the rain does not fall during the proper rainy season. 'Dubbhikkhaṃ' means the difficulty of obtaining almsfood. 'Dussassaṃ' means having bad crops due to the insufficiency of various kinds of grain. 'Setaṭṭhikaṃ' means while the crops are flourishing, white-stalk insects (mildew) fall upon them; because of being bitten by those insects, the emerging heads of rice become white and pithless. Referring to this, it is called 'setaṭṭhika'. 'Salākāvuttaṃ' means all the sown crops turn out to be merely like stalks and do not bear fruit. 'Yakkhā' means the chiefs of the demons. 'Vāဠေ amanusse ossajjantī' means they release fierce non-humans (demons) onto the paths where humans travel; those demons, having found the opportunity, bring many people to the end of their lives.

## 7. Vacchagottasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'mahapphalaṃ' means having great fruit or result. In the phrase 'dhammassa cānudhammaṃ vyākarontī', 'dhamma' refers to the spoken word (the teaching), and 'anudhamma' refers to repeating or explaining in accordance with that teaching. 'Sahadhammiko' means being with reason and cause. 'Vādānupāto' means following after the doctrine. 'Gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ' means a blameworthy ground or cause. The meaning is this: the reasoned doctrine spoken by the Venerable Gotama does not come to any blameworthy ground. Or else, it is a question: does the reasoned doctrine spoken by those others come to any blameworthy ground?
143:
'Antarāyakaro hoti' means one who causes danger, destruction, difficulty in acquisition, and opposition. 'Pāripanthiko' means a thief who commits destruction on the road. 'Khato ca hoti' means one who is uprooted by the digging up of virtues. 'Upahato' means one who is ruined by the destruction of virtues.

'Candanikā' refers to a cesspool of filth. 'Oligalla' refers to a muddy pit where water flows from a drain. 'So ca' refers to the aforementioned virtuous Arahant. 'Sīlakkhandhena' means by the aggregate of virtue. The same method applies to the remaining terms such as the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and so on. Here, 'vimuttiñāṇadassana' refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) (the knowledge that reviews the fruit of Arahantship). That knowledge is called 'asekha' (beyond training) because it arises in an asekha person. The others, such as the aggregate of virtue, are also called asekha because they have reached the end of the training to be practiced. Although those aggregates of virtue and so on are supramundane (lokuttara), reviewing knowledge is only mundane (lokiya).

'Rohiṇīsu' refers to red-colored cows. 'Sarūpāsu' refers to cows that are similar in color to their own calves. 'Pārevatāsu' refers to pigeon-colored cows. 'Danto' means one who is tamed or free from opposition. 'Puṅgavo' means a bull. 'Dhorayho' means one who carries a burden. 'Kalyāṇajavanikkamo' means one who goes with a good and straight speed. 'Nāssa vaṇṇaṃ parikkhare' means they do not examine the body color of that ox, but only examine its ability to carry a burden. 'Yasmiṃ kasmiñci jātiye' refers to one born in any family without distinction. 'Yāsu kāsuci etāsu' refers to one born in any of those various families such as the Khattiya, and so on.

'Brahmacariyassa kevalī' means one who is complete in the holy life, one endowed with the state of perfection. Truly, an Arahant is called one who has lived the entire holy life. Therefore, this is said. 'Pannabhāro' means one who has laid down the burden. It means one who remains having laid down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of the cords of sensual pleasure. 'Katakicco' means one who remains having performed the tasks (the sixteen tasks) through the four paths. In the phrase 'pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ', the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are called 'sabbadhamma' (all phenomena). He is called 'pāragū' (one who has gone to the further shore) because he has reached the six kinds of shores: the shore of direct knowledge (abhiññā), the shore of full understanding (pariññā), the shore of abandoning (pahāna), the shore of development (bhāvanā), the shore of realization (sacchikiriyā), and the shore of attainment (samāpatti). 'Anupādāya' means without clinging or grasping. 'Nibbuto' means one who is free from the heat of defilements. 'Viraje' means in one who is free from the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion.
144:
'Avijānantā' (not knowing) means not knowing the good field of merit, which is the recipient. 'Dummedhā' (unwise) means being devoid of wisdom. 'Assutāvino' (unlearned) means lacking hearing or knowledge regarding the judgment of the good field. 'Bahiddhā' (outside) means outside of this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Na hi sante upāsare' (they do not attend upon the peaceful ones) means they do not approach the noble men, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants. 'Dhīrasammate' (regarded as wise) means those who are recognized and praised by the wise. 'Mūlajātā patiṭṭhitā' (rooted and established)—by this statement, the faith of a Stream-enterer is shown. 'Kule vā idha jāyare' (born here in families) means they are born in this human world in the families of Khattiyas, Brahmins, or Vessas. These three alone are called the perfection of family (kulasampatti). 'Anupubbena nibbānaṃ adhigacchanti' (gradually they attain Nibbāna) means they reach Nibbāna in due order after fulfilling these qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

## 8. Tikaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, 'Tikaṇṇa' is the name of that Brahmin. 'Upasaṅkamī' (approached) means he approached after having breakfast, surrounded by many people, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is wise; I will go to him." 'Bhagavato sammukhā' (in the presence of the Blessed One) means sitting in front of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). Regarding the phrase 'vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati' (speaks praise), why does he speak it? It is said that this Tikaṇṇa Brahmin had never before come to the presence of the Tathāgata. Then it occurred to him: "The Buddhas are difficult to approach; if I do not speak first, he may or may not speak. If he does not speak, then in the assembly of Brahmins, they will rebuke me, saying, 'Why did you speak there? Even though you went to the presence of the ascetic Gotama, you did not receive even a single word.' Therefore, by speaking thus, I will be free from this blame." Thinking so, he speaks. Although he speaks the praise of the Brahmins, he speaks only with the intention of testing the Tathāgata's knowledge. 'Evampi tevijjā brāhmaṇā' (thus the Brahmins of the three Vedas) means the Brahmins endowed with the three Vedas are thus wise, thus steady, thus clever, thus learned, thus speakers, and thus recognized. 'Itipi' (also thus)—by this word, the distinction of their qualities such as being wise is shown. "For this many reasons they are called wise... for this many reasons they are recognized"—this is the meaning here.

"Brahmin, in what way do the Brahmins..." (yathā kathaṃ pana brāhmaṇā)—here, 'yathā' is a word indicating the reason, and 'kathaṃ pana' is a word of questioning. The intended meaning is: "Brahmin, in what way do the Brahmins designate the three Vedas? Tell me the reason by which this designation of the three Vedas can be known."
145:
(The Buddha asked), "How do the Brahmins prescribe the threefold knowledge? Tell me the reason by which it is possible to know the prescription of these three knowledges." Hearing these words, the Brahmin named Tikaṇṇa, with a joyful mind, thinking, "The Fully Enlightened One asks me only in the area where I have knowledge, not in the area where I lack knowledge," said the words beginning with, "Master Gotama, in this world..."

In that passage beginning with "Idha bho Gotama," "Ubhato" means from both sides, the mother's side and the father's side. For a Brahmin whose mother is a Brahmin woman, her mother is a Brahmin woman, and her mother's mother is a Brahmin woman; whose father is a Brahmin, his father is a Brahmin, and his father's father is a Brahmin. That Brahmin is well-born from both sides, from the mother and from the father. "Saṃsuddhagahaṇika" means that the mother's womb of that Brahmin is pure; "gahaṇī" means the womb. However, in the passage "Samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā," the digestive fire produced by kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) is called "gahaṇī."

In the passage "Yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā," the father's father is called "Pitāmaha" (grandfather). The lifespan of the grandfather is called "Pitāmahayuga." By the word "Yuga," the lifespan is intended. This word "Yuga" is merely a designation; in meaning, the grandfather himself is "Pitāmahayuga." All ancestors above the grandfather are also included by the term "Pitāmaha." Thus, it shows that up to the seventh generation of men, the mother's womb is pure; or in other words, one is not rejected or reproached because of birth-related talk.

"Akkhitto" means not rejected or discarded in such a way as "Remove this person, what use is there for him?" "Anupakkuṭṭho" means not scolded or blamed, having never before reached a state of being scolded or blamed. For what reason? Because of birth-related talk. It means (not being blamed) by words of such nature as "For this reason, this Brahmin is of low birth."

The word "Ajjhāyako" (arose from): "Vāseṭṭha, now these people do not meditate, now these people do not meditate; therefore, the third syllable 'Ajjhāyaka' (non-meditator) appeared nearby." Thus, in the beginning of the aeon, words of blame arose for Brahmins who were devoid of jhāna. But now, they use it as a word of praise with the meaning that one recites or studies the Vedas. Because of bearing the Vedas (mantras), one is called "Mantadhara."

"Tiṇṇam vedānam" refers to (reaching the end of) the three Vedas: Iruveda, Yajuveda, and Sāmaveda. Because of reaching the far shore by means of the impact of the lips (recitation), one is called "Pāragū" (Master). Because of being together with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha treatises, they are called "Sanighaṇḍukeṭubha." "Nighaṇḍu" is a treatise that explains the synonyms of names such as trees. "Keṭubha" is a treatise consisting of various deliberations on rituals for the benefit of the wise. Together with...
146:
"Sākkharappabhedānaṃ" means being together with the Akkharappabheda treatise. Akkharappabheda refers to the Sikkhā (phonetics) and Nirutti (etymology) treatises. "Itihāsapañcamānaṃ" means those Vedas which have Itihāsa as the fifth, making the Atharvaveda the fourth. Itihāsa refers to ancient stories connected with words such as "Thus it has been, thus it has been," or it refers to the Khattavijjā (science of the ruling class). One who studies and knows the words of those Vedas with Itihāsa as the fifth, and the remaining Veyyākaraṇa (grammar), is called "Padaka" and "Veyyākaraṇa."

"Lokāyata" refers to the Vitaṇḍavāda treatise (the science of sophistry that agitates the minds of the wise). "Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa" is a treatise that explains the marks of Great Men such as the Buddha, having a length of twelve thousand texts. In that treatise, there are "Buddhamantas" (Buddha-mantras) amounting to sixteen thousand verse-lines. By the power of those Buddhamantas, this distinction is known: "Those endowed with these marks are called Buddhas; with these marks, Paccekabuddhas, the two Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, the Buddha's Mother, the Buddha's Father, the Chief Male Attendant, the Chief Female Attendant, and the Cakkavatti King."

"Anavaya" means one who is able to perform completely without deficiency in these Lokāyata and Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa treatises, thus not being "Avaya" (incomplete). One who is called "Avaya" is one who is unable to maintain those treatises either in meaning or in text. Alternatively, "Anavaya" is "Anu-avaya," where the 'u' sound is elided by way of sandhi (conjunction). It means one who has repeatedly non-deficient, complete knowledge.

Regarding the words "Tena hi," the Blessed One, seeing that Brahmin entreating Him and knowing, "Now is the time to answer the question for him," spoke these words. Its meaning is: "Because you entreat Me, therefore listen." The words beginning with "Vivicceva kāmehi" (secluded from sensual pleasures) have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Here, however, these words are spoken to show the preliminary practice of the threefold knowledge. In that regard, the sequential explanation and the method of development of the two knowledges have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Paṭhamā vijjā" (the first knowledge) is called "Paṭhamā" because it arises first; it is called "Vijjā" in the sense of making something known. What does it make known? It makes known the sequence of past aggregates (Pubbenivāsa). "Avijjā" (ignorance) refers to the delusion (moha) that covers that very Pubbenivāsa so it is not known. "Tama" (darkness) refers to that same delusion in the sense of covering. "Āloka" (light) refers to that same knowledge (vijjā) in the sense of producing radiance. Here, the statement "Knowledge has been attained" is...
147:
This is the meaning. The remaining words are words of praise. The connection of meaning here is: this person has attained this knowledge (vijjā), and by attaining knowledge, his ignorance (avijjā) is destroyed and perished. Why? Because knowledge has arisen. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases.

In the phrase 'yathā taṃ', 'yathā' is a simile, and 'taṃ' is just a particle. It means: for one who is diligent (appamatta) because of non-separation from mindfulness; for one who is ardent (ātāpī) because of effort that burns away defilements; and for one who is resolute (pahitatta), meaning one whose mind is sent towards Nibbāna without regard for body and life. This is what is meant: Just as for one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, ignorance is destroyed and knowledge arises, and darkness is destroyed and light arises; even so, for him, ignorance is destroyed and knowledge has arisen. Darkness is destroyed and light has arisen. He has obtained the fruit appropriate to such application of exertion.

In the 'Cutūpapāta-kathā' (Discourse on Passing Away and Reappearance), 'vijjā' is the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). 'Avijjā' is the ignorance that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings. The rest is as previously stated.

In the third knowledge, by the phrase 'so evaṃ samāhite citte' (with the mind thus concentrated), the fourth jhāna mind which is the basis for insight (vipassanā) should be understood. 'Āsavānaṃ khaya-ñāṇāya' (for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints) is for the sake of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). The path of Arahantship is called 'the destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khaya) because it destroys the taints, and this knowledge is included therein. 'Cittaṃ abhininnāmeti' means he directs the insight-mind. In the phrases 'so idaṃ dukkhaṃ' (this is suffering) etc., he knows and penetrates according to reality by penetrating the individual essence (sarasalakkhaṇa) that 'this much is suffering, there is nothing beyond this' regarding the whole truth of suffering. He knows and penetrates according to reality the craving that causes that suffering as 'this is the origin of suffering' (dukkha-samudaya); the Nibbāna which is the cessation where both [suffering and origin] cease upon reaching it as 'this is the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha); and the Noble Path that leads to that Nibbāna as 'this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā) by penetrating the individual essence.

Having shown the truths by their nature, now to show them figuratively by way of defilements, he said 'ime āsavā' (these are the taints) etc. 'Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato' (for him thus knowing, thus seeing) refers to the teaching of the Path that has reached the summit along with insight to that monk. 'Kāmāsavā' means from the taint of sensual desire. By the word 'vimuccati' (is liberated), the path-moment (magga-kkhaṇa) is shown. At the path-moment, the mind is being liberated from the taints.
148:
At the fruit-moment (phala-kkhaṇa), it is liberated (from the taints). By the words 'when liberated, there is the knowledge that it is liberated', the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) is shown. By the words 'birth is exhausted' (khīṇā jāti) etc., the object of that reviewing knowledge is shown. With that knowledge, when that Arahant reviews, he understands 'birth is exhausted' etc. in detail. What kind of birth is exhausted for that Arahant, and how does he know that exhaustion?

For that Arahant, past birth is not exhausted (now) because it was already exhausted before; future birth is not exhausted because there is no effort in the future; present birth is not exhausted because it is currently manifest. Rather, the birth that would have arisen in the one-constituent, four-constituent, or five-constituent existence (ekavokāra, catuvokāra, pañcavokāra bhava) as one, four, or five aggregates if the Noble Path had not been developed—that birth, because the Noble Path has been developed, has reached the state of non-arising and is thus exhausted. That Arahant, having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the Path, understands that because there are no defilements, even the existing kamma cannot produce rebirth in the future.

'Vusitaṃ' means lived, done, practiced, or reached completion. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' means the holy life of the Path. Indeed, the seven trainees (sekha) along with the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) are still living the holy life; the Arahant is one who has lived the holy life. Therefore, that Arahant, reviewing his living of the holy life, understands: 'The holy life has been lived'. 'Kataṃ karaṇီyaṃ' means the sixteen-fold task regarding the Four Truths—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development through the four paths—has been completed. Indeed, persons such as the virtuous worldling are still doing that task; the Arahant is one who has done what was to be done. Therefore, that Arahant, reviewing his task, understands: 'What was to be done has been done'.

'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means he understands: 'There is no further task of developing the path for the sake of these sixteen-fold path-tasks or for the sake of the destruction of defilements.' Alternatively, 'itthattāya' means: 'Beyond this current continuity of aggregates, there is no other future continuity of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, being fully understood, remain like trees with their roots cut. Upon the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel.' Here, 'vijjā' is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. 'Avijjā' is the ignorance that covers the Four Truths. The rest is as previously stated.

'Anuccāvacasīlassa' (of one whose virtue is not high and low): One whose virtue sometimes decreases and sometimes increases is called one with 'high and low' virtue.
