But the virtue of an Arahant is only ever perfected. Therefore, that Arahant is called one with 'not high and low' (unwavering) virtue.
149:
"Vasībhūtaṃ" means having attained mastery. "Susamāhitaṃ" means being well-concentrated, well-placed on the object. "Dhīraṃ" means being endowed with fortitude. "Maccuhāyinaṃ" means standing having abandoned death. "Sabbappahāyinaṃ" means standing having abandoned all unwholesome states. "Buddhaṃ" means one who knows the Four Noble Truths. "Antimade hīnaṃ" means one who bears the very last body. "Taṃ namassanti gotamaṃ" means that the disciples of the Buddha pay homage to that Buddha of the Gotama clan. Alternatively, it means a disciple of the Gotama Buddha is also called Gotama; the gods and humans pay homage to that group of disciples of the Gotama clan.

"Pubbenivāsaṃ" refers to the sequence of aggregates lived in the past. "Yoveti" means he who knows. There is also a variant reading "yovedī," which means he who stands having made it manifest. "Saggāpāyañca passati" means seeing the six heavens of the sense sphere, the nine Brahma worlds, and the four states of deprivation. "Jātikkhayaṃ patto" means having attained Arahantship. "Abhiññāvosito" means having reached the completion of the task through direct knowledge. "Muni" means an Arahant sage endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya). "Etāhi" means by these knowledges of past lives, etc., mentioned below. "Nāññaṃ lapitalāpanaṃ" means I do not call one a 'tevijja' (possessor of the three knowledges) merely because others speak of him as such; I call one 'tevijja' only if, having known for himself by direct experience, he can also teach the three knowledges to others. "Kalaṃ" means a fraction (a part). "Nāggahati" means it is not worth (it does not reach). Now, the brahmin, being pleased with the words of the Blessed One, performs the gestures of one who is pleased and addresses Him with "Abhikkantaṃ" (Excellent) and so forth.

## 9. Jāṇussoṇisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "yassassu" means to whom there may be. In the terms such as "yañño," it is called "yañña" because it should be sacrificed; this is a name for the gift (deyyadhamma). "Saddhaṃ" means food offered in dedication to the deceased (matakabhatta). "Thālipāko" means food suitable to be given to noble persons. "Deyyadhammaṃ" means any other gift not yet mentioned. By the phrase "tevijjesu brāhmaṇesu dānaṃ dadeyya," it is shown that all these gifts should be given to brahmins who possess the three knowledges; only brahmins with the three knowledges are worthy of receiving them. The remaining meanings here are just as explained below.

## 10. Saṅgāravasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "Saṅgāravo" is the name of a brahmin official in the city of Rājagaha who was in charge of repairing old buildings. "Upasaṅkami" means he approached, surrounded by a large crowd, after having had his breakfast. "Mayamassūti ettha"...
150:
The word "assu" is a mere particle. "O Gotama, we are called brahmins"—this is the only meaningful phrase here. "Yaññaṃ yajāmā" (we perform sacrifice) refers to the kind of sacrifice involving the killing of living beings, such as in groups of four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, one hundred, or five hundred, according to the beliefs of external traditions. It was with reference to such animal sacrifices that the brahmin Saṅgārava spoke thus. 

"Anekasārīrika" means occurring in many bodies. "Yadidaṃ" refers to that practice known as merit. "Yaññādhikaraṇa" means on account of performing sacrifice or on account of causing others to perform sacrifice. Indeed, whether one person gives by himself or causes others to give to many, or whether many people give by themselves or cause others to give to many, the practice known as merit is said to be "occurring in many bodies." It was with reference to this that it was said. Whether one says, "I sacrifice for you and for you," or commands, "You sacrifice and you sacrifice," the practice of merit is indeed "occurring in many bodies." It was also with reference to this that it was said.

"Yassa vā tassa vā" means because of this or because of that. "Tames only one's self" means taming only one's own self through the power of restraining one's faculties. "Calms only one's self" means calming only one's own self through the power of subsiding lust and so forth. "Extinguishes" means one extinguishes through the total cooling of lust and so forth. "Evamassāyaṃ" means even though it is so, this practice of merit.

Thus, upon hearing the words of the brahmin, the Teacher thought: "This brahmin speaks of the practice of merit involving many bodies, which is a great sacrifice involving the slaughter of animals. But he calls the practice of merit based on renunciation a practice involving only one body. This brahmin knows neither the practice involving one body nor the practice involving many bodies. Now, I shall teach him the practice involving one body and the practice involving many bodies." Thinking thus, He expanded the discourse further and said, "Brahmin, if that is so," and so forth.

In that discourse, "How does it please you?" means in what manner do you prefer? The passage beginning with "A Tathāgata arises in this world" has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "This is the path" means "Come, I shall instruct you; this is the path." "This is the practice" is a synonym for that very word "path." "Practicing in which way" means by which path one has practiced. "The unsurpassed foundation of the holy life" means Nibbāna, which is the unsurpassed foundation, the supreme attainment of the holy life known as the Path of Arahantship. "Iccāyaṃ" should be resolved as "iti ayaṃ."

"Appaṭṭhatarā" refers to the practice of merit where there is no need for many workers or equipment. "Appasamārambhatarā" refers to the practice of merit where there is no destruction of the livelihood of many people...
151:
There is no undertaking (samārambha) characterized by the affliction of body and mind. This was said with the intention: "Just as I honor the Venerable Gotama and the Venerable Ānanda, so do I honor such persons; only you two are the ones I honor and praise." It is said that this thought occurred to the Brahmin Saṅgārava: "The Elder Ānanda wishes me to answer this very question; indeed, there is no one who is displeased when their own virtues are spoken of." Therefore, not wishing to answer the question, he attempted to divert attention by speaking of [Ānanda's] virtues, and said this.

"Na kho tyāhaṃ" means "Na kho te ahaṃ" (I do not [ask] you this). The Elder Ānanda also thought: "This Brahmin is twisting and turning, not wishing to answer the question; I will make this very Brahmin answer it." Therefore, he said this to the Brahmin.

"Sahadhammikaṃ" means with reason (legitimate). "Saṃsādeti" means to cause to sink or falter. "No vissajjeti" means he does not answer. "If only I could release both of them from this affliction" means "If only I could release both from this harassment and fatigue." For the Brahmin was afflicted by not being able to answer the question asked by Ānanda, and Ānanda was also afflicted by wanting the non-answering Brahmin to answer. Thinking, "I will release both from this affliction," the Buddha said this. "Kā nvajjā" should be analyzed as "Kā nu ajja" (What is the talk today?). "Antarākathā udapādi" is a question asking what conversation arose in the midst of other talks. At that time, it is said that a conversation concerning the three miracles had arisen in the royal palace; intending to ask about that talk, the Teacher said this. Then the Brahmin, thinking "Now I will be able to speak," and wishing to report the talk that had arisen in the palace, said "Ayaṃ khvajjā, bho Gotama," and so on.

In that passage, "Ayaṃ khvajjā" means "Ayaṃ kho ajja" (This indeed today). In the phrase "Pubbe sudaṃ," "sudaṃ" is merely a particle. "Uttari manussadhammā" refers to states superior to the human Dhamma known as the ten courses of meritorious action (kusala kammapatha). "Iddhi-pāṭihāriyaṃ dassesuṃ" refers to the flying through the air that occurred in the past, referring to monks who went for alms and traveled only through the sky. "But now the monks are more numerous"—the Brahmin said this with the view: "In the past, monks did this thinking 'We will generate the four requisites,' but now, knowing that requisites are abundant, they spend their time in sleep and negligence."
152:
"Pāṭihāriyāni" are so called because they dispel opposing wrong views. "Iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ": "Iddhi" is by way of accomplishment; "Pāṭihāriya" is by way of dispelling opposing wrong views. Since the various psychic powers (iddhividha) are themselves miracles of power, it is called "Iddhipāṭihāriya." The same method applies to the remaining [Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya] and Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya. The meaning and method of development for terms such as "anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ" (manifold psychic powers) have been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Nimittena ādisati" (points out by means of a sign) means speaking of what will happen, such as "This particular benefit or harm will occur," by observing signs of coming, going, or standing. In this regard, there is this story: Once, a king held three pearls in his hand and asked his chaplain, "Teacher, what is in my hand?" The chaplain looked here and there. At that moment, a lizard ran out thinking, "I will catch a fly," but at the moment of capture, the fly escaped. Because the fly was released (muttā), he said, "Pearls (muttā), Great King." The king asked again, "Let the pearls be; how many pearls are there?" The chaplain again looked for a sign. Then, in a place not far away, a cock crowed three times. The Brahmin said, "Three, Great King." In this way, some speak by means of a sign of coming. By this method, speaking by signs of going or standing should also be understood. "Evampi te mano" means "Thus is your mind, whether it is joyful or sorrowful, or associated with sensual thoughts, etc." The second phrase is merely a synonym for the first. "Itipi te cittaṃ" means "Your mind of such a nature is arising while thinking of this or that matter." "Bahuṃ cepi ādisati" means even if he says much, "Tatheva taṃ hoti" means it happens exactly as spoken.

"Amanussānaṃ" refers to yakkhas, ghosts (pisācas), etc. "Devatānaṃ" refers to the devas of the Cātumahārājikā realm, etc. "Saddaṃ sutvā" (having heard the sound) means hearing the voices of those devas or non-humans who speak after knowing another's mind. "Vitakkavipphārasaddaṃ" refers to the sound of muttering or talking in one's sleep by those who are asleep or negligent, produced by the spreading of thoughts. "Sutvā" means having heard that sound, and by the power of that thought which arose in the person thinking, one points out, "Thus is your mind."

In this regard, there are these stories: A man, thinking "I will conduct a lawsuit," went from his village to the city. From the moment he set out, he thought, "I will say this and that to the King and the great ministers in the court." He acted as if he had reached the royal palace, as if he were standing before the King, and with his opponent...
153:
It was as if he were speaking with a judge. Hearing the sound emerging through the force of his thinking, a man asked, "For what purpose are you going?" He replied, "I am going on a legal matter." The man said, "Go, you will be successful." He went, conducted the legal case, and achieved success.

Another elder was wandering for alms in Moḷiyagāma. Then, a girl, being distracted by something else, did not see the elder as he was leaving. Standing at the village gate, he turned back and looked, and seeing her, he went along thinking. While going, he spoke aloud, "What was that girl doing that she did not see me?" A man standing nearby heard this and said, "Venerable sir, did you wander in Moḷiyagāma?"

"Manosaṅkhārā paṇihitā" means mental formations are well-established. "Vitakkessatī" means knowing that one will think or will bring about. In such knowing, there is knowing by arrival, knowing by the preliminary stage, and knowing by observing the mind within an attainment.

"Knowing by arrival" means that even during the preliminary work for a kasina, one knows, "By this manner, this person, having undertaken the kasina meditation, will produce the first jhāna... or the fourth jhāna, or the eight attainments."

"Knowing by the preliminary stage" means that even when the initial insight is undertaken, one knows, "By this manner, this person, having undertaken insight, will produce the path of stream-entry... or the path of arahantship."

"Knowing by observing the mind within an attainment" means knowing, "By this manner, this person's mental formations are well-established; immediately after this mind, he will think such a thought; for this person who has emerged from this attainment, there will be concentration partaking of decline (hānabhāgiya), or concentration partaking of stability (ṭhitibhāgiya), or concentration partaking of distinction (visesabhāgiya), or concentration partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), or supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) will arise."

In that regard, a worldling (puthujjana) who has attained the knowledge of encompassing others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) knows only the minds of worldlings, not of the noble ones (Ariyas). Among the noble ones, one at a lower path does not know the mind of one at a higher path, but one at a higher path knows the mind of one at a lower path. Among those, a stream-enterer enters the attainment of the fruition of stream-entry... an arahant enters the attainment of the fruition of arahantship. A higher person does not enter a lower attainment of fruition. This is because the lower attainments of those persons occur only within those respective persons. Likewise...
154:
"Tatheva taṃ hoti" means it happens exactly as indicated. This is because there is no such thing as that which is known through the power of the knowledge of encompassing others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) becoming otherwise.

"Think thus" means think by bringing about thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) and so forth. "Do not think thus" means do not think by bringing about thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka) and so forth. "Reflect thus" means reflect on the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) or any one of the perceptions such as the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā). "Not thus" means do not reflect with the mind in the manner of "permanent" and so forth. "This" means abandon this lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Having also attained this" means dwell having attained, reached, and accomplished only the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), which is divided into the four paths and fruits.

"It appears as if having a nature similar to magic" means it appears as if having a cause and origin similar to magic. Indeed, a magician takes water and makes it oil, or takes oil and makes it water; in this way, he shows various forms of magic. "This miracle also has such a nature" means "O Gotama, this miracle also appears to me as if having a nature similar to magic," which is said in reference to its similarity to the Cintāmaṇika art. For those who know the Cintāmaṇika art, just by seeing someone coming, they know, "This person is coming while thinking such a thought." Likewise, they know, "He is standing while thinking such a thought, sitting while thinking such a thought, lying down while thinking such a thought."

"Abhikkantataraṃ" means more excellent. "Paṇītataraṃ" means more sublime. In this context, "The Venerable Gotama [is one who has attained the state] without thought and without examination (avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ)..." the Brahmin does not regard the remaining miracle of manifestation (ādesanā-pāṭihāriya) as an external art. The Brahmin said all these words only wishing to praise the qualities of the Blessed One. "Addhā kho tyāyaṃ" means "Certainly you [referring to this person]." "Words spoken by touching upon and bringing near" means words spoken by touching upon my qualities and bringing them near to my qualities. "Indeed, I shall answer you" means "Indeed, I alone shall preach to you." The remaining words have clear meanings.

## The First Chapter: The Chapter on Brahmins (Brāhmaṇavagga) is finished.
155:
## (7) 2. Mahāvagga ## 1. Titthāyatanasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the second vagga, 'titthāyatanāni' refers to the places where views, which are like fords (tittha), arise, or the places where sectarians (titthiya) arise. In this context, one should understand the ford (tittha), the ford-maker (titthakara), the sectarian (titthiya), and the sectarian's disciple (titthiya-sāvaka). The 'ford' (tittha) refers to the sixty-two types of wrong views. The 'ford-maker' (titthakara) refers to those like Pūraṇa Kassapa who originate those wrong views. The 'sectarian' (titthiya) refers to those who delight in and accept those wrong views. The 'sectarian's disciple' (titthiya-sāvaka) refers to the donors and supporters of those sectarians.

Regarding 'āyatana', in the context of 'Kamboja is the āyatana of horses, Dakkhiṇāpatha is the āyatana of cattle,' āyatana means the place of origin (sañjātiṭṭhāna).

'Birds frequent the pleasant āyatana; those seeking shade go for shade, those seeking fruit go for the fruit-eaters.' In this verse, āyatana means the place of assembly (samosaraṇaṭṭhāna). In the passage, 'Monks, there are these five bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana),' āyatana means cause (kāraṇa). All these meanings are applicable to the term 'titthāyatana' here.

This is because all those with wrong views, when they arise, arise only within these three positions; when they assemble, they assemble and meet only in these three positions; and these three are the very causes for their status as holders of wrong views. Thus, they are called 'titthāyatana' in the sense of being bases (āyatana) like fords, through meanings such as place of origin. For that same reason, they are also called 'titthāyatana' as the bases of sectarians.

'Samanuyuñjiyamānāni' means when they are questioned, 'What kind of views are these?' 'Samanugāhiyamānāni' means when they are properly scrutinized and asked, 'For what reason did these views arise?' 'Samanubhāsiyamānāni' means when they are properly exhorted, 'Abandon these evil wrong views.' Alternatively, all three of these are synonyms for investigative questioning. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: 'Samanuyuñjati, samanuggāhati, or samanubhāsati—these are all the same in meaning, equal in part, and identical in nature.'

'Parampi gantvā' means having reached any lineage, whether it be the lineage of teachers, the lineage of views, or the lineage of successive existences. 'Akiriyāya saṇṭhahanti' means they stand merely in non-action (akiriya). 'Our teacher is a proponent of the view that everything is due to past deeds (pubbekata-vādī), our teacher's teacher was such a proponent, and our teacher's teacher's teacher was such a proponent. Our teacher...'
156:
"...is one who holds the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord (issara-nimmāna-vādī); our teacher's teacher is one who holds the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord; our teacher's teacher's teacher is one who holds the doctrine of creation by a Supreme Lord. Our teacher is one who holds the doctrine of no cause and no condition (ahetu-apaccayavādī); our teacher's teacher is one who holds the doctrine of no cause and no condition; our teacher's teacher's teacher is one who holds the doctrine of no cause and no condition." Thus proceeding, these doctrines are said to go through the lineage of teachers.

"Our teacher held the view of past actions; our teacher's teacher... [pe]... our teacher's teacher's teacher held the view of no cause and no condition." Thus proceeding, these are said to go through the lineage of views.

"The existence (attabhāva) of our teacher had its cause in what was done in the past; our teacher's teacher's... [pe]... the existence of our teacher's teacher's teacher was without cause and without condition." Thus proceeding, these are said to go through the lineage of existences. Even though they go back to such a great distance, they come to a standstill in mere non-action; not even a single person among these holders of wrong views is known as the doer or the one who causes others to do.

'A person' (purisapuggalo) means a being (satta). Although it is said as 'man' (purisa) or 'person' (puggalo), it simply refers to a being. However, this is called conventional speech (sammuti-kathā); whatever one understands, it is spoken to him in that way.

'Experiences' (paṭisaṃvedeti) means one knows the feeling that has arisen in one's own continuity, makes it known, or experiences it.

'Due to what was done in the past' (pubbekata-hetu) means due to the cause of kamma done in the past; the meaning is that one experiences only because of the condition of past kamma. By this, they reject kamma-feeling and functional (kiriya) feeling, and accept only resultant (vipāka) feeling. Alternatively, eight types of diseases are mentioned: those originating from bile, those originating from phlegm, those originating from wind, those originating from a combination of the three, those produced by seasonal changes, those produced by improper conduct, those produced by external effort, and those produced by the result of kamma. Among these, they reject seven and accept only resultant feeling.

Also, three groups of kamma are mentioned: kamma to be experienced in the present life, kamma to be experienced in the next life, and kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparapariyāya-vedanīya). Among these, they reject two and accept only subsequent kamma. Also, three groups of results (vipāka) are mentioned: result in the present life, result in the next life, and result in subsequent lives. Among these, they also reject two and accept only subsequent result. Also, four groups of volition (cetanā) are mentioned: wholesome volition, unwholesome volition, resultant volition, and functional volition. Among these, they also reject three and accept only resultant volition.

'Due to creation by a Supreme Lord' (issara-nimmāna-hetu) means due to the cause of creation by a Supreme Lord; the meaning is that one experiences because of being created by a Supreme Lord. This is their intention—these three...
157:
(They hold that) feelings experienced in the present cannot be due to one's own actions, or due to the actions of others (at one's command), or due to past actions, or without cause and condition; rather, these feelings are experienced solely because of the creation by a supreme Lord (Issara). Those who speak thus reject all eight types of diseases mentioned below, without acknowledging even one. They reject all three groups of kamma, three groups of results (vipāka), and four groups of volition (cetanā) mentioned below, without acknowledging even one.

'Ahetu-apaccayā' means experiencing without cause and without condition, solely by chance. This is their intention: these three types of feelings in the present cannot be experienced due to one's own actions, or due to the actions of others, or due to past actions, or due to the creation by a supreme Lord; rather, these feelings are experienced solely without cause and condition. Those who speak thus reject everything, including the diseases mentioned below, without acknowledging even one.

Having thus laid down the matrix (mātikā), the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with "Tatra, bhikkhave" in order to analyze and demonstrate it. In those words, saying "Thus I speak" is shown for the purpose of establishing them in their own view. For if they are rebuked without their view being established, they might shift from their view to another, saying, "Venerable Gotama, we do not hold the view that everything is caused by past actions," and so on. But once their view is firmly established, they have no opportunity to shift, and thus they are well-rebuked. Therefore, He said "Thus I speak" to establish their view.

"Tenahāyasmanto" means "In that case, venerable sirs." What does this mean? If what you say is true, then according to your view, people would become killers of living beings solely because of past actions. Whoever in the world kills living beings, all of them would be killers solely because of past actions. Why? Because it is your view that the act of killing cannot be experienced due to one's own actions, or due to the actions of others, or due to the creation by a supreme Lord, or without cause and condition, but is experienced solely because of past actions. Just as those who kill living beings (would do so because of past kamma), so too those who abstain from killing would abstain solely because of past actions. In this way, the Blessed One took their own view and applied the rebuke to them. In the same manner, the application should be understood for terms such as "adinna-ādāyino" (those who take what is not given).
158:
For those who take it as the essence (as the highest), it is said 'sārato paccāgacchanti'. 'Desire' (chanda) refers to the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). Regarding the phrase "This should be done or this should not be done," the meaning is: there is no desire to act (kattukamyatā) or personal effort (paccatta-purisakāra) for the purpose of performing a wholesome deed that should be done, or for the purpose of not performing an unwholesome deed that should not be done. If desire and effort are absent, there can be no "this should be done" or "this should not be done."

Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not found or established as true and firm, it means: if it were possible to do what should be done and to abstain from what should not be done, then "what should be done" and "what should not be done" would be found as true and firm. Since this person cannot find both, they are not found as true and firm. This is the meaning of "when both are not found."

'Muṭṭhassatīnaṃ' refers to those who are forgetful or whose mindfulness is lost. 'Anārakkhānaṃ viharataṃ' refers to those who live without guarding the six sense doors. "Na hoti paccattaṃ sahadhammiko samaṇavādo" means that for you who are like this, the claim of being a recluse (samaṇa) along with its reason is not possible and cannot be fulfilled. This is because being a recluse is solely due to past causes, and not being a recluse is also solely due to past causes. 'Sahadhammiko' means "along with the reason." 'Niggaho hoti' means "there is my rebuke," and those recluses and brahmins are rebuked.

Having thus rebuked those who hold the view of past actions (pubbekata-vāda), He now spoke the words beginning with "Tatra, bhikkhave" to rebuke those who hold the view of creation by a Lord (issara-nimmāna-vāda). The meaning of those words should be understood in the same way as explained for the view of past actions. The same applies to the view of causelessness (ahetuka-vāda).

Thus, He showed the emptiness and the non-liberating nature of these wrong views because they lead to the state of non-action (akiriyā). He showed how they are like someone pounding husks because they lack essence, and like someone blowing on a firefly thinking it is a fire. Among those with wrong views, because those of the past, middle, and future cannot see the meaning, He showed their similarity to a line of blind men (andhaveṇu). Those who accept these views based on mere sound and think they have essence are like the young rabbit who, hearing the "thud" of a ripe wood-apple falling to the ground, mistakenly thought "the world is collapsing" and fled. Now, in order to show the essential nature and the liberating quality of the Dhamma He Himself taught...
159:
The Buddha spoke the words beginning with, 'Monks, this Dhamma is...'. In that passage, 'aniggahito' means a Dhamma that is not suppressed by others, or cannot be suppressed. 'Asaṃkiliṭṭho' means a Dhamma that is free from defilements and pure, such that even those who strive saying, 'We will defile it,' are unable to do so. 'Anupavajjo' means a Dhamma that is free from reproach or blame. 'Appaṭikuṭṭho' means a Dhamma that is not rejected or reviled in the manner of saying, 'What is the use of this Dhamma? Cast it away.' 'Viññūhi' means by the wise. This is said because the words of the ignorant, who speak without knowing, are not a standard (pamāṇa).

Now, to demonstrate that Dhamma, the Buddha asked the question, 'Monks, what is it?' and laid down the matrix (mātikā) with the method beginning with, 'These six elements.' Desiring to analyze and show them in order, He spoke again the words beginning with, 'These six elements.' In that matrix, 'dhātuyo' refers to natures (sabhāva). The meaning of 'element' (dhātu) is the sense of nature that reveals the state of being non-soul (nijjīva) and non-being (nissatta). 'Phassāyatanāni' are called bases (āyatana) in the sense of being the location for resultant contacts. 'Manopavicārā' are the various mental explorations of the mind in eighteen ways through the 'feet' of initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra).

Earth element (pathavī-dhātu) is the nature of support. Water element (āpo-dhātu) is the nature of cohesion. Fire element (tejo-dhātu) is the nature of maturation. Air element (vāyo-dhātu) is the nature of distension. Space element (ākāsa-dhātu) is the nature of non-contact. Consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu) is the nature of cognizing. Thus, this meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) is presented. It is appropriate to explain this meditation on elements both briefly and in detail where it appears in brief. Where it appears in detail, it is not appropriate to explain it briefly, but only in detail. In this Titthāyatana Sutta, however, this meditation appears briefly by way of the six elements. It is appropriate to explain that meditation in both brief and detailed ways.

One who discerns the meditation by way of the six elements in brief discerns it thus: these four—earth element, water element, fire element, and air element—are the Great Elements (mahābhūta), and the space element is derived matter (upādā-rūpa). When one derived matter, the space element, is seen, the remaining twenty-three types of derived matter should be regarded as already seen. 'Viññāṇa-dhātu' is the mind and constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The feeling (vedanā) arisen together with that mind is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); perception (saññā) is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); and contact (phassa) and volition (cetanā) are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). These four are called the mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha/arūpa-kkhandha). As for the four Great Elements and the four Great Elements'...
160:
...derived matter is called the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Among those five aggregates, the four mental aggregates are called 'nāma' (mind), and the aggregate of matter is called 'rūpa' (matter); thus, there are only these two phenomena: mind and matter. Beyond this mind and matter, there is no being (satta) or soul (jīva). Thus, for a monk, the meditation that leads to the fruit of Arahantship by way of the six elements in brief should be understood.

However, one who discerns in detail, having discerned the four great elements, discerns the twenty-three types of derived matter following the discernment of the space element. Thereafter, while investigating their causes, he sees again the four great elements themselves. Among those great elements, he groups them by way of parts: the earth element has 20 parts, the water element has 12, the fire element has 4, and the air element has 6 parts. Having thus defined the 42 parts of the great elements and including the 23 types of derived matter within those great elements, he defines 65 types of matter. Those 65 types of matter, together with the heart-base matter (vatthu-rūpa), become 66; thus, he sees 66 types of matter. As for the consciousness element, by way of mundane consciousness, there are 81 types of consciousness. All these are called the aggregate of consciousness. Since feeling and the others arising together with those consciousnesses are also the same in number (81 each), the 81 feelings are the aggregate of feeling, the 81 perceptions are the aggregate of perception, and the 81 volitions are the aggregate of formations. When these four mental aggregates are taken by way of the three planes (tebhūmaka), they become 324 phenomena. Thus, when all these mental phenomena and the 66 types of material phenomena are combined, there are only two phenomena: mind and matter. Beyond this mind and matter, there is no being or soul. Having thus defined the five aggregates by way of mind and matter, and searching for their causes, he sees the causes thus: they arise because of ignorance (avijjā), because of craving (taṇhā), because of kamma, and because of nutriment (āhāra). Thinking, "In the past, this round of existence (vaṭṭa) proceeded because of these causes; in the future, it will proceed because of these causes; and now also, it proceeds because of these very causes," he overcomes doubt regarding the three periods of time. Practicing in due order, he reaches the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, the meditation that leads to the fruit of Arahantship by way of the six elements in detail should also be understood.

"Cakkhu phassāyatanan" (eye-contact base) means a source (ākara), like a mine for gold and such, because it is the place of origin for the seven contacts that arise together with these seven consciousnesses: two eye-consciousnesses, two receiving consciousnesses, and three investigating consciousnesses. In the passages such as "sotaṃ phassāyatanan" (ear-contact base), the method is the same. Mano...
161:
In this term "base of mind-contact" (manophassāyatana), twenty-two types of resultant contact (vipāka-phassa) should be combined. Thus, this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) comes by way of the six bases of contact (phassāyatana). This meditation subject is taught both in brief and in detail.

To speak first in brief—in this meditation subject, the first five bases are called derived matter (upādā-rūpa); when these five bases are seen, the remaining derived matter is also seen. The sixth base is the mind, which is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The remaining three mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha), such as feeling (vedanā) and so on, which arise together with that mind, should be understood as the meditation subject that leads to the attainment of Arahantship, both in brief and in detail, according to the method mentioned below.

"Having seen a form with the eye" (cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā) means seeing a visible form with eye-consciousness. "A basis for joy" (somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ) means the cause of joy. "Wanders over" (upavicarati) means it occurs by approaching the object, causing the mind to wander over that object. The same method applies to the remaining terms. In this context, whether it is a pleasant or unpleasant object, the visible form that gives rise to joy when seen is called "a basis for joy" (somanassaṭṭhāniya). The visible form that gives rise to grief (domanassa) when seen is called "a basis for grief" (domanassaṭṭhāniya). The visible form that gives rise to equanimity (upekkhā) when seen should be known as "a basis for equanimity" (upekkhāṭṭhāniya). The same method applies to sounds and so on. Thus, this meditation subject comes in brief. In a place where it comes in brief, it is appropriate to teach it both in brief and in detail. In a place where it comes in detail, it is not appropriate to teach it in brief. However, in this Titthāyatana Sutta, this meditation subject comes in brief by way of the eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra). It is appropriate to teach this meditation subject both in brief and in detail.

To speak first in brief among these two—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, smell, and taste: these nine are derived matter (upādā-rūpa). When these nine types of derived matter are seen, the remaining derived matter is also seen. Tangible object (phoṭṭhabba) consists of three great primary elements (mahābhūta); when these three great primary elements are seen, the fourth is also seen. Mind is the aggregate of consciousness; the three mental aggregates such as feeling and so on, which arise together with that mind, should be understood as the meditation subject that leads to the attainment of Arahantship, both in brief and in detail, according to the method mentioned below.

"Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni) means the truths that make one noble, or the truths penetrated by the Noble Ones. This is just a brief explanation of this term; in detail, this term has been explained in the Visuddhimagga. For what purpose did He begin this statement, "Monks, these six elements"? He began it for the sake of easy understanding. For when the Tathāgata wishes to teach the twelve-linked cycle of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) to someone, He shows the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) which has its root in the descent into the womb (gabbhāvakkanti). When the round of rebirth called the descent into the womb is shown, it is easy to teach and easy to make others understand. Thus, it should be understood that He began this statement for the sake of easy understanding.
162:
It should be understood that this discourse was undertaken for the sake of easy understanding, as it is also easy to make others understand. In that sutta, "six elements" refers to the earth element and so on, mentioned below. "Dependent upon" (upādāya) means based on. By this term, He shows the mere condition (paccaya). This means: "Because of the condition of the six elements, the descent of the embryo into the womb occurs."

By the condition of whose six elements does the descent of the embryo into the womb occur? Is it the mother's or the father's? It is neither the mother's nor the father's. In fact, it is only by the condition of the six elements of the being who is taking rebirth (paṭisandhi) that the so-called descent of the embryo into the womb occurs. This "embryo" (gabbha) is of various kinds: an embryo in hell, an embryo in the animal realm, an embryo in the realm of hungry ghosts, an embryo among humans, and an embryo among devas. However, in this context, the human embryo is intended. "Descent occurs" (avakkanti hoti) means the descent into the womb, the arising, the manifestation. How does it occur? It occurs through the meeting of three factors.

It is also taught thus: "Monks, through the meeting of three factors, the descent of the embryo into the womb occurs. What three? Here, the mother and father have come together, but the mother is not in her season, and the gandhabba (the being to be reborn) is not present; then there is no descent of the embryo. Here, the mother and father have come together, and the mother is in her season, but the gandhabba is not present; then too there is no descent of the embryo. But, monks, when the mother and father have come together, and the mother is in her season, and the gandhabba is present—through the meeting of these three factors, the descent of the embryo into the womb occurs." (Majjhima Nikāya).

In this context of "When there is descent into the womb, there is mind and matter (nāmarūpa)," as in the teaching "With consciousness as condition, mind and matter come to be," the thirty-three states—namely, the heart-decad (vatthu-dasaka), the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), and the three mental aggregates—are taken. However, in this context of "When there is descent into the womb, there is mind and matter," it should be understood that thirty-four states are taken by including the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) at the moment of rebirth for womb-born beings. Just as the manifestation of mind and matter when there is descent into the womb is shown by "With mind and matter as condition, the six bases (saḷāyatana) come to be," etc., so too He shows the manifestation of the six bases when there is mind and matter, the manifestation of contact when there are the six bases, and the manifestation of feeling when there is contact.
163:
In this word 'vediyamānassa', one who experiences a feeling is called 'vediyamāna', and one who knows is also called 'vediyamāna'. In this passage (from the Cūḷavagga Commentary), 'Venerable Sir, I know and experience (the offense); let the Saṅgha recognize me as one who knows and experiences,' 'vediyamāna' refers to the one who experiences. However, in this passage (from the Majjhima Nikāya, etc.), 'When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows, "I experience a pleasant feeling,"' 'vediyamāna' refers to the one who knows. Here also, only the one who knows is intended. 'I declare: This is suffering' means that for a being who knows thus, I declare, make known, and cause to understand: 'This phenomenon occurring in the three planes is suffering; suffering is only this much; there is no suffering beyond this.' The same method applies to the terms 'This is the origin of suffering' and so forth.

Regarding those Truths such as suffering, the definitive explanation is as follows: Excluding craving, the five aggregates belonging to the three planes are called 'suffering' (dukkha). The previous craving that produces that suffering is called the 'origin of suffering' (dukkhasamudaya). The cessation of both these truths by way of non-arising is called the 'cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodha). The Noble Eightfold Path is called the 'practice leading to the cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā). Thus, even when the Blessed One says, 'When there is descent (okkanti), there is name-and-form,' He speaks only to one who knows. Whether He says, 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise,' or 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises,' or 'With contact as condition, feeling arises,' or 'Bhikkhus, I declare "This is suffering" only to one who knows,' or when He declares 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' He speaks only to one who knows.

Now, wishing to elaborate on the meaning of those Truths placed in order, He said the words beginning with 'Bhikkhus, what is...'. All of that has been explained in every detail in the Visuddhimagga. It should be understood exactly according to the method stated in that text. However, there is this distinction: In that Visuddhimagga, it appears according to the scriptural text, 'The Noble Truth of the origin of suffering is that craving which leads to renewed existence,' but in this discourse, it appears by way of the mode of conditions (Dependent Origination) as 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise.' And in that Visuddhimagga, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering is explained according to the scriptural text, 'It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving,' but in this discourse, it is explained by way of the cessation of Dependent Origination as 'Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance.'

In that passage, 'asesavirāganirodhā' means through remainderless fading away and through remainderless cessation. Both these terms are just synonyms for each other. 'Saṅkhāranirodho' means of formations...
164:
...it is the cessation by way of non-arising of formations. The same method applies to the remaining terms such as the cessation of consciousness. In fact, by these terms such as 'through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance,' the Dhamma of Nibbāna is indicated, depending on which ignorance and so forth cease; in terms of meaning, it is a description of Nibbāna. Indeed, Nibbāna is called by the name 'Cessation' (nirodha) of those respective phenomena, such as 'cessation of ignorance' or 'cessation of formations.' 'Kevalassa' means of the whole. 'Dukkhakkhandhassa' means of the mass of suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). 'Nirodha hoti' means non-occurrence happens. In that passage, since the cessation (nirodha) of ignorance and so forth is called the state of exhaustion (khīṇākāra), and also Arahattaphala and Nibbāna, it should be understood that in this teaching of Dependent Origination, by way of showing the state of exhaustion, Arahattaphala is spoken of in twelve places, and Nibbāna is also spoken of in twelve places. In the phrase 'This is called,' the word 'This' (idaṃ) is said referring only to Nibbāna. 'Aṭṭhaṅgiko' (eightfold) means there is no other path separate from the eight factors. Just as when one says 'a musical instrument with five factors,' it means the collection of five factors itself is the instrument; so too here, it should be understood that the collection of eight factors itself is the Path. 'Aniggahito' means unrefuted or unsuppressed. Indeed, one who suppresses shows (the original teaching) by either decreasing it, increasing it, or changing it. Among those ways, regarding the Four Noble Truths, one cannot show them by decreasing them as 'These are not four, but two or three,' nor by increasing them as 'five or six,' nor by changing them as 'These are not the four Noble Truths, but four others.' Therefore, this Dhamma is called 'unrefuted' (aniggahita). The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## 2. Bhayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second discourse, 'amātāputtikāni' means mother and son are called 'mātāputta'; because there is no mother or son capable of protecting (from danger) therein, they are called 'amātāputtikā' (dangers where mother and son cannot help). 'Yaṃ' means at which time. It means when that (danger of fire) arises, the mother does not get to see the son, and the son does not get to see the mother. 'Bhayaṃ hoti' means the fear of mental terror arises. 'Aṭavisaṅkopo' means destruction due to the forest. Here, by the word 'aṭavī' (forest), the robbers living in the forest should be understood. Indeed, when those robbers descend from the forest to the countryside and attack and plunder villages, market towns, and royal capitals, it is called 'aṭavisaṅkopa' (forest uprising); He said this referring to that situation. In the phrase 'cakkasamārūḷhā' (mounted on wheels), the wheel of postures (iriyāpathacakka) is suitable, and the wheel of a vehicle (yānacakka) is also suitable. Indeed, when danger arrives, those who have vehicles load their belongings onto them and flee. Those who have vehicles...
165:
Those without vehicles flee either by carrying loads with a yoke or on their heads. They are said to have mounted the wheel of postures or the wheel of a cart. 'Pariyāyantī' means wandering here and there. 'Kadāci' means at some time. 'Karahaci' is a synonym for that same 'kadāci'. 'A mother also finds her son' means she gets the opportunity to see her son who is coming, going, or hidden in a certain place. 'Udakavāhako' means a river full of water. 'A mother also finds her son' means seeing the son drifting along, clinging to a raft, a float, a clay vessel, or a piece of wood; or seeing him standing in a village or forest after safely crossing over to land.

Having thus shown the figurative 'dangers where mother and son do not find each other' (amātāputtika-bhaya), he now says 'tīṇimāni' etc., to show them literally. In that context, 'jarābhayaṃ' is the danger arising on account of old age. The same method applies to the remaining terms. This was also said: 'On account of old age, there arises fearful danger, trembling, hair-standing-on-end, and terror of mind. On account of sickness, and on account of death, there arises fearful danger, trembling, hair-standing-on-end, and terror of mind.' The remaining phrases are clear in all places.

## 3. Venāgapurasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'Kosalesu' means in the country named Kosala. 'Cārikaṃ caramāno' means while traveling on a long journey. The Blessed One's wandering on tour is of two kinds: 'turitacārikā' (quick tour) and 'aturitacārikā' (leisurely tour). Therein, seeing a person capable of realization even in a distant place and going quickly for the purpose of their realization is called 'turitacārikā'. This should be understood in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. Traveling through villages and towns in succession, covering a distance of one league or half a league daily, benefiting the world through alms-round and so forth, is called 'aturitacārikā'. With reference to this leisurely tour, it is said 'cārikaṃ caramāno'. The detailed explanation of the tour is stated in the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary. 'Brāhmaṇagāmo' refers to a village where brahmins assemble or a fief-village of brahmins. Here, a village where brahmins reside and assemble is intended. 'Tadavasari' means he arrived there. Since the monastery is not specified here, it should be understood that he went to a forest grove suitable for Buddhas located not far from that village.
166:
There is a forest grove suitable for Buddhas; it should be understood that the Teacher went to that forest grove. 'Assosuṃ' means they heard, they obtained, they knew according to the sequence of the sound of words reaching the ear-door. 'Kho' is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa) or as a mere filler (padapūraṇa). Between these two, in the sense of emphasis, it should be understood as 'they indeed heard, and there was no obstacle to their hearing.' In the sense of a filler, it is merely for the smoothness of the phrasing.

Now, to reveal the matter they heard, it is said 'The ascetic Gotama, indeed, sirs...' and so forth. Therein, he is known as 'Samaṇa' (ascetic) because he has calmed evil. 'Khalu' is a particle in the sense of hearsay. 'Bho' is a mere address among themselves. 'Gotamo' is a designation of the Blessed One by his clan name; therefore, 'The ascetic Gotama, indeed, sirs' should be understood as 'The ascetic of the Gotama clan, sirs, it is said.' 'Sakyaputto' is a designation of the Blessed One's high birth. 'Sakyakulā pabbajito' is a designation of his going forth out of faith; it means he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that family which was not overcome by any loss and was not diminished. 'Taṃ kho pana' is the accusative case in the sense of 'regarding such a person' (itthambhūtākhyāna), meaning 'of that venerable Gotama.' 'Kalyāṇa' means endowed with good qualities, meaning 'excellent.' 'Kittisadda' means fame or the sound of praise. 'Abbhuggata' means having spread, pervading the world including the devas. How? 'For this reason, the Blessed One is... [pe]... Buddha, Bhagavā.' Here, the connection of words is: 'For this reason, the Blessed One is Arahaṃ, for this reason, he is Sammāsambuddha... [pe]... for this reason, he is Bhagavā.' It means 'for this reason and for that reason.'

Therein, 'The Blessed One is to be known as Arahaṃ for these reasons: because of being remote (from defilements), because of having destroyed the enemies (defilements) and the spokes (of the wheel of saṃsāra), because of being worthy of requisites, and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil,' and so forth. Having laid down the table of contents (mātikā) in this manner, all these terms are explained in detail in the Buddhānussati-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga; therefore, their detailed explanation should be taken from there. The Blessed One is to be known as 'Arahaṃ' because of being remote from defilements, because of killing the enemies that are defilements, because of destroying the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because of being worthy of receiving the four requisites, and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil. 'So imaṃ lokaṃ' means that venerable Gotama reveals this world of space (okāsaloka) which will be mentioned. 'Sadevakaṃ' means together with the six deva realms.
167:
By the phrase 'He, this world' (so imaṃ lokaṃ), the Venerable Gotama points out this world which is about to be described. 'With its devas' (sadevakaṃ) means the world together with the devas. Similarly, 'with its Maras' (samārakaṃ) means together with Mara; 'with its Brahmas' (sabrahmakaṃ) means together with Brahma; 'with its recluses and brahmins' (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ) means together with recluses and brahmins. Because beings are produced, they are called 'generation' (pajā); it refers to those beings. 'With its devas and humans' (sadevamanussaṃ) means together with devas and humans. Among these terms, by the word 'sadevaka', it should be understood that the five types of sense-sphere devas are included. By the word 'samāraka', the sixth sense-sphere deva is included. By the word 'sabrahmaka', the Brahmas such as the Brahma-kayika are included. By the word 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī', both the recluses and brahmins who are opponents and enemies of the Dispensation, as well as those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil or removed evil, are included. By the word 'pajā', the world of beings (sattaloka) is included. By the word 'sadevamanussa', the conventional gods (kings) and the remaining humans are included. Thus, it should be understood that in this context, the world of beings together with the world of locations (okāsaloka) is taken by three terms, and the world of beings alone is taken by two terms through the power of 'generation' (pajā).

Another way: By the view of 'sadevaka', the formless realm (arūpāvacara) is included. By the view of 'samāraka', the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included. By the view of 'sabrahmaka', the fine-material Brahma realm (rūpāvacara) is included. By the view of 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa' etc., the human world together with conventional gods is included through the power of the fourfold assembly, or all the remaining world of beings. However, the ancient teachers said: 'sadevaka' means the remaining world together with the deities; 'samāraka' means the remaining world together with Mara; 'sabrahmaka' means the remaining world together with the Brahmas. Thus, having included all beings who have reached the three states of existence into the three terms by three modes, he again said 'with its recluses and brahmins, this generation, with its devas and humans' (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajā sadevamanussaṃ) to encompass them without remainder by two terms. Thus, it is said that by these five terms, the three planes are encompassed without remainder in various ways.

In the phrase 'Having realized it himself through direct knowledge, he makes it known' (sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti), 'sayaṃ' means by himself, not being led by others. 'Abhiññā' means having known with higher knowledge, with superior knowledge. 'Sacchikatvā' means having witnessed/realized; by this word, knowledge through inference and so on is excluded. 'Pavedeti' means he makes it known, he makes it understood, he declares it clearly.

That Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, having relinquished even the incomparable bliss of seclusion...
168:
He teaches the Dhamma. When he teaches that Dhamma, whether a little or a lot, he teaches it only in a manner that is beautiful in the beginning and so on. It means that he teaches by making it good and faultless in the beginning, and he teaches by making it good and faultless in the middle and in the end as well.

Regarding that (beauty in the beginning, middle, and end), just as there is a beginning, middle, and end of the Teaching (desanā), there is also a beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (sāsana). In the Teaching, in a verse of four lines, the first line is called the beginning, the next two lines are called the middle, and the one remaining line at the end is called the end. In a Sutta with a single connection, the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, the concluding words 'Thus he spoke' is the end, and the text between the two is the middle. In a Sutta with many connections, the first connection is the beginning, the last connection is the end, and the one, two, or many connections in the middle are simply the middle.

In the Dispensation, virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā) are called the beginning. It has also been said: 'What is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and straight view are the beginning of wholesome states.' The Noble Path, spoken of as 'Monks, there is a Middle Way (majjhima paṭipadā) fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,' is called the middle. Fruition (phala) and Nibbāna are called the end. In the passage, 'Brahmin, therefore, this holy life has this (Fruition of Arahantship) as its shore, this as its end,' Fruition is called the end. In the passage, 'Friend Visākha, the holy life merges into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, has Nibbāna as its end,' Nibbāna is called the end. Here, however, the beginning, middle, and end of the Teaching are intended. For the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, shows virtue in the beginning, shows the Path in the middle, and shows Nibbāna at the end. Therefore, it is said: 'He teaches the Dhamma, beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, beautiful in the end.' Therefore, another Dhamma preacher, when preaching the Dhamma:

'Should show virtue in the beginning, should clarify the Path in the middle,
Should show Nibbāna at the end; this is the systematic structure of preachers.'

In the phrase 'with meaning and phrasing' (sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ), if a person's teaching is based on praising rice-gruel, boiled rice, women, men, and so on, he does not teach a Dhamma that is with meaning. The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such kinds of teaching, teaches a teaching based on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and so on. Therefore, 'with meaning...'
169:
It is said, "He preaches with phrasing (savyañjana)." If a person's preaching is associated with only one of the syllables such as the lax (sithila), or if it consists entirely of syllables recited without touching the lips, or entirely of syllables recited as released, or entirely of syllables recited by pressing the points of articulation, then that preaching is called "preaching without phrasing" (abyañjana), because it lacks the completeness of phrasing, similar to the languages of the Damiḷa, Kirāta, Yavana, and other foreigners (milakkha).

However, the Blessed One—

"Lax (sithila) and aspirated (dhanita), long (dīgha) and short (rassa), light (lahuka) and heavy (garuka), and nasalized (niggahīta);
Connected (sambandha), distinct (vavatthita), and released (vimutta)—thus there are ten divisions in the knowledge of phrasing."

Without violating these ten kinds of phrasing mentioned thus, He preaches the Dhamma by making it possess complete phrasing. Therefore, it is said, "He preaches with phrasing."

In the phrase "entirely complete" (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ), "kevala" is a term for the whole. "Paripuṇṇa" is a term for being neither deficient nor excessive. This is what is meant: He preaches only that which is entirely complete; there is not even a single portion of the preaching that is incomplete. "Pure" (parisuddhaṃ) means free from the defilements that cause impurity. If a person preaches with the thought, "Depending on this Dhamma preaching, I shall obtain gain and honor," his preaching is called impure. The Blessed One, however, being regardless of worldly gain, preaches with a heart made tender by the meditation on loving-kindness that spreads welfare, and with a mind established in the nature of lifting beings up [from the whirlpool of saṃsāra]. Therefore, it is said, "He preaches purely."

In the phrase "He proclaims the holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti), "brahmacariya" refers to the entire Dispensation (sāsana) encompassed by the Threefold Training (sikkhā-ttaya). Therefore, it should be understood in this context that as the Blessed One preaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... and pure, He proclaims the holy life of the entire Dispensation encompassed by the Threefold Training. "Brahmacariya" means the practice that is noble (brahma) in the sense of being excellent, or it means the practice of those who have become noble, such as the Buddhas.

"It is good indeed" (sādhu kho pana) means it is truly excellent; it means it brings welfare and happiness. "Such Arahants" (tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ) refers to Arahants like the Venerable Gotama, who are of such a nature—those who are difficult to see even for hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons; whose delightful bodies are graced with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty minor marks, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance; whose appearance one can never tire of beholding; whose voice of Dhamma is exceedingly sweet; and who have attained the title of "Arahant" in the world due to their realization of true qualities. "It is good to see" (dassanaṃ hoti) means that even the mere act of opening one's clear and serene eyes to behold them is truly excellent. If we were to hear even a single word of the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One with His noble voice (brahmassara) endowed with eight qualities, it would be even more excellent.
170:
With the intention, "It will be especially good," they "approached where the Blessed One was," which means they came with joyful hearts, having abandoned all other business. Regarding the phrase "with hands joined in salutation" (añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā), those people were associated with both sides [wrong view and right view], and they thought thus: "If those with wrong view question us, 'Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?', we shall reply to them, 'Does merely joining the hands amount to paying homage?' If those with right view question us, 'Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?', we shall reply to them, 'Does paying homage only occur when one strikes the ground with one's head? Is the act of joining hands not also indeed paying homage?'"

"Name and clan" (nāmagottaṃ) means they made their names known by saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am the son of such-and-such, named Datta, named Mitta, and I have come here." They made their clans known by saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am of the Vāseṭṭha clan, of the Kaccāna clan, and I have come here." It is said that these people, being from poor and decayed families, acted thus with the thought, "We shall become well-known by name and clan in the midst of the assembly." Those who sat down in silence, however, were the cunning and the extremely foolish. Among them, the cunning ones sat in silence to free themselves from the obligation of giving, thinking, "If we speak a word or two, we will become familiar; and once there is familiarity, it would not be proper to remain without offering a meal or two." The extremely foolish ones, due to their ignorance, sat in silence in various places like lumps of clay cast down on the ground.

"Venāgapurika" means a resident of Venāgapura. "He addressed these words" means that while looking at the body of the Tathāgata from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair, he saw the Tathāgata's body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, shining with the eighty minor marks, and surrounded by the dense Buddha-rays of six colors that emerged from the body and overspread the surrounding area for about eighty cubits. Filled with wonder, and wishing to praise His qualities, he spoke these words: "It is wonderful, Master Gotama," and so forth.

In that context, "yāvañcidaṃ" is a term indicating an extreme degree or measure. It should be connected with the word "vippasanna" (serene). The meaning is "exceedingly serene" or "serene to an extreme degree." "Faculties" (indriyāni) refers to the six faculties, such as the eye-faculty. For that Brahmin, the serenity of the five faculties was evident upon seeing the serenity of the places where the eye and other faculties are situated. Furthermore, since that serenity occurs only when the mind is serene—for there is no such thing as serenity of the faculties for those with un-serene minds—the serenity of his mind-faculty (manindriya) also became evident to him. He...
171:
Taking the clarity (of the Brahmin's faculties), he said, "The faculties are very clear." *Parisuddha* means being without impurity. *Pariyodāta* means brilliantly pure. *Sārada badarapaṇḍu* refers to a jujube fruit produced in the autumn season that is not yet overripe. Such a jujube fruit is both clean and brightly pure. *Tālapakka* refers to a well-ripened palm fruit. *Sampati bandhanā pamutta* refers to a fruit that has just been released (fallen) from its stalk at that very moment. When the base of the stalk of that ripe palm fruit is removed and it is placed on a wooden board facing upwards, it appears clean and brightly pure to those looking at the area of about four finger-breadths. Intending this, he spoke thus. *Nekkha jambonada* refers to an ingot of Jambonada gold which has an extremely red hue. *Dakkhakammāraputtasuparikammakata* refers to that which is well-fashioned and polished by a skilled son of a goldsmith. *Ukkāmukhe sukusalasampahaṭṭha* means the state of being well-fashioned and well-polished by a very skilled goldsmith through smelting in a furnace, striking, rubbing, and burnishing. *Paṇḍukambale nikkhitta* refers to (a gold ingot) that has been smelted by fire, rubbed with a stone, prepared with red earth, and then placed on a red woolen blanket. *Bhāsate* means it shines because of the radiance produced. *Tapate* means it glows because it destroys darkness. *Virocati* means it is beautiful, shining brilliantly.

In the phrase *uccāsayanamahāsayanāni*, a couch or bench that exceeds the standard measurements is called *uccāsayana* (high bed). An unallowable bedding that is wide and extensive in length and breadth is called *mahāsayana* (large bed). Now, wishing to show those items, he said, "*Seyyathidaṃ āsandī*" and so on. Among those terms, *āsandī* is a seat or chair that exceeds the standard measurements. *Pallanka* is a couch made with animal figures carved on its legs. *Gonaka* is a large long-haired rug. It is said that the hairs of that rug are longer than four finger-breadths. *Cittaka* is a woolen coverlet variegated with floral designs. *Paṭikā* is a white coverlet made of wool. *Paṭalikā* is a woolen coverlet variegated with thick floral designs; it is also called *āmalakapaṭṭa*. *Tūlikā* is a bedding stuffed with one of the three types of cotton. *Vikatikā* is a woolen coverlet variegated with figures of lions, tigers, etc. *Uddalomī* is a woolen coverlet with hair on both sides. Some teachers say it is a coverlet with flowers appearing on one side. *Ekantalomī* is a woolen coverlet with hair on only one side. Some teachers say it is a coverlet with flowers appearing on both sides. *Kaṭṭissa* is a coverlet made of silk threads embroidered with gems. *Koseyya* is a coverlet made of silk threads also embroidered with gems. *Kuttaka* is a large woolen coverlet large enough for sixteen dancing women to stand and dance upon. *Hatthatthara* and so forth are coverings spread on the backs of elephants and so on.
172:
There are also coverings made by showing figures of elephants and so on. *Ajinappaveṇī* is a multi-layered covering made by sewing together skins of the black antelope to the size of a couch. The remaining meaning is just as stated below.

*Nikāmalābhī* means obtaining as much as desired, or obtaining whenever desired. *Akicchalābhī* means obtaining without pain. *Akasiralābhī* means obtaining abundantly or obtaining what is noble; it is said with the thought that he obtains only very noble beds and seats. This Verañja Brahmin was one who gave weight to beds and seats; seeing the state of the Blessed One's exceptionally clear faculties, he thought, "Surely this Venerable Gotama sits and lies on such high and large beds and seats. Therefore, his faculties are exceptionally clear, and his complexion is clean and brilliantly pure." Thinking thus, he spoke in praise of these lodgings.

In the phrase "even if obtained, they are not allowable," some certain beds and seats are allowable. Indeed, a pure silk coverlet is allowable to be spread even on a couch. Large rugs (*gonaka*) and so forth are allowable by using them as floor coverings, or by cutting off the legs of the long chair (*āsandī*), or by breaking the animal figures (*vāla*) of the couch (*pallanka*), or by opening up the cotton-stuffed coverlet (*tūlikā*) and making it into a pillow (*bimmohana*). According to the words (in the Cullavagga), these beds and seats also become allowable through such a procedure. However, with reference to what is unallowable, it is said that all of them are not allowable.

"I enter only the forest" means entering only the jungle. "*Yadeva*" means whatever (grass and leaves) they are. "Having folded the legs crosswise" (*pallankaṃ ābhujitvā*) means sitting with the thighs bound all around. "Having set the body erect" (*ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya*) means placing the upper body straight, aligning the eighteen vertebrae end to end. "Having set up mindfulness in front" (*parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā*) means setting up mindfulness towards the meditation subject, or it means having grasped the mindfulness that leads to liberation. For it was said: "*Pari* has the sense of grasping. *Mukha* has the sense of liberation. *Sati* has the sense of setting up. Therefore, it is said: having set up mindfulness in front." "I dwell having attained" (*upasampajja viharāmi*) means I dwell having obtained and realized it.

Being such a person, having become possessed of one of the first jhāna and so forth, he says, "At that time, this walking path of mine is a divine walking path (*dibbacankama*)." For the walking of one who walks after attaining the four fine-material jhānas is called a divine walking path; the walking of one who walks after emerging from the attainment is also a divine walking path. The same method applies to standing and other postures. Likewise, it should be understood in the same way for the other two abidings (the Divine Abiding and the Noble Abiding).
173:
With the words "I know thus: 'My lust has been abandoned,'" [the Buddha] spoke, wishing to show only the lust that was abandoned by the Path of Arahantship at the Mahābodhi throne. The same method applies to the remaining terms. What is meant by this statement? It refers to the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that reflects on the abandoned defilements; by reviewing knowledge, fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti) is meant. For one who has entered fruition attainment, as well as for one who has emerged from it, their walking and so forth are "noble walking" (ariya-caṅkama) and so on. The rest of the meaning here is clear.

## 4. Commentary on the Sarabha Sutta

In the fourth sutta, "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name. "On the Gijjhakūṭa mountain": it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak) either because it has peaks shaped like vultures or because vultures live on its peaks. By this, the dwelling place of the Blessed One is shown, who lived making Rājagaha his resort for alms. A monastery was built on Gijjhakūṭa dedicated to the Tathāgata; its name was simply the Gijjhakūṭa Monastery. At that time, the Blessed One was staying there. "A wanderer named Sarabha had recently left": this means a wanderer named Sarabha, having gone forth in this Dispensation, left not long after; the meaning is that he had recently disrobed.

When the Fully Enlightened One appeared in the world, the sectarians (titthiyas) lost their gains and honor, while great gains and honor arose for the Triple Gem. As it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One was revered, respected, esteemed, honored, and venerated, and he received the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not revered, respected, esteemed, honored, or venerated, and they did not receive the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."

Those sectarians, numbering about five hundred, whose gains and honor had thus declined, gathered in a wanderers' park and consulted together: "Sirs, since the time the Ascetic Gotama appeared, our gains and honor have diminished. Let us investigate some fault in the Ascetic Gotama and his disciples. By spreading [news of] that fault..."
174:
"...we shall disparage his Dispensation and generate gains and honor for ourselves." While searching for a fault, they said: "It is not possible to see any fault in the Ascetic Gotama in these four areas: the three doors [of action] and livelihood. Leave these four areas aside and look elsewhere." Then, one among those sectarians said: "I see nothing else, but these [monks] gather once a fortnight, close the doors and windows, and do not even allow novices to enter. Even devoted supporters who are like their own lives do not get to see them. They accumulate and practice a deceptive art called Āvaṭṭanī, and by enticing the people, they consume [their offerings]. If we can acquire that art, our gains and honor will become magnificent." Another sectarian stood up saying the same thing. All were of one opinion. Then they said: "Whoever is able to acquire that art, we shall make him the leader in our sect."

Then, starting from the end of the line, they asked, "Can you do it? Can you do it?" When many said, "I cannot, I cannot," they asked Sarabha: "Teacher, can you do it?" He said: "It is no burden to acquire it, provided you stand by your word and make me the leader." They said: "Teacher, it is no burden. Please acquire it; you are already our leader." Sarabha said: "One who acquires that art cannot do so by stealing or plundering. Rather, one must act like a disciple of the Ascetic Gotama, pay homage to his disciples, perform major and minor duties, and eat alms-food from their bowls to acquire it. Do you agree to the performance of such acts?" They said: "Acquire it by any means and give it to us."

"In that case, behave as if you do not see me even if you do," he signaled to the wanderers. Rising early the next morning, he went to the Gijjhakūṭa Great Monastery and prostrated with the five-point contact at the feet of every monk he saw. The monks said: "Other wanderers are fierce and harsh, but this wanderer seems to have faith and devotion." Sarabha said: "Venerable sirs, you have gone forth in a suitable place with understanding. We, however, without reflection, have entered a place that is not a 'ford' (atittha) and are wandering on a path that does not lead to liberation." Having spoken thus, he repeatedly prostrated to every monk he saw, prepared water for bathing and so on, made ready allowable tooth-sticks, washed and anointed their feet, and ate the leftover alms-food he received.
175:
A certain Great Elder, seeing Sarabha the Wanderer living in such a manner, said: "Wanderer, you have faith and devotion; why do you not ordain?" He replied: "Venerable Sir, who would ordain me? For a long time, we have lived as enemies of the Venerable Ones." The Great Elder said: "If you wish to ordain, I myself will ordain you," and he ordained him. From the time of his ordination, he constantly applied himself to the major and minor duties. Then, the Great Elder, pleased with his performance of duties, soon granted him higher ordination (upasampadā). On an Uposatha day, having entered the Uposatha hall with the monks, he saw the monks reciting the Pātimokkha with great effort and thought: "These monks, by reciting in this manner (like a deceptive art), mislead the people and get their food. I too will learn this art within two or three days." He went to the front of the monastery, paid respects to his preceptor (upajjhāya), and asked: "Venerable Sir, what is the name of this Dhamma?" "Friend, it is called the Pātimokkha," he replied. "Venerable Sir, this must be a very noble Dhamma." "Yes, friend, this training (sikkhā) is what upholds the entire Dispensation (Sāsana)," he said. "Venerable Sir, if this training is noble, I will learn this first." The Elder consented, saying: "Friend, learn it."

While he was learning, when he met the wanderers and they asked: "Teacher, how is the situation?" he said: "Friends, do not worry; I will bring it within two or three days," and he soon mastered it. Then he asked his preceptor: "Venerable Sir, is this all, or is there more?" "Friend, this is all," he replied. On the following day, dressed and robed as usual, and in his usual manner, he took his bowl and descended from Gijjhakūṭa Hill to the park of the wanderers. When the wanderers saw him, they surrounded him, saying: "Teacher, how is the situation? We thought you were unable to bring the āvaṭṭanī-māyā (the deceptive art of turning others around) that can mislead the people." He said: "Friends, do not worry; I have brought the āvaṭṭanī-māyā. From today, our gains and honor will be great. Be united among yourselves; do not quarrel." They said: "Teacher, if you have learned it well, teach it to us too." He then recited the Pātimokkha from the beginning. Then all those wanderers said: "Come, friends, let us wander through the city and speak dispraise of the Samana Gotama." Even before the city gates were opened, they went near the gates and entered first as soon as the gates were opened. Thus, referring to Sarabha the Wanderer who departed while still in his monk's form, it is said: "The wanderer named Sarabha has recently departed (acirapakkanto)."
176:
Thus, referring to Sarabha the Wanderer who departed while still in his monk's form, it is said: "The wanderer named Sarabha has recently departed." On that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world, saw this matter: "Today, the wanderer named Sarabha will wander through the city and make a public display (pakāsanīyakamma). Speaking dispraise of the Three Jewels, he will pour out the poison (of his words) and go to the park of the wanderers. I too shall go to that park. The four assemblies will also gather there. In that gathering, eighty-four thousand beings will drink the nectar of the Deathless (Nibbāna)." Then, thinking, "Let there be an opportunity for Sarabha the Wanderer; let him spread dispraise as he pleases," he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, inform the Sangha of monks in the eighteen great monasteries to wander for alms only with me." The Elder did so. The monks, taking their bowls and robes, surrounded the Teacher. The Blessed One, taking the Sangha of monks, wandered for alms only in the village near the city gate.

Sarabha the Wanderer also entered the city with the wanderers and, going to various places such as the midst of assemblies, the palace gates, main roads, and crossroads, said: "I have understood the Dhamma of the Sakyaputta monks," and so on. Referring to such speech, it was said: "He speaks such words in the midst of the assembly in the city of Rājagaha," and so on. In that context, "Aññāto" means understood, realized, or mastered by making it clear. "Aññāya" means having known. "Apakkanto" means departing while still in his monk's form. He spoke thus to show this meaning: "If there were any essence (such as virtue, concentration, etc.) in the Dispensation of the Samana Gotama, I would not have departed. Indeed, the Dispensation of that Samana Gotama is without essence, devoid of essence; the monks use the deceptive art of turning others around (āvaṭṭanī-māyā) to mislead the world and get their food."

"Then many monks (Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū)" means that while the wanderer was speaking thus, five hundred forest-dwelling monks, not knowing that the Teacher had gone to such-and-such a place for alms, entered the city of Rājagaha for alms at the time of alms-round.
