Referring to those monks, this was said. "Assosuṃ" means they heard. "Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu" means they approached with the intention: "We shall report this matter to the Blessed One."

"Sippinikātīraṃ" means the bank of the river named Sippinikā. "The Blessed One consented by silence (Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena)" means he did not move his limbs or speech, but bore it with patience internally, consenting only with his mind. Having consented thus, he again thought: "Today, when I go to refute the doctrine of Sarabha the Wanderer, should I go alone or accompanied by the Sangha of monks?" Then [he thought], "If I go accompanied by the Sangha of monks..."
177:
(He reflected,) "Should I go alone, or should I go surrounded by the community of monks?" Then, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If I go surrounded by the community of monks, the multitude will think: 'The ascetic Gotama, when going to a place where a dispute over doctrine has arisen, takes a faction with him and, by the strength of the assembly, crushes the doctrine that has arisen; he does not allow other teachers to raise their heads.' In truth, I do not need to make others my companions to crush a doctrine that has arisen; I will go and crush it myself. It is not surprising that I, having now become a Buddha, should crush a doctrine that has arisen against me. For even when I was born in a state of a rootless animal while practicing the perfections, there was no one else capable of bearing the burden I had to bear."

To prove this matter, this Kaṇha Jātaka should be brought forth:
"Wherever the burden is heavy,
Wherever the path is deep and difficult,
At such times, they yoke the black bull,
And that black bull carries that burden."

In the past, a merchant stayed at the house of an old woman. At that time, one of the merchant's cows gave birth at dawn. That cow gave birth to a young calf. From the moment the old woman saw the calf, a motherly love for him arose as if he were her own son. The next day, the merchant's son said, "Take this as payment for the house rent." The old woman said, "I have no need for anything else; just give me this calf." The merchant's son said, "Mother, take him," and gave him to her.

The old woman took the calf and raised him by feeding him milk, gruel, rice, grass, and so on. As the calf grew up, he became beautiful in appearance, endowed with strength and energy, and well-behaved; he was known by the name 'Kaṇha'.

Then, the wheel of a wagon belonging to a merchant traveling with five hundred wagons got stuck in a place where the road had been washed away by water. Although that merchant tried to pull it out by yoking ten, twenty, or thirty oxen, he was unable to do so. He approached the black bull Kaṇha and said, "Dear one, I will give you a fee; please pull up my wagon for me." Having said this, he took the black bull and, thinking "There is no other capable of bearing the burden with this black bull," he tied the rope to the lead wagon and yoked only that one bull. That black bull pulled the wagon up onto dry ground, and in this same manner, he pulled out all five hundred wagons. After pulling out the very last wagon and being released from the harness, he made the sound 'Su' and lifted his head.
178:
The merchant thought, "This black bull did not act like this (groan) when pulling so many wagons; I suppose he is making the 'Su' sound for the sake of the fee." He took coins according to the number of wagons and tied a bundle of five hundred coins around the bull's neck. The bull, not allowing others to come near him, went straight home. When the old woman saw him and untied the bundle, she realized it was money and said, "My son, why did you do this? Do not think, 'This old woman shall live on the wealth I have earned by working.'" She bathed the bull with warm water, anointed him with oil, and admonished him, saying, "From today onwards, do not do this again." In this way, the Teacher reflected, "Even when I was born in a state of a rootless animal while practicing the perfections, there was no one else capable of bearing the burden I had to bear," and he went alone. To show that he went alone, the words beginning with "Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" were spoken.

In those words, "paṭisallānā" means withdrawing the mind from various objects and being in seclusion, or entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Tenupasaṅkami" means that the wanderers, having made themselves famous throughout the city, left the city and gathered in the wanderers' park, asking, "Friend Sarabha, if the ascetic Gotama comes, what will you do?" (Sarabha replied), "If the ascetic Gotama speaks one word, I will speak two; if he speaks two, I will speak four; if four, five; if five, ten; if ten, twenty; if twenty, thirty; if thirty, forty; if forty, fifty; if fifty, a hundred; if a hundred, I will speak a thousand." While they were sitting there raising such bold talk like a lion's roar to one another, the Blessed One approached.

When he approached, because the path to the wanderers' park was through the middle of the city, he dressed in his well-dyed double undergarment, put on his noble great robe, and like a king with great power but without an escort, he went alone through the middle of the city. When those with wrong view saw him, they thought, "The wanderers have disgraced the ascetic Gotama; I suppose that ascetic Gotama is following them to appease them," and they followed him. Those with right view also thought, "The Fully Enlightened One has come out alone taking his bowl and robes; today there will be a great Dhamma battle with the wanderer Sarabha. We too shall be witnesses in that assembly," and they followed him. The Teacher approached the wanderers' park while the great multitude was watching.
179:
The wanderers (paribbājakas) saw the dense six-colored rays of the Buddha emerging from between the trunks, branches, and twigs of the trees. They looked up, saying, "At no other time has there been such a radiance; what could this be?" and then said, "The ascetic Gotama is coming." Upon hearing those words, the wanderer Sarabha sat with his head between his knees, looking downwards. At that time, the Blessed One approached that park and sat on the prepared seat. Indeed, because the Tathāgata was born into a noble family on the surface of Jambudīpa, he was worthy of the highest seat; therefore, in all places, a seat was always prepared for the Buddha. Thus, he sat on the prepared Buddha-seat worthy of the noble ones.

Those wanderers said this to the wanderer Sarabha. While the Sammasambuddha was speaking these words with the wanderer Sarabha, the Saṅgha of monks, following in the footsteps of the Teacher, arrived at the park of the wanderers. The fourfold assembly also descended and gathered in the park of the wanderers. Then those wanderers, following the will of the Sammasambuddha, all said: "The deed of the ascetic Gotama is truly wonderful! Having traveled throughout the entire city, those enemies, rivals, and adversaries who came after spreading dispraise and performing acts of public denunciation, yet upon coming into their presence, he does not speak even a single word of contentious talk. From the moment he arrived, he speaks only sweet and pleasant words, as if anointing them with oil cooked a hundred times, or as if giving them the drink of the Deathless (Nibbāna) to drink."

"Yāceyyāsi" means entreat verbally, entreat mentally, or cherish. "Tuṇhībhūto" means having attained the state of silence. "Maṅkubhūto" means having become crestfallen (devoid of radiance). "Pattakkhandho" means with a bent neck (shoulders dropped). "Adhomukho" means with the face turned downwards. "Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato" means of you who claim, "I am the Sammasambuddha; all dhammas have been fully realized by me." "Anabhisambuddhā" means these certain dhammas have not been fully realized by you. "Tattha" means in those dhammas shown as not being fully realized. "Anyena vā anyaṃ paṭicariyyati" means he will cover one statement with another statement, or it means when asked one thing, he will answer another. "Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmessati" means he will dismiss the previous talk by bringing in another external, extraneous talk. "Appaccayaṃ" means he will manifest dissatisfaction or an unpleasant manner. In this context, "appaccaya" refers to mental displeasure (domanassa); the two preceding terms refer to anger in its weak and strong forms.
180:
Thus, the Blessed One, having roared the lion's roar with the first Knowledge of Intrepidity (Vesārajja-ñāṇa), and wishing to roar again with the second and subsequent knowledges, said the words beginning with "Yo kho maṃ paribbājakā." In that passage, "Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito" means for the sake of which Path (Magga) or Fruit (Phala) the Four Noble Truths were taught by you. "So na niyyāti" means that Dhamma does not lead out (from the suffering of the round), does not depart; it means it cannot accomplish that benefit (of the Path and Fruit). "Takkarassa" means for the person who practices it, who fulfills the practice. "Sammā dukkhakkhayāya" means for the complete ending of the suffering of the round through the proper causal method.

Alternatively, "Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito" means for which benefit the Dhamma was taught by you. Those benefits are: the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) for the removal of lust (rāga); the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) for the removal of hatred (dosa); the five dhammas (learning, hearing, memorizing, practicing, and reflecting on the aggregates, etc.) for the removal of delusion (moha); and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) for the cutting off of applied thought (vitakka). "So na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya" means that for the person who practices that Dhamma as it was taught, that Dhamma does not lead out, does not depart, and does not accomplish the benefit of ending the suffering of the round through the proper causal method. "Seyyathāpi sarabho paribbājako" means just as this wanderer Sarabha sits brooding and speechless, so too will he sit.

Thus, having roared the lion's roar with these three phrases, as the Tathāgata was concluding the discourse, the assembly of eighty-four thousand beings gathered in that place drank the beverage of the Deathless (Nibbāna). The Teacher, knowing that the assembly had drunk the beverage of the Deathless, rose into the air and departed. To show that matter, the words beginning with "Atha kho bhagavā" were said. Therein, "Sīhanādaṃ" means the noble roar, the fearless roar, the peerless roar. "Vehāsaṃ pakkāmi" means having attained the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and having emerged and made a determination, he flew into the sky together with the Saṅgha of monks. Having thus flown, he arrived at the Great Monastery of Gijjhakūṭa mountain in that very moment.

"Vācāya sannitodakena" means with the goad of speech. "Sañjambharimakaṃsu" means they made it thoroughly and continuously permeated; it means they pierced from above. "Brahāraññe" means in the great forest. "Sīhanādaṃ nadissāmi" means seeing the manner of a roaring lion, [the jackal] thought: "This creature is an animal, and I am an animal; this lion has four legs, and I have them too; I will also roar the lion's roar in this very same way." That jackal, in order to roar in the presence of the lion...
181:
When that jackal went to the lion's hunting ground, he tried to roar alone. At that time, only the sound of a jackal came out of him. Therefore, it is said, "He roars only the sound of a jackal." "Bheraṇḍaka" is a synonym for that very jackal. Alternatively, it means he roars with a broken, unpleasant sound. By this simile, the wanderers made the Blessed One like a lion and made the wanderer Sarabha like a jackal.

"Ambukasañcarī" refers to a young hen. "I will cry like the karavīka-sound of men" means that upon seeing a large rooster crowing, she thought, "This rooster has two legs and two wings; I also have the same. I too will cry with such a sound." But being unable to cry in the presence of that rooster, when the rooster had left, she cried, yet only the sound of a hen came out. Therefore, it is said, "She cries only the cry of an ambukasañcarī." "Usabha" refers to a bull. "Suññāya" means in a herd devoid of chief bulls. "He thinks he should roar deeply" means he thinks he should roar with a deep sound similar to the roar of a chief bull. The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all respects.

## 5. Kesamuttisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Kālāmānaṃ nigamo" refers to the market town of the nobles named Kālāmas. "Kesamuttiyā" refers to the residents of the market town of Kesamutta. "They approached" means they approached while having medicines such as ghee and fresh butter, as well as the eight kinds of drinks, brought along. "They showed only their own views" means they spoke only of their own beliefs. "They illumined" means they made them clear. "They oppressed" means they harassed. "They reviled" means they looked down upon. "They despised" means they treated as inferior. "They made them soiled" means they treated them as discarded, picking them up and throwing them away.

"Venerable sir, others also"—it is said that the market town of Kesamutta was at the entrance to a forest; therefore, those who had crossed the forest and those who wished to cross it stayed there. Among them, those who arrived first showed their own beliefs and left. Those who arrived later said, "What do they know? They are just our pupils; they have learned some arts from us," and after showing their own beliefs, they left. The Kālāmas were unable to remain firm even in a single belief. Showing this matter and reporting it to the Blessed One, they said, "Venerable sir, regarding them, for us..." and so on. In that passage, "hotēva kaṅkhā" means doubt indeed arises. "Vicikicchā" is a synonym for that "kaṅkhā". "Alaṃ" means it is appropriate.
182: "Mā anussavena" means do not accept by mere oral tradition. "Mā paramparāya" means do not accept by lineage of teaching. "Mā itikirāya" means do not accept by hearsay, thinking "it is said to be thus." "Mā piṭakasampadānena" means do not accept by thinking "it agrees with our scriptural tradition." "Mā takkahetu" means do not accept by mere reasoning. "Mā nayahetu" means do not accept by logical inference. "Mā ākāraparivitakkena" means do not accept by reflecting on reasons, thinking "this reason is good." "Mā diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā" means do not accept by thinking "it agrees with the view we have reflected upon and accepted." "Mā bhabbarūpatāya" means do not accept by thinking "this monk appears competent; it is proper to accept his words." "Mā samaṇo no garū" means do not accept by thinking "this ascetic is our teacher; it is proper to accept his words." "Samattā" means when completed. "Samādinnā" means when taken up by grasping wrongly. "Yaṃsa hoti" means whatever reason occurs to that person. Non-greed and so on should be understood by way of being the opposites of greed and so on. By the words "vigatābhijjo" and so on, the preliminary stage of the meditation on loving-kindness is spoken. Now, wishing to teach the meditation subjects such as loving-kindness, he said "mettāsahagatena" and so on. Whatever should be said in that discussion of meditation subjects, or in the method of development, or in the commentary on the Pali text, has all been stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Evaṃ averacitto" means thus, due to the absence of the enmity of unwholesomeness and the enmity of persons, he is one with a mind free from enmity. "Abyāpajjacitto" means due to the absence of the mind of anger, he is one with a mind free from suffering. "Asaṅkiliṭṭhacitto" means due to the absence of defilements, he is one with an undefiled mind. "Visuddhacitto" means he is one with a pure mind due to the absence of the stain of defilements. "Tassa" means to such a noble disciple. "Assāsā" means supports or foundations. "Sace kho pana atthi paro loko" means if there is a world beyond this world. "Athāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā parammaraṇā... upapajjissāmi" means there is this reason: "After the breaking up of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world." The method should be understood thus in all places. "Anīghaṃ" means free from suffering. "Sukhiṃ" means endowed with happiness. "Ubhayeneva visuddhaṃ attānaṃ samanupassāmi" means I do not do evil, and even for one who does, it is not considered done; by both these reasons, I see myself as pure. The rest of the words have clear meanings in all places. Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta. In the sixth sutta, "Migāranattā" means the grandson of the wealthy merchant Migāra. "Sekhuniyanattā" means the grandson of the wealthy merchant Sekhuniya. "They approached" means they approached after eating their morning meal, surrounded by servants and workers. It is said that for those two donors named Sāḷha, a problem had arisen in their house even before breakfast. Having no opportunity to solve that problem, they thought, "We will ask about that problem," and went to Venerable Nanda, paid homage, and sat in silence. The Elder, knowing the minds of those two donors named Sāḷha, thinking "They must have come to ask about the problem that occurred in their house," and wishing to start with that very problem, said "Etha tumhe sāḷha" and so on. There, with the word "atthi lobho", he asked, "Is there the nature of greed and attachment?"
183:
## 6. Sāḷhasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, 'Migāranattā' refers to the grandson of the merchant Migāra. 'Sekhuniyanattā' refers to the grandson of the merchant Sekhuniya. Having finished their breakfast, they approached [the Elder] accompanied by their servants and workers. It is said that for these two lay devotees named Sāḷha, a problem had arisen at home in the morning before breakfast, but there was no opportunity to resolve it. Thinking, "We shall hear the answer to that problem," they went to the Elder, paid homage, and sat down in silence. The Elder, knowing their thoughts, "They must have come to ask about the problem that arose at home," began with that very problem, saying, "Come, Sāḷhas," and so on. In those words, with the phrase "Is there greed?" he asks whether the nature of attachment exists. "Sāḷha, I call this meaning 'covetousness' (abhijjhā)" means that he explains the meaning of the problem that arose by saying, "I call that very meaning known as greed 'covetousness' or 'craving' (taṇhā)." The same method should be applied to all sections.

"He knows thus" means that the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka), who remains after developing the four divine abodes (brahma-vihāra), knows thus when he emerges from meditative attainment and begins insight meditation (vipassanā). "There is this [suffering]" means that knowing by discerning the group of five aggregates, known as the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), through the power of mind and matter (nāmarūpa), is called "knowing thus that there is this suffering." "Lowly state" refers to the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca). "Exalted state" refers to the truth of the path (magga-sacca). "Beyond this perception, there is an escape" means that Nibbāna is the escape beyond this perception known as insight-perception (vipassanā-saññā); by saying "it exists," he shows the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). By the phrase "knowledge that when liberated, one is liberated," he speaks of the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). "Formerly there was greed in me" means that in the past, greed existed in me. "Then it was unwholesome" means that greed was called unwholesome, or at that time, it was called unwholesome. "Thus this is wholesome" means that the absence of that unwholesome state is wholesome; he says this referring to the security of the wholesome state, which is the absence of that unwholesome. "One without hunger" (nicchāto) means one without craving (taṇhā). "One who is quenched" (nibbuto) means one who is quenched due to the absence of defilements (kilesas) that cause internal burning. "One who has become cool" (sītibhūto) means one who has become cooled. "One who experiences happiness" (sukhappaṭisaṃvedī) means the experience of both bodily and mental happiness. "By becoming Brahma" (brahmabhūtena) means by becoming the most excellent. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.
184:
## 7. Kathāvatthusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'kathāvatthūni' means the causes of talk, the grounds or foundations of talk. In the phrase 'Monks, whether in the past time,' the past duration refers to both time and the aggregates (khandhas). The same method applies to the future and the present. Among these three, one who speaks in this way: 'In the past time, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha named Kassapa appeared; the King of Kāsi named Kikī was his chief attendant; his lifespan was twenty thousand years,' is said to engage in talk concerning the past. One who speaks in this way: 'In the future time, the Buddha named Metteyya will appear; the King named Saṅkha will be his chief attendant; his lifespan will be eighty thousand years,' is said to engage in talk concerning the future. One who speaks in this way: 'At present, the King of such a name is a righteous king,' is said to engage in talk concerning the present.

'Kathāsampayogena' means by coming into contact through talk. 'Kaccho' means one who is fit to be talked with. 'Akaccho' means one who is unfit to be talked with. Regarding the categorical answer (ekāṃsavyākaraṇīya) and others: when asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?', one should answer categorically, 'Yes, it is impermanent.' The same method applies to the ear and so on. This is a question to be answered categorically (ekāṃsavyākaraṇīya-pañha). However, if asked, 'Is impermanence the eye?', one should answer by analytical division: 'Not only the eye is impermanent; the ear is also impermanent, the nose is also impermanent.' This is a question to be answered by analytical division (vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya-pañha). If asked, 'As the eye is, so is the ear? As the ear is, so is the eye?', one should ask a counter-question, 'In what sense do you ask?' If the reply is, 'I ask in the sense of seeing,' one should answer, 'No.' If the reply is, 'I ask in the sense of impermanence,' one should answer, 'Yes.' This is a question to be answered with a counter-question (paṭipucchā-vyākaraṇīya-pañha). If asked, 'Is the soul the same as the body?' and so on, one should set it aside, saying, 'This has not been declared by the Blessed One'; this question should not be answered. This is a question to be set aside (ṭhapanīya-pañha).

'Ṭhānāṭhāne na saṇṭhāti' means not being able to stand in what is a reason and what is not. In this regard, the method is: an eternalist (sassatavādī) is able to refute an annihilationist (ucchedavādī) with a valid reason; the annihilationist, being refuted by him, thinks, 'Why should I speak of annihilation?' and shows only the state of being an eternalist, unable to stand in his own view. In this same way, when the annihilationist is capable, the eternalist [fails]; when the personalist (puggalavādī) is capable, the void-teacher (suññatavādī) [fails]; when the void-teacher is capable, the personalist [fails]. This is what is meant by not standing in what is a reason and what is not.
185:
"Does not stand in conjecture"—this phrase applies to both asking and answering questions. How? Someone thinks, 'I will ask a question,' and clears his throat. When another person says to him, 'You will ask such-and-such a question,' he realizes that his intention is known and says, 'It is not this; I will ask another question.' Also, one who is asked a question thinks, 'I will answer the question,' and clears his chin. When another person says to him, 'You will give such-and-such an answer,' he realizes it is known and says, 'It is not this; I will give another answer.' This is called 'not standing in conjecture.'

"Does not stand in unknown speech" means not standing in what is known. How? Someone asks a question. Another says to him, 'You have asked a pleasant question; where did you learn this?' Even though he asked the question according to the proper method of asking, because of the other's words, he becomes doubtful, thinking, 'Did I ask something that is not a question?' Another person, being asked, gives an answer. Another says to him, 'You have answered the question well; where did you learn it? One who answers a question should answer in this way.' Even though he answered the question according to the proper method of answering, because of the other's words, he becomes doubtful, thinking, 'Did I answer something that is not a question?'

"Does not stand in the practice" means not standing in the duties. It means asking in an inappropriate place without knowing the duties. Such a question should not be answered when asked in the courtyard of a Cetiya; likewise, on the alms-round path, while wandering for alms in a village, while sitting in the assembly hall (āsanasālā), while sitting after taking gruel or food, while sitting after eating, or while going to the place of day-rest. However, when sitting in the place of day-rest, it should be answered for one who asks after requesting permission; it should not be answered for one who asks without requesting permission. One who asks without knowing these duties is said to 'not stand in the practice.' Bhikkhus, when such reasons exist, this person is called 'unfit for conversation' (akaccho).

## Ṭhānāṭhāne saṇṭhātīti
"Stands in what is possible and impossible" means an Eternalist (Sassatavādī) is able to refute an Annihilationist (Ucchedavādī) with appropriate reasons. Even when being refuted by him, the Annihilationist says, 'Even if I am refuted by you a hundred times, I am still an Annihilationist.' In this same way, the method should be applied to Eternalists, Personalists (Puggalavādī), Void-proponents (Suññatavādī), and so on. Thus, in what is possible and impossible...
186:
...is called 'standing.' 'Stands in conjecture' means while clearing the throat with the thought, 'I will ask a question,' when told, 'Will you ask such-and-such?' he says, 'Yes, I will ask that very question.' While clearing the chin with the thought, 'I will answer the question,' when told, 'Will you give such-and-such an answer?' he says, 'Yes, I will give that very answer.' This is called 'standing in conjecture.'

'Stands in acknowledgment' means after asking this question, when told, 'You have asked the question well; one who asks should ask in this way,' he accepts it and does not give rise to doubt. After answering a question, when told, 'You have answered the question well; one who answers should answer in this way,' he accepts it and does not give rise to doubt.

'Stands in the practice' means having [the teacher] sit in the house, offering gruel, snacks, etc., and while sitting there until the meal is finished, he asks a question. Or, taking medicines such as ghee, the eight kinds of drinks, robes, flowers, perfumes, etc., going to the monastery, offering them, and then entering the place of day-rest, he asks the question after requesting permission. Thus, one who asks knowing the duties to be performed by questioners is said to 'stand in the practice.' It is proper to answer the question of such a person.

'Evades one thing with another' means covering one statement with another, or when asked one thing, answering another. 'Diverts the talk to external matters' means introducing extraneous talk and thereby pushing the original topic aside. In this matter, there is this story: It is said that the bhikkhus assembled and said to a young monk, 'Friend, have you committed such-and-such an offense?' He said, 'Venerable sirs, I went to Nāgadīpa.' 'Friend, we do not care about your going to Nāgadīpa; we are asking whether you committed an offense.' 'Venerable sirs, having gone to Nāgadīpa, I ate fish.' 'Friend, we have no business with your eating fish; we are asking because we heard you committed an offense.' The young monk said, 'Venerable sirs, the fish was not well-cooked and caused me discomfort.' 'Friend, we have no business with your comfort or discomfort; we are asking if you committed an offense.' 'Venerable sirs, as long as I lived there, I only experienced discomfort.' Thus, it should be understood as diverting the talk to external matters by means of extraneous conversation.

'Overwhelms' means bringing in scriptures from here and there and covering [the topic]. Like the Elder Tepiṭaka Tissa. It is heard that: Formerly, bhikkhus assembled in the courtyard of the Mahācetiya, performed Saṅgha duties, gave exhortations to the bhikkhus, and then engaged in mutual discussion of questions. There, this Elder would bring in scriptures from the three Piṭakas from here and there and would not allow even a single question to be concluded during the day. 'Crushes' means...
187:
He crushes [the opponent] by bringing forth a reason. 'Anupajagghati' means laughing loudly while clapping one's hands, whether the other person asks a question or gives an answer. Because of such laughter, the other person feels doubt: "Did I ask something that should not be asked? Did I say something that should not be said?" 'Khalitaṃ gaṇhāti' means seeking faults even in minor slips of the tongue. If a syllable, word, or phrase is mispronounced, he goes about finding fault, saying, "This word should be said in this way." 'Saupaniso' means being together with a support or cause.

'Ohitasoto' means lending an ear (listening attentively). 'Abhijānāti ekaṃ dhammaṃ' means knowing with higher knowledge the one wholesome state, which is the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). 'Parijānāti ekaṃ dhammaṃ' means fully understanding the one state of the Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasacca) through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā). 'Pajahati ekaṃ dhammaṃ' means abandoning, dispelling, and eliminating the one state of all unwholesome qualities. 'Sacchikaroti ekaṃ dhammaṃ' means realizing either the one state of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) or the Truth of Cessation (Nirodhasacca). 'Sammāvimuttiṃ phusati' means touching and experiencing the liberation of the Fruit of Arahantship through the right method and cause with the touch of knowledge.

Monks, "Etadatthā bhikkhave kathā" means the talk shown by the phrase "through engagement in talk" (kathāsam-payogena) has the Fruit of Arahantship as its benefit. This Fruit of Arahantship is the ground or foundation of that talk. This liberation of the mind from defilements without clinging is the subject matter; thus, the connection (yojanā) should be understood in all phrases. 'Etadatthā mantanā' means that among those who should and should not be consulted, consulting with those who should be consulted is also only for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship. 'Etadatthā upanisā' means the support (upanissaya) described as "listening attentively with a cause" is also only for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship. 'Etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ' means the lending of the ear for that support is also only for that same purpose. 'Anုpādā' means not grasping through the four types of clinging (upādāna). 'Cittassa vimokkho' means the liberation of the Fruit of Arahantship. Having concluded the Sutta by saying that all this talk is for the sake of the Fruit of Arahantship, the Buddha spoke the verses starting with "Ye viruddhā" to reach the climax.

In those verses, 'viruddhā' means being opposed through anger, which is known as opposition. 'Sallapanti' means they engage in conversation. 'Viniviṭṭhā' means being obsessed. 'Samussitā' means being well-elevated by the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya). 'Anariyaguṇamāsajjā' means they speak by relying on the talk of the qualities of those who are not Noble Ones (anariya). Indeed, talk that attacks [another's] qualities is called the talk of non-noble ones, not the talk of Noble Ones.
188:
The meaning is that they speak such talk (of non-noble ones). 'Aññoññavivaresino' means seeking each other's flaws and faults. They delight in what is badly spoken (dubbhāsitaṃ), in minor slips of the tongue (vikkhalitaṃ), and in the confusion and defeat of one another caused by minor verbal faults. [The wise] does not practice so, nor does he speak so. Talk spoken by one established in the Dhamma is both established in the Dhamma and connected with that Dhamma; therefore, it is called 'dhammaṭṭhapāṭisaṃyuttā'. [One should speak] with a mind that is not distracted, being without disparagement (apaḷāsa) through the power of rivalry, and without rashness (asāhasa) through the power of the rashness of greed, hatred, and delusion.

One should not be envious, and one should not disparage what is badly spoken. One should not learn the habit of carping (upārambha), which has the characteristic of excessive argumentation. One should not seize upon a minor slip of the tongue, saying, "This is your fault." One should not overwhelm. One should not crush [the opponent] by bringing up a single reason. One should not speak words connected with falsehood. One should speak for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of inspiring confidence. One should not be elevated by the arousal of conceit. The wise do not speak while being conceited; rather, they should consult, speak, and converse only while not being elevated by conceit.

## 8. Aññatitthiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, 'bhagavaṃmūlakā' means those teachings have the Blessed One as their root. This is the intended meaning: "Venerable Sir, these teachings of ours were brought forth in the past by the Blessed One Kassapa. When that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, during the interval between two Buddhas, no other recluse or brahmin was able to bring forth these teachings. But these teachings of ours have been brought forth by the Blessed One. It is only by depending on the Blessed One that we know these teachings and penetrate them. Therefore, Venerable Sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root." 'Bhagavaṃnettikā' means the Blessed One is the leader, the trainer, and the guide of the teachings. Because he shows them by taking each name individually according to its nature, the teachings have the Blessed One as their guide.
189:
... are so named. 'Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇa' means that when the states of the four planes come into the range of the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa), they resort to (rely on) the Blessed One; thus they are called 'Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇa'. 'Paṭisarantī' means they resort to, they converge. In another way, to the Blessed One seated at the Great Bodhi-maṇḍa, through the power of penetration, Contact (Phassa) comes and asks, "Blessed One, what is my name?" (The Blessed One replies,) "You are named Contact because of the sense of touching the object." Feeling (Vedanā), Perception (Saññā), Mental Formations (Saṅkhāra), and Consciousness (Viññāṇa) also come and ask, "Blessed One, what is my name?" (The Blessed One replies,) "You are named Consciousness because of the sense of cognizing the object." In this way, taking the respective names of the states of the four planes according to their nature, the Blessed One penetrates and knows the Dhamma; thus they are called 'Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇa'. "Bhagavantamyeva paṭibhātu" means: let the meaning of these spoken words be revealed to the Blessed One's knowledge alone; may you alone please preach it to us.

"Rāgo kho" refers to lust (rāga) that occurs through the power of attachment. "Appasāvajjo" means having little fault, either through the power of worldly fault (lokavajja) or through the power of the fault of ripening (vipākavajja); because it is of little fault in both ways, it is called 'appasāvajjo' (of little fault) or 'appadoso'. How so? Parents, elder brothers, elder sisters, and so on, arrange the marriage ceremonies (āvāha-vivāha) for their children and younger siblings. In this way, such lust is first of all of little fault through the power of worldly fault. Lust based on contentment with one's own wife (saddārasantosa), however, does not cause rebirth in the states of deprivation (apāya); thus it is of little fault through the power of the fault of ripening. "Dandhavirāgī" means that when that lust fades, it fades slowly; it is not quickly released. Like a stain of oil-mixed ink, it follows for a long time; even after passing through two or three future lives, it does not depart; thus it is called 'dandhavirāgī' (one whose lust is slow to fade).

In this matter, there is this story: A certain man committed misconduct with his elder brother's wife. To that woman, he was even more dear than her own husband. That woman said to the man, "If this matter becomes known, there will be great reproach; kill your elder brother." That man rebuked her, saying, "Perish, you wretch! Do not say such a thing again." That woman remained silent, but after a few days, she spoke again, and the man's mind became divided. Then, when she spoke for the third time, he asked, "How shall I do it to get the opportunity?" Then the woman told him the means: "Do exactly as I say. There is a landing place near a large Kakudha tree in such-and-such a place; take a sharp billhook and wait there." The man did so. His elder brother also returned home after working in the forest. That woman, acting as if she were tender-hearted toward her husband,
190:
said, "Come, lord, I will look for lice in your head." While looking for lice, she said, "Your head is dirty," and gave him a lump of emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) paste, saying, "Go to such-and-such a place, wash your head, and come back." He went to the very landing place mentioned by the woman, smeared his head with the emblic myrobalan paste, went down into the water, and bowed his head to wash it. Then the other (the younger brother) came out from between the trees, struck him on the neck bone, deprived him of life, and went home.

The other (the elder brother), being unable to abandon his affection for his wife, was reborn in that very house as a large centipede (mahādhammani). That centipede would go and fall on her body whether she was standing or sitting. Then the woman, thinking, "This creature must be him," had it killed. He was reborn again in that very house as a dog because of his affection for her. From the time he could walk on his feet, he followed closely behind that woman. Even when she went to the forest, he went along with her. Seeing this, people mocked her, saying, "The dog-huntress has come out; where will she go?" That woman had the dog killed again.

He was reborn again in that very house as a young calf. In the same way, he followed closely behind that woman. At that time too, when people saw them, they mocked her, saying, "The cowherdess has come out; where will the cows graze?" In that life too, the woman had the young calf killed. At that time, still unable to cut off his affection for that woman, he was reborn for the fourth time in her very womb as one who remembers past births (jātissara). That boy, seeing that he had been killed by that woman in all four successive lives, reflected, "I have been reborn in the womb of such an enemy," and from then on, he would not let himself be touched by that woman's hand. If she touched him, he would scream and cry. Then, only his grandfather looked after him. Later, when the boy had grown up, the grandfather asked, "Dear son, why do you not let yourself be touched by your mother's hand? Why do you cry and lament loudly if she touches you?" When asked by the grandfather, he told the whole story, saying, "This woman is not my mother; she is only an enemy." The grandfather embraced his grandson and wept, saying, "Come, dear son, there is no reason for us to live in such a place." He took his grandson and left, went to a monastery, and they both ordained as monks. Living there, both of them attained Arahantship.
191:
Maha-savajjo means being greatly blameworthy for two reasons: by way of being socially blameworthy (lokavajja) and by way of being blameworthy through its result (vipākavajja). How? A person corrupted by the force of anger (dosa) offends his mother, father, brothers, sisters, and so on, as well as the monks. In every place he goes, he receives great blame, with people saying, 'This person offends his parents, his siblings, and even the monks.' This is how it is greatly blameworthy by way of being socially blameworthy. Furthermore, due to an act with immediate result (ānantariya kamma) committed through anger, he boils in hell for an entire aeon (kappa). This is how it is greatly blameworthy by way of being blameworthy through its result.

Khippa-virāgī means quickly fading in attachment (or being quickly released from the fault). Even if a person corrupted by anger offends his parents, a shrine (cetiya), a Bodhi tree, or the monks, he confesses his fault, saying, 'Please forgive me.' Along with that forgiveness, that kamma returns to its original state (becoming free of fault).

Delusion (moha) is also greatly blameworthy for two reasons. A person confused by delusion offends his parents, a shrine, a Bodhi tree, or the monks, and receives blame wherever he goes. This is how it is greatly blameworthy by way of being socially blameworthy. Furthermore, due to an act with immediate result committed through delusion, he boils in hell for an entire aeon. This is how it is greatly blameworthy by way of being blameworthy through its result. Dandha-virāgī means slowly fading away. The kamma committed by one confused by delusion is only slowly released. Just as a bear skin (acchacamma) does not become white even if washed a hundred times, the kamma committed by one confused by delusion is not quickly released but is released only slowly. The remaining words here are clear.

## 9. Akusalamūlasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the ninth, the Akusalamūla Sutta: 'Akusalamūlāni' means the roots of the unwholesome. Or, it means those states which are both unwholesome and roots. 'Yadapi, bhikkhave, lobho' means 'Monks, whatever greed there is.' 'Tadapi akusalamūlaṃ' means that greed is also called an unwholesome root. Or, it is appropriate to say 'tadapi' in reference to the unwholesome root here. This method should be applied in all places.

'Abhisaṅkharoti' means he strives, accumulates, or piles up. 'Asatā dukkhaṃ uppādayati' means he causes suffering by speaking of another's non-existent faults through what is untrue or non-existent. The phrase 'vadhena vā' (or by killing) and so on is stated to show the manner in which he causes suffering. Therein, 'jāniyā' means by loss of wealth. 'Pabbājanāya' means by banishment from a village or a country.
192:
By the act of banishment (pabbājanīya kamma). 'Balavamhi' means 'I am powerful.' In the word 'balattho,' it means speaking either as 'I have a purpose with power' or 'I stand on power.'

'Akālavādī' means one who does not speak at the proper time but speaks at an improper time. 'Abhūtavādī' means one who does not speak the truth but speaks what is untrue. 'Anatthavādī' means one who does not speak what is beneficial but speaks what is unbeneficial. 'Adhammavādī' means one who does not speak the Dhamma but speaks what is not Dhamma. 'Avinayavādī' means one who does not speak the Vinaya but speaks what is not Vinaya.

'Tathā hāyaṃ' should be resolved as 'tathā hi ayaṃ.' For that very reason, this person does not make an effort for the purpose of exposing and clarifying that which is untrue. 'Itipetaṃ atacchaṃ' means for this reason also, this is not true. The remaining term 'itipetaṃ abhūtaṃ' is merely a synonym (vevacana) for that word 'atacchaṃ.'

'Duggati pāṭikaṅkhā' means that only a miserable destination such as hell is to be expected; it means that he will inevitably be reborn in that miserable destination. 'Uddhasto' means destroyed from above. 'Pariyonaddho' means enveloped or entwined from all around. 'Anayaṃ āpajjati' means reaching non-prosperity, and 'byasanaṃ āpajjati' means reaching ruin. Indeed, in the summer season, when the pods of the Māluvā creeper burst, the seeds scatter and fall at the foot of trees such as the Banyan. If three seeds from three directions fall at the foot of that tree, when it is rained upon by a heavy monsoon cloud, three sprouts arise from those three seeds and cling to the tree. From then on, the tree deities are unable to remain in their original state. Those sprouts, growing and becoming creepers, climb the tree, entwine all the large and small branches, and envelop the tree from above. That tree, being entwined by the Māluvā creepers and covered by the thick, large Māluvā leaves, breaks and collapses here and there when it rains or when the wind blows, leaving only a stump. With reference to this, the words 'Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, māluvā' and so on were spoken.

'Evameva kho'—here, to compare the simile and the thing illustrated: this being should be regarded like one of the trees such as the Sāla tree. The three unwholesome roots should be regarded like the three Māluvā creepers. The period before the greed and so on reach the sense-doors should be regarded like the period when those creepers are climbing straight up before reaching the branches of the tree.
193:
The māluvā creepers grow and climb that tree, entwining all the branches and overshadowing it from above. When that tree is entwined by the māluvā creepers and covered by their thick, large leaves, it breaks and falls in various places when it rains or when the wind blows, leaving only a stump. Referring to such remaining, the Blessed One said, "Monks, just as a māluvā creeper..." and so forth.

In this phrase "Evameva kho", the correlation between the simile and the thing illustrated is as follows: This sentient being should be understood as one of the trees, such as a sal tree. The three unwholesome roots should be understood as the three māluvā creepers. The period when greed and so forth have not yet reached the sense-doors should be understood as the time when the creepers are climbing straight up the tree before reaching the branches. The time of moving through the sense-doors should be understood as the time of moving along the branches. The time of being oppressed by greed and so forth should be understood as the time of being entwined and overshadowed by the creepers. The time of committing minor and very minor offenses through the power of defilements that have reached the sense-doors should be understood as the time when small branches break. The time of committing a grave offense (garuka-āpatti) should be understood as the time when large branches break. The time of being reborn in the four woeful planes after successively committing the four pārājika offenses should be understood as the time when the tree falls to the ground because its roots are soaked by water descending along the creepers.

The wholesome side (sukkapakkha) should be understood in the opposite way from the unwholesome side already mentioned. In this context, the correlation of the simile for "Evameva kho" is: This sentient being should be understood as a tree such as a sal tree. The three unwholesome roots should be understood as the three māluvā creepers. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the man who comes to prevent those creepers from growing. Wisdom should be understood as the hoe. The basket of faith should be understood as the hoe-basket. Insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) should be understood as the digging tool that digs all around. The time of cutting the root of ignorance (avijjā) with insight knowledge should be understood as the cutting of the root with the digging tool. The time of seeing through the power of the aggregates should be understood as the time of cutting into pieces. The time of eradicating defilements with path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) should be understood as the time of splitting the wood. The time of the five aggregates being present should be understood as the time of making charcoal. The time of not taking rebirth in a new existence, having ceased through the cessation of the aggregates of grasping (upādinnaka-kkhandha) without further linking, should be understood as the time of being blown away in a strong wind and not occurring again. In this sutta, the cycle of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 10. Uposathasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "tadahuposathe" means on such a day that is an Uposatha day, on that Uposatha day; it means on the fifteenth-day (pannarasī) Uposatha. "Upasaṅkami" means approaching while holding perfumes, flowers, and so forth in hand, having undertaken the Uposatha factors. The particle "handa" is used in the sense of relinquishment. In the phrase "divā divassa", what is called "divā" of the day is the noon time; it means at the time when it is midday. By the phrase "kuto nu tvaṃ āgacchasi" (where do you come from?), he asks, "What work are you doing as you wander about?" "Gopālaka-uposatho" means the Uposatha observed together with herdsmen. "Nigaṇṭha-uposatho" means the Uposatha observed by the Nigaṇṭhas. "Ariya-uposatho" means the Uposatha observed by the Noble Ones. "Seyyathāpi visākhe" means "Visākhā, for example..."
194:
In the evening, "handing over the cows to the owners" means: Herdsmen look after cows by taking them for daily wages, or for a fixed period of five days, ten days, half a month, a month, six months, or a year. Here, however, it is said with reference to a herdsman who looks after them for daily wages. "Handing over" means giving them back, saying, "These are your cows."

"He reflects thus" means after going to his own home and eating, he reflects in this way while lying on his couch. "Accompanied by covetousness (abhijjhā)" means with a mind associated with craving (taṇhā). "Visākhā, such is the Herdsman's Uposatha" means that although this Uposatha is indeed the Uposatha of the Noble Ones, it stands in the position of the Herdsman's Uposatha because of impure thoughts. "It is not of great fruit" means it does not have great fruit in terms of its resultant (vipāka) fruit. "It is not of great benefit" means it does not have great benefit in terms of its resultant benefit. "It is not of great splendor" means it does not have great splendor in terms of the splendor of the resultant. "It is not of great pervasiveness" means it is not of great pervasiveness because the pervasiveness of the resultant is not great.

"Samaṇajātikā" means they are indeed ascetics. "Beyond a hundred yojanas" means crossing a hundred yojanas and being in a place beyond that. "Lay down the rod among them" means lay down the rod towards the beings who exist in those places beyond a hundred yojanas; it means "be one who has laid down the rod." "I am not anywhere, for anyone, in any attachment (kiñcana)" means I do not exist anywhere in the oppression of another. "Kiñcana" is called oppression (palibodha); it means "I am not an oppression." "And for me, there is no attachment anywhere in anything" means for me also, whether internally or externally, there is no state of attachment even in a single requisite; there is no hindrance (palibodha); it means "I am one whose hindrances are cut off."

"Bhoga" refers to couches, stools, gruel, rice, and so forth. "He consumes only what is not given" means on the next day, whether lying on a couch, sitting on a stool, drinking gruel, or eating rice, he consumes those enjoyments without the owner having given them. "It is not of great fruit" means it is fruitless. Here, only the words remain, but the meaning is without remainder (it is completely fruitless). For an Uposatha observed in this way, there is not even a slight resultant fruit that is desirable, pleasant, or agreeable. Therefore, it should be understood as simply fruitless. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

"Of the defiled mind"—why is this said? Because it is shown that an Uposatha observed with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, the great fruitfulness of an Uposatha observed with a pure mind is thereby authorized. Therefore, in order to show the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by which the mind is purified, the meditation subject for purifying the mind, he said this.
195:
He spoke these words. In that text, 'upakkameṇa' means by a cause accomplished through one's own effort or by a means. 'Recollects the Tathāgata' means recollecting the qualities of the Tathāgata through eight reasons. Here, by the phrase 'Itipi so bhagavā' (Thus indeed is the Blessed One), all mundane and supramundane qualities of the Buddha, such as being endowed with such virtue and such concentration, are included. By terms such as 'Arahaṃ', the specific qualities are individually indicated. 'The mind of one recollecting the Tathāgata becomes clear' means that for a person recollecting the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Tathāgata, the arising of consciousness is purified.

'Defilements of the mind' refers to the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Kakka' refers to the powder of the myrobalan (āmalaka) fruit. 'Appropriate effort' means the effort of anointing, rubbing, and washing with that myrobalan powder suitable for purification. 'Cleansing occurs' means the act of making pure. Indeed, if the head is dirty, one does not look beautiful even when adorned and playing at a celestial festival; however, if that head is pure, one looks beautiful when adorned and playing at a celestial festival. In the same way, an Uposatha observed by undertaking the factors of the Uposatha with a defiled mind is not of great fruit; but an Uposatha observed by undertaking the factors of the Uposatha with a pure mind is of great fruit. With this intention, He spoke thus. In the phrase 'observes the Brahma-Uposatha', the Perfectly Enlightened One is called 'Brahma'; this Uposatha, observed by way of recollecting His qualities, is called 'Brahma-Uposatha', and one observes that Uposatha. 'Dwells together with Brahma' means dwelling together with the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'With reference to Brahma' means with reference to the Perfectly Enlightened One.

'Recollects the Dhamma' means recollecting the supramundane Dhamma along with the scriptures (pāḷi). 'Sotti' refers to the Kuruvindaka scouring stone. Indeed, they mix the powder of the touchstone with lac to make ruby-like beads, pierce them, string them together, and then, holding that string of beads from both ends, rub the back; with reference to such rubbing, it is said, 'depending on the sotti'. 'Cuṇṇa' refers to bathing powder. 'Appropriate effort' means the effort suitable for that purification, such as extracting, rubbing, and washing. 'Dhamma-Uposatha' is so called because this Uposatha is observed with reference to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma along with the scriptures. Here too, based on the term 'cleansing', the explanation should be applied in the same manner as before.

'Recollects the Sangha' means recollecting the qualities of the eight noble persons. 'Depending on steam' means depending on the steam that has been made to be taken two or three times. There is also a reading 'usañca'.
196:
This is the meaning. 'Khāra' means ash. 'Gomaya' means cow urine or goat dung. In this term 'cleansing' (pariyodapanā) as well, the explanation should be applied in the same manner as before. This Uposatha is called 'Sangha-Uposatha' because it is observed with reference to the qualities of the eight noble persons.

'Sīlāni' means the virtues of a layperson if one is a layperson, or the virtues of a monk if one is a monk. The meaning of terms such as 'akhaṇဍāni' (unbroken) has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Vālaṇḍupaka' means a scouring pad made of horsehair or fibers such as sunn hemp. 'Appropriate effort' means the effort of rubbing with the hair-pad after moistening with oil, knowing the moist state of the dirt, and adding ash. Based on this term 'cleansing', the explanation should be applied thus: a body adorned and decorated does not look beautiful when viewed in a dirty mirror, but it looks beautiful in a pure mirror. In the same way, an Uposatha observed with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, but an Uposatha observed with a pure mind is of great fruit. 'Sīla-Uposatha' is the name of the Uposatha observed by way of recollecting one's own virtue. 'Together with virtue' means together with one's own five precepts or ten precepts. 'With reference to his virtue' means with reference to the five precepts and the ten precepts.

'Recollects the deities' means recollecting one's own qualities such as faith, placing the deities in the position of witnesses. 'Ukka' means a furnace. 'Loṇa' means saline earth. 'Geruka' means red earth powder. 'Nāḷikasaṇဍāsa' means the blowpipe and the tongs for turning. 'Appropriate effort' means the suitable effort such as putting into the furnace, blowing, and turning. Based on this term 'cleansing', the meaning should be understood thus: those adorned with ornaments made of defiled gold do not look beautiful when playing at a celestial festival, but they look beautiful with ornaments made of pure gold. In the same way, the Uposatha of one with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, but that of one with a pure mind is of great fruit. 'Devatā-Uposatha' is the name of the Uposatha observed by recollecting one's own qualities, placing the deities in the position of witnesses. Everything else that should be said regarding these meditation subjects, such as the recollection of the Buddha, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.
197:
Pāṇātipāta means the killing of living beings. 'Pahāya' means having abandoned that lack of virtue known as the intention to kill. 'Paṭiviratā' refers to those who abstain, specifically those who have turned away from that lack of virtue from the time of abandonment. 'Nihitadaṇḍā nihitasatthā' means those who have laid down the rod and laid down the weapon, as they no longer carry a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others. In this context, except for the walking stick, all other implements that can harm beings should be understood as 'weapons' (sattha). Although monks travel carrying a walking stick, a small knife for cutting tooth-wood, or a razor, these are not for the purpose of harming others. Therefore, they are still rightly called 'those who have laid down the rod and laid down the weapon.' 'Lajjī' means one endowed with shame, which has the characteristic of loathing evil. 'Dayāpannā' means one who has attained a state of loving-kindness. 'Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī' means one who is always compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings; it means having a mind that desires the welfare of all beings precisely because of that state of loving-kindness. 'Ahampajja' should be resolved as 'I too, today.' 'Imināpi aṅgena' means by this factor of virtue. 'Arahataṃ anukaromi' means that just as one following behind follows the one going in front, so too, by performing this virtue previously practiced by the Noble Arahants, I imitate those Arahants. 'Uposatho ca me upavuttho bhavissati' means that by doing so, I will be imitating the Arahants and I will also be observing the Uposatha.

Adinnādāna means taking what belongs to another and is not given by the owner; it means theft or robbery. One is called 'dinnādāyī' because they take only what is given. One is called 'dinnapāṭikaṅkhī' because even in their mind, they desire only what is given. One who steals is called 'thena'; one who does not steal is 'athena.' It means they live with a pure self because they do not steal.

Abrahmacariya means unholy conduct. One is called 'brahmacārī' because they practice the sublime (brahma) conduct. One is called 'ārācārī' because they practice far away from unholy conduct. 'Methunā' refers to the practice of the low, called 'methuna' because it is practiced by those known as 'methunaka' (couples) who are similar due to the arousal of lust. 'Gāmadhammā' means the practice of villagers.

Musāvādā means false speech or empty speech. One is called 'saccavādī' because they speak the truth. One is called 'saccasandhā' because they bond truth with truth (consistently); it means they do not speak lies in between.
198:
The meaning is: a certain man sometimes speaks lies and sometimes speaks the truth. Because his truth is interrupted by lies, the previous truth and the subsequent truth do not connect. Therefore, he is not one who is bonded to truth (saccasandha). These [Arahants], however, are not like that; even for the sake of their lives, they do not lie and they bond truth with truth; thus they are 'saccasandhā.' 'Theta' means firm; it means having stable speech. A certain person is not one of stable speech, like the color of turmeric, like a stump fixed in a heap of chaff, or like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back. Another person is one of stable speech, like an inscription on stone or like an Indakhīla (threshold pillar); even if their head is being cut off with a sword, they do not speak two different words. Such a person is called 'theta.' 'Paccayika' means having words that should be believed; it means being trustworthy. For a certain person is not trustworthy; if it is asked, 'Who said this? So-and-so said it,' it becomes necessary to say, 'Do not believe his words.' Another person is trustworthy; if it is asked, 'Who said this? So-and-so said it,' it becomes necessary to say, 'If he said it, this alone is the standard; now there is nothing to reject; it is exactly so.' Such a person is called 'paccayika.' 'Avisāṃvādaka lokassa' (not deceiving the world) means that because of that habit of speaking the truth, they do not deceive the world.

Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna is the cause of heedlessness, known as the intention to drink distilled and fermented intoxicants. Regarding 'ekabhattika' (one-meal-a-day), there are two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Among them, the morning meal is defined as being within the noon period; the other is from after noon until dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within the noon period, they are still 'ekabhattika.' It is with reference to that single mealtime that 'ekabhattika' is said. 'Rattibhojana' is the night meal; because of abstaining from it, one is 'rattūparata.' Eating from after noon until sunset is called 'vikālabhojana' (wrong-time eating); because of abstaining from it, one is 'one who abstains from wrong-time eating.'

'Visūkadassana' refers to watching spectacles that are contrary [to the teaching] because they are inconsistent with the Dispensation. 'Naccagīitavādita-visūkadassana' refers to dancing, singing, and music performed by oneself or by causing others to perform, and even watching spectacles such as the dancing of peacocks. Engaging in dancing and so on oneself, causing others to engage in them, or watching them being performed is not permissible for monks or for nuns.
199:
Among the words beginning with *mālā*, *mālā* refers to any kind of flower. *Gandha* refers to any kind of scent or fragrance. *Vilepana* refers to cosmetic paste or ointment that causes the coloring of the skin. In the phrase *mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhāna*, one who wears flowers is said to 'wear' (*dhāreti*). One who fills in low or deficient spots is said to 'adorn' (*maṇḍeti*). One who enjoys through the power of scent or the power of skin-coloring is said to 'beautify' (*vibhūseti*). *Ṭhāna* means cause or reason. Therefore, it means abstaining from that unwholesome intention of a person lacking virtue, by which the masses perform acts such as wearing flowers and so on.

*Uccāsayana* refers to a couch or bed with legs exceeding the measurement of eight finger-breadths of the Buddha (equivalent to one cubit of an ordinary person). *Mahāsayana* refers to unallowable rugs or coverings such as lion skin, leopard skin, and so on. It means abstaining from those high and great places of sitting and sleeping.

*Kīvamahapphalo* means 'how much fruit or benefit does it have?' In the remaining words such as *kīvamahānisaṃse*, the method is the same. *Pahūtarattaratanānaṃ* means countries endowed with many precious jewels, which are filled with the seven kinds of jewels up to waist-height, making the entire surface of Jambudīpa like the surface of a great drum. *Issariyādhipaccaṃ* means either the state of being a lord or the supreme lordship which is true sovereignty. It is also called *issariyādhipaccaṃ* because there is no act of violence or oppression (*sāhasikakamma*) in this lordship. *Rajjaṃ kāreyya* means one should exercise such universal kingship (*cakkavatti*). The words beginning with *Aṅgānaṃ* are the names of those provinces or countries. *Kalaṃ nāgghati soḷasiṃ* means that if the merit of the Uposatha observed for one day and night is divided into sixteen parts, it is not worth even one of those sixteen parts. It means that the result and fruit of even one-sixteenth part of the merit of a single night's Uposatha is much greater than the wealth of those sixteen kingdoms of Jambudīpa. *Kapaṇaṃ* means a small amount.

*Abrahmacariyā* means abstaining from non-noble conduct. *Rattiṃ na bhuñjeyya vikālabhojanaṃ* means that a person observing the Uposatha should not eat at night nor eat at the wrong time during the day (after noon). *Mañce chamāyaṃva sayetha santhate* means one should sleep on an allowable couch with legs the height of a fist, or on the ground prepared with lime and so on, or on a spread made by spreading grass, leaves, straw, and so on. *Etaṃ hi aṭṭhaṅgikāmāhuposathaṃ* means that the Uposatha observed by not practicing killing and so on is called *aṭṭhaṅgika* (eightfold) because it is endowed with eight factors. A person observing that Uposatha should consider the arrangement of food and so on even today, thinking, 'Tomorrow I will be an Uposatha observer,' and saying, 'Do this and that.' On the Uposatha day, early in the morning, in the presence of a monk, a nun, or a male or female lay follower who knows the characteristics of the ten precepts, one should [break] the silence...
200:
...by speaking, the Uposatha factors should be properly undertaken. However, a person who does not know the Pali should resolve: 'I undertake the Uposatha prescribed by the Buddha.' If one cannot find another person [to administer the precepts], one should resolve by oneself, but the verbal utterance must definitely be made. A person observing the Uposatha should not manage affairs connected with the oppression of others, nor should they spend time calculating income and expenditure. Having eaten at home like a monk who receives regular meals, one should go to the monastery and either listen to the Dhamma or reflect on one of the thirty-eight meditation subjects.

*Sudassanā* means those with beautiful sight. *Obhāsayanti* means illuminating. *Anupariyanti* means they wander or roam. *Yāvatā* means as far as the place extends. *Antalikkhagā* means those who go through the sky. *Pabhāsanti* means they shine or emit light. *Disāvirocanā* means being radiant in all directions. Alternatively, *pabhāsanti* means they illuminate from direction to direction. *Virocanā* means being radiant. In the word *veḷuriya*, although it says *maṇi* (gem), it shows the nature of a genuine precious stone. A genuine precious stone called *veḷuriya* (beryl) has the color of a one-year-old bamboo. He said this referring to that genuine gem. *Bhaddakaṃ* means beautiful. *Siṅgīsuvaṇṇa* is gold named thus because it arose looking like a bull's horn. *Kañcanaṃ* is gold produced in mountains. *Jātarūpaṃ* is gold with the color of the Teacher (the Buddha). *Haṭakaṃ* is gold brought out by ants. *Nānubhavanti* means they cannot reach or match. *Candappabhā* is a word in the nominative case used in the sense of the possessive, meaning 'of the moonlight.' *Upavassuposathaṃ* means having observed the Uposatha. *Sukhudrayāni* means having happy results, or results consisting of pleasant feeling. *Saggamupenti ṭhānaṃ* means they go to the place called heaven; being unblamed by anyone, they are reborn in the deva world. Here, the remaining words not mentioned in between should be understood according to the method already stated.

## The Second Great Chapter (Mahāvagga).

## (8) 3. Ānanda Chapter (Ānandavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Channa Sutta

In the first sutta of the third chapter, *Channa* is the wandering ascetic named Channa. He asks: 'Friends, just as we prescribe the abandoning of lust and so on, do you also prescribe it thus?' Then the Elder [thinks]: 'This wanderer says we prescribe the abandoning of lust and so on; there is no...'
201:
Wishing to reject the statement "Pana etaṃ bāhirasamaye" (But this is in the external tradition), he said, "Friends, we alone..." and so forth. In the passage beginning with "Mayaṃ kho," the word "kho" is an emphatic (avadhāraṇa) particle, meaning "We alone prescribe [this]." Then the wanderer (paribbājaka) thought, "This Elder has discarded the external tradition and said, 'We alone.' Seeing what kind of fault do these people prescribe the abandonment of lust and so forth?" Then, wishing to question the Elder, he said, "How is it for you, sirs?" and so forth. The Elder, wishing to answer the wanderer, said, "One who is lustful..." and so forth. In that passage, "attattha" (one's own benefit) refers to one's own welfare, described as the benefit in the present life, the benefit in the future life, and mundane and supramundane benefits. The same method applies to the benefit of others (parattha) and the benefit of both (ubhayattha).

In the terms beginning with "andhakaraṇa" (making blind), lust is called "andhakaraṇa" because it makes one blind by preventing the seeing of things as they really are. It is called "acakkhukaraṇa" because it does not produce the eye of wisdom. It is called "aññāṇakaraṇa" because it does not produce knowledge. It is called "paññānirodhika" (destroying wisdom) because it causes the cessation of these three kinds of wisdom—wisdom of ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-paññā), wisdom of meditative absorption (jhāna-paññā), and wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā)—by preventing their occurrence. It is called "vighātapakkhika" (siding with distress) because it leads to the side of affliction known as suffering (dukkha) by yielding undesirable results. It is called "anibbānasaṃvattanika" because it does not lead to the quenching of defilements (Nibbāna). "Friend Ānanda, if such a practice exists, it is indeed fitting and appropriate for your heedfulness; friends, practice heedfulness." Saying this, he rejoiced in the Elder's words, said "Sādhu," and departed. In this sutta, the Noble Path (ariya-magga) mixed with the supramundane is taught. The remaining words in this sutta have clear meanings.

## 2. Ājīvakasuttavaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, regarding the phrase "Householder, in that case...", it is said that the Elder thought: "This householder did not come here with a desire to know; he came only to investigate. I will make this householder himself speak the answer to the question he asked." Having thought thus, and wishing to make the householder himself speak, he said, "In that case" and so forth. In that passage, "tena hi" (in that case) is a term indicating a reason. It means, "Since you ask in this way, I will therefore question you in return on that very matter." "Kesaṃ no" means "By whom is the good Dhamma well-taught?" "Sadhammukkansanā" means exalting and upholding one's own doctrine. "Paradhammāpasādanā" means attacking, disparaging, and belittling the doctrines of others. "Āyatanēva dhammadēsanā" means teaching the Dhamma only on appropriate grounds. "Attho ca vutto" means "The meaning of the question I asked..."
202:
...is clearly shown. "We are of such a nature" refers only to oneself; it is not brought forward to others. There is also a reading "nupanīto."

## 3. Mahānāmasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "gilānā vuṭṭhito" means having recovered from illness. "Gelaññā" means because of the state of being ill. "Upasaṅkami" means that after having eaten his morning meal, he approached, taking flowers, perfumes, etc., and being surrounded by a large retinue. "Bāhāyaṃ gahetvā" (taking by the arm) should be understood not as pulling him by the arm, but as rising from his seat, going to Mahānāma, and signaling with his thumb on Mahānāma's right arm to lead him to a suitable place. Then, to that Mahānāma, he taught the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the seven types of trainees (sekha) by the method beginning with "Mahānāma, the virtue of a trainee also..." and so forth. When teaching the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the non-trainee (asekha) by way of the fruit of Arahantship above that, he showed: "After trainee-concentration, trainee-insight-knowledge and non-trainee-fruition-knowledge arise; and after trainee-insight-knowledge, non-trainee-fruition-concentration arises." However, the occurrence of the associated concentration and knowledge should be understood as being simultaneous, without before or after.

## 4. Nigaṇṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "Kūṭāgārasālāyam" refers to the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) built with two gables and covered in the hansa-vaṭṭaka style. "Apari-sesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti" means claiming all knowledge and vision without leaving even a small remainder. "Satataṃ samitaṃ" means occurring at all times and continuously. "Ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ" shows that "Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is always present before me." "Purāṇānaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to old kammas that were previously accumulated. "Tapasa byantībhāvaṃ" means making an end of cessation through difficult austerities. "Navānaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to new kammas to be accumulated now. "Akaraṇā" means through non-accumulation. By the word "setughātaṃ" (destroying the bridge), he teaches the destruction of the cause. "Kammakkhayā dukkhakkhayo" means the end of suffering through the end of the round of kamma. "Dukkhakkhayā vedanākkhayo" means the end of feeling through the end of the round of suffering. For when the round of suffering is exhausted, the round of feeling is also exhausted. "Vedanākkhayā sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissati" means that by the end of feeling, the entire suffering of the round will be worn away and destroyed. "Sandiṭṭhikāya" means that which is to be personally realized. "Nijjarāya"...
203:
"For purification" (Visuddhiyā) means for the purification of beings through the practice that wears away defilements, or because of the wearing away of defilements. "Overcoming occurs" (Samatikkamo hoti) means the overcoming of the entire suffering of the round of rebirth. "Venerable Sir, what did the Blessed One say in this practice? Does He prescribe only this practice of wearing away defilements, or another?" is the question.

"Knowing" (Jānatā) means knowing with unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). "Seeing" (Passatā) means seeing with the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu). "For purification" (Visuddhiyā) means for the sake of reaching purification (Nibbāna). "For overcoming" (Samatikkamāya) means for the sake of overcoming. "For cessation" (Atthaṅgamāya) means for the sake of reaching cessation. "For the attainment of the method" (Ñāyassa adhigamāya) means for the sake of attaining the Path along with insight (vipassanā). "For the realization of Nibbāna" (Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya) means for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is unconditioned (apaccayaniibbāna). "Does not perform new kamma" (Navañca kammaṃ na karoti) means not accumulating new kamma. "Old kamma" (Puraṇañca kammaṃ) is kamma accumulated in the past. "Touching and touching, he makes an end" (Phussa phussa byantī karoti) means making an end by repeatedly touching; the meaning is that by repeatedly touching resultant contact (vipākaphassa), he exhausts that kamma. "Visible here and now" (Sandiṭṭhikā) means to be seen by oneself. "Timeless" (Akālikā) means not performing the function of giving results at another time. "Inviting one to come and see" (Ehipassikā) means worthy of being shown as "Come and see." "Worthy of being brought inward" (Opaneyyikā) means worthy of being brought into one's own mind, associated with what should be adhered to. "To be personally known by the wise" (Paccattaṃ veditabbā viññūhi) means to be known by the wise only in their own mental continuums, but difficult for the foolish to know. Thus, two paths and two fruits are spoken of by the power of virtue. For the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) are those who practice to fulfill the virtues. However, by the fulfillment of concentration (samādhisampadā) starting with "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," three paths and three fruits are spoken of. For the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) noble disciple is said to be one who practices to fulfill concentration. By the words "through the destruction of taints" (āsavānaṃ khayā), etc., the fruit of Arahatship is spoken of. Some teachers, however, say that in this context, virtue and concentration are also intended as those associated with the fruit of Arahatship. That statement is presented separately for the sake of showing the practice according to each individual.

## 5. Nivesakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "ministers" (amaccā) means friends with good hearts. "Relatives" (ñātī) means the groups of the mother-in-law and father-in-law. "Kinsmen" (sālohitā) means those with the same blood, such as brothers and sisters. "Unwavering confidence" (aveccappasāde) occurs in the unwavering confidence that arises from knowing the virtues. "Alteration" (aññathattaṃ) means the state of being in another way.
204:
The occurrence of a state in another way (alteration). In the words "of the earth element" (pathavīdhātuyā), etc., there might be an alteration of the earth element which exists in twenty parts in the form of hardness; of the water element which exists in twelve parts in the form of cohesion in liquid; of the fire element which exists in four parts in the form of maturing; and of the air element which exists in six parts in the form of supporting. "But never" (na tveva) shows that while an alteration might occur in these four great elements by their turning into one another, such an alteration would never occur for the noble disciple. Here, "alteration" (aññathattaṃ) refers to the alteration of confidence and the alteration of destination (gati). That [alteration] does not happen to that [noble disciple]. However, the alteration of state (bhāvaññathattaṃ) does occur. For a noble disciple, having been a human, becomes a deva or a brahma. But his confidence does not vanish even in another life, nor does he reach the alteration of destination known as the woeful states (apāya). The Teacher, wishing to show that very meaning, said "Therein, this is the alteration" (tatraidaṃ aññathattaṃ), etc. The rest here is clear in meaning.

## 6. Paṭhamabhava-sutta-vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "ripening in the sense sphere" (kāmadhātuvepakkaṃ) is kamma that ripens in the sense sphere. "Sense-sphere existence" (kāmabhavo) is the rebirth existence in the sense sphere. "Kamma is the field" (kammaṃ khettaṃ) means wholesome and unwholesome kamma is like a field in the sense of being the place of growth. "Consciousness is the seed" (viñညာဏံ bījaṃ) means the co-nascent volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) is like a seed in the sense of growing. "Craving is the moisture" (taṇhā sneho) means craving is called water by way of supporting and nourishing. "Of those hindered by ignorance" (avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ) means of those obstructed by ignorance.
